#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Configure SMTP for the Kodely contact form.
#
#   ./setup-smtp.sh staging     configure staging only
#   ./setup-smtp.sh prod        configure prod only
#   ./setup-smtp.sh both        configure both
#
# Prompts for the mailbox password with hidden input, so it is never typed
# into a chat, never lands in shell history, and never appears in any log.
set -euo pipefail

TARGET="${1:-}"
case "$TARGET" in
  staging|prod|both) ;;
  *) echo "usage: $0 [staging|prod|both]"; exit 1 ;;
esac

read -rp "SMTP host [mail.nxeon.cloud]: " HOST; HOST="${HOST:-mail.nxeon.cloud}"
read -rp "SMTP port [587]: " PORT; PORT="${PORT:-587}"
read -rp "SMTP username (mailbox, e.g. noreply@kodely.me): " USER
[ -n "$USER" ] || { echo "username is required"; exit 1; }
read -rsp "SMTP password (hidden): " PASS; echo
[ -n "$PASS" ] || { echo "password is required"; exit 1; }
read -rp "From address [Kodely <${USER}>]: " FROM; FROM="${FROM:-Kodely <${USER}>}"
read -rp "Deliver contact mail to [hello@kodely.me]: " TO; TO="${TO:-hello@kodely.me}"

# Escape single quotes so a password containing ' can't break the .env line.
esc() { printf "%s" "$1" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g"; }

write_env() {
  local dir="$1" svc="$2" port="$3"
  local env="$dir/.env"
  echo
  echo "== $dir =="
  cp "$env" "$env.bak.$(date +%s)"

  # Drop any previous SMTP/mail settings, then append the new ones.
  grep -vE '^(SMTP_HOST|SMTP_PORT|SMTP_USER|SMTP_PASS|MAIL_FROM|CONTACT_TO)=' "$env" > "$env.tmp" || true
  {
    echo "SMTP_HOST='$(esc "$HOST")'"
    echo "SMTP_PORT='$(esc "$PORT")'"
    echo "SMTP_USER='$(esc "$USER")'"
    echo "SMTP_PASS='$(esc "$PASS")'"
    echo "MAIL_FROM='$(esc "$FROM")'"
    echo "CONTACT_TO='$(esc "$TO")'"
  } >> "$env.tmp"
  mv "$env.tmp" "$env"
  chmod 600 "$env"
  echo "  .env updated (mode 600, backup kept alongside)"

  sudo systemctl restart "$svc"
  sleep 4
  echo "  $svc: $(systemctl is-active "$svc")"

  echo "  sending a test message through the running app..."
  local code
  code=$(curl -s -o /tmp/smtp-test.out -w '%{http_code}' -m 45 \
    -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:$port/api/contact" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"name":"SMTP setup test","email":"'"$USER"'","message":"Automated test from setup-smtp.sh. If this arrives, the contact form works."}')
  echo "  HTTP $code  $(cat /tmp/smtp-test.out)"
  rm -f /tmp/smtp-test.out
  if [ "$code" = "200" ]; then
    echo "  ✅ accepted — check $TO for the test message"
  else
    echo "  ❌ not sent. Check credentials, then: journalctl -u $svc -n 40 --no-pager"
  fi
}

[ "$TARGET" = staging ] || [ "$TARGET" = both ] && write_env /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging 3001 || true
[ "$TARGET" = prod ]    || [ "$TARGET" = both ] && write_env /opt/kodely         kodely         3000 || true

echo
echo "Done. Password was never echoed, and is stored only in the .env files (mode 600)."

  *) echo "usage: $0 [staging|prod|both]"; exit 1 ;;
esac

read -rp "SMTP port [587]: " PORT; PORT="${PORT:-587}"
read -rp "SMTP username (mailbox, e.g. noreply@kodely.me): " USER
[ -n "$USER" ] || { echo "username is required"; exit 1; }
read -rsp "SMTP password (hidden): " PASS; echo
[ -n "$PASS" ] || { echo "password is required"; exit 1; }
read -rp "From address [Kodely <${USER}>]: " FROM; FROM="${FROM:-Kodely <${USER}>}"
read -rp "Deliver contact mail to [hello@kodely.me]: " TO; TO="${TO:-hello@kodely.me}"

# Escape single quotes so a password containing ' can't break the .env line.
esc() { printf "%s" "$1" | sed "s/'/'\\\\''/g"; }

write_env() {
  local dir="$1" svc="$2" port="$3"
  local env="$dir/.env"
  echo
  echo "== $dir =="
  cp "$env" "$env.bak.$(date +%s)"

  # Drop any previous SMTP/mail settings, then append the new ones.
  grep -vE '^(SMTP_HOST|SMTP_PORT|SMTP_USER|SMTP_PASS|MAIL_FROM|CONTACT_TO)=' "$env" > "$env.tmp" || true

    echo "SMTP_PORT='$(esc "$PORT")'"
    echo "SMTP_USER='$(esc "$USER")'"
    echo "SMTP_PASS='$(esc "$PASS")'"
    echo "MAIL_FROM='$(esc "$FROM")'"
    echo "CONTACT_TO='$(esc "$TO")'"
  } >> "$env.tmp"
  mv "$env.tmp" "$env"
  chmod 600 "$env"
  echo "  .env updated (mode 600, backup kept alongside)"

  sudo systemctl restart "$svc"
  sleep 4
  echo "  $svc: $(systemctl is-active "$svc")"

  echo "  sending a test message through the running app..."
  local code
  code=$(curl -s -o /tmp/smtp-test.out -w '%{http_code}' -m 45 \
    -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:$port/api/contact" \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \

  rm -f /tmp/smtp-test.out

  else

  fi

[ "$TARGET" = prod ]    || [ "$TARGET" = both ] && write_env /opt/kodely         kodely         3000 || true

Making that work would mean opening a firewall port, widening Postfix's relay policy to the whole VM subnet (letting *any* VM send as any domain), and still landing in spam. Worse security for worse deliverability — not a trade worth making.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# deploy.sh — push this tree's committed work to kodely.me.
#
#   ./deploy.sh            staging -> verify -> prod -> verify
#   ./deploy.sh --staging  stop after staging
#
# This is the PROD checkout, so there is no cherry-picking and no personal
# divergence to guard against (unlike ship.sh in the personal instance).
# Commit, run this, done.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30
STAGING_ONLY="${1:-}"

say() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree dirty — commit first"

# A dependency change means the VM must reinstall; deploy.sh on the VM runs
# npm ci, so this is handled — but warn, since it makes the deploy slower and
# a bad lockfile is the known way to break it.
git fetch -q origin main
if ! git diff --quiet origin/main -- package-lock.json; then
  echo "  note: package-lock.json differs from origin/main (dependency change)"
fi

if [ -n "$(git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD)" ]; then
  say "Pushing to origin/main"
  git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | sed 's/^/  /'
  git push -q origin main
else
  echo "  nothing to push; deploying current origin/main"
fi
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short origin/main)
echo "  main = $NEW"

ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

verify() {
  local env="$1" url="$2" dir="$3"
  local head behind build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  behind=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  behind_main=$behind  BUILD_ID=$build"
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env HEAD ($head) != main ($NEW)"
  [ "$behind" = "0" ]  || die "$env is $behind commits behind main"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

say "Deploying staging"; vm "/home/kodely/deploy.sh staging 2>&1 | tail -2"
say "Verifying staging"; verify staging https://staging.kodely.me /opt/kodely-staging

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

say "Deploying prod"; vm "/home/kodely/deploy.sh prod 2>&1 | tail -2"
say "Verifying prod"; verify prod https://kodely.me /opt/kodely

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK"

content.thinking:
The user's asking a good question about workflow direction. The key point is that "live" is just a deploy target, not an editing location—the real choice is which checkout to edit: kodely-prod, which tracks main and flows straight to deploy, versus the personal branch, which requires cherry-picking into main first. Nothing flows backward from live itself.

So the answer is: default to editing in kodely-prod, reserve the personal instance for generation testing or house-style experiments, and periodically rebase the personal branch onto main to stay in sync. I want to lay this out as a simple mental model with three places and one direction, then give the default workflow, the exception, and concrete commands—keeping it tight since they've already had a lot of detail, and noting clearly that editing directly on the VM is what causes the mess in the first place.

content.text:
## The mental model

You never edit "live." The VM is a **deploy target**, not a place to work — `deploy.sh` does `git reset --hard origin/main`, so anything edited there is destroyed on the next deploy. That's precisely how this got tangled in the first place.

Everything flows one direction:

```
kodely-prod  ──commit──▶  origin/main  ──deploy.sh──▶  staging ──▶ kodely.me
```

`main` on GitHub is the single source of truth. Both servers are just checkouts of it.

## Default: edit in `kodely-prod` (99% of the time)

```bash
cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod
```

Edit → check on **:3002** → then:

```bash
git add -A && git commit -m "What changed" && ./deploy.sh
```

That pushes, deploys staging, verifies, deploys prod, verifies, and prints a rollback point. Use `./deploy.sh --staging` to stop and eyeball it first.

No porting. No cherry-picking. No guard needed — this checkout has nothing dangerous in it.

## The exception: the personal instance

`Desktop\Kodely` (:3000) exists for **one reason** — generation runs on your Claude subscription instead of a metered API key, so testing costs nothing. Use it for:

- Testing site generation
- Refining `skills/kodely-house-style/SKILL.md`

If you build something there worth shipping:

```bash
./ship.sh
```

That cherry-picks onto `main` and refuses any commit touching `lib/agent.ts` and friends.

## Answering your question directly

> should i just make the changes on live and push to local

**Neither** — but the closer half is right. Edit in **`kodely-prod`** and push *up* to live. Nothing ever flows back from live, because live holds no unique code.

The only backward flow is keeping the personal instance current when `main` moves:

```bash
cd "/c/Users/edmem/OneDrive/Desktop/Kodely" && git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main
```

## The one rule

**Never edit files on the VM.** If you catch yourself SSH-ing in to change code, stop — it'll be wiped, and it's what made the last cleanup necessary.

---

**Quick reference**

| I want to… | Where | Command |
|---|---|---|
| Change UI / marketing / API | `kodely-prod` (:3002) | `./deploy.sh` |
| Test generation for free | `Desktop\Kodely` (:3000) | — |
| Ship something from personal | `Desktop\Kodely` | `./ship.sh` |
| Sync personal after main moves | `Desktop\Kodely` | `git rebase origin/main` |

I verified each candidate against the real code, and found something worse than the card says.

## Verified state (not what the board claims)

| # | Card | Reality |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | Service-key rotation runbook | ✅ **Already done** — shipped this session; board is stale |
| 10 | Auto-SEO on generated output | ❌ **Worse than carded** — see below |

| 15 | "Built with Kodely" badge | ❌ Not present anywhere |

## The finding

Every generated site's HTML head is literally this:

```html
<title>Kodely Site</title>
```

No meta description, no OG tags, no sitemap, no favicon — and **zero SEO instruction in the agent prompt**. So every site your users publish shows *"Kodely Site"* in the browser tab, in Google results, and in every Slack/WhatsApp/Twitter share preview.

That's not a missing enhancement; it's a hardcoded placeholder leaking into production on every customer site. For a product whose pitch is *"puts it online at a real, working URL,"* it actively undercuts the promise — and it's the kind of thing a user notices immediately and screenshots.

## My recommendation: card 10 first

- **Highest visible value per effort** — improves *every* site ever generated, retroactively for new builds
- **Self-contained** — the foundation template plus the agent prompt; no schema, no infra, no new deps
- **Needs nothing from you** — no credentials, no pricing decisions
- **Easy to verify** — generate a site, inspect the `<head>`

The strongest counter-argument is **card 11 (moderation)**: you *host* what gets generated, so phishing/brand-clone sites are your liability — the board rates it URGENT. I'd still do SEO first, because moderation done properly needs a real classifier, and your own code comments explicitly refuse to fake it with a weak heuristic. It's a bigger, separate piece of work.

content.text:
Both done. **Yes — I can create stages, move cards, and comment**, and I've now done all three.

## Auto-SEO shipped → prod `d8fd1d3`

**The root cause wasn't a missing feature.** The builder prompt listed `index.html` under *"already correct, leave them alone"* — the agent was **explicitly forbidden** from editing the one file containing `<title>`. Every published site shipped as *"Kodely Site"* in the browser tab, search results, and every link preview.

Fixed at three levels so a bad title can't reach a visitor:

1. **Prompt** — `index.html` is now a stated exception; the agent must write a real title/description/OG per site
2. **Foundation** — head scaffolding so the agent can see exactly what to fill
3. **Serve-time backstop** — placeholder title → project name, missing tags filled, but **anything the agent wrote is preserved verbatim**. Because it rewrites on read, it also fixes already-published sites with no regeneration.

Plus generated `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` per request (the visitor-facing host differs between the branded subdomain and staging path form, so a baked file would be wrong on one). Added `xml` to the MIME map — without it crawlers ignore the sitemap entirely.

I also fixed a self-inflicted bug mid-build: my empty `content=""` scaffolding wouldn't have been filled, because the check only tested whether tags *existed*.

## Board restructured

`Backlog → In Progress → Bug Testing → Needs Attention → Blocked → Done`

| Card | Stage | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Auto-SEO | **Bug Testing** | Shipped, but prod has **0 published sites** — never run against a real generation |
| Service-key rotation runbook | **Done** | Written and live |
| Tier numbers | **Needs Attention** | A decision, not engineering — cheapest unblock on the board |
| Content moderation | **Needs Attention** | Verified: publish runs *only* `scanForSecrets`. Highest risk, since you host what's generated |

content.text:
Published a site and verified the SEO work live — and it surfaced two real bugs.

## ✅ Live and verified

**https://my-first-site-pmiq0.kodely.site**

```
<title>My first site</title>
<meta name="description" content="My first site — built with Kodely." />
<link rel="canonical" href="https://my-first-site-pmiq0.kodely.site" />
<meta property="og:url" content="https://my-first-site-pmiq0.kodely.site" />
```

`sitemap.xml` → `application/xml` ✓, `robots.txt` → `text/plain` ✓. The "Kodely Site" placeholder is gone.

## 🐛 Bug 1 — found only because I tested through the real edge

`canonical` said **https** but `og:url` said **http**.

Your Cloudflare SSL is **Flexible**, so TLS terminates at the edge and the origin is spoken to over plain HTTP — nginx forwards `x-forwarded-proto: http` even though the visitor is on HTTPS. My code trusted it.

It was nearly invisible because Cloudflare's Automatic HTTPS Rewrites silently repairs `href="http://"` (canonical) but **not** `content="http://"` (og:url). Only the OG tag stayed broken — and only through the real edge, never locally. Fixed in `572a07a`.

## 🚨 Bug 2 — your deploys are broken, and were lying about it

**The VM can no longer fetch from GitHub.** The deploy key is fine (verified — still registered, matches exactly). It's the SSH transport:

| From VM | Result |
|---|---|
| `ssh -T git@github.com` (port 22) | Connection closed — 3/3 |
| `ssh -T -p 443 git@ssh.github.com` | Connection closed |
| HTTPS git | **Works** |

Worse: `/home/kodely/deploy.sh` runs `git fetch … && git reset --hard origin/main`. When the fetch fails, `origin/main` is a **stale ref**, so the reset "succeeds" against old code and the script **reports a healthy deploy of the wrong commit**. It did exactly that twice today — my `deploy.sh`'s `HEAD == main` check is the only reason we caught it.

I shipped `572a07a` via a git bundle over my existing SSH access as a workaround. Both environments are on it and verified.

**Needs your action:** either find why GitHub refuses SSH from `51.79.162.96` (likely OVH egress or a GitHub IP block), or switch the VM remote to HTTPS with a fine-grained PAT — HTTPS already works. Either way, `deploy.sh` should fail loudly rather than reset to a stale ref.

Both are on the board: SEO comment added, and a new **URGENT/BUG** card in Needs Attention with the full diagnosis.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# deploy.sh — push this checkout's committed work to kodely.me.
#
#   ./deploy.sh            staging -> verify -> prod -> verify
#   ./deploy.sh --staging  stop after staging
#
# Transport note: the VM cannot currently reach GitHub over SSH (see the board
# card "VM cannot reach GitHub over SSH"). Its own /home/kodely/deploy.sh runs
# `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`, and when that fetch
# fails it resets to a STALE remote-tracking ref and reports a healthy deploy
# of the WRONG commit — it did that twice on 2026-08-21.
#
# So this script does not rely on the VM pulling. It still pushes to GitHub
# (that works from here, and keeps origin authoritative), then ships the actual
# commits over the existing SSH path as a git bundle and builds in place. When
# the VM's GitHub access is restored, the bundle step can be dropped.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30
STAGING_ONLY="${1:-}"

say() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"

# deploy.sh — push this tree's committed work to kodely.me.
#
#   ./deploy.sh            staging -> verify -> prod -> verify
#   ./deploy.sh --staging  stop after staging
#
# This is the PROD checkout, so there is no cherry-picking and no personal
# divergence to guard against (unlike ship.sh in the personal instance).
# Commit, run this, done.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30
STAGING_ONLY="${1:-}"

die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree dirty — commit first"

# npm ci, so this is handled — but warn, since it makes the deploy slower and
# a bad lockfile is the known way to break it.
git fetch -q origin main
if ! git diff --quiet origin/main -- package-lock.json; then
  echo "  note: package-lock.json differs from origin/main (dependency change)"
fi

if [ -n "$(git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD)" ]; then
  say "Pushing to origin/main"
  git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | sed 's/^/  /'
  git push -q origin main
else
  echo "  nothing to push; deploying current origin/main"
fi
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short origin/main)
echo "  main = $NEW"

ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

verify() {
  local env="$1" url="$2" dir="$3"
  local head behind build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  behind=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  behind_main=$behind  BUILD_ID=$build"
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env HEAD ($head) != main ($NEW)"
  [ "$behind" = "0" ]  || die "$env is $behind commits behind main"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"

  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

say "Deploying prod"; vm "/home/kodely/deploy.sh prod 2>&1 | tail -2"
say "Verifying prod"; verify prod https://kodely.me /opt/kodely

say "Shipped"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# deploy.sh — push this checkout's committed work to kodely.me.
#
#   ./deploy.sh            staging -> verify -> prod -> verify
#   ./deploy.sh --staging  stop after staging
#
# Transport note: the VM cannot currently reach GitHub over SSH (see the board
# card "VM cannot reach GitHub over SSH"). Its own /home/kodely/deploy.sh runs
# `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`, and when that fetch
# fails it resets to a STALE remote-tracking ref and reports a healthy deploy
# of the WRONG commit — it did that twice on 2026-08-21.
#
# So this script does not rely on the VM pulling. It still pushes to GitHub
# (that works from here, and keeps origin authoritative), then ships the actual
# commits over the existing SSH path as a git bundle and builds in place. When
# the VM's GitHub access is restored, the bundle step can be dropped.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30
STAGING_ONLY="${1:-}"

say() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree dirty — commit first"

git fetch -q origin main || die "cannot reach GitHub from here"
if [ -n "$(git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD)" ]; then
  say "Pushing to origin/main"
  git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | sed 's/^/  /'
  git push -q origin main
fi
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
echo "  main = $NEW"

ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

# --------------------------------------------------------------- transport
# Bundle only what the VM is missing, using prod's current HEAD as the base.
say "Bundling commits for the VM"
BASE=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse HEAD')
if [ "$BASE" = "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" ]; then
  echo "  VM already at $NEW — nothing to transport"
else
  git cat-file -e "$BASE^{commit}" 2>/dev/null || die "prod is on commit $BASE which this checkout does not have — fetch/rebase first"
  git bundle create /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle "$BASE..HEAD" >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "  $(git rev-list --count "$BASE..HEAD") commit(s), $(du -h /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle | cut -f1)"
  base64 -w0 /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle > /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64
  B64=$(cat /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64)
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" \
    "echo '$B64' | ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM 'base64 -d > /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle'" \
    || die "could not transfer the bundle to the VM"
  vm "cd /opt/kodely && git bundle verify /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle >/dev/null 2>&1" \
    || die "bundle failed verification on the VM"
  echo "  transferred and verified"
fi

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_env staging /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging https://staging.kodely.me

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

deploy_env prod /opt/kodely kodely https://kodely.me

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK"

content.text:
Two different "token costs" are in play here, and the answer differs for each.

## 1. Kodely's own generation cost — depends on the **engine**, not the machine

| | Cost per build |
|---|---|
| `KODELY_ENGINE=api` (metered key) | ~90 credits, real $ |
| `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk` (your subscription) | **1 credit, $0** |

That's the 90× difference we measured today. And it's set per-environment, not per-location — **prod is already on `sdk`**, so generating on kodely.me right now costs the same as generating locally: nothing metered.

So no — running locally doesn't make *site generation* cheaper. Switching engines did that, and it's already done everywhere except local `:3003`, which just needs its token.

## 2. My token usage — local is somewhat cheaper, but it's not the main lever

Working locally is modestly cheaper because I edit and read files directly, instead of every command going through nested SSH (`host → VM`) and returning output I have to read back. Same for logs and DB queries.

But that's a rounding error next to the real cost driver: **how many iterations something takes.**

The clearest example is today's prompt-box glow. That burned far more than anything else in this session — not because of where the files were, but because my sandbox browser can't render, so I guessed six times before your DevTools output pinpointed it in one shot. Contrast that with the auto-SEO work: I could verify each step myself, so it landed quickly despite being a bigger change.

**The things that actually cost:**
- Debugging what I can't observe (visual/animation bugs are the worst case)
- Re-reading large files or long logs
- Vague scope that leads to rework

**What's cheap:**
- Anything I can verify with a command
- Tight, specific asks
- Handing me a paste of real output when something looks wrong on your screen

So: keep working locally on `:3003` because the feedback loop is faster and you can *see* the result — not because it saves tokens. When something's visual or environment-specific, one screenshot or console paste from you is worth several of my guessing rounds.

content.text:
**No — please don't.** That's the specific thing that created the mess we spent this morning untangling.

## Why editing on the VM is a trap

**1. Your deploy script deletes uncommitted work.** `/home/kodely/deploy.sh` runs:

```bash
git fetch -q origin main && git reset --hard origin/main
```

A `--hard` reset discards every uncommitted change in that checkout. Anything you edit directly on staging is one deploy away from being gone, with no undo.

**2. The VM can't push to GitHub.** SSH from it is blocked — that's the open URGENT card. So you couldn't push edits from there anyway without reversing the bundle workaround.

**3. No preview, no editor, no history.** You'd be editing production infrastructure over SSH with no local diff and no way to try something and back out.

## The split that actually works

These are two different jobs, and only one of them needs the server:

| Job | Where | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Edit code** | Local `kodely-prod` (`:3003`) | Fast, version-controlled, previewable, reversible |
| **Test generation** | staging | Needs the server's SDK credentials |

Local generation being broken doesn't affect editing at all — UI, marketing, auth, pricing, blog, contact all work fine on `:3003`. You just can't *generate a site* there, and staging covers that.

So the loop stays:

```bash
cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && git add -A && git commit -m "..." && ./deploy.sh --staging
```

Test on staging → then `./deploy.sh` to promote.

## The one rule worth keeping

**The VM is a deploy target, never an editing surface.** Every change reaches it through git. That's what makes `git log` an accurate history of what's running, and what makes rollback possible — both of which stop being true the moment someone edits in place.

If the local editing experience is what's bothering you, tell me what's annoying about it and I'll fix that instead — that's a much cheaper problem to solve than losing work to a hard reset.

content.text:
✅ **Credit metering is live on all three environments** (`4ff10e8`).

## What changed

The tokens were always there — the SDK's result carries `modelUsage`, which its own docs call the correct field for token accounting (it spans the main loop *plus* subagents and internal calls). The engine was just discarding it and reporting zeros.

Now every build charges real credits:

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Local build | 1 credit | **246** ($0.4913) |
| Staging build | 1 credit | **224** |

Verified the arithmetic against your rate card exactly — 491,279 micros → `ceil(/2000)` = 246. The SDK's concrete model id is normalised onto `MODEL_RATES` families, and anything unrecognised falls through to the conservative `default` rate, so an unknown model **over**-estimates rather than under-bills.

This also restores the instrument you'd lost: `/admin`'s cost/margin dashboard now has real data again, so "riskiest assumption #1" is measurable during the testing period.

## Two things to be clear about

**1. These costs are imputed, not billed.** No money moves on the subscription. They're real token counts priced against the API rate card — *what the build would have cost* on metered billing. That's exactly what makes the credit system testable now, but `/admin` figures are a model, not a statement. It's documented at the top of `agent-sdk.ts` so nobody later mistakes them for spend.

**2. Testing is no longer credit-free.** At ~225–250 credits per build against a 750-credit signup grant, a test account gets **~3 builds** before hitting zero. That's the real economics you wanted to exercise — but it means test accounts will now run dry. You have `scripts/promote-admin.mjs` for admin, and topping up credits is a DB write if you need it.

That second point is worth a decision: it's realistic, but it'll slow down casual testing. Want me to add a simple way to grant credits to an account?

content.content:
### ★ Roadmap overview — how to read this
Build order anchored to the 5 launch-gating blockers and the 4 riskiest assumptions. Phases are SEQUENTIAL GATES — don't start a phase until the previous phase's exit criteria pass. Every other card on the board slots into a phase by its priority/labels.
The 5 gates: (1) funded Anthropic key + capacity, (2) egress-isolated sandbox on a separate box, (3) DR + off-site backups, (4) the Nxeon partner-API contract, (5) committed pricing numbers.
Woven through from Phase 1, never bolted on later: transparent credits + no-charge-on-failure, security-by-default, and the Nxeon hosting monetization.
Principle: prove the core loop cheaply (Phase 1) BEFORE building real backend/infra (Phase 2). Kill-criteria gate the jump.

### Phase 0 — Foundation & Unblock (the 5 gates)
GOAL: remove the blockers that make everything else impossible. No product work until these clear.
IN SCOPE:
• Funded Anthropic key + org quota + hard spend caps + multi-key pool (the standing BLOCKER — sister Nxeon agent is already stuck on this).
• Rotate the exposed Anthropic/Cloudflare keys; stand up a secret vault + rotation runbook.
• Core data model / schema (User, Org, Project, Build, Deployment, Domain, CreditLedger, Subscription, Template, Event, ApiToken).
• CI/CD + staging + build-isolation for Kodely itself (no build-in-prod).
• Stand up the isolated Firecracker sandbox pool on a SEPARATE box (NOT the live .200 Soul Pilates machine) with an egress/SSRF firewall blocking the Nxeon control plane.

## TECH & ARCHITECTURE (42)

**T1 — WebContainers licensing / Safari limits** — Decide whether StackBlitz WebContainers are viable given SharedArrayBuffer + COOP/COEP + no-Safari + commercial licence; conclusion is "optional add-on, not core." • OPTIMISATION (research/decision) • Deps: none • **S** • Partly moot — you already build server-side, so this is a "don't do it" decision.

**T2 — Sandpack/Nodebox in-browser preview** — Free-tier zero-infra client-side preview of generated React before graduating to a real sandbox. • OPTIMISATION (COGS) • Deps: none (parallel path to server build) • **M** • Competes with existing server-side `vite build`; only worth it as a latency/cost play.

**T3 — Pick cloud sandbox vendor (E2B/Daytona/Modal/Fly)** — Buy-vs-buy comparison for server-side code execution; isolation (Firecracker) vs persistence (containers). • FOUNDATIONAL (decision gate) • Deps: **blocks/blocked-by T4** — mutually exclusive build-vs-buy • **S** (decision) / **M** with benchmarks.

**T4 — Self-host Firecracker microVMs on Proxmox** — Run own microVM sandbox fleet on Nxeon hardware to kill per-second vendor fees and keep code on owned infra. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: **is the sandbox dependency** — needed by T10, T15, T17, T18, T32, T33, T34, A4, A8; needs T39 (separate sandbox VM w/ nested KVM) • **XL**.

**T5 — Default stack Vite+React+TS+Tailwind+shadcn** — Ship the Lovable-style SPA template as the default generation target. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: none • **M** • **LIKELY ALREADY SATISFIED** — the locked pre-installed dependency tree implies this template already exists; card reduces to formalising it.

**T6 — Next.js full-stack template** — Second first-class template (SSR + API routes + Prisma/Postgres) matching Nxeon's own stack. • FOUNDATIONAL for full-stack tier • Deps: needs **per-project DB (T33)**, a real server runtime, and hosting (T11) — cannot ride the locked-dep `vite build` path • **L**.

**T7 — Backend choice: Supabase vs Convex vs Neon vs Nxeon Postgres** — Decide the default generated-app backend; recommends Nxeon-hosted Postgres+Prisma. • FOUNDATIONAL (decision) • Deps: gates T6, T8, T17, T33 • **S** decision / **L** to implement.

**T8 — Batteries-included auth scaffold per template** — Pre-wired login/signup/session + protected route in every template instead of letting the model invent it. • FOUNDATIONAL (quality) • Deps: T7 (backend), T33 for full-stack • **M** (SPA-only variant is **S**).

**T9 — Object storage for generated apps** — S3-compatible store (MinIO/Supabase) with upload helper + signed URLs, tenant-isolated prefixes. • SCALING • Deps: T7; tenant isolation model • **M**.

**T10 — Live preview + hot reload wiring** — Run the framework dev server inside the sandbox, expose via `<id>.preview.kodely` proxy subdomain, stream writes to disk so HMR pushes to the iframe. • FOUNDATIONAL (UX core) • Deps: **hard dep on sandbox (T3/T4)** + wildcard TLS + proxy router (related to T41) • **L** • Note: fundamentally different from today's build-then-serve model; this is a real architecture change.

**T11 — One-click deploy: Nxeon first, then Vercel/Netlify/CF** — Deploy button ships to Nxeon hosting (turning builders into hosting customers), with portability escapes. • FOUNDATIONAL (this is the monetisation moat) • Deps: **hosting infra**; T19 go-live flow; T30 partner API • **L**.

**T12 — Bi-directional GitHub sync** — Push generated code and pull external commits back so the AI works on true current state; GitHub App with per-repo tokens. • SCALING (retention of devs) • Deps: checkpoint/file-tree store (exists); conflict handling vs snapshots • **L**.

**T13 — Custom domains + automated SSL** — Attach user domains to deployed builds via existing Nxeon DNS/TLS automation. • SCALING • Deps: **hosting infra (T11)**, T41 router • **M** (reuses Nxeon pipeline).

**T14 — Project persistence: snapshot the filesystem, not just chat** — Git repo + periodic tarball snapshot + DB schema so a project rehydrates into a fresh sandbox. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: object storage; sandbox for rehydration • **M** • **LARGELY SATISFIED** — checkpoint snapshots of the full file tree already exist; remaining delta is git-as-source-of-truth and DB/migration capture.

**T15 — Multi-tenant isolation for sandboxes/previews** — Kernel/VM-level isolation, egress control, quotas, no shared creds; hard gate before real users. • FOUNDATIONAL (security gate) • Deps: **sandbox (T4)**, T32, T33 • **L** • Only becomes relevant once untrusted code *executes*; today's locked-tree `vite build` still runs untrusted code, so a scoped version is needed now.

**T16 — Secrets: encrypted vault + runtime injection, never in prompts** — Per-project vault, env injection into sandbox, output guardrail scanning commits for real secrets. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: sandbox for injection • **M** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — publish-time secret scanning exists; the vault + runtime injection half does not.

**T17 — Per-branch preview envs with DB branching** — Throwaway preview URL + branched Postgres per AI iteration/branch. • OPTIMISATION (polish) • Deps: **T10 preview infra + T33 per-project DB** — near the top of the dependency chain • **L**.

**T18 — Sandbox cost control: hibernate, scale-to-zero, quotas** — Auto-hibernate idle projects, fast rehydrate from snapshot, per-plan CPU/RAM/runtime caps. • SCALING • Deps: **sandbox (T4)** + T14 snapshots • **M** • Mostly N/A until long-lived sandboxes exist; today's ephemeral build model has no idle burn.

**T19 — Go-live flow across Kodely↔Nxeon** — CTA → SSO account-link → signed partner API deploy + hosting subscription + coupon + card capture → `deploy.succeeded` webhook returns live URL. • FOUNDATIONAL (revenue path) • Deps: **hosting infra**, T30 contract, T26 webhooks • **L**.

**T20 — Cinematic scroll hero: how the effect works** — Explainer: scroll-scrubbed pre-rendered clip vs real 3D; division of labour between video model, scroll lib, and codegen. • OPTIMISATION (marketing/template) • Deps: none • **S** (it's a note) • Feeds T21/T22/T23.

**T21 — Zero-API procedural WebGL hero ($0 marginal)** — R3F + GSAP/Lenis + Bloom hero rendered live in the visitor's browser; default cinematic path, zero COGS. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: none • **M**.

**T22 — Seedance hero: prompt + scroll-scrub code (premium)** — Credit-gated bespoke path: AI-generated clip → ffmpeg image sequence → GSAP scrub. • OPTIMISATION (upsell) • Deps: credit system (A12); asset hosting • **M**.

**T23 — Working procedural WebGL hero demo (reference)** — A built proof of T21 exists at `scratchpad/kodely-webgl-hero.html`. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: none • **S** (done; needs productising) • **ALREADY BUILT** as a demo artifact.

**T24 — Recommended whole-system stack** — Master architecture card: Next.js/TS/Prisma/Postgres app, BullMQ+Redis worker queue, Claude router + caching, in-browser preview first then Firecracker, two output templates, Nxeon hosting. • FOUNDATIONAL (the spine) • Deps: names nearly every other card; **explicitly recommends deferring Firecracker until full-stack demand justifies it** • **XL** as a programme • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — model router + prompt caching + the agent loop already exist; the **build worker/queue (BullMQ+Redis)** is called out here and is a prerequisite for T28, T37, T18.

**T25 — Core data model / schema** — User, Org, Project, Build, Deployment, Domain, CreditLedger, Subscription, Template, Event, ApiToken. • FOUNDATIONAL — **do first; nearly everything reads/writes it** • Deps: none • **M**.

**T26 — Public API + webhooks** — REST API + project/deploy events; backs API tokens and the Nxeon go-live bridge. • SCALING • Deps: T25, T30 • **L**.

**T27 — Kodely CLI (init/deploy/pull)** — Power-user CLI reinforcing own-your-code positioning. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: T26 public API • **M**.

**T28 — Rate limiting, quotas, queue autoscaling** — Per-plan limits, build quotas, autoscale the build-worker pool. • SCALING • Deps: **build worker/queue (T24)**; T25 • **M** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — coarse per-user rate limits exist; quotas + autoscaling do not.

**T29 — Disaster recovery + off-site backups (epic)** — Off-site backups, per-project DB+FS snapshot/restore, RTO/RPO, restore drills. Called the biggest infra gap. • FOUNDATIONAL (gate for hosting others' prod) • Deps: **hosting infra + per-project DB (T33)**; T14 • **L**.

**T30 — Kodely↔Nxeon partner API contract (formal spec)** — Signing, versioning, idempotency, auth, error semantics, webhook retry/DLQ. • FOUNDATIONAL — the monetisation moat rides on it • Deps: none to spec; blocks T19/T26 • **M**.

**T31 — CI/CD + staging + build isolation for Kodely itself** — Promote pipeline, migration gating, never build in the prod tree. • FOUNDATIONAL (Phase 0) • Deps: T39/T40 infra • **M**.

**T32 — Sandbox egress / SSRF firewall** — Allowlist blocking generated code from reaching internal metadata/DB/control plane. Hard pre-GA gate. • FOUNDATIONAL (security) • Deps: **sandbox (T4)** + T39 network topology • **M**.

**T33 — DB-per-project lifecycle + isolation** — Provisioning, isolated credentials, teardown, quota, backup per generated app. Security boundary, not a feature. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: T7 backend choice; **blocks T6, T8 full-stack, T17, T29** • **L**.

**T34 — Sandbox base-image supply chain + CVE patching** — Golden image with provenance and scheduled rebuilds. • SCALING • Deps: **sandbox (T4)** • **M** • Note: your existing single locked dependency tree is exactly this problem in miniature and already needs a patch cadence.

**T35 — Distributed tracing / request correlation** — End-to-end traces across app → queue → sandbox → partner API. • SCALING • Deps: **queue + sandbox** exist first • **M**.

**T36 — Data residency / region strategy** — EU pinning for generated apps + user data. • SCALING • Deps: **hosting infra**, multi-region sandbox pool • **L**.

**T37 — Load/chaos/capacity test of build-worker pool** — Validate autoscaling and rate limits under spike/failure before GA. • SCALING • Deps: **build worker/queue (T24) + T28** • **M**.

**T38 — Anthropic capacity: multi-key pool, org quota, spend caps** — Prevent a spike exhausting the key or the budget. • FOUNDATIONAL (launch blocker) • Deps: plugs into the existing model router • **M** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — model router exists as the insertion point; key pool + hard spend caps do not.

**T39 — Kodely infra home: dedicated VMs isolated from Nxeon** — `kodely-app` VM (Next.js + worker + own Postgres) and a **separate** `kodely-sandbox` VM with nested KVM + Firecracker + hard egress firewall; capacity noted as sufficient to start. • FOUNDATIONAL — **the physical prerequisite for T4, T15, T32, T40** • Deps: Proxmox host • **L**.

**T40 — Staging environment (staging.kodely.me)** — prod + staging trees, staging Postgres, sandbox-staging target, CI promote with migration gating. Phase-0. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: T39 • **M**.

**T41 — *.kodely.site wildcard routing + subdomain router** — Separate PSL-listed domain, wildcard DNS + Cloudflare Universal SSL, plus a **new reverse-proxy component** mapping Host header → deployment; slug assignment, collisions, reserved names, takedown. • FOUNDATIONAL for free user hosting • Deps: **hosting infra + deployments must exist**; Phase 2 dispatch needs the sandbox • **L** (placeholder wildcard proving DNS/SSL is **S**).

**T42 — Credit burn is the #1 complaint; win on transparency** — Live credit meter, pre-flight cost estimate, never charge for a failed build. • FOUNDATIONAL (positioning wedge) • Deps: token metering (A12); **"never charge for a failed build" needs the existing self-repair loop's build-result signal** • **M**.

---

## AI / CODEGEN ENGINE (21)

**A1 — Flow-engineered agent loop (plan→generate→run→read errors→fix)** — Explicit state machine rather than one-shot generation; called the single most important engine decision. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: error capture (A4) • **L** • **SUBSTANTIALLY SATISFIED** — the self-repair loop (one retry with error fed back) is this loop in minimal form. Delta: multi-step planning, n>1 iterations, fix/ignore user choice.

**A2 — Diff-based edits over full-file rewrites** — Targeted patches for token cost + latency; full writes only for new files/large refactors. • OPTIMISATION (large, though) • Deps: none; pairs with A8 tools • **M**.

**A3 — Sonnet default, escalate to Opus for planning** — Model tiering behind a router. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: none • **S** • **ALREADY SATISFIED** — model router with configurable model + effort per build phase exists. Card is now just tuning.

**A4 — Instrument the sandbox to feed real errors back** — Capture build output, dev-server logs, runtime exceptions, **browser console errors**, structured into the next turn. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: **sandbox for the runtime/console half**; build-output half needs nothing • **M** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — build errors already feed the repair loop; runtime + browser-console capture requires a live dev server, i.e. T10/T4.

**A5 — Context management: retrieve, don't dump** — Send tree/manifest but only relevant file bodies; context-rot degrades accuracy well before window limits. • FOUNDATIONAL for project growth (SCALING in timing) • Deps: A9 index • **L**.

**A6 — Prompt caching — biggest cost lever** — Cacheable stable prefixes (system prompt, tool defs, static project context). • OPTIMISATION • Deps: none • **S** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — caching on the system prompt exists; tool definitions and project-context prefixes are the remaining ~2 breakpoints.

**A7 — Context compaction / conversation summarization** — Summarize resolved turns, trim stale tool output, keep a rolling project-state summary. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: A1 loop • **M**.

**A8 — Tool-use design: fs, terminal, npm, console tools** — Lean composable tool set (write_file, apply_diff, read_file, run_command, install_package, read_logs, restart_dev_server). • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: **`run_command`/`install_package`/`restart_dev_server` require the sandbox and directly conflict with the locked-dependency-tree model** — install_package cannot exist without abandoning "never npm install per generation" or adding a curated allowlist • **M**.

**A9 — Retrieval/index over the project (tree + embeddings)** — Live symbol map + embeddings on pgvector so the agent searches instead of reading whole files. • SCALING • Deps: Postgres+pgvector; feeds A5, A21 • **L**.

**A10 — System prompt design + structured artifact output format** — Strict parseable schema (plan block, then file-write/shell actions) so the runner never parses prose. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: none; **prerequisite for making A6 caching effective** • **M** • Partially exists implicitly in the current builder.

**A11 — Stream generation to the UI** — Stream tokens, show each file as it's written, show plan up front, allow early interrupt. • FOUNDATIONAL (UX) • Deps: A10 output format • **M**.

**A12 — Token metering + credit system** — Per-user token/compute metering, credit balance, cost-per-project tracking, tied to Nxeon billing. Business-survival item. • FOUNDATIONAL • Deps: T25 (CreditLedger); **blocks T42, T22, T17 gating** • **L**.

**A13 — Execution-based evals: pass@k + regression harness** — Representative prompt suite that generates, boots, and asserts the app builds and core flows work; run on every prompt/model change. • FOUNDATIONAL (quality gate for every other engine change) • Deps: **needs a sandbox to boot apps for the flow-assertion tier**; the build-only tier works today with `vite build` • **L**.

**A14 — Guardrails: prompt-injection, secrets, code-injection scanners** — Input sanitisation of untrusted content (repos, issues, pastes) + output scanning (SecretsScanner, CodeInjectionScanner) as a launch gate. • FOUNDATIONAL (security) • Deps: T12 GitHub sync makes the injection surface real • **M** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — publish-time secret scanning exists; prompt-injection input guardrails and code-injection scanning do not.

**A15 — shadcn/ui component retrieval for consistent UI** — Curated component/block library + a retrieval tool so the model composes known components instead of inventing markup. • OPTIMISATION (quality + tokens) • Deps: T5 template; A9-style retrieval • **M** • Fits today's locked dependency tree cleanly — no new install path needed.

**A16 — Model routing + graceful degradation/fallback** — Task-based routing, secondary provider on outage/rate-limit, degraded-mode banner, capped backoff retries. • OPTIMISATION/resilience • Deps: pairs with T38 key pool • **M** • **PARTIALLY SATISFIED** — router exists; fallback provider, degradation banner, and retry caps do not.

**A17 — Optional multi-agent decomposition (planner/coder/reviewer)** — Flag-gated reviewer pass for complex/paid builds; multiplies token cost. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: **A13 evals must exist to justify it**; A1 loop • **L** • Explicitly "start single-agent" — defer.

**A18 — Auto-SEO for generated sites** — Meta tags, OG/Twitter images, sitemap, structured data in every generated site. • OPTIMISATION (high value/effort ratio) • Deps: none — pure template + prompt work • **S–M**.

**A19 — Accessibility + performance budget on output** — a11y checks + Lighthouse budget on generated output with auto-fix. • OPTIMISATION • Deps: **needs to run the built site** — headless browser in the build path (lighter than a full sandbox) • **M**.

**A20 — Prompt/guardrail library + eval harness** — Versioned prompts/guardrails so engine changes are regression-tested. • FOUNDATIONAL (process) • Deps: **overlaps A13 and A14 — dedupe these three** • **M**.

**A21 — Large-project context management** — Diff edits + file targeting + retrieval so quality holds as projects outgrow the context window. • SCALING • Deps: **duplicate/umbrella of A2 + A5 + A9 — dedupe** • **L**.

---

## Dependency clusters (sequencing signal)

**Server-side sandbox (Firecracker/microVM) required:** T4, T10, T15, T17, T18, T32, T34, T35(partly), A4(runtime half), A8(run_command/install/restart), A13(boot-and-assert tier). Root prerequisite: **T39** (dedicated `kodely-sandbox` VM with nested KVM). T3 is the buy-instead alternative. Note T24 explicitly recommends deferring this until full-stack demand justifies it.

**Per-project database isolation required:** T33 is the root; it gates T6 (Next.js full-stack), T8 (full-stack auth), T17 (DB branching), T29 (per-project DR). T7 is the decision that unblocks T33.

**Build worker / queue required:** named in T24 (BullMQ + Redis); gates T28 (quotas/autoscaling), T37 (load/chaos test), T18 (hibernation scheduling), T35 (tracing across hops). Not yet in the "exists today" list — this is the largest un-flagged foundational gap.

**Hosting infrastructure required:** T11, T13, T19, T29, T36, T41 — plus T26/T30 as the API contract layer. T30 (partner API spec) is cheap, blocks T19 and T26, and should precede both.

**Phase-0 with no external dependency (do first):** T25 (schema), T30 (partner API spec), T39 + T40 + T31 (infra/staging/CI), A10 (output format), A6-completion (cache the tool defs), A12 (metering — gates the T42 wedge), A18 (auto-SEO).

**Already satisfied or near-satisfied — descope these cards:** A3 (fully), A1 (minimal form shipped), T14 (snapshots), T5 (template), T23 (demo built), and partially T16, T28, T38, A4, A6, A14, A16, T42's build-result signal.

**Dedupe candidates:** A13 / A20 (eval harness stated twice), A21 vs A2+A5+A9, T21 vs T23, T3 vs T4 (mutually exclusive — pick one).</result>

Yes — **26 cards**, and I read that column directly earlier rather than delegating it. It's the third-largest build column after Tech & Architecture (42) and Builder/Editor UX (30).

## What's actually in it

**Analytics & instrumentation (9)** — overview dashboard, first-party event pipeline, activation funnel, per-user journey timeline, retention/cohorts, revenue (MRR/churn/LTV/CAC), UTM attribution, end-user site analytics, cost & margin.

**Engine ops (3)** — model router + spend caps console, build success-rate/eval dashboard, prompt & build log inspector.

**Users & safety (4)** — user/team management + impersonation, admin RBAC + 2FA + audit log, projects registry + takedown, abuse/fraud console.

**Money (2)** — billing/credits/refunds/dunning, coupons + referral/affiliate.

**Content & config (4)** — template/wizard CMS, blog CMS for the 253 SEO pages, feature flags + pricing config + kill switches, Nxeon hosting-bridge admin.

**Compliance & support (4)** — GDPR export/delete/retention, support inbox + feedback board, system health/observability, API token oversight.

## Where it stands today

**1 of 26.** Only the read-only cost/margin dashboard exists at `/admin`, plus a CLI script to promote an admin. My code audit found no analytics tables at all — the schema has 9 models and none of them is an `Event`.

## The dependency that decides its phasing

**The first-party event pipeline is the root.** Six or seven of those dashboards — funnel, retention, cohorts, attribution, journey timeline, overview — are all just different queries over one event stream. Build the pipeline once and they become views; skip it and each dashboard invents its own tracking.

That single card is cheap and unblocks the most, so it lands early. But most of the *rest* of the admin panel is genuinely late-phase: revenue analytics needs revenue, abuse console needs public signups, hosting-bridge admin needs the Nxeon bridge, GDPR tooling needs real user data.

The exceptions that earn their place early are **spend caps + kill switches** (your #1 existential risk is cost) and **build success-rate tracking** (it measures "riskiest assumption #2", green-build-first-try — which the board says must gate the jump to Phase 2 but currently has no instrument).

content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
