Kodely · board audit · 21 Aug 2026

Kodely Build Sequence

Every card on the research board, read and sorted into what to build, in what order — and the five contradictions that have to be settled before most of it means anything.

707cards total
302build work
253SEO briefs
130research
18shipped

Contents

Where you are Five reconciliations Merge & kill Dependency spine 0 · Unblock 1 · Trust the loop 2 · Finish the builder 3 · The fork 4 · Go-live 5 · Launch 6 · Moat Parallel tracks

Ground truth

Where you actually are

Taken from the codebase, not the board — the board is stale in both directions. Nine database models, eighteen API routes, thirteen pages.

Working today

Prompt → a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind site, built server-side against one locked dependency tree. Chat editing, live preview, checkpoint and restore, read-only code view. One-click publish to a *.kodely.site subdomain over HTTPS, with a secret scan that blocks the publish. Credits metered per build with no charge on failure. Auth, a seeded onboarding project, and 56 of 251 SEO pages live.

Not built

Click-to-edit. Diff-based edits — the prompt still says “always pass the complete final file, never a diff.” Code export or GitHub sync. Any backend in generated output: no database, auth, or payments. Custom domains. A build worker or queue. An event pipeline. Content moderation. Twenty-five of twenty-six admin panel cards.

The gate that got skipped

The board defines Phase 0 as five hard gates and says “no product work until these clear.” In practice Phase 1 is roughly 80% built while Phase 0 was never finished: the Anthropic key is unfunded, there is no sandbox, no off-site backups, no partner-API contract, and pricing numbers are still undecided. Nothing on the board records that this happened.

That isn't necessarily wrong — proving the loop cheaply first was the right instinct, and it worked. But the phases below are re-cut against what is actually shipped, rather than pretending the original gate order held.

Settle first

Five reconciliations

These aren't engineering tasks. Each one invalidates a block of cards until it's decided, and three of them are actively dangerous to publish against.

1 · The Nxeon hosting funnel doesn't exist ~10 cards

Ten cards assume a paid Nxeon hosting subscription, custom domains, a first-month-free promo, always-on vs sleeping free sites, backups tiering, and Nxeon Mail. Today hosting is a free subdomain and nothing else.

Why it matters: this is where most of the monetization thinking lives. Killing these cards leaves a revenue gap; keeping them means committing to build a hosting product. One or the other, explicitly.

2 · Subscription tiers don't exist ~9 cards

Nine cards assume monthly plans with included credit allowances — per-plan ceilings, plan pickers, “removable on paid”. The product sells one-off credit packs and has no tiers. One card records a decision for a hybrid tier model that shipped behaviour now contradicts.

Resolve as: re-affirm the hybrid model and build it, or formally reverse it. Everything about paywalls and feature fences is blocked until then.

3 · Your credit is 125× smaller than a competitor's marketing hazard

A Kodely credit is $0.002 of model spend. A Rocket credit is roughly $0.25. Six cards compare raw credit counts across the two, and all of that arithmetic is meaningless.

Live risk: “500 credits for $9” reads stingy beside “100 credits for $25”, while “750 free credits” sounds generous but is $1.50 of inference. Publishing a pricing page before fixing this actively misleads. The fix is a plain “what one credit buys” mapping, and it blocks any pricing or comparison page.

4 · “A live business” overclaims frontend-only output positioning

The positioning line is “Claude writes code. Kodely gives you a live business.” Generated sites have no database, auth, or payments. The wizard cards ask “needs login? payments?” and the slash-command set includes “wire an API” — none of which the generator can produce.

Consequence: comparison pages and the messaging house are built on this. Either narrow the claim to what ships, or move backend up the plan and earn it.

5 · The preview runtime is undecided — and it's the root dependency decision

In-browser sandbox, rented cloud sandbox, or self-hosted Firecracker on your own metal. Two cards propose mutually exclusive answers (buy vs build) and a third argues for deferring the sandbox until full-stack demand justifies it.

Blocks: auto-backend, full-stack preview, autonomous testing, the verification loop, production guardrails, per-branch previews, and the egress firewall. Nothing full-stack can be honestly scoped until this is answered.

Housekeeping

Merge and kill

302 overstates the real work. These pairs describe the same build from two columns; one card in each pair should win and the other should be closed as a duplicate.

Duplicate setKeep as
Auto backend (DB + auth) — appears in Features and DifferentiationOne epic; it's the biggest lift on the board
Don't bill for failed generations ×2One policy card + one build card
Plan/estimate before spending ×2One card, paired with the credit mapping
Template gallery ×3 (GTM, Design, Features)One epic — it's SEO surface, onboarding and viral loop
Teams / collaboration ×2One, post-PMF
Eval harness ×2 in the engine columnOne
Badge + referral ×2 · launch plan ×2 · affiliate vs KOL programOne each
Cloud sandbox vendor vs self-hosted FirecrackerMutually exclusive — pick one, delete the other
Large-project context ⊃ diff edits + retrieval + indexingUmbrella card; keep the three specifics

Sequencing

The dependency spine

Build order isn't a preference — six things force it. Everything else can move around them.

  • Diff-based editsEvery generation currently rewrites whole files. It's a cost multiplier on everything downstream, and now that metering is live the saving is measurable. Do it first.
  • The data modelOrg, Deployment, Domain, Subscription, Template, Event, ApiToken don't exist yet. Cheap to add, and almost everything later reads or writes them.
  • The event pipelineSeven admin dashboards — funnel, retention, cohorts, attribution, journey, overview — are all queries over one event stream. Build it once or each dashboard invents its own tracking.
  • The verification loopTypecheck, build, lint, smoke-test before the user sees output. “Never charge for failures” is only honest once you can define failure as more than “the build errored”.
  • The runtime decisionReconciliation 5. Until it lands, nothing full-stack can be scoped.
  • Per-project database isolationThe security boundary the entire backend tier stands on. Gates full-stack templates, auth scaffolding, branch previews and per-project disaster recovery.

One gap is worth naming because no card flags it as foundational: the build worker and queue. It's mentioned once inside an architecture card, doesn't exist, and is a prerequisite for quotas, autoscaling, hibernation and tracing.

The plan

Seven phases

Re-cut from the board's own Phase 0–4, which stay valid in intent. Sizes are focused-work estimates: S under a day · M 2–5 days · L 1–3 weeks · XL a month or more.

Phase 0

Unblock

Close the gates that were skipped. None of this is product work, and all of it is currently exposed.

  • SRotate four exposed credentialsAnthropic key, Google client secret, Postgres password, VM OAuth token — all leaked into chat or screenshots today. Procedures already written in the runbook.
  • SFix the VM's GitHub accessSSH is blocked in both directions; deploys run on a bundle workaround. The VM's own deploy script silently ships stale code when a fetch fails.
  • MFund the Anthropic key, add a multi-key pool and hard spend capsThe standing launch blocker. The key currently has no credit — generation only works because it runs on a subscription.
  • MExtend the data modelOrg, Deployment, Domain, Subscription, Template, Event, ApiToken.
  • decideSettle reconciliations 1–5Hosting funnel, tiers, credit units, positioning, runtime. Roughly 25 cards are unplannable until these land.
  • SPut numbers on the four kill-criteriaGreen-build rate, margin per build, design preference, hosting attach. They're meant to gate the jump to backend work and are currently unset, so they gate nothing.

ExitNo live credential is compromised; deploys fail loudly rather than silently; the five reconciliations are written down as decisions.

Phase 1

Trust the loop

Make what already works measurable and cheap to run. Highest leverage per day of work on the entire board.

  • MDiff-based editsThe single biggest cost lever. Every edit currently regenerates whole files.
  • MUser-set spend caps and budget alertsBill shock is the category's deepest trust wound — one competitor billed $607 against a $25 plan in three days.
  • M“What one credit buys” mapping and pre-flight estimatorBlocks every pricing and comparison page. Reconciliation 3 has no other fix.
  • MEvent pipeline, North Star and activation funnelFirst successful published build. Unlocks seven admin dashboards as views.
  • MBuild success-rate instrumentMeasures green-build-first-try — the assumption meant to gate Phase 3.
  • LVerification loopTypecheck, build, lint and a headless smoke test before output reaches the user, with a hard cap on fix attempts.

ExitCost per build is trending down and visible; the four kill-criteria have real readings; no user can be surprised by a bill.

Phase 2

Finish the builder

Close the table-stakes gaps that need no sandbox and no backend. This is the largest cluster of user-visible value on the board.

  • LClick-to-edit on the canvasThe biggest single table-stakes gap. Chat plus a read-only code view is two of three editing modes; the DOM-to-source mapping is the real work.
  • MCode exportCheap, and it's the only thing currently backing the “you own the code” claim.
  • LDiff view with per-hunk approve and rejectThe trust mechanism for “it changed the wrong thing”.
  • MBrand and style step feeding design tokens into the promptThe most demoable differentiator — it's the direct answer to generic “AI purple” output, and it fits frontend-only perfectly.
  • SAuto-enhance rough prompts into an editable specBest effort-to-impact ratio in the design column.
  • LTemplate gallery with remixThree duplicate cards merged. Kills the blank canvas, and doubles as SEO surface and social proof.
  • MContent moderation on publishYou host what you generate, so a phishing site is your liability. Publish currently runs only a secret scan.
  • MNotifications and lifecycle emailBuild finished, site live, credits low.

ExitA non-technical user builds, visually edits, and publishes a site they'd put their own name on — without touching chat for every change.

Phase 3

The fork

Reconciliation 5 comes due. Everything here is XL and irreversible in architecture terms — don't start it until Phase 1's kill-criteria say the loop is worth scaling.

  • decideRuntime: buy a sandbox, build Firecracker, or deferOne architecture card explicitly recommends deferring until full-stack demand justifies the cost. Deferring is a legitimate answer.
  • LDedicated sandbox VM with nested virtualisation and an egress firewallPhysical prerequisite for everything below. Must block the Nxeon control plane and cloud metadata.
  • LPer-project database isolation and lifecycleA security boundary, not a feature. Gates full-stack templates, auth scaffolding and per-project recovery.
  • XLAuto backend — Postgres, auth, storage from a promptThe biggest lift on the board and the largest capability gap against competitors. Unblocks payments, RLS checks, and production guardrails.
  • MSecrets vault with runtime injectionPublish-time scanning exists; storing and injecting secrets safely does not.
  • LProduction guardrailsSnapshots, destructive-operation confirmation, dev/prod separation — the Replit lesson, and only meaningful once generated apps hold real data.

ExitA generated app with a database and login runs in an isolated sandbox that cannot reach your control plane, and can be restored from a snapshot.

Phase 4

Go-live and monetization

Turn hosting into revenue. Every card here depends on reconciliations 1 and 2 having been answered yes.

  • MCustom domains with guided DNS and automatic SSLThe industry's standard paid fence, and the thing the whole go-live upsell hangs on.
  • LOff-site backups and disaster recoveryFlagged repeatedly, never built. You cannot host other people's production sites without it.
  • MPartner API contractSigning, versioning, idempotency, webhook retries. Cheap to specify, blocks the go-live flow and the public API.
  • LGo-live flow and hosting subscriptionOnly exists if reconciliation 1 says build it.
  • MBilling UX, spend ceilings, invoices, self-serve cancelStripe is wired and inert; it needs real keys and committed numbers.
  • M“Built with Kodely” badge and referralNear-zero-CAC loop — but badge removal needs a paid fence to sit behind.
  • MAdmin: billing, abuse console, moderation and takedownNow genuinely needed, because there's revenue and public signups to police.

ExitA user attaches their own domain, pays, and the site stays up — with backups you have actually restored from in a drill.

Phase 5

Launch

Open the doors. Growth loops only pay once the funnel underneath them converts.

  • MWaitlist and staged invite wavesControls load and creates the launch moment.
  • LDocs, help centre, changelog, public roadmapTrust surface and long-tail SEO.
  • MLegal pack — ToS, Privacy, AUP, DPA — plus GDPR rights and cookie consentRequired before public signups, and non-negotiable for any EU user.
  • MStatus page, SLOs, error budgets, on-callPeople hosting real sites need to see health.
  • MLoad and chaos test the build-worker poolNeeds the queue that doesn't exist yet.
  • LLaunch: Product Hunt, HN, founder video, creator seeding, DiscordFour duplicate cards merged into one moment.
  • LAffiliate program with attribution and payoutsCuts CAC from $500–800 to $150–250 at competitor benchmarks.

ExitA sustained signup → activation → paid funnel, with SLOs holding under real traffic.

Phase 6

Moat

Post-PMF expansion. Nothing here should start before revenue retention is proven.

  • LTwo-way GitHub syncIndependent of the backend spine — could pull earlier if developers become the lead segment.
  • XLTeams, agency white-label, client workspacesHigher-ACV, and needs orgs, seats, custom domains and branding first.
  • LPublic API, webhooks, CLIReinforces the ownership positioning.
  • LTemplate and component marketplaceSupply-side network effect on top of the Phase 2 gallery.
  • MBYOK tierOffloads inference cost for power users and agencies.
  • LAccessibility checks, performance budgets, i18n, SOC 2 pathEnterprise and agency readiness.

ExitNet revenue retention above 100%.

Alongside

Two parallel tracks

SEO content — 253 briefs, 56 live

This runs continuously and isn't a phase. It's already producing at roughly fourteen pages per wave. But about eighty of the briefs — most of the Guides and Feature & Integrations columns — describe Stripe, Supabase, Postgres, Clerk, S3, GitHub export and custom domains. Writing them today means publishing a roadmap as though it were a product.

Decision needed: drop them, hold them until Phases 3–4 make them true, or rewrite them as honest “not yet” pieces. This has been flagged twice in shipped notes and is still open.

Research — 130 cards

Competitor teardowns, market segmentation and risk analysis. These are reference material, not work — but two of them carry live warnings: unit economics is the standing existential risk, and one card self-flags its own market figures as stale.

Compiled from all 707 cards on the Kodely Research board, cross-checked against the deployed codebase rather than the board's own status. Where the two disagreed — and they did, in both directions — the code won.

Prompt → a real Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind site, built server-side against one locked dependency tree. Chat editing, live preview, checkpoint and restore, read-only code view. One-click publish to a *.kodely.site subdomain over HTTPS, with a secret scan that blocks the publish. Credits metered per build with no charge on failure. Auth, a seeded onboarding project, and 56 of 251 SEO pages live.

Not built

Click-to-edit. Diff-based edits — the prompt still says “always pass the complete final file, never a diff.” Code export or GitHub sync. Any backend in generated output: no database, auth, or payments. Custom domains. A build worker or queue. An event pipeline. Content moderation. Twenty-five of twenty-six admin panel cards.

The gate that got skipped

The board defines Phase 0 as five hard gates and says “no product work until these clear.” In practice Phase 1 is roughly 80% built while Phase 0 was never finished: the Anthropic key is unfunded, there is no sandbox, no off-site backups, no partner-API contract, and pricing numbers are still undecided. Nothing on the board records that this happened.

That isn't necessarily wrong — proving the loop cheaply first was the right instinct, and it worked. But the phases below are re-cut against what is actually shipped, rather than pretending the original gate order held.

Settle first

Five reconciliations

These aren't engineering tasks. Each one invalidates a block of cards until it's decided, and three of them are actively dangerous to publish against.

1 · The Nxeon hosting funnel doesn't exist ~10 cards

Ten cards assume a paid Nxeon hosting subscription, custom domains, a first-month-free promo, always-on vs sleeping free sites, backups tiering, and Nxeon Mail. Today hosting is a free subdomain and nothing else.

Why it matters: this is where most of the monetization thinking lives. Killing these cards leaves a revenue gap; keeping them means committing to build a hosting product. One or the other, explicitly.

2 · Subscription tiers don't exist ~9 cards

Nine cards assume monthly plans with included credit allowances — per-plan ceilings, plan pickers, “removable on paid”. The product sells one-off credit packs and has no tiers. One card records a decision for a hybrid tier model that shipped behaviour now contradicts.

Resolve as: re-affirm the hybrid model and build it, or formally reverse it. Everything about paywalls and feature fences is blocked until then.

3 · Your credit is 125× smaller than a competitor's marketing hazard

A Kodely credit is $0.002 of model spend. A Rocket credit is roughly $0.25. Six cards compare raw credit counts across the two, and all of that arithmetic is meaningless.

Live risk: “500 credits for $9” reads stingy beside “100 credits for $25”, while “750 free credits” sounds generous but is $1.50 of inference. Publishing a pricing page before fixing this actively misleads. The fix is a plain “what one credit buys” mapping, and it blocks any pricing or comparison page.

4 · “A live business” overclaims frontend-only output positioning

The positioning line is “Claude writes code. Kodely gives you a live business.” Generated sites have no database, auth, or payments. The wizard cards ask “needs login? payments?” and the slash-command set includes “wire an API” — none of which the generator can produce.

Consequence: comparison pages and the messaging house are built on this. Either narrow the claim to what ships, or move backend up the plan and earn it.

5 · The preview runtime is undecided — and it's the root dependency decision

In-browser sandbox, rented cloud sandbox, or self-hosted Firecracker on your own metal. Two cards propose mutually exclusive answers (buy vs build) and a third argues for deferring the sandbox until full-stack demand justifies it.

Blocks: auto-backend, full-stack preview, autonomous testing, the verification loop, production guardrails, per-branch previews, and the egress firewall. Nothing full-stack can be honestly scoped until this is answered.

Housekeeping

Merge and kill

302 overstates the real work. These pairs describe the same build from two columns; one card in each pair should win and the other should be closed as a duplicate.

Duplicate setKeep as
Auto backend (DB + auth) — appears in Features and DifferentiationOne epic; it's the biggest lift on the board
Don't bill for failed generations ×2One policy card + one build card
Plan/estimate before spending ×2One card, paired with the credit mapping
Template gallery ×3 (GTM, Design, Features)One epic — it's SEO surface, onboarding and viral loop
Teams / collaboration ×2One, post-PMF
Eval harness ×2 in the engine columnOne
Badge + referral ×2 · launch plan ×2 · affiliate vs KOL programOne each
Cloud sandbox vendor vs self-hosted FirecrackerMutually exclusive — pick one, delete the other
Large-project context ⊃ diff edits + retrieval + indexingUmbrella card; keep the three specifics

Sequencing

The dependency spine

Build order isn't a preference — six things force it. Everything else can move around them.

  • Diff-based editsEvery generation currently rewrites whole files. It's a cost multiplier on everything downstream, and now that metering is live the saving is measurable. Do it first.
  • The data modelOrg, Deployment, Domain, Subscription, Template, Event, ApiToken don't exist yet. Cheap to add, and almost everything later reads or writes them.
  • The event pipelineSeven admin dashboards — funnel, retention, cohorts, attribution, journey, overview — are all queries over one event stream. Build it once or each dashboard invents its own tracking.
  • The verification loopTypecheck, build, lint, smoke-test before the user sees output. “Never charge for failures” is only honest once you can define failure as more than “the build errored”.
  • The runtime decisionReconciliation 5. Until it lands, nothing full-stack can be scoped.
  • Per-project database isolationThe security boundary the entire backend tier stands on. Gates full-stack templates, auth scaffolding, branch previews and per-project disaster recovery.

One gap is worth naming because no card flags it as foundational: the build worker and queue. It's mentioned once inside an architecture card, doesn't exist, and is a prerequisite for quotas, autoscaling, hibernation and tracing.

The plan

Seven phases

Re-cut from the board's own Phase 0–4, which stay valid in intent. Sizes are focused-work estimates: S under a day · M 2–5 days · L 1–3 weeks · XL a month or more.

Phase 0

Unblock

Close the gates that were skipped. None of this is product work, and all of it is currently exposed.

  • SRotate four exposed credentialsAnthropic key, Google client secret, Postgres password, VM OAuth token — all leaked into chat or screenshots today. Procedures already written in the runbook.
  • SFix the VM's GitHub accessSSH is blocked in both directions; deploys run on a bundle workaround. The VM's own deploy script silently ships stale code when a fetch fails.
  • MFund the Anthropic key, add a multi-key pool and hard spend capsThe standing launch blocker. The key currently has no credit — generation only works because it runs on a subscription.
  • MExtend the data modelOrg, Deployment, Domain, Subscription, Template, Event, ApiToken.
  • decideSettle reconciliations 1–5Hosting funnel, tiers, credit units, positioning, runtime. Roughly 25 cards are unplannable until these land.
  • SPut numbers on the four kill-criteriaGreen-build rate, margin per build, design preference, hosting attach. They're meant to gate the jump to backend work and are currently unset, so they gate nothing.

ExitNo live credential is compromised; deploys fail loudly rather than silently; the five reconciliations are written down as decisions.

Phase 1

Trust the loop

Make what already works measurable and cheap to run. Highest leverage per day of work on the entire board.

  • MDiff-based editsThe single biggest cost lever. Every edit currently regenerates whole files.
  • MUser-set spend caps and budget alertsBill shock is the category's deepest trust wound — one competitor billed $607 against a $25 plan in three days.
  • M“What one credit buys” mapping and pre-flight estimatorBlocks every pricing and comparison page. Reconciliation 3 has no other fix.
  • MEvent pipeline, North Star and activation funnelFirst successful published build. Unlocks seven admin dashboards as views.
  • MBuild success-rate instrumentMeasures green-build-first-try — the assumption meant to gate Phase 3.
  • LVerification loopTypecheck, build, lint and a headless smoke test before output reaches the user, with a hard cap on fix attempts.

ExitCost per build is trending down and visible; the four kill-criteria have real readings; no user can be surprised by a bill.

Phase 2

Finish the builder

Close the table-stakes gaps that need no sandbox and no backend. This is the largest cluster of user-visible value on the board.

  • LClick-to-edit on the canvasThe biggest single table-stakes gap. Chat plus a read-only code view is two of three editing modes; the DOM-to-source mapping is the real work.
  • MCode exportCheap, and it's the only thing currently backing the “you own the code” claim.
  • LDiff view with per-hunk approve and rejectThe trust mechanism for “it changed the wrong thing”.
  • MBrand and style step feeding design tokens into the promptThe most demoable differentiator — it's the direct answer to generic “AI purple” output, and it fits frontend-only perfectly.
  • SAuto-enhance rough prompts into an editable specBest effort-to-impact ratio in the design column.
  • LTemplate gallery with remixThree duplicate cards merged. Kills the blank canvas, and doubles as SEO surface and social proof.
  • MContent moderation on publishYou host what you generate, so a phishing site is your liability. Publish currently runs only a secret scan.
  • MNotifications and lifecycle emailBuild finished, site live, credits low.

ExitA non-technical user builds, visually edits, and publishes a site they'd put their own name on — without touching chat for every change.

Phase 3

The fork

Reconciliation 5 comes due. Everything here is XL and irreversible in architecture terms — don't start it until Phase 1's kill-criteria say the loop is worth scaling.

  • decideRuntime: buy a sandbox, build Firecracker, or deferOne architecture card explicitly recommends deferring until full-stack demand justifies the cost. Deferring is a legitimate answer.
  • LDedicated sandbox VM with nested virtualisation and an egress firewallPhysical prerequisite for everything below. Must block the Nxeon control plane and cloud metadata.
  • LPer-project database isolation and lifecycleA security boundary, not a feature. Gates full-stack templates, auth scaffolding and per-project recovery.
  • XLAuto backend — Postgres, auth, storage from a promptThe biggest lift on the board and the largest capability gap against competitors. Unblocks payments, RLS checks, and production guardrails.
  • MSecrets vault with runtime injectionPublish-time scanning exists; storing and injecting secrets safely does not.
  • LProduction guardrailsSnapshots, destructive-operation confirmation, dev/prod separation — the Replit lesson, and only meaningful once generated apps hold real data.

ExitA generated app with a database and login runs in an isolated sandbox that cannot reach your control plane, and can be restored from a snapshot.

Phase 4

Go-live and monetization

Turn hosting into revenue. Every card here depends on reconciliations 1 and 2 having been answered yes.

  • MCustom domains with guided DNS and automatic SSLThe industry's standard paid fence, and the thing the whole go-live upsell hangs on.
  • LOff-site backups and disaster recoveryFlagged repeatedly, never built. You cannot host other people's production sites without it.
  • MPartner API contractSigning, versioning, idempotency, webhook retries. Cheap to specify, blocks the go-live flow and the public API.
  • LGo-live flow and hosting subscriptionOnly exists if reconciliation 1 says build it.
  • MBilling UX, spend ceilings, invoices, self-serve cancelStripe is wired and inert; it needs real keys and committed numbers.
  • M“Built with Kodely” badge and referralNear-zero-CAC loop — but badge removal needs a paid fence to sit behind.
  • MAdmin: billing, abuse console, moderation and takedownNow genuinely needed, because there's revenue and public signups to police.

ExitA user attaches their own domain, pays, and the site stays up — with backups you have actually restored from in a drill.

Phase 5

Launch

Open the doors. Growth loops only pay once the funnel underneath them converts.

  • MWaitlist and staged invite wavesControls load and creates the launch moment.
  • LDocs, help centre, changelog, public roadmapTrust surface and long-tail SEO.
  • MLegal pack — ToS, Privacy, AUP, DPA — plus GDPR rights and cookie consentRequired before public signups, and non-negotiable for any EU user.
  • MStatus page, SLOs, error budgets, on-callPeople hosting real sites need to see health.
  • MLoad and chaos test the build-worker poolNeeds the queue that doesn't exist yet.
  • LLaunch: Product Hunt, HN, founder video, creator seeding, DiscordFour duplicate cards merged into one moment.
  • LAffiliate program with attribution and payoutsCuts CAC from $500–800 to $150–250 at competitor benchmarks.

ExitA sustained signup → activation → paid funnel, with SLOs holding under real traffic.

Phase 6

Moat

Post-PMF expansion. Nothing here should start before revenue retention is proven.

  • LTwo-way GitHub syncIndependent of the backend spine — could pull earlier if developers become the lead segment.
  • XLTeams, agency white-label, client workspacesHigher-ACV, and needs orgs, seats, custom domains and branding first.
  • LPublic API, webhooks, CLIReinforces the ownership positioning.
  • LTemplate and component marketplaceSupply-side network effect on top of the Phase 2 gallery.
  • MBYOK tierOffloads inference cost for power users and agencies.
  • LAccessibility checks, performance budgets, i18n, SOC 2 pathEnterprise and agency readiness.

ExitNet revenue retention above 100%.

Alongside

Two parallel tracks

SEO content — 253 briefs, 56 live

This runs continuously and isn't a phase. It's already producing at roughly fourteen pages per wave. But about eighty of the briefs — most of the Guides and Feature & Integrations columns — describe Stripe, Supabase, Postgres, Clerk, S3, GitHub export and custom domains. Writing them today means publishing a roadmap as though it were a product.

Decision needed: drop them, hold them until Phases 3–4 make them true, or rewrite them as honest “not yet” pieces. This has been flagged twice in shipped notes and is still open.

Research — 130 cards

Competitor teardowns, market segmentation and risk analysis. These are reference material, not work — but two of them carry live warnings: unit economics is the standing existential risk, and one card self-flags its own market figures as stale.

Compiled from all 707 cards on the Kodely Research board, cross-checked against the deployed codebase rather than the board's own status. Where the two disagreed — and they did, in both directions — the code won.

Good, so diff-based edits already work on the SDK path — the gap is just the API engine, which shifts priorities. Now for parallelizing agents, I need to avoid having multiple agents edit the same repo simultaneously since that risks git and build conflicts, and the deploy pipeline is serial with some work blocked on pending decisions — so I should assign agents to non-overlapping workstreams, each in its own isolated space.

I'm considering using worktree isolation so each agent gets its own git worktree, but that complicates merging their work back, especially since my session's working directory is the personal Kodely instance rather than kodely-prod where the actual work needs to land. Given that risk, the safer path is to launch agents on tasks that don't touch the shared repo at all — research, analysis, and writing work instead.

A more practical compromise is to assign each agent a disjoint set of files within kodely-prod, have them implement and typecheck without committing or deploying, then I review and deploy everything serially myself. I'm sketching out four candidate features with mostly independent files: a code export/ZIP download feature, spend caps with budget alerts, a credit estimator page, and an event pipeline — though I notice the spend caps and credit estimator both touch lib/credits.ts, and several features overlap on the Prisma schema, so I'll need to sequence those carefully to avoid conflicts.

Since the schema is the real collision point, I'm restructuring so only one agent (or myself) touches prisma/schema.prisma. I'll give three agents disjoint, schema-free features — code export, content moderation on publish, and an auto-enhance prompt feature — each working only with new files, while I handle the schema-touching work like the event pipeline and spend caps myself, serially. I also want to make sure each agent gets a tight brief on codebase conventions before starting.

I should be upfront with the user that deploys are inherently serial and schema changes are a single point of contention, so parallelism only helps so much here. I'll write prompts specifying the working directory, the feature to implement, required verification steps (tsc and eslint), and explicit restrictions against committing, deploying, or touching the schema or credits file, plus a requirement to report back changes. I'm also realizing that even with disjoint file scopes, three agents running builds simultaneously in the same working tree could still collide on shared build artifacts.

I'll tell each agent to skip `npm run build` entirely and only run tsc/eslint, saving the actual build for when I integrate everything myself. Now I'm ready to launch the agents.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. **Primary Request and Intent:**

The user is building "Kodely", an AI website builder (Next.js 16 + Prisma + Postgres, deployed at kodely.me). Requests in chronological order:
- Set up the local app (Postgres, .env, build, dev server)
- Fix hydration error; add password show/hide toggle on login/signup
- Set up "Kodely Board" (a nested Kanban app) and fix its UX: light mode, single-screen layout, voice-to-text, click-to-edit descriptions, smoother drag-drop, drag-to-delete, search, all stages visible, narrower columns
- Fix the prompt-box glow (many iterations — "vigorously vet this issue because I'm tired of giving you prompt after prompt"), then soften it, add rotating colors + pulsing, reduce intensity
- Add a contact page with a form to hello@kodely.me; later make it actually send email
- Establish a clean local→GitHub→staging→prod workflow ("this whole thing is a mess, what can we do moving forward")
- Make all Kodely environments use the Claude Agent SDK (subscription) instead of the metered API key: *"i want our kodely sites we using during this testing period to always use the sdk"* and *"no i dont want to use api key for for testing phase on production"*
- Fix local builds so generation can be tested locally
- *"are you able to add credit logic based off the amount of tokens are used to build a site so we can test this feature"*
- Analyze the entire Kodely Research board (707 cards) and produce a phased build plan
- *"lets build all of it, or as much as we can"* + *"launch agents to take care of everything we need to in this session at the same time"*

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
- Next.js 16.3.1 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19.2.8, Prisma 6.19.3, PostgreSQL 18
- Claude Agent SDK (`@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) vs Anthropic API (`@anthropic-ai/sdk`)
- `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk|api` env flag pattern; `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` vs `~/.claude/.credentials.json`
- Credit ledger: 1 credit = $0.002 model spend (`MICROS_PER_CREDIT = 2000`); `costMicros()` uses `MODEL_RATES` (USD per MTok, numerically = micros per token)
- `modelUsage` from SDK result (inputTokens, outputTokens, cacheReadInputTokens, cacheCreationInputTokens)
- Generated sites: Vite + React + TS + Tailwind, server-side `vite build` against ONE locked pre-installed dependency tree (never npm install per generation), served from DB under strict CSP
- git bundle transport (VM cannot reach GitHub over SSH)

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Downloads via `fetch` + blob so failures surface in the existing error strip rather than saving a JSON error body as a `.zip`.

**None.** No `npm install`, `package.json` untouched. Deflate comes from Node's built-in `zlib`.

## Auth path reasoning
`requireUser()` (not `getCurrentUser()` — every existing route under `app/api/projects` uses `requireUser().catch(() => null)`, and `requireUser` is just `getCurrentUser` + throw, so this is the same session check in the repo's idiom). Unauthenticated → 401 before any DB read. The project lookup is `findFirst({ where: { id, userId: user.id } })` — ownership is in the same query as the id, so a wrong-user id returns no row and yields a 404 indistinguishable from a nonexistent project. Files are then fetched by `project.id` from that already-ownership-scoped row, never from the raw route param.

**Both**, routed on the `ENGINE` export from `lib/agent.ts` — the two branches were ~20 lines each, so honouring both was cheaper than picking one.
- `api` → `anthropic.messages.create` with `MODELS.enhancer`, `max_tokens: 1500`. No `thinking`, no `output_config.effort` — Haiku 4.5 rejects `effort`, and a 220-word brief isn't a reasoning task. No `cache_control` either: the system prompt sits under the ~1k-token minimum cacheable prefix, so a breakpoint would be silently ignored.
- `sdk` → `query()` with `model: MODELS.enhancer`, `allowedTools: []`, `maxTurns: 1`, `settingSources: []`, `cwd: tmpdir()`. The tool/settings/cwd lockdown means the agent has nothing to read and cannot wander into the repo or pick up its `CLAUDE.md`. It first does a bare `await import("./agent-sdk")` **for the module-scope side effect** — that module strips `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` so nothing spawned can quietly bill the metered key on a subscription box. Enhance can be the first SDK call a process makes, so it must not skip that. This is commented at the call site.

This environment runs `KODELY_ENGINE=sdk` with no `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, so the SDK branch is the live one here.

### The enhance prompt
`ENHANCE_SYSTEM` in `lib/enhance.ts`. Structure:
1. **"What actually gets built"** — a single-page site; layout, sections, copy, visual style; no backend of any kind. Then an explicit never-list: databases/stored submissions/search over real data; accounts, sign-in, member areas, dashboards, admin; payments, checkout, carts, real bookings; server code, APIs, cron, email sending, contact forms that deliver; **anything loaded from another host** (CDN scripts, web fonts, remote/stock images, embedded maps, video embeds, analytics, social feeds, live prices). It names the CSP as the reason and adds the key nuance: a form or "Book now" button may exist as a *visual element* — describe it that way, never as something that works. Images are inline SVG/CSS gradients; type is the system stack.
2. **"What to write"** — plain text, no fences, under 220 words, in the user's own language, under exactly five headings: `Audience`, `Goal`, `Tone and visual style`, `Sections`, `Key content`.
3. **Rules** — be specific (real headline wording, never "your headline here"); **invent no facts about a real business** (no addresses, phone numbers, prices, hours, testimonials, statistics) — use bracketed placeholders like `[your address]`; keep every choice the user already made, expand don't replace; output the brief and nothing else.

The 220-word ceiling is a product decision as much as a cost one — a spec nobody reads is worse than no spec.

### Failure handling
The governing rule: **Enhance is a convenience and must never stand between someone and their build.**
- Hard deadlines in `lib/enhance.ts` (25s API / 60s SDK — the SDK spawns a process, cold start alone eats seconds), merged with `req.signal` so a closed tab or an impatient user also cancels the in-flight model call. `maxDuration = 90` on the route so *our* deadline fires with a friendly message rather than the platform's blank 504.
- Timeout, refusal, empty spec, or SDK-not-authenticated all collapse to one 502 with `"Couldn't expand that just now — you can still build with what you wrote."` Internals go to `console.error` only.
- On the client, failure is non-destructive by construction: the typed prompt is still in the box, the Build/send button was never disabled by enhance, and the error renders as a quiet neutral line, not a red alarm — it isn't the user's fault.
- Enhance is **not credit-charged and creates no build row** — a preview of what you're about to buy cannot itself cost credits. That's why the abuse ceiling is the rate limiter rather than the credit meter.

### UI decisions
The spec lands **in the composer's own textarea** rather than a modal or preview pane. That textarea is already editable and is already what the send button reads, so *accept* = press Build, *edit* = type, *discard* = **Revert** (a small strip above the box, with a `Sparkles` glyph in `var(--accent)` on the hero, plain `text-black/40` in the editor). Zero new design patterns; rows grow 2→12 (hero) and 3→12 (editor) so the spec is actually reviewable.

Two things worth flagging:
- **I caught and fixed a bug in my own change:** with a multi-line spec in the box, the existing `Enter`-submits handler would have fired a build on the first paragraph break the user typed. Enter now inserts a newline while a spec is showing, in both surfaces.
- Re-enhancing always re-sends the **original** one-liner, never a spec we already produced — re-expanding an expansion compounds invention instead of adding detail.

### Rate limiting
`checkEnhanceRateLimit` is **in-memory and synchronous**, unlike its two DB-backed siblings, because an enhance leaves nothing in the database to count (no files, no build row, no credits) and a throwaway suggestion doesn't justify a schema migration — which I'm also forbidden from making. Per-process, resets on deploy: a speed bump, exactly the weight the contact form's throttle carries, and right for a call costing a fraction of a cent. The real spending gates (`checkGenerateRateLimit` + credit meter) still sit in front of the only thing that costs money. The map is bounded at 5000 entries. `Retry-After` is computed from when the oldest hit in the window ages out, not a flat hour. Limit is deliberately **above** the 20 builds/hour generate limit — enhancing several drafts before committing to one build is the whole point.

### Incomplete / worth knowing
1. **The hero's Enhance is signed-in-only.** `/api/enhance` is auth-gated per spec, and most hero visitors are anonymous, so the button appears only after a `/api/auth/me` probe confirms it would work — same pattern the mic already uses for feature detection. A button that 401s on click is worse than no button. Cost is negligible: `getCurrentUser()` returns null without touching the DB when there's no cookie.
2. **Pre-existing quirk this exposes:** `PromptHero.submit()` pushes *everyone* to `/signup`, including signed-in users — who are exactly the population that now sees Enhance there. Their spec does survive (sessionStorage → `destinationAfterAuth` → new project), but the redirect is odd. Out of scope; not introduced by me.
3. **`npx tsc --noEmit` reports 3 errors**, all in the concurrent agent's root scratch files (`__modbuild.mts`, `__modcheck.mts`). Zero from my files.
4. **`npx eslint` reports 5 errors in `PromptHero.tsx`** — all pre-existing. I verified this by linting the file at `HEAD`: identical 5 (the `any`-typed SpeechRecognition shims and the existing `setSpeechSupported` effect). My additions introduce none; every other changed file lints clean.
5. Per instructions I did not run `npm run build`, and nothing was committed, pushed, or deployed. The SDK path is unexercised at runtime — verifying it would mean an actual `query()` spawn, which I did not run.</result>

Closed by stripping `className`/`class` values before proximity matching, so the window measures text distance rather than Tailwind volume; that widened the film-blog margin from marginal to several hundred characters and let me drop the window to 120.
3. *formsubmit.co* — a normal static-site contact backend. Closed by requiring it within 900 chars of a password field; the gallery fixture (contact form + separate staff login) passes clean while the webmail fixture (password inside the formsubmit form) blocks.

Residual known FP: an educational page with a seed-phrase input in a live demo would trip HIGH unless phrased as a warning.

**One finding from the build pass worth your attention:** in the drainer fixture the minifier stripped the `/* setApprovalForAll */` comment, leaving only calldata — the name-based rule went silent on dist while passing on source. I added the raw 4-byte selectors (`0xa22cb465`, `0x39509351`, `0x23b872dd`, `0x42842e0e`, `0xf242432a`, `0x2eb2c2d6`) which survive minification. Anything relying on identifier names in built output is unreliable; that's noted in the code.

Unrelated: `lib/build-site.ts`'s Windows junction to the foundation `node_modules` creates without error but doesn't resolve on this machine, so every local build fails with `Cannot find module`. I worked around it in the throwaway harness only and changed nothing. Worth someone looking at separately.

## Deliberately not attempted

No logo/visual similarity detection, no OCR, no domain-reputation or URL-blocklist feed, no drainer-kit domain list (goes stale, and staleness reads as coverage), no LLM call in the publish path, no homoglyph/IDN analysis, no cross-project or per-user pattern correlation, no scanning of `.css`/`.map`. No keyword blocklist — nothing fires on prose alone. And no attempt at an evasion-resistant design: string-splitting or runtime-assembled markup defeats all of this, which the module header says plainly.

## DB column I'd want (not added)

A `ModerationFinding` table — `id, projectId, publishedAt, provider, rule, severity, path, evidence, action ("blocked" | "recorded"), reviewedAt, reviewedBy, outcome` — one row per finding per publish attempt. Today the sub-HIGH signals go only to `console.warn`, which is enough to reconstruct one site after it's reported but not enough to query proactively. With that table you could: pull every `low`/`medium` on a reported site instantly; measure the real FP rate by reviewing `blocked` rows (currently unknowable, which is the main obstacle to promoting any MEDIUM rule to blocking); and rank users by accumulated findings, which is a much better abuse signal than any single page. A cheaper interim version is a `Project.moderationFindings Json?` column holding the last result — loses history but needs no new model.</result>

content.text:
Everything's built, green, and running locally. Here's where things stand.

## Your new list → 18 cards on the board

| Column | Cards |
|---|---|
| AI / Codegen Engine | Learning mode (feedback loop), chat replies as quality signal, golden-set eval harness, skills library |
| Features & Table-Stakes | Asset library (parent, with ~16 categories brainstormed), asset search tool, CDN/optimisation, brand kit, AI-gen fallback |
| Builder / Editor UX | Logo pre-loader, build animation, live progress narration, wake agent, low-credit warning |
| Pricing & Monetization | Social credit gifts (4×50), verified social connections |
| Risks & Pitfalls | Anti-abuse for credit gifts |

Two of those carry warnings you should see before they're picked up:

- **Wake agent** — I couldn't tell which of two things you meant (resume a stalled build vs. an idle agent that wakes on a trigger), so the card names both and recommends the first.
- **Social verification** — Discord membership is genuinely checkable via their API. Instagram, Facebook, and LinkedIn have no follower-check API worth relying on. The card says: decide the abuse tolerance before building, and don't ship an honour-system button that grants credits on click.

I also shipped the **low-credit warning** rather than just carding it, since it was cheap.

## What shipped in code

Three agents finished — code export (dependency-free ZIP writer, streamed), publish moderation (`lib/moderation.ts`, conjunction-based rules, verified against 13 fixtures both as source and as real `vite build` output), and prompt auto-enhance (`/api/enhance`, Haiku, not credit-charged).

Mine, on top:
- **Analytics** — `Event` model + `lib/events.ts` with a closed event vocabulary, wired into signup, project creation, build start/success/failure, and publish. Activation funnel and green-build-first-try now render on `/admin`.
- **`Build.repairAttempts`** — the green-build-first-try metric your roadmap gates on had nothing measuring it. Now it does, per build, and it's a column in the admin table.
- **Spend cap** — `User.spendCapCredits`, enforced in `/api/generate` before anything is spent, with `/settings` to set it.
- **Credit meter** — real bar on the dashboard, amber before the dead end, "about N more builds" from *your* measured average rather than a constant.

## Two corrections

**I was wrong about an admin leak.** I told you mid-turn that `/admin` was unauthenticated and exposing cost, margin, and customer prompts. It wasn't — [layout.tsx:6](app/admin/layout.tsx:6) has always gated it on `role === "ADMIN"`. I'd read `page.tsx` and `middleware.ts` and jumped. Nothing was ever exposed. I kept a page-level check as defence-in-depth and rewrote the comment that stated the false claim.

**Local builds are fine.** The moderation agent reported the Windows junction doesn't resolve and every local build fails. I reproduced that, then realised both of us had made the same mistake — running a test harness without loading `.env`, so `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` fell back to the Linux path and created a dangling junction. With the env loaded, `buildSite` compiles and returns output correctly.

I also **corrected `estimateCredits`** — it claimed 8–30 credits for a build when the measured figure is ~144. It's currently unused, so nothing displayed the wrong number, but on a product whose headline promise is no bill shock that was a landmine.

`npm run build` passes. TypeScript clean. The 12 ESLint errors all exist at HEAD — I verified by stashing and re-linting.

## Two things need you

**Nothing is committed or deployed yet**, deliberately — `deploy.sh` doesn't run Prisma migrations, and this adds a table and a column. Shipping the code first would break production on the first build query. The order has to be `prisma db push` on `/opt/kodely-staging` and `/opt/kodely`, *then* deploy. Say the word and I'll run the whole sequence.

**No ADMIN user exists**, so you can't actually open `/admin` — pre-existing, not something I changed. To promote yourself locally:

```bash
psql -d kodely_personal -c "UPDATE \"User\" SET role='ADMIN' WHERE email='haxkodi@gmail.com';"
```

content.content:
1	---
2	title: proxy.js
3	description: API reference for the proxy.js file.
4	related:
5	  title: Learn more about Proxy
6	  links:
7	    - app/api-reference/functions/next-request
8	    - app/api-reference/functions/next-response
9	---
10	
11	> **Note**: The `middleware` file convention is deprecated and has been renamed to `proxy`. See [Migration to Proxy](#migration-to-proxy) for more details.
12	
13	The `proxy.js|ts` file is used to write [Proxy](/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) and run code on the server before a request is completed. Then, based on the incoming request, you can modify the response by rewriting, redirecting, modifying the request or response headers, or responding directly.
14	
15	Proxy executes before routes are rendered. It's particularly useful for implementing custom server-side logic like authentication, logging, or handling redirects.
16	
17	> **Good to know**:
18	>
19	> Proxy is meant to be invoked separately of your render code and in optimized cases deployed to your CDN for fast redirect/rewrite handling, you should not attempt relying on shared modules or globals.
20	>
21	> To pass information from Proxy to your application, use [headers](#setting-headers), [cookies](#using-cookies), [rewrites](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#rewrite), [redirects](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/next-response#redirect), or the URL.
22	
23	Create a `proxy.ts` (or `.js`) file in the project root, or inside `src` if applicable, so that it is located at the same level as `pages` or `app`.
24	
25	If you’ve customized [`pageExtensions`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/pageExtensions), for example to `.page.ts` or `.page.js`, name your file `proxy.page.ts` or `proxy.page.js` accordingly.
26	
27	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
28	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
29	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
30	
31	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
32	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
33	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
34	}
35	
36	export const config = {
37	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
38	}
39	```
40	
41	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
42	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
43	
44	// This function can be marked `async` if using `await` inside
45	export function proxy(request) {
46	  return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/home', request.url))
47	}
48	
49	export const config = {
50	  matcher: '/about/:path*',
51	}
52	```
53	
54	## Exports
55	
56	### Proxy function
57	
58	The file must export a single function, either as a default export or named `proxy`. Note that multiple proxy from the same file are not supported.
59	
60	```js filename="proxy.js"
61	// Example of default export
62	export default function proxy(request) {
63	  // Proxy logic
64	}
65	```
66	
67	### Config object (optional)
68	
69	Optionally, a config object can be exported alongside the Proxy function. This object includes the [matcher](#matcher) to specify paths where the Proxy applies.
70	
71	### Matcher
72	
73	The `matcher` option allows you to target specific paths for the Proxy to run on.
74	
75	Without a `matcher`, Proxy runs on **every request**, including static files (`_next/static`), image optimizations (`_next/image`), and assets in the `public/` folder. Consider using a [negative match pattern](#negative-matching) to exclude these paths, otherwise auth logic or redirects can unintentionally block CSS, JS, or images from loading.
76	
77	You can specify paths in several ways:
78	
79	- For a single path: Directly use a string to define the path, like `'/about'`.
80	- For multiple paths: Use an array to list multiple paths, such as `matcher: ['/about', '/contact']`, which applies the Proxy to both `/about` and `/contact`.
81	
82	```js filename="proxy.js"
83	export const config = {
84	  matcher: ['/about/:path*', '/dashboard/:path*'],
85	}
86	```
87	
88	Additionally, the `matcher` option supports complex path specifications using regular expressions. For example, you can exclude certain paths with a regular expression matcher:
89	
90	```js filename="proxy.js"
91	export const config = {
92	  matcher: [
93	    // Exclude API routes, static files, image optimizations, and .png files
94	    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|.*\\.png$).*)',
95	  ],
96	}
97	```
98	
99	This enables precise control over which paths to include or exclude.
100	
101	The `matcher` option accepts an array of objects with the following keys:
102	
103	- `source`: The path or pattern used to match the request paths. It can be a string for direct path matching or a pattern for more complex matching.
104	- `locale` (optional): A boolean that, when set to `false`, ignores locale-based routing in path matching.
105	- `has` (optional): Specifies conditions based on the presence of specific request elements such as headers, query parameters, or cookies.
106	- `missing` (optional): Focuses on conditions where certain request elements are absent, like missing headers or cookies.
107	
108	```js filename="proxy.js"
109	export const config = {
110	  matcher: [
111	    {
112	      source: '/api/:path*',
113	      locale: false,
114	      has: [
115	        { type: 'header', key: 'Authorization', value: 'Bearer Token' },
116	        { type: 'query', key: 'userId', value: '123' },
117	      ],
118	      missing: [{ type: 'cookie', key: 'session', value: 'active' }],
119	    },
120	  ],
121	}
122	```
123	
124	The `source` path patterns:
125	
126	1. MUST start with `/`
127	2. Can include named parameters: `/about/:path` matches `/about/a` and `/about/b` but not `/about/a/c`
128	3. Can have modifiers on named parameters (starting with `:`): `/about/:path*` matches `/about/a/b/c` because `*` is _zero or more_. `?` is _zero or one_ and `+` _one or more_
129	4. Can use regular expression enclosed in parenthesis: `/about/(.*)` is the same as `/about/:path*`
130	5. Are anchored to the start of the path: `/about` matches `/about` and `/about/team` but not `/blog/about`
131	
132	Read more details on [path-to-regexp](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp#path-to-regexp-1) documentation.
133	
134	> **Good to know**:
135	>
136	> - The `matcher` values need to be constants so they can be statically analyzed at build-time. Dynamic values such as variables will be ignored.
137	> - For backward compatibility, Next.js always considers `/public` as `/public/index`. Therefore, a matcher of `/public/:path` will match.
138	
139	## Params
140	
141	### `request`
142	
143	When defining Proxy, the default export function accepts a single parameter, `request`. This parameter is an instance of `NextRequest`, which represents the incoming HTTP request.
144	
145	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
146	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
147	
148	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
149	  // Proxy logic goes here
150	}
151	```
152	
153	```js filename="proxy.js" switcher
154	export function proxy(request) {
155	  // Proxy logic goes here
156	}
157	```
158	
159	If you prefer a shorthand, you can use the `NextProxy` type. It infers the parameter types for both `request` (`NextRequest`) and `event` (`NextFetchEvent`) automatically:
160	
161	```tsx filename="proxy.ts"
162	import type { NextProxy } from 'next/server'
163	
164	export const proxy: NextProxy = (request, event) => {
165	  event.waitUntil(Promise.resolve())
166	  return Response.json({ pathname: request.nextUrl.pathname })
167	}
168	```
169	
170	> **Good to know**:
171	>
172	> - `NextRequest` is a type that represents incoming HTTP requests in Next.js Proxy, whereas [`NextResponse`](#nextresponse) is a class used to manipulate and send back HTTP responses.
173	
174	## NextResponse
175	
176	The `NextResponse` API allows you to:
177	
178	- `redirect` the incoming request to a different URL
179	- `rewrite` the response by displaying a given URL
180	- Set request headers for API Routes, `getServerSideProps`, and `rewrite` destinations
181	- Set response cookies
182	- Set response headers
183	
184	<AppOnly>
185	
186	To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
187	
188	1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route)) that produces a response
189	2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
190	
191	> **Good to know**: For redirects, you can also use `Response.redirect` instead of `NextResponse.redirect`.
192	
193	</AppOnly>
194	
195	<PagesOnly>
196	
197	To produce a response from Proxy, you can:
198	
199	1. `rewrite` to a route ([Page](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/pages-and-layouts) or [Edge API Route](/docs/pages/building-your-application/routing/api-routes)) that produces a response
200	2. return a `NextResponse` directly. See [Producing a Response](#producing-a-response)
201	
202	</PagesOnly>
203	
204	## Execution order
205	
206	Proxy will be invoked for **every route in your project**. Given this, it's crucial to use [matchers](#matcher) to precisely target or exclude specific routes. The following is the execution order:
207	
208	1. `headers` from `next.config.js`
209	2. `redirects` from `next.config.js`
210	3. Proxy (`rewrites`, `redirects`, etc.)
211	4. `beforeFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
212	5. Filesystem routes (`public/`, `_next/static/`, `pages/`, `app/`, etc.)
213	6. `afterFiles` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
214	7. Dynamic Routes (`/blog/[slug]`)
215	8. `fallback` (`rewrites`) from `next.config.js`
216	
217	> **Good to know:** [Server Functions](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-server) are not separate routes in this chain. They are handled as POST requests to the route where they are used, so a Proxy matcher that excludes a path will also skip Server Function calls on that path.
218	>
219	> A matcher change or a refactor that moves a Server Function to a different route can silently remove Proxy coverage. Always verify authentication and authorization inside each Server Function rather than relying on Proxy alone. See the [Data Security guide](/docs/app/guides/data-security#authentication-and-authorization) for recommended patterns.
220	
221	## Runtime
222	
223	Proxy defaults to using the Node.js runtime. The [`runtime`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route-segment-config/runtime) config option is not available in Proxy files. Setting the `runtime` config option in Proxy will throw an error.
224	
225	## Advanced Proxy flags
226	
227	In `v13.1` of Next.js two additional flags were introduced for proxy, `skipProxyUrlNormalize` (formerly `skipMiddlewareUrlNormalize`) and `skipTrailingSlashRedirect` to handle advanced use cases.
228	
229	`skipTrailingSlashRedirect` disables Next.js redirects for adding or removing trailing slashes. This allows custom handling inside proxy to maintain the trailing slash for some paths but not others, which can make incremental migrations easier.
230

312	### Using Cookies
313	
314	Cookies are regular headers. On a `Request`, they are stored in the `Cookie` header. On a `Response` they are in the `Set-Cookie` header. Next.js provides a convenient way to access and manipulate these cookies through the `cookies` extension on `NextRequest` and `NextResponse`.
315	
316	1. For incoming requests, `cookies` comes with the following methods: `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete` cookies. You can check for the existence of a cookie with `has` or remove all cookies with `clear`.
317	2. For outgoing responses, `cookies` have the following methods `get`, `getAll`, `set`, and `delete`.
318	
319	```ts filename="proxy.ts" switcher
320	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
321	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
322	
323	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
324	  // Assume a "Cookie:nextjs=fast" header to be present on the incoming request
325	  // Getting cookies from the request using the `RequestCookies` API
326	  let cookie = request.cookies.get('nextjs')
327	  console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
328	  const allCookies = request.cookies.getAll()
329	  console.log(allCookies) // => [{ name: 'nextjs', value: 'fast' }]
330	
331	  request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => true
332	  request.cookies.delete('nextjs')
333	  request.cookies.has('nextjs') // => false
334	
335	  // Setting cookies on the response using the `ResponseCookies` API
336	  const response = NextResponse.next()
337	  response.cookies.set('vercel', 'fast')
338	  response.cookies.set({
339	    name: 'vercel',
340	    value: 'fast',
341	    path: '/',
342	  })
343	  cookie = response.cookies.get('vercel')
344	  console.log(cookie) // => { name: 'vercel', value: 'fast', Path: '/' }
345	  // The outgoing response will have a `Set-Cookie:vercel=fast;path=/` header.
346	
347	  return response
348	}
349	```

440	#### RSC requests and rewrites
441	
442	During RSC requests, Next.js strips internal Flight headers from the `request` instance in Proxy. For example, headers like `rsc`, `next-router-state-tree`, and `next-router-prefetch` are not exposed through `request.headers`. This is to prevent accidentally handling an RSC request differently than the HTML request as both need to align.
443	
444	When you use `NextResponse.rewrite()`, Next.js automatically propagates the required RSC rewrite headers upstream.
445	
446	If you implement custom rewrite logic with `fetch()` instead of `NextResponse.rewrite()`, you can run into missing RSC headers unless you forward them manually.

448	For custom `fetch` rewrite setups, you can also enable `skipProxyUrlNormalize` in `next.config.js` so your rewrite logic can receive the necessary URL shape and RSC headers from the provided request object:

456	### CORS
457	
458	You can set CORS headers in Proxy to allow cross-origin requests, including [simple](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#simple_requests) and [preflighted](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/CORS#preflighted_requests) requests.
459	
460	```tsx filename="proxy.ts" switcher
461	import { NextResponse } from 'next/server'
462	import type { NextRequest } from 'next/server'
463	
464	const allowedOrigins = ['https://acme.com', 'https://my-app.org']
465	
466	const corsOptions = {
467	  'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS',
468	  'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': 'Content-Type, Authorization',
469	}
470	
471	export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
472	  // Check the origin from the request
473	  const origin = request.headers.get('origin') ?? ''
474	  const isAllowedOrigin = allowedOrigins.includes(origin)
475	
476	  // Handle preflighted requests
477	  const isPreflight = request.method === 'OPTIONS'
478	
479	  if (isPreflight) {
480	    const preflightHeaders = {
481	      ...(isAllowedOrigin && { 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': origin }),
482	      ...corsOptions,
483	    }
484	    return NextResponse.json({}, { headers: preflightHeaders })
485	  }
486	
487	  // Handle simple requests
488	  const response = NextResponse.next()
489	
490	  if (isAllowedOrigin) {
491	    response.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin)
492	  }
493	
494	  Object.entries(corsOptions).forEach(([key, value]) => {
495	    response.headers.set(key, value)
496	  })
497	
498	  return response
499	}
500	
501	export const config = {
502	  matcher: '/api/:path*',
503	}
504	```

603	
604	The `matcher` config allows full regex so matching like negative lookaheads or character matching is supported. An example of a negative lookahead to match all except specific paths can be seen here:
605	
606	```js filename="proxy.js"
607	export const config = {
608	  matcher: [
609	    /*
610	     * Match all request paths except for the ones starting with:
611	     * - api (API routes)
612	     * - _next/static (static files)
613	     * - _next/image (image optimization files)
614	     * - favicon.ico, sitemap.xml, robots.txt (metadata files)
615	     */
616	    '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico|sitemap.xml|robots.txt).*)',
617	  ],
618	}

676	The `NextFetchEvent` object extends the native [`FetchEvent`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/FetchEvent) object, and includes the [`waitUntil()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/ExtendableEvent/waitUntil) method.
