input.description: Brand kit for generated sites
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: a brand kit — let a customer supply their own logo and colours so generated sites look like *their* business rather than a nice generic template.

## The constraint that decides the whole design
Generated sites are static files under a CSP with **no external hosts**: `default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'` and **no `font-src`**. Read `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` yourself. Consequences you must work within:
- A logo must be **inlined** — SVG markup or a data URI. There is no remote image and no upload CDN.
- **Custom web fonts are impossible, including base64 ones**: with no `font-src`, fonts fall back to `default-src 'self'`, which does not admit `data:` the way `img-src` does. Do not build a font picker.
- Everything the builder writes passes through the model's context as tokens, so **size is cost**. A 200 KB base64 PNG logo is roughly 270 KB of base64 in a prompt. Work out what is actually affordable and say so with numbers.

## Read before designing
- `lib/assets/patterns.ts` — 30 curated gradients and palettes with stable ids already exist. **Reuse them as the palette vocabulary**; do not invent a second one.
- `lib/agent.ts` SYSTEM — how the builder is instructed, including its rules against inventing business facts. **READ ONLY.**
- `lib/foundation.ts` — the starting project, including `src/index.css`. Tailwind v4 uses an `@theme` block; a palette can be seeded there as CSS variables, which is far cheaper than describing colours in prose. **READ ONLY.**
- `prisma/schema.prisma` — `ProjectFile.content` is a `String`, so an SVG logo can live there as an ordinary project file. **You may not change the schema**; work within it.
- `components/marketing/PromptHero.tsx` — there is already an image-attach path that downscales client-side to a data URL. Learn from it; do not duplicate it.

## Build
1. **`lib/brand-kit.ts`** — the model: a logo (SVG preferred, raster accepted with a hard size cap you justify), a palette chosen from the existing catalogue or as explicit hexes, and a business name. Plus the code that turns a brand kit into (a) a `@theme` block for `src/index.css` and (b) a short, precise instruction fragment for the prompt.
2. **An API route** under `app/api/projects/[id]/brand/` to read and write a project's brand kit. Auth via `requireUser()`, ownership scoped in the same query as the id — match the convention in `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts`.
3. **A UI** under `components/brand/` to set it.

## Hard requirements
- **An uploaded SVG is untrusted input and SVG is executable.** It can carry `<script>`, `onload=`, `<foreignObject>`, external `href`s and entity expansion. It will be inlined into a page served on `*.kodely.site`. **Sanitise it server-side** — allowlist elements and attributes, do not blocklist — and say exactly what you allow. Getting this wrong is stored XSS on a customer's own site. There is no sanitiser dependency available; hand-roll it and be conservative. If you are not confident, restrict to a very small element set and say so.
- **Colour must reach the model as exact hex values plus a catalogue preset id, never as adjectives.** "Warm and modern" produces exactly the generic look this feature exists to kill.
- **State the token cost** of whatever logo format you allow, with real arithmetic.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT: `lib/brand-kit.ts`, `app/api/projects/[id]/brand/**`, `components/brand/**`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, any other lib file, other app/api routes, app/projects/** (another agent is in there — if the editor needs an entry point, describe the exact line), app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.

## Constraints
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **No new white text on the brand gradient** (fails contrast — known accepted issue). Real labels, visible `focus-visible:` states, no keyboard traps.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components` must stay clean — currently ZERO errors and ZERO warnings.** Other agents are active in `lib/credits.ts`, `app/api/generate/route.ts`, `app/projects/[id]/**`, `app/api/site/**`; transient errors there are not yours.
- Verify with a real project you create and delete. **Test your SVG sanitiser against actual attack payloads** — script tags, event handlers, `javascript:` hrefs, `<foreignObject>`, nested entities — and report what each one did.

## Report back
Your sanitiser allowlist and the payloads you tested with results, the logo size cap and its token arithmetic, how colour reaches the model, what you need outside your scope, and anything you refused to build.

## Policy chosen: charge attempt 1 only; every repair pass is free

`settleBuild(model, attempts)` in `lib/credits.ts` bills `attempts[0]` — the customer's own request — and waives everything after it. Added as **rule 4** of the anti-bill-shock contract.

### Why this and not the alternatives

**"Charge the successful attempt"** is wrong in two ways. The repair pass re-reads a project attempt 1 just grew, so it can cost *more* than attempt 1 — you'd sometimes charge more for a repaired run than a clean one, which inverts the promise. And it bills the patch rather than the product: attempt 1 wrote the site, attempt 2 fixed a semicolon. Worse, it creates a real gaming gradient (big attempt 1 + tiny attempt 2 = near-free build), which is exactly the incentive we must not build.

**"Cap at what a clean attempt would have cost"** — the only honest value for that cap is attempt 1's metered cost, and since `total ≥ attempt1` always, `min(total, attempt1) ≡ attempt1`. It's this policy with extra steps. Any *other* cap is a constant, i.e. the "flat guess" rule 2 forbids.

**Attempt 1 is the right answer because its metered cost *is* "what a clean run of this request would have cost"** — a real measurement, not a cap, not a constant. It makes the charge for a repaired run arithmetically indistinguishable from a clean one. The promise, stated as arithmetic.

### Verified against the two existing rules
- **Failed build → zero**: both failure paths set `creditsCharged: 0` and never call `chargeForBuild`; the catch path leaves the ledger untouched. Unchanged, and re-proved.
- **Metered, not guessed**: the charge path is `usage` SSE events → `costMicros(model, usage)` → `creditsFor`. No constant anywhere in it. `estimateCredits` is display-only.

## Margin impact

Effective cost per *charged* credit becomes `$0.002 × (1 + r·k)`, where `r` = share of successful builds that repair and `k` = repair cost ÷ first-attempt cost. My measured fixture had `k ≈ 0.51` (the repair pass is a smaller diff but a bigger cache read).

| | starter ($0.018/cr) | pro ($0.015/cr, thinnest) |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | 88.9% | 86.7% |
| r=10%, k=0.5 | 88.3% | 86.0% |
| r=20%, k=0.5 | 87.8% | 85.3% |
| r=20%, k=1.0 | 86.7% | 84.0% |
| r=30%, k=1.0 | 85.6% | 82.7% |
| **r=100%, k=1.0 (hard floor)** | **77.8%** | **73.3%** |

The floor is real and cheap to state: `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS = 2` means at most **one** waived pass, so absorbed cost can never exceed 1× billed cost. Even if *every single build* needed a repair, gross margin bottoms out at ~73% on the worst pack. This is affordable by a wide margin.

I could not measure `r` — the local DB has only 2 successful builds, both `repairAttempts = 0`. `greenBuildRate` is the instrument; `1 − greenBuildRate` is `r`.

## Can it be gamed? No

1. **The free pass does no work the user chose.** The repair prompt is fixed and user-untouchable (`"The last change failed to build. Fix it and keep the rest of the change. Build error: …"`). Its only mandate is making attempt 1's output compile. It cannot add features.
2. **Inducing a repair gains nothing.** You'd pay attempt 1's cost — which you'd have paid anyway — and receive a compiling site, which is what a clean run gives you. Same price, same product.
3. **No downward gradient.** The charge is *invariant* to the repair's size. Proved: a repair pass 24× larger than the original still charged the identical 267 credits, and the run's charge is never below a clean run's.
4. **No loop to farm** — `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS` is unchanged at 2. One free pass per run, maximum.
5. Rate limit and the user's own spend cap still sit in front of everything.

## What I proved (38/38, real local Postgres, all rows deleted after)

Compiled the *real* `lib/credits.ts` + `lib/events.ts` to CJS and drove them against `kodely_personal`, creating and deleting a real User/Project/Build/CreditLedger set. Build count returned to 10.

```
  A clean    : cost $0.5340  charged 267 cr  repairs 0
  B repaired : cost $0.8040  charged 267 cr  repairs 1
  C failed   : cost $0.8040  charged   0 cr  repairs 1
  old policy would have charged B: 402 cr  (customer overcharged 50.6% / 135 cr ≈ $2.43 retail)
```

Read back **from Postgres**, asserted: B charged identically to A; B's `costMicros` records the whole run and exceeds A's; B's token columns are the full run; B is under-recovered by exactly the waived $0.2700 while A is fully recovered (rounding only, $0.0000); failed build charged zero with no ledger row; `repairAttempts` preserved 0/1/1; both charge rows still read `reason = "build"`; balance chain consistent; `averageBuildCredits` correct; `greenBuildRate` correctly counts B as not-first-try (3/4); the admin recovery query shows cost $2.1420 vs recovered $1.0680 — the absorbed repair is visible to an admin.

Also replayed the route's per-attempt accumulator with **two** `usage` events in attempt 1 (the SDK engine can emit more than one) to prove they land in one bucket rather than splitting across attempts. Plus edge cases: zero-telemetry run still charges 0, empty attempt list settles to 0/0, `billed + waived === costMicros`.

## Implementation

`app/api/generate/route.ts`: replaced the single `totals` accumulator with `attemptUsage: Usage[]` — a fresh bucket pushed per loop iteration. `totals` is now `sumUsage(attemptUsage)` at settle time and still populates the Build token columns unchanged.

**One addition beyond the brief, flagged deliberately:** both failure paths now record their token columns and `costMicros`. Rule 3 claims a failed build is *"recorded with its true cost and charged ZERO"* — the recording half was missing, so every failure showed `$0.0000` in `/admin`. Under rule 4 that matters more, not less: a run that burned two attempts and still failed is the single most expensive thing we absorb, and it was invisible. `creditsCharged: 0` is untouched. **Heads-up: `freeCostMicros` on `/admin/analytics` will jump once this ships** — that's the truth arriving, not a regression.

## Ledger encoding: deliberately unchanged

`describeReason` in `app/dashboard/billing/ledger.ts` is a closed allowlist that never echoes `reason` (it can carry a Stripe session id or an account hash). **Any** new string — `"build:repair_waived"` or otherwise — falls to its unknown branch and *downgrades* the statement row from "Site build" to a bare "Credits used". So the reason stays exactly `"build"`, and the reasoning is written into `chargeForBuild`'s docblock rather than only living here.

The statement doesn't need an encoding: it already joins `CreditLedger.build`, and `repairAttempts > 0 && costMicros > creditsCharged * MICROS_PER_CREDIT` *is* "repaired and absorbed".

## What the customer sees now, and the four UI changes needed

The `done` SSE event now carries `repairAttempts`, `repairWaived: boolean`, `waivedCredits: number`. `Editor.tsx` ignores unknown fields, so this is live and safe today but not yet rendered.

1. **`app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx`**, `done` handler ~line 261 (after `setBalance(event.remaining)`): when `event.repairWaived`, show e.g. *"The first attempt didn't compile. We fixed it and didn't charge you for the fix — 135 credits waived."*
2. **`app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx`** ~line 85: extend the existing join to `build: { select: { repairAttempts: true, costMicros: true, creditsCharged: true, project: {...} } }`, then render a second line on qualifying rows: *"Includes a repair we didn't charge for."*
3. **`app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx` lines 336–340 are now WRONG.** Currently: *"the whole run is charged once, together: the first attempt and the repair."* Replace with: *"If a build doesn't compile, Kodely repairs it and tries again — and the repair is free. You're charged for your original attempt only, the same as if it had compiled first time."*
4. **`app/legal/terms/page.tsx` lines 78–80** carry the same now-false claim, and it's the *disclosed term*. Replace with: *"If a build doesn't compile the first time, Kodely repairs it and tries again. The repair attempt is never charged: a run that succeeds after a repair costs the same as if it had compiled first time. We don't bill you for our own mistake."* (Shipping ahead of this text is safe — we'd be charging less than disclosed, never more.)

Also stale: the comments in `app/admin/page.tsx` (~72–79) and `app/admin/analytics/page.tsx` (~305–315) asserting the charged-minus-cost delta "can only ever return rounding noise". It's now genuinely negative. The "Given away" footnote filters on `creditsCharged = 0`, so it misses partially-waived builds — it wants `SUM(costMicros) − SUM(creditsCharged) × MICROS_PER_CREDIT` as an "absorbed" figure.

## Schema I'd want

- **`Build.billedMicros Int @default(0)`** — the billable attempt's metered spend. Today it's reconstructable only to within rounding from `creditsCharged × MICROS_PER_CREDIT`. With it, `/admin/analytics` could split absorbed cost into its three distinct causes, which currently collapse into one bucket: *repaired our own mistake* / *build failed* / *telemetry missing*. Highest value of the set.
- **`Build.attemptUsage Json?`** — per-attempt token breakdown. Makes any future policy change auditable retrospectively and lets support answer "why was I charged this" from the record rather than by inference.
- `Build.waivedMicros` is redundant if `billedMicros` exists (`costMicros − billedMicros`); one of the pair is enough.
- `CreditLedger.waivedCredits Int @default(0)` would let the statement render the saving without a join — but the billing page already joins `Build`, so I'd rank this last.</result>

content.text:
Card moved as the work landed — that's the discipline from here on.

## The fair-metering result is the best reasoning of the session

The policy is **charge attempt 1 only; every repair pass is free**. What makes it right is the rejection of the obvious alternative:

"Charge the *successful* attempt" sounds fairer and is wrong twice. The repair re-reads a project attempt 1 just grew, so it can cost **more** than attempt 1 — you'd sometimes charge more for a repaired run than a clean one, inverting the promise. And it creates a gaming gradient: a big first attempt plus a tiny repair becomes a near-free build.

"Cap at what a clean attempt would have cost" collapses into the same policy, since `total ≥ attempt1` always means `min(total, attempt1) ≡ attempt1`. Any *other* cap is the flat guess rule 2 forbids.

Attempt 1 is correct because its metered cost **is** what a clean run of that request would have cost — a measurement, not a constant.

Proven with 38 assertions: clean build 267 credits, repaired build **267 credits**, failed build 0 — while `costMicros` still records the whole run. Under the old behaviour that repaired build would have charged 402, a **50.6% overcharge**. And it can't be farmed: a repair pass 24× larger than the original still charged the identical amount.

The margin floor is bounded and cheap to state — `MAX_BUILD_ATTEMPTS = 2` means at most one waived pass, so even if *every* build needed repair, gross margin bottoms out around 73% on the thinnest pack.

## It caught that my own copy was now false

Both the billing page and the **terms page** stated the old policy: *"charged once, for the whole run including the repair attempt."* That's now wrong — in the customer's favour, but a disclosed term shouldn't be wrong in either direction. Both fixed.

I also renamed the `/admin` tile from "Meter rounding" to **"Meter recovery"** and made it amber when negative. My earlier comment claimed that delta "can only ever be rounding noise, bounded at $0.0019" — true when I wrote it, false now. A negative number there is the promise working.

It also found a gap in rule 3: failed builds recorded `creditsCharged: 0` but **no cost at all**, so every failure showed $0.0000 in admin. A run that burned two attempts and still failed is the most expensive thing absorbed, and it was invisible.

## Contact forms solved the CSP question without widening it

The generated page POSTs to `/__forms/<name>` on **its own origin** — which on the sites domain is already us, because `proxy.ts` rewrites that host into our route. `form-action 'self'` permits it as written. Neither copy of the CSP constant had to change by a character.

## How I solved schema drift

**`prisma migrate diff --from-schema-datasource prisma/schema.prisma --to-schema-datamodel prisma/schema.prisma --script`**, with an `information_schema` fallback.

- **No shadow database needed** — I verified this empirically. A shadow DB is only required when a migration *history* is replayed (`--from-migrations`/`--to-migrations`). Both endpoints here are direct, so nothing is replayed and nothing is created. It ran clean with no `--shadow-database-url` and no `CREATEDB` rights.
- **`--from-schema-datasource`, not `--from-url`** — this was the deciding detail. It reads `DATABASE_URL` out of the datasource block, so the connection string never enters `argv` and never lands in a process listing.
- It knows types, defaults, nullability, indexes and uniques — a name-only comparison silently passes a column that exists with the *wrong type*, which is exactly what a half-finished `db push` leaves behind.
- **Direction is classified, not just presence.** The SQL is parsed: `CREATE TABLE` / `ADD COLUMN` / `CREATE INDEX` = DB behind code = BLOCKER. `DROP …` = DB ahead = WARNING only (safe, and the expected shape after a code rollback, since the runbook forbids rolling schema back). An `ALTER COLUMN` whose direction can't be inferred is printed verbatim and counted as a blocker rather than guessed at.
- Fallback (`--no-prisma-diff`, or automatic when the CLI errors non-connectively) parses `schema.prisma` into tables/columns and compares to `information_schema`. It is coarser — no types — and **says so in its own summary line** rather than presenting a weaker answer as the same one.

I proved the classifier against a real Prisma-generated `--from-empty` script (the max-drift case): it correctly extracted all 17 tables including all 8 release models, and on a mixed script it separated `table Event`/`column User.spendCapCredits`/`index …` (missing) from `column Build.legacyField`/`table OldThing` (extra). The schema parser correctly excludes relation fields and finds `Build.repairAttempts`.

- `lib/agent.ts`, `lib/agent-sdk.ts`, `lib/build-site.ts`, `lib/enhance.ts` — model calls and real builds; that's `scripts/eval`.

Note that `lib/credits.ts` and `lib/flags.ts` *are* imported (they pull in `./db` transitively) — constructing a `PrismaClient` opens no connection, and no test issues a query.</result>

<result>Done. Both gates are clean (`npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components`: zero errors, zero warnings), and all test fixtures are deleted.

## The CSP change: there isn't one, and that's the finding

**Neither `SANDBOX_CSP` constant changed by a single character.** They are still byte-identical (verified). Only the comments around them changed, identically in intent, in both files.

The hint in the brief is the whole design. `form-action 'self'` resolves `'self'` to the **document's** origin — `https://<slug>.kodely.site` — not to ours. So posting to `https://kodely.me/api/forms/...` would be cross-origin and would have forced `form-action 'self' https://kodely.me` onto every customer site on the platform. That is unnecessary, because **`<slug>.kodely.site` is already us**: `proxy.ts` rewrites every request on that host into `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts`. A form whose action is `/__forms/contact` is a same-origin POST that lands in the same route handler that served the page. `form-action 'self'` permits it as written.

What an attacker gains from the change: **nothing new.** A generated page could already POST to its own origin; the only thing that changed is that one path on that origin now does something. The phishing shape the directive was added for — a generated page collecting what a visitor types and shipping it to an attacker's server — is exactly as impossible as before. `connect-src 'none'` is untouched, and is why the endpoint answers with HTML rather than JSON: a form POST is a navigation, not a scripted request.

One consequence I chose rather than papered over: the editor's **draft preview iframe is sandboxed without `allow-same-origin`**, so it sits in an opaque origin where `'self'` matches nothing and a form there is inert. Re-enabling it would mean naming an origin in the preview CSP — the app's own origin — and would mean draft submissions either landing in the owner's real inbox as fake enquiries or needing a second discard path. Forms are tested on the live site after publishing. Both comment blocks say so, and say the change belongs in both copies if it is ever revisited.

## Abuse controls

Three layers, cheapest first:
1. **In-process burst limiter**, 8 per 5 min per hashed IP, no DB query — sheds a flood before Postgres is touched. Bounded map that evicts expired-then-LRU, never `clear()` (a wholesale clear is a way for an attacker to reset the counter throttling them — the mistake `checkEnhanceRateLimit` and `app/api/contact` make on lower-value paths).
2. **Durable per-IP**: 15/hour, 50/day, counted from stored rows.
3. **Durable per-project**: 60/hour, 300/day. Refusal wording is identical to the per-IP one so a visitor is never told someone else filled the quota.

Plus: `Origin` must match a host allowed to serve that slug; only `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`; body capped at 32 KB read from the stream (Content-Length is only a fast pre-check, never trusted); 12 fields, 64-char keys matching `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}`, 5000-char values; over-cap is **refused, never truncated**. Honeypot `_gotcha` and an advisory `_t` timing token flag as `spam: true` — stored, not dropped (the schema comment asks for that), never emailed, and still consuming quota so flagging isn't a cheap way to write rows. `ipHash` is a salted SHA-256 with a stable salt; the raw IP comes from `cf-connecting-ip` only, never `x-forwarded-for` (that's finding M3 and this does not repeat it).

**What still gets through**, stated in a RESIDUALS block in the file: origin-IP access forges `cf-connecting-ip`; `Origin` is trivially forged by non-browsers; the burst limiter is per-process and resets on deploy; refused requests write nothing so they aren't counted by the durable limits and cost reads (only the burst limiter bounds that); the per-IP count has no dedicated index (schema is fixed) so it's a bounded range scan of `FormSubmission_createdAt_idx`; and nothing here classifies content.

## Markup contract for the SYSTEM prompt

```jsx
<form method="post" action="/__forms/contact">
  <label htmlFor="name">Your name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" type="text" required />

  <label htmlFor="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required />

  <label htmlFor="message">Message</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message" required />

  {/* Spam trap — must be present, must stay invisible and unlabelled to humans */}
  <p style={{ position: "absolute", left: "-9999px" }} aria-hidden="true">
    <input name="_gotcha" type="text" tabIndex={-1} autoComplete="off" />
  </p>
  {/* Optional timing signal */}
  <input type="hidden" name="_t" defaultValue={Date.now()} />

  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
```

Rules the builder must follow:
- **Action** is exactly `/__forms/<formName>`, root-relative. `<formName>` is `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,31}` — `contact`, `quote`, `booking`, `newsletter`. One per form on the site.
- **`method="post"`**, default encoding. No `enctype` (multipart is refused, no file uploads). No `onSubmit`, no `fetch` — `connect-src 'none'` blocks it and the native navigation is the mechanism.
- **Field names**: `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}`. Max 12; empty ones are dropped. Max 5000 chars each, 32 KB total.
- A field named **`email`** holding a valid address becomes the notification's `Reply-To`. Name it `email` or the owner cannot reply.
- **`_`-prefixed names are reserved** and never stored: `_gotcha` (honeypot, required), `_t` (optional timing token), `_next` (optional same-site path to land on, e.g. `/thanks`).
- The default reply is a plain Kodely thank-you page with a link back. Use `_next` for a custom one.
- **Only on a published site.** A draft, and the editor preview, will not submit.

## Delivery

Email goes to the project owner resolved from the DB (never an address from the request), via `sendMail`, fired after the write and never awaited. Plain text is the real message; the HTML alternative is built from the same values and escapes every one. Submitted content reaches exactly one header — `Reply-To` — and only through a strict address regex that admits no CR, LF, comma, semicolon, angle bracket or quote; a value that fails is simply not used. Skipped for spam-flagged rows and past 10 submissions/hour per project, so a form flood never becomes an inbox flood.

Owner UI at `/projects/[id]/submissions` (server component + `SubmissionList.tsx`), with inbox/filtered tabs, mark read/unread and spam/not-spam via `PATCH /api/forms/[projectId]`. Values render as React children only — no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` anywhere, and both files say so in comments.

**Editor.tsx needs a link to it** — I could not touch that file. Suggested: a "Submissions" link next to Publish, ideally with the unread count (`FormSubmission where projectId, readAt: null, spam: false`). Until then the page is reachable only from the notification email or by URL.

## What I proved

Against a real published project (created and since deleted) on a live dev server: **35/36 + 10/10 + 17/17 + 3/3** automated checks.

- A submission from `<slug>.kodely.site` lands; fields stored verbatim (`<script>` intact as text); `ipHash` is a hash, not the address.
- Unpublished project → 404, nothing stored. Unknown slug → identical 404. `kodely.me/api/site/<slug>/__forms/contact` → 404.
- Foreign/missing Origin → 403. JSON → 415. 40 KB body → 413. 6000-char field → 413. 20 fields → 400. Empty → 400.
- Honeypot → 200, stored, `spam: true`, honeypot value not stored, no email. Instant fill flagged; 30s fill not.
- `_next=/thanks` → 303; `//attacker.example` and `https://attacker.example` ignored (no open redirect). Path-form base resolves to `/api/site/<slug>/`.
- Burst limit: statuses `200×8, 429, 429`, and the refused requests stored **0** rows. Durable per-IP and per-project limits both trip when seeded.
- Against a real SMTP sink: exactly one message, to the owner from the DB, envelope sender ours, `Reply-To: ada@example.com`. **Header injection attempt** (`attacker@example.com\r\nBcc: victim@example.com`) → **no `Bcc` header, no `Reply-To` at all, one envelope recipient**; the attempt survives only as body text. Good progress — down to 4 failures now: the American flag search picking the wrong asset, an overly strict AND condition making "coffee shop" return nothing, and two cases where "generic"/"bland" wording is being misclassified as visual feedback when it should be content feedback. I'm looking at fixing the classification logic so those words route correctly.

The generic/bland/boring adjectives shouldn't be tied to visual alone since "generic copy" is content while "generic design" is visual — I'm working out whether to strip those words from the visual pattern entirely and instead let context (presence of a content noun like copy/wording/text vs a visual noun) decide the classification, or to check content signals ahead of visual ones just for these ambiguous cases without breaking things like "make the colors warmer" which should stay visual.

I'll move `generic|bland|boring` out of the visual pattern and add a separate vague-complaint rule checked after content, mapping vague looks-complaints back to visual. Testing this against phrases like "the copy is generic" (content), "this looks really generic" (visual), and "make the colors warmer" (visual) confirms it resolves the ordering issue correctly.

Switching to the asset search tie-break problem for "american flag" — the cleanest fix is boosting the sovereign country's score directly in the demonym scoring logic rather than restructuring the whole ranking.

Given the low practical impact, I'll deprioritize the demonym tie-break and focus on fixing the coffee shop search returning nothing, which is the more serious bug. For the tie-break, a reasonable general heuristic is to prefer the entry with the shorter name string, which correctly resolves France vs French Guiana and United Kingdom vs British Indian Ocean Territory, even if it's not perfect for United States vs American Samoa.

For the coffee shop issue, the AND-matching requires every token to score against an entry, but "shop" doesn't correspond to anything in the icon catalog, causing valid matches to be dropped entirely. A better fix is to detect tokens that match nothing across the whole catalogue and treat them as non-discriminating, effectively ignoring them during scoring rather than letting them zero out otherwise-good matches.

I realize the intent was preference, not a hard requirement, but my implementation enforced it strictly. I should fix it by scoring matched tokens with a bonus instead of dropping entries missing some tokens, just ranking them lower — matching "prefers" rather than requiring all.

Given limited context left, I'll be efficient and tackle three fixes together: the feedback-intent scoring, the asset AND-ness matching the docstring, and the tie-break sort by matched count then total, then implement them carefully.

content.text:
The test suite paid for itself on its first run. **209 tests, zero failures, exit 0** — and every bug it found is fixed.

## Six real bugs, two of them mine

**The worst was in code I wrote.** In a JavaScript string replacement, `$` is a substitution sigil — `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$1` all expand — and `escapeHtml` doesn't escape `$`. So a project called "Everything $1 Store" silently lost the `$1`, and a value containing `` $` `` **spliced the entire preceding document into a meta attribute**. I reproduced it before fixing:

```
replace with $`  ->  <head><title>X<head>Y</title></head>
```

`applySeo` runs on every read of every published site, so that was live on the serving path. It was in `lib/site-seo.ts` *and* in the SEO route I'd written an hour earlier. Fixed with replacer functions in both.

**My entity fix was incomplete.** I decoded before escaping for `description` and missed `og:title` — the tag link previews read *first*. "Bloom & Co" was still reaching share cards as "Bloom & Co".

**Four more prototype-chain guards.** I'd fixed two occurrences and assumed that was the class. It wasn't — `lib/flags.ts`, `app/admin/health`, `app/admin/users`, `app/admin/content` all still used `in`. The flags one was the serious one: that guard is the only thing stopping `setFlag` — a Server Action, a public endpoint — from writing a junk key.

**And the demonym fix I was pleased with only worked by luck.** "french flag" → France and "british flag" → UK passed because the alphabetical tie-break happened to run the right way (`flag:fr` < `flag:gf`). For the US it runs the wrong way, so "american flag" returned American Samoa. Now tie-broken on the shorter canonical name.

Plus: `findAssets("coffee shop")` — the docstring's own example — returned **nothing**, because multi-token search was a hard AND when the doc says "prefers". And "the copy is generic" bucketed as *visual*, despite being the module header's headline example of a *content* complaint.

## Contact forms shipped without touching the CSP

The agent found that `form-action 'self'` resolves to the **document's** origin — `<slug>.kodely.site` — which `proxy.ts` already rewrites into our own route handler. So a form posting to `/__forms/contact` is same-origin and permitted as written. Neither CSP constant changed by a character, and an attacker gains nothing new.

Its header-injection test is the one I'd want: `attacker@example.com\r\nBcc: victim@example.com` produced **no Bcc, no Reply-To at all, one envelope recipient** — the attempt survived only as body text.

Build green, lint zero, 41 cards in Done. Two agents still running.

content.text:
Brand kit is in and wired. **42 cards in Done**, 209 tests passing, build green.

## The sanitiser is the substance, and it's well built

SVG is executable and gets inlined onto a customer's live site — get this wrong and it's stored XSS. Two structural properties do the real work, and both are better than an allowlist alone:

**Everything is re-serialised** from the sanitiser's own writer, so nothing from the input reaches the output as bytes. A parser differential can mangle a logo; it can't invent an element.

**Every `id` is renumbered** to `bk1..bkN` with references repointed, which makes an off-document reference structurally impossible and kills page-wide id collisions as a side effect.

It **refuses** rather than silently strips, on the grounds that a silent strip hides an attack — and the payload table covers the ones that matter: `<script>` in three spellings, `<foreignObject>`, external `use href`, entity-obfuscated `javascript:`, billion laughs, XXE, CDATA, and `<set attributeName="href">` retargeting. Real Illustrator, Figma and Inkscape exports all still work.

Its own tests caught a bug: the id renumberer was treating bare `#` on **paint** attributes as a dangling reference and silently deleting `stop-color="#F72570"`.

## The token arithmetic is why the caps exist

A logo lives in a source file, so `describeFiles()` re-sends it every turn, and only SYSTEM is cache-controlled. A naive 200 KB PNG works out at **~88,900 tokens ≈ $1.07 per four-turn build** — more than the rest of the build. Rejected. SVG is capped at 12,288 sanitised chars (~$0.046/build), and real logos land at 213–322 chars.

I wired it into the generate route myself — prepended to the **first** request only, since the repair loop is about a compile error, not the brand.

## Also wired

`/wizard` had nothing linking to it. Added the side-door line under the composer — deliberately a quiet link *below* rather than a button *beside*, because the plan is explicit that the raw box stays the default and the wizard is never a gate.

I've messaged the click-to-edit agent with the two remaining mounts it's the only one able to make (brand panel, submissions link), and told it plainly that if click-to-edit isn't achievable in scope, an honest partial beats a convincing stub.

## What I verified about the sandbox (measured, not assumed)

I could not use the Browser pane — it silently refuses to load any iframe carrying a `sandbox` attribute without `allow-same-origin`, so nothing renders there. I instead drove real headless Chrome (CDP over Node's built-in WebSocket) against servers reproducing the preview's exact sandbox + CSP.

**Parent → iframe:** `contentDocument` is `null`; `contentWindow.location` and `.document` both throw `SecurityError`. `contentWindow.postMessage(msg, "*")` **does** get through. Targeting an exact origin is silently dropped; `targetOrigin: "null"` throws `SyntaxError`. So `"*"` is mandatory.

**Iframe → parent:** works. `event.origin` arrives as the literal string `"null"` — worthless for auth. `event.source === iframe.contentWindow` is the only real check, and even that only proves *the frame* sent it, not *our agent*.

**Three findings that changed the design:**
1. Built `index.html` references `/assets/index-*.js` absolutely. `GET /assets/…` on the app origin is a **404** (published sites work only because `proxy.ts` rewrites the sites domain; there is no equivalent for the editor).
2. **Every subresource request from inside the opaque-origin frame is `sec-fetch-site: cross-site` and carries no cookie.** A cookie-authenticated `/api/preview/[id]/assets/…` therefore 401s. There is no header-only fix.
3. Vite emits `<script type="module" crossorigin>`; module scripts are always CORS-mode, so they additionally need `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. Stripping `crossorigin` does not help (verified).

**Any one of those makes the preview blank. The in-editor preview has never rendered anything** — no CSS, no JS, just `<div id="root">`. That is a pre-existing bug, not something I introduced.

## Mechanism

The parent (where cookies work) fetches `index.html` + assets, **inlines** them into one self-contained document, injects the selection agent, and hands it to the iframe via `srcdoc`. Zero subresources means zero cross-site requests. The `sandbox` attribute is **byte-identical** — still `allow-scripts allow-forms`, still opaque origin, `contentDocument` still `null` (re-checked on the live frame at the end of the run). No out-of-scope file was needed.

Because a `srcdoc` document has no response headers, the policy travels in-band as `<meta http-equiv>`, first child of `<head>`. It is **stricter** than the header it replaces (`default-src 'none'`, everything inlined). Verified: an external `<script src>` is blocked and never requested, and `fetch()` rejects.

## What works end to end

Against a real generated site (Copperleaf Tea Room, real 204KB bundle), with a real CDP mouse click:

```
Change the <h1> element reading "A quiet room, a warm pot, and time to slow down."
in section 2 of 5 ("A quiet room, a warm pot, and time to slow down."),
at section#top > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > h1:
```

Click-select, hover outline, in-frame arrow keys (parent/child/sibling), Escape to exit, parent-driven move buttons, clear, and the prompt pre-fill all verified working. **The preview now actually renders** as a side effect.

Two defects the E2E run caught and I fixed: in-frame keys never reached the agent (the pick cancels the click, so focus never entered — added an agent-owned focus sink, no `tabindex` on generated elements); and containers reported run-together `textContent` ("Since 2014A quiet room") as if it were their own text — now own-text vs. subtree is distinguished, and the reference says *"a container whose contents begin…"* rather than *"reading"*, using source-faithful casing so the string is greppable.

**Not built:** direct text editing without a generation. Editing text means editing JSX and rebuilding — a server round trip with no endpoint in scope. Every change still goes through a normal build, and the UI copy says exactly that.

## Files

New: `app/projects/[id]/preview-agent.ts`, `app/projects/[id]/SelectionPanel.tsx`. Modified: `PreviewFrame.tsx`, `Editor.tsx`, `page.tsx`.

## Judgment call for review

Feeding the iframe `srcdoc` instead of `src` is a real change to how the preview is served, made entirely inside my scope. It is what makes the feature possible *and* fixes the blank preview. Trade-off: the preview document can no longer load any external resource at all — previously it couldn't either, so nothing regresses, but a future generated site wanting a non-`data:` image would need `img-src` widened.

Also worth flagging: generated content can forge a `selected` message. Bounded by `normalizeSelection` (validates and clamps every field), text-only rendering, and never auto-submitting — worst case is editable text appearing in the prompt box.

## Coordinator's two additions

Both done. `BrandKitPanel` mounted as a fifth "Brand" view with `onSaved={refreshFiles}`. Submissions link added next to Publish **with** a live unread count — `page.tsx` is inside my scope, so I added a `db.formSubmission.count` using the same `readAt: null, spam: false` filter the submissions page uses, no fragile plumbing. Both also added to the command palette so it doesn't go stale.

Untouched and intact: progress narration, building overlay, thumbs-up/down, zip download, Enhance/Revert, low-credit warning, Stop/cancel, device-frame preview, ⌘K palette (window-level Escape net preserved), connection-loss recovery, cost estimate, SEO panel. No new white-on-gradient text; `focus-visible:` rings on every new control; selection is fully keyboard-operable from the editor's own tab order, not just inside the frame.

**Gates:** `npx tsc --noEmit` clean, `npx eslint app lib components` **0 errors 0 warnings**, tests **209/209 pass**. Both `/projects/[id]` and `/projects/[id]/submissions` compile and 307 to login on the dev server.

## Recommended follow-up (outside my scope)

`app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts` carries a comment claiming `form-action 'self'` is effectively `'none'` because `'self'` matches nothing in an opaque origin. I measured the opposite: `'self'` resolves to the serving origin and the policy works as written. Worth correcting so nobody relies on the wrong model.</result>

content.text:
All agents are done. **43 cards in Done**, 209 tests passing, build green, lint at zero.

## The biggest finding: your editor preview has never worked

While building click-to-edit, the agent discovered the in-editor preview **has never rendered anything** — no CSS, no JS, just an empty `<div id="root">`, for every project, the whole time.

Three independent causes, any one of which blanks it:

1. Built `index.html` references `/assets/index-*.js` absolutely, and `GET /assets/…` on the app origin is a 404. Published sites work only because `proxy.ts` rewrites the sites domain; the editor has no equivalent.
2. Every subresource from an opaque-origin sandboxed frame is `sec-fetch-site: cross-site` and carries **no cookie**, so a cookie-authenticated asset route 401s. No header-only fix exists.
3. Vite emits `<script type="module" crossorigin>`, and module scripts are always CORS-mode, so they need `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` on top. Stripping `crossorigin` doesn't help — verified.

Fixed by inlining everything in the parent (where cookies work) and handing the frame one self-contained `srcdoc`. The sandbox attribute is byte-identical; `allow-same-origin` was never added.

**This means every visual check anyone did in the editor before now was of a blank page.** I've carded it as needing your eyes after deploy — it was verified against one real 204KB bundle, and sites with unusual asset shapes haven't been tried.

## A disagreement I recorded rather than resolved

Two agents measured the CSP `'self'` behaviour in an opaque origin and got **opposite results**. One concluded it matches nothing; the other, driving real headless Chrome over CDP, measured it resolving to the serving origin.

They may have been testing different setups — the preview is now `srcdoc` rather than `src`, which changes how the origin is established. Rather than pick a winner, I've marked that comment **DISPUTED** with both measurements and a note that nobody has re-run the original case. The practical impact is nil either way, but a confident-sounding mechanism that might be wrong is worse than an honest unknown.

## Where things stand

Every agent I launched has reported. The tree is green on all four gates: TypeScript, lint, 209 tests, production build.

The blocking sequence hasn't changed, and the first item is the one the preflight tool caught: **nothing is committed.** 124 changed files, `HEAD` still at `4ff10e8`, including `prisma/schema.prisma`. Then `prisma db push` on staging and prod, then the code, then the ungated blog corrections — with the dentist/chiropractor fix going first, since it doesn't depend on the export deploy.

input.description: Multi-page generated sites
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

TASK: make generated sites support multiple pages. This is the single largest capability gap after the backend, and it blocks a whole category of demand.

## Why it matters
Generated sites are single-page apps. `lib/agent.ts`'s SYSTEM prompt says so explicitly: *"Multi-page: this is a single-page app. Build distinct sections/routes as components conditionally rendered or scrolled to, not separate .html files."*

That one line blocks: "build a blog with AI", "add an About page", every service-page SEO strategy, internal linking, and multi-page site structure guides. A content audit found live blog posts already claiming *"a multi-page app with working navigation"* — which is false today.

## The constraints that shape the answer
Read all of these before proposing anything:
- `lib/foundation.ts` — the starting project. **Only `react` and `react-dom`.** No router package, and no way to add one: `lib/build-site.ts` symlinks ONE shared pre-installed dependency tree and never runs `npm install` per generation.
- `lib/build-site.ts` — `vite build`, 60s timeout, output read back as a flat file map.
- `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` — how a published site is served, including what happens for a path that is not a real file. **This is the crux: a client-side router needs unknown paths to serve index.html, and a hash router does not.**
- `lib/site-seo.ts` — `sitemapXml()` currently assumes one page.
- `proxy.ts` — the `<slug>.kodely.site` rewrite.

## Decide the mechanism, and argue it
Real options, each with a genuine cost:
- **Hash routing** (`#/about`) — needs no server change at all, works today, but the URLs are ugly and historically weaker for SEO. Verify rather than assume the current SEO position.
- **Path routing with a server fallback** — real URLs, needs the site route to serve `index.html` for unknown paths, and needs care that it does not mask genuine 404s or shadow `robots.txt`/`sitemap.xml`/`/__forms/*`.
- **Genuinely separate HTML entry points** — multiple Vite inputs. Best for SEO (each page is a real document with its own `<head>`), but it changes the build config, and `vite.config.ts` is on the protected-paths list precisely because the agent must not write it.
- A hand-rolled router in the foundation, since no package can be added.

Pick one, implement it, and state what you gave up. **SEO is the reason multi-page is wanted at all**, so weigh that heavily — a mechanism that produces one crawlable document defeats the purpose.

## Deliver
1. The foundation change in `lib/foundation.ts` — routing primitive, nav, and a shape the builder can follow.
2. Whatever `app/api/site/[slug]/**` needs, if your mechanism needs it. **Do not break** the existing `siteHostAllowed` host check, the form endpoint, `robots.txt` or `sitemap.xml`.
3. `sitemapXml()` emitting one entry per page, if your mechanism makes pages discoverable. `lib/site-seo.ts` is editable for this.
4. **The exact replacement text for the SYSTEM prompt paragraph.** `lib/agent.ts` is NOT yours to edit — write the new wording in your report and I will apply it.

## Scope — ONLY: `lib/foundation.ts`, `lib/site-seo.ts`, `app/api/site/[slug]/**`
DO NOT modify: lib/agent.ts, lib/build-site.ts, prisma/schema.prisma, other lib files, other app/api routes, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.

## Constraints
- **No new npm dependencies, and none for generated sites either** — that is the hard architectural constraint, not a preference.
- Every page must still work under the sandbox CSP: no external requests, inline SVG/CSS/data: only.
- Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint app lib components`, and `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` must ALL pass — currently 0/0/209.** `tests/site-seo.test.mjs` covers `sitemapXml`; update it if you change that function's contract, and say so.
- **Prove it compiles.** Build a real multi-page site through `buildSite` from `lib/build-site.ts` and confirm the output. `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` must be set — it is in `.env`; load it, or the foundation path falls back to a Linux default and every build fails with a misleading "Cannot find module".

## Report back
The mechanism and what you gave up, the SEO consequence with evidence rather than assumption, the exact SYSTEM prompt replacement text, proof it compiles, and anything that still cannot be done.

input.description: Editor diff view and undo
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: two Builder/Editor features. Bundled because both touch `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` and parallel edits there would collide.

## 1. Diff view — see what changed before and after a build
Today a build rewrites files and the user sees only the preview. There is no way to know *what* changed. `Build.filesSnapshot` already stores the complete file tree after every successful build (see `prisma/schema.prisma`), and `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/[buildId]/restore/route.ts` already restores from it — so the data for a diff exists and nothing reads it that way.

Build a per-build diff: which files changed, added, removed, and a readable line-level diff for each. **No diff library** — hand-roll a simple LCS or line-based diff; the files are small.

The board card is "Diff view with approve / reject before applying". Read it and be honest in your report about whether approve/reject is achievable: the build has already written to the database by the time the user sees anything, so "reject" means restoring the previous snapshot, not preventing a write. If that is what you build, say that is what it is — do not present a restore as a pre-apply gate.

## 2. Undo / redo across AI and manual edits
`Build.filesSnapshot` gives you a checkpoint per successful build, and History already lists them. What is missing is a cheap one-step undo — "that last change was wrong, put it back" — without opening History and picking.

Note `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/route.ts` now filters to builds whose snapshot still exists (the retention job clears old ones), so an undo target can legitimately disappear. Handle that honestly rather than showing a control that fails.

## Scope — ONLY files under `app/projects/[id]/`
READ anything. If you need an API route outside that directory, describe it precisely in your report rather than creating it.

## Do not regress — this file is dense now
Read `Editor.tsx` in full first. It carries: live progress narration, building overlay, thumbs-up/down, zip download, Enhance/Revert, low-credit warning, Stop/cancel, device-frame preview, ⌘K command palette, connection-loss recovery, a cost estimate, an SEO panel, a Brand panel, a Submissions link with unread count, and click-to-edit selection. **All of it must keep working.**

Traps already hit in this exact file:

Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: a build and prompt log inspector for the admin panel — the tool for answering "why did this generation go wrong".

## Why
`/admin` shows the last 50 builds in a table and `/admin/users/[id]` shows one customer's history, but neither lets you actually investigate a build: read the prompt in full, see the error, see which files it wrote, compare a failed run against a successful one. When a customer says "it built the wrong thing", there is nothing to look at.

## Read first
- `prisma/schema.prisma` → `Build` carries `prompt`, `error`, `model`, `status`, all four token columns, `costMicros`, `creditsCharged`, `repairAttempts`, and `filesSnapshot` (the complete file tree after a successful build).
- `app/admin/health/errors.ts` — an error-family classifier already exists. **Reuse it**; do not write a second one.
- `app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx` — query patterns and the visual idiom. `app/admin/users/ui.tsx` has shared primitives.
- `lib/auth.ts` → `getAdminUser()`. `lib/admin-audit.ts` → the recording contract.
- `lib/events.ts` — `build.rated` events carry a rating and reason per build.

## Build
1. **A build list** — filterable by status, model, error family, and whether it needed a repair. Searchable by prompt text. Paginated. **No N+1** — read how `app/admin/users/page.tsx` solves this.
2. **A build detail page** — the full prompt, the assistant's reply if stored, the error with its classified family, token counts and cost, repair attempts, which files the snapshot contains, and any rating the customer left. Link to the project and the owner.
3. **Comparison is the point.** Make it easy to see a failed build next to the project's last successful one. That is the actual debugging move.

## This is the most privacy-sensitive admin surface yet
Prompts are customer content, and `filesSnapshot` is their generated source.
- **Audit-log every read.** `lib/admin-audit.ts` has a closed vocabulary; `build.viewed` and `build_list.viewed` do NOT exist in it and you may NOT edit that file. Use the closest existing names if any genuinely fit, or state in your report exactly which names should be added and where. Do not invent a name by string literal.
- **Never dump `filesSnapshot` content.** List paths and sizes; do not render file bodies. That is the customer's source code and there is no operational reason to read it here.
- Truncate prompts in list views; full text only on the detail page.
- Never put prompt text or a search query into `meta` on an audit row — the rule is stated at the top of `lib/admin-audit.ts` and searching here means searching customer prompts.

## Scope — ONLY: `app/admin/builds/**`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, anything under lib/, app/api/**, other app/admin/** subtrees, app/projects/**, app/globals.css, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.

## Constraints
- `getAdminUser()` at the top of every page, `notFound()` if null — the layout gates the section but must not be the sole boundary.
- **Guards on query params must use `Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`, never the `in` operator.** `in` walks the prototype chain; `?status=constructor` has produced reachable 500s in three separate files in this codebase already.
- Match the admin idiom: `rounded-xl border border-black/10 dark:border-white/10`, `text-sm`, `tabular-nums`, monochrome. No new white-on-brand-gradient text.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint app lib components`, and `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` must ALL pass — currently 0 errors, 0 warnings, 209 tests.**
- Local Postgres has ~10 builds, 8 of them failed on SDK auth. Build a real low-data state and say so.

## Report back
What you built, which audit action names you need added and why, how you avoided N+1, what you deliberately do not display, and what you verified against the real database.

input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

TASK: extend the data-retention job to cover the tables that have appeared since it was written, and close a gap the privacy policy currently has to admit.

## Read first
`lib/retention.ts` and `docs/retention.md`. The existing job has four rules, a `--dry-run` default, batched deletes, and a `NEVER_PRUNED` list. **Match its design exactly** — same structure, same discipline of naming a reader before pruning anything, same honesty about what it gives up.

## The tables it does not yet cover
Every one of these was added after that job was written, and several accumulate on hot paths:

- **`FormSubmission`** — public, unauthenticated writes from published sites. The agent that built it explicitly flagged that a retention rule is needed and that the policy judgement was not theirs to make. Note `spam: true` rows are kept deliberately so a false positive is recoverable and the rate is measurable — decide whether they should age out faster than real ones, and justify it.
- **`AdminAuditLog`** — an accountability record. **Think hard before pruning this at all.** A short retention on an audit log defeats its purpose; too long and it is a growing store of who-looked-at-whose-account. One measurement to weigh: a short browsing session generated 144 rows, because `site.viewed` records every render.
- **`ModerationFinding`** — evidence about abuse. Reviewed and unreviewed rows are not the same thing.
- **`EmailLog`** — the idempotency guard for transactional email. **Pruning this can cause a DUPLICATE SEND.** Read how `dedupeKey` works before touching it, and if the safe retention is "never", say so.
- **`LoginAttempt`** — already self-prunes inside `lib/rate-limit.ts`; the author argued deliberately that it does not belong in `retention.ts`. **Read that reasoning and either agree or rebut it** — do not silently duplicate the pruning, which would be worse than either choice.
- **`Event`** — already has a rule at 400 days. Re-check whether it still holds now that ratings and follow-up intents are stored there.

## Method — the part that matters
For each table: **find who reads it before you propose pruning it.** The existing job refused to prune `Build` rows and `Build.prompt` on exactly that basis, and it was right. Grep for the readers, name them in a comment, and where a reader would be affected say so rather than quietly accepting the loss.

Where the honest answer is "never prune this", say that and put it in `NEVER_PRUNED` with the reasoning.

## Also update `docs/retention.md`
It is the document the privacy policy quotes. `app/legal/privacy/page.tsx` currently has to say some data is retained indefinitely — your rules are what let that become a real commitment, so the doc must state each period plainly enough to quote.

## Scope — ONLY: `lib/retention.ts`, `scripts/retention.mjs`, `docs/retention.md`
DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, any other lib file, app/**, .env, package.json, other docs.

## Constraints
- **`--dry-run` stays the default.** Deleting requires `--apply`. Never weaken that.
- **Do not prune `CreditLedger`.** It is an auditable financial record, it is what stops reward-credit farming across account deletions, and it carries the Stripe payment record.
- Deletes must stay batched and bounded.
- Test in dry-run against the local database. If you want to prove a delete path, create your own throwaway rows and remove them. **Do not `--apply` against data you did not create** — note that command has been blocked by the permission system before, so plan around needing dry-run plus seeded fixtures.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint app lib components`, and `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` must ALL pass — currently 0 errors, 0 warnings, 209 tests.**

## Report back
Each table with its proposed period and the reader you checked, anything you refused to prune and why, your verdict on the `LoginAttempt` question, the `EmailLog` duplicate-send risk, and dry-run counts against the real database.

content.text:
Five agents launched on the remaining actionable work.

| Agent | Scope |
|---|---|
| Site import (wizard step 3) | SSRF-defended fetching of the user's current site and a reference site |
| Multi-page sites | The single largest remaining capability gap |
| Editor diff view + undo | Reads `Build.filesSnapshot`, which nothing currently uses that way |
| Admin build inspector | The "why did this generation go wrong" tool |
| Retention for new tables | Eight tables have appeared since that job was written |

Three of these carry constraints where the wrong answer is worse than no answer, so I stated them explicitly:

**Site import is an SSRF problem, not a fetching problem.** It's pulling arbitrary user-supplied URLs from a server inside a private network holding real credentials. I required DNS resolution with a check on the *resolved IP* rather than the hostname, manual redirect following with every hop re-validated, and an explanation of how it closes the TOCTOU re-bind hole — checking DNS and then letting the HTTP client resolve again is a real bypass. If it can't close any one of those, it ships without that path.

**Multi-page has no free option.** No router package can be added — `build-site.ts` symlinks one shared dependency tree and never installs per generation. Hash routing needs no server change but weakens the SEO that's the entire reason multi-page is wanted; path routing needs the site route to serve `index.html` for unknown paths without masking real 404s or shadowing `robots.txt` and `/__forms/*`. It has to pick and say what it gave up.

**Retention's hardest call is what *not* to prune.** `EmailLog` is the idempotency guard for transactional email — pruning it can cause a duplicate send. `AdminAuditLog` is an accountability record where short retention defeats the purpose and long retention becomes a growing store of who-looked-at-whose-account. And `LoginAttempt`'s author argued deliberately that it does *not* belong in the retention job; I asked this agent to read that reasoning and either agree or rebut it, because silently duplicating the pruning would be worse than either choice.

The board discipline holds — I'll move each card as its agent reports.

Direct answer: **no, and deliberately not.** Nothing has been scraped, and I wouldn't without asking you first.

The 461 assets are all hand-authored geometry or arithmetically derived — the agent that built them reported the provenance explicitly: no path data copied from any icon library, free or licensed. Two reasons scraping would be the wrong move here:

**Licensing.** Scraped images have owners. These get inlined into *customers'* commercial websites, so an unlicensed asset transfers a legal problem to them — the kind of thing that surfaces months later as a demand letter to a barber shop.

**Architecture makes it moot for photography anyway.** The CSP blocks every external host, so an image has to be inlined as base64 and passes through the model's context as tokens. input.description: Kodely Pro foundation spike
input.prompt:
Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Next.js 16 + Prisma, an AI website builder called Kodely).

BUILD: one real proof-of-concept foundation for "Kodely Pro" — the tier that generates full applications rather than marketing sites.

## Read the plan first
The board is SQLite at `C:\Users\edmem\OneDrive\Desktop\Kodely\Kodely Board\board.sqlite` (`node:sqlite`, `DatabaseSync`, **READ ONLY — never write to it**). Board id `720aa8c1-d259-4e49-b777-c58965efabd1`, column `Kodely Pro — Full Apps`, 41 cards. **Read the DECISION cards first** — the research concluded that the blocker is architectural, not a prompting problem, and those cards carry the options and a recommendation.

## The thesis you are testing
The owner's idea is that pre-built foundations for app types (CRM, booking, inventory) make generation both **easier and credit-cheaper**, because the model writes less. **That is a measurable claim and this task is the measurement.**

## The constraint that decides the shape
Read `lib/foundation.ts`, `lib/build-site.ts`, `app/api/site/[slug]/**` (the CSP), and `lib/agent.ts`. Generated sites are static, `react` + `react-dom` only, no npm install per generation, `connect-src 'none'` — **no server, no database, no auth, no network.**

So a shared, multi-user CRM is not reachable. A **single-user, client-only** app absolutely is: `localStorage` or IndexedDB gives real persistence on one device with no backend at all. That is a genuine product for a sole trader tracking clients or bookings, and it is honest about what it is.

**Build the client-only version.** Do not pretend it is multi-user, and make the foundation itself say so.

## Deliver
1. **`lib/foundations/` — one complete, working app foundation.** Pick the strongest candidate from the board (a simple CRM/client tracker or a booking/appointment log) and build it properly: data model, persistence layer, list/detail/create/edit, empty states, and the same quality bar `lib/agent.ts` demands of generated sites (responsive to 380px, dark mode, real focus states, no external requests).
2. **Prove it compiles** through `buildSite` from `lib/build-site.ts`. Load `.env` first — `KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR` must be set or the path falls back to a Linux default and every build fails with a misleading "Cannot find module".
3. **MEASURE THE CREDIT CLAIM.** Count the tokens in the foundation versus what the model would have to write without it. You do not need to run a real generation to do this usefully — compare file sizes and reason about what `describeFiles()` re-sends per turn versus what the model would otherwise author. **Show the arithmetic.** If the foundation turns out to make builds *more* expensive (it is re-sent on every turn as context), say so plainly — that would be the most valuable finding here and it is a real possibility.
4. **A short `docs/pro-foundations.md`**: what this foundation is, what it honestly cannot do, and what the next 3-4 would be.

## Scope — ONLY: `lib/foundations/**` and `docs/pro-foundations.md`
DO NOT modify: lib/foundation.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/build-site.ts, prisma/schema.prisma, any other lib file, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json. If wiring it in needs a change elsewhere, describe it precisely in your report.

## Constraints
- **No new npm dependencies**, for the foundation or the repo. That is the architectural constraint, not a preference.
- Data lives on the device. Say so in the UI — a user must never believe their client list is backed up when it is one browser-cache clear from gone. That honesty is the whole difference between this being a product and being a trap.
- No new npm dependencies. Do NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`.
- **HARD GATE: `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npx eslint app lib components`, and `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` must ALL pass — currently 0 errors, 0 warnings, 209 tests.**

## Report back
Which foundation you built and why that one, proof it compiles, **the credit arithmetic with your actual numbers and an honest verdict on whether the thesis holds**, what it cannot do, and what would have to change architecturally for a genuinely multi-user app.

content.text:
Seven agents running. On your question about assets, one thing worth flagging as a decision rather than leaving implicit:

## Photography is a strategic dead end, not a backlog item

The SEO audit found this independently: **photographer, wedding, real-estate, hotel, salon and interior-design verticals are all unservable**, and the photographers article already live on kodely.me tells readers to add their own photos after launch — a step the product cannot perform, before or after any deploy. That agent recommended rewrite-or-unpublish rather than a patch.

That's not fixable by growing the asset library. It needs one of:

- **Image upload with Kodely-hosted delivery** — a CSP change (`img-src` widened to our own host), storage, and a delivery path. Unblocks every one of those verticals at once.
- **AI image generation** — already carded, but it's per-call cost on the build path and needs its own credit line item.
- **Accept the boundary** and stop selling to those verticals, which means correcting several live pages.

I'd put image upload well above more icons in value — the asset library is genuinely good now, and the thing blocking those customers isn't a shortage of vector art.

## Running

| Agent | Testing |
|---|---|
| Site import | SSRF defences — DNS re-bind, redirect chains, metadata addresses |
| Multi-page sites | Whether any mechanism gives crawlable pages without a router package |
| Editor diff + undo | Whether "approve/reject" is honest when the write already happened |
| Admin build inspector | The debugging tool for "why did this generation go wrong" |
| Retention | What must **never** be pruned — `EmailLog` pruning causes duplicate sends |
| Illustrations | Hand-authored only, provenance stated |
| Kodely Pro spike | **Whether the credit-saving thesis actually holds** |

That last one is the one I'd watch. Your idea was that foundations make Pro builds cheaper because the model writes less — but a foundation is re-sent as context on every turn, so it could plausibly make builds *more* expensive. I've told the agent that if the arithmetic comes out that way, saying so is the most valuable result it can produce.

Board is at 43 done, 79 comments, tree green.

1	// SEO for PUBLISHED sites (served by app/api/site/[slug]/...).
2	//
3	// Why any of this exists at serve time rather than purely in generation:
4	// the builder prompt is told to fill in index.html's <head>, but a prompt is
5	// guidance, not a guarantee. Everything here is a backstop that runs on the
6	// way out, so a site can never be published with the foundation's placeholder
7	// title — which is exactly what shipped before (every site was "Kodely Site",
8	// in the browser tab, in Google, and in every link preview).
9	//
10	// It also fixes ALREADY-published sites with no regeneration, because it
11	// rewrites on read rather than at build time.
12	
13	const SITES_BASE = process.env.KODELY_SITES_BASE ?? "kodely.site";
14	
15	// The foundation's placeholder. If this survives to serve time the agent
16	// didn't personalise the head, so we substitute the real project name.
17	const PLACEHOLDER_TITLE = "Kodely Site";
18	
19	/**
20	 * Public base URL of a published site, as a visitor sees it.
21	 *
22	 * Two shapes, because the proxy rewrites the branded subdomain onto an
23	 * internal path:
24	 *   <slug>.kodely.site/         -> internally /api/site/<slug>
25	 *   staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>/   (no wildcard DNS off prod)
26	 *
27	 * Canonical/OG URLs must use the EXTERNAL form or they point somewhere the
28	 * visitor's browser never went, so this keys off the Host header.
29	 */
30	export function siteBaseUrl(req: Request, slug: string): string {
31	  const host = req.headers.get("host") ?? "";
32	  const bare = host.split(":")[0];
33	
34	  // Deliberately NOT derived from x-forwarded-proto. Cloudflare's SSL mode
35	  // here is Flexible: it terminates TLS at the edge and talks to the origin
36	  // over plain HTTP, so nginx forwards `x-forwarded-proto: http` even though
37	  // the visitor is on https. Trusting it emitted http:// canonical and og:url
38	  // on sites that are only reachable over https.
39	  //
40	  // That was invisible in testing because Cloudflare's Automatic HTTPS
41	  // Rewrites silently repairs href="http://..." (canonical) but NOT
42	  // content="http://..." (og:url) — so only the OG tag stayed wrong, and
43	  // only when checked through the real edge.
44	  //
45	  // Every published site is reachable only via the Cloudflare HTTPS edge, so
46	  // anything that isn't loopback is https by definition.
47	  const isLocal = bare === "localhost" || bare === "127.0.0.1" || bare === "::1";
48	  const proto = isLocal ? "http" : "https";
49	  // Branded subdomain: the site lives at the host root.
50	  if (bare.endsWith(`.${SITES_BASE}`)) return `${proto}://${host}`;
51	  // Otherwise it is served under a path (staging, localhost).
52	  return `${proto}://${host}/api/site/${slug}`;
53	}
54	
55	/**
56	 * The public URL of ONE built HTML file — the single definition of a page's
57	 * address.
58	 *
59	 * Sites are multi-page now (see lib/foundation.ts): `vite build` emits one real
60	 * document per page, and the site route serves `about.html` for a request to
61	 * `/about`. Three things have to agree on what a page's address IS — its
62	 * <link rel="canonical">, its og:url, and its <loc> in sitemap.xml — and they
63	 * agree by all coming from here. A sitemap advertising /about while the page at
64	 * /about canonicalises elsewhere is a self-cancelling instruction: Google drops
65	 * the URL rather than guessing which half to believe.
66	 *
67	 * Extensionless is the canonical form, so /about and /about.html — the route
68	 * answers both — collapse onto one indexable URL instead of competing as two.
69	 */
70	export function pageUrl(baseUrl: string, htmlPath: string): string {
71	  return baseUrl.replace(/\/$/, "") + pagePath(htmlPath);
72	}
73	
74	/** "index.html" -> "", "about.html" -> "/about", "blog/index.html" -> "/blog". */
75	function pagePath(htmlPath: string): string {
76	  const stripped = htmlPath
77	    .replace(/^\/+/, "")
78	    .replace(/\.html?$/i, "")
79	    // A directory index IS the directory: blog/index.html is /blog, and a bare
80	    // index at the root is the site root itself.
81	    .replace(/(^|\/)index$/i, "$1")
82	    .replace(/\/+$/, "");
83	  return stripped ? `/${stripped}` : "";
84	}
85	
86	function escapeHtml(s: string): string {
87	  return s
88	    .replace(/&/g, "&")
89	    .replace(/</g, "<")
90	    .replace(/>/g, ">")
91	    .replace(/"/g, """);
92	}
93	
94	function escapeXml(s: string): string {
95	  return escapeHtml(s).replace(/'/g, "'");
96	}
97	
98	/**
99	 * Undo the entity encoding in text pulled back OUT of the HTML.
100	 *
101	 * The title is read from inside <title>…</title>, where it is already encoded —
102	 * a site called "Bloom & Co" is stored as "Bloom & Co". Composing the
103	 * fallback description from that string and then escaping it again produced
104	 * "Bloom &amp; Co", and the literal entity showed up in every link preview.
105	 * Decoding first, then escaping once, is the round trip that holds.
106	 *
107	 * Only the five entities escapeHtml/escapeXml can produce. A general HTML
108	 * entity decoder is not wanted here: this exists purely to invert our own
109	 * escaping, and anything else the builder wrote should pass through untouched.
110	 */
111	function decodeHtml(s: string): string {
112	  return s
113	    .replace(/</g, "<")
114	    .replace(/>/g, ">")
115	    .replace(/"/g, '"')
116	    .replace(/'/g, "'")
117	    // Ampersand LAST, so "&lt;" decodes to "<" rather than "<".
118	    .replace(/&/g, "&");
119	}
120	
121	/** Absolutise a root-relative URL against the site's public base. */

# Pexels API Guidelines & Terms of Use

## Attribution Requirements

**Required:** You must display prominent attribution to Pexels and photographers.

- "Whenever you are doing an API request make sure to show a **prominent link to Pexels**."
- Credit photographers when possible: "Photo by [Name] on Pexels" with a link to the photo page.

## Rate Limits

Default: "200 requests per hour and 20,000 requests per month." Higher limits available upon request with demonstrated proper attribution.

Violation warning: "Abuse of the Pexels API, including attempting to work around the rate limit, will lead to termination of your API access."

## Prohibited Uses

You "may not copy or replicate core functionality of Pexels (including making Pexels content available as a wallpaper app)."

## Response Headers

Rate limit status is provided via response headers (`X-Ratelimit-Limit`, `X-Ratelimit-Remaining`, `X-Ratelimit-Reset`) on successful requests.

**Note:** The documentation doesn't explicitly address local caching, hotlinking, or image storage policies beyond the general requirement for attribution and prohibition against replicating Pexels' core functionality.

content.text:
That changes my answer, and I overstated something earlier. Let me correct it.

## I was wrong that photography is architecturally impossible

I said "impossible, not un-built." That's true only for **inlining base64**. Pexels routes around the thing I was actually objecting to: if the model references an image by ID or URL instead of embedding it, the token cost collapses from ~88,900 tokens to a handful. My main technical objection doesn't apply.

And it isn't scraping — it's a licensed API. The Pexels License is genuinely permissive: commercial use allowed, modification allowed, **attribution not required**, and it explicitly covers the case we need.

## But the API terms are stricter than the license, and that's the catch

The license says attribution isn't required. **The API guidelines say it is:**

> "Whenever you are doing an API request make sure to show a **prominent link to Pexels**."

So using their API to find images means putting *our supplier's branding on a customer's business website*. A barber shop's site would carry a "Photos from Pexels" link. That's a real product decision, not a technical one.

Three other constraints that shape any design:

- **200 requests/hour, 20,000/month.** If we search once per generation, that's a hard ceiling of 200 builds/hour across the whole platform.
- **"You may not copy or replicate core functionality of Pexels."** A browsable photo picker inside Kodely edges toward that. Photos *embedded in generated sites* clearly don't.
- **CSP.** `img-src 'self' data:` still blocks pexels.com. The clean fix is proxying through our own origin — which satisfies `'self'` without widening anything, and avoids leaking visitor IPs to a third party. But a proxy that permanently stores images sits less comfortably with "prominent link to Pexels" than hotlinking does.

## The decision is yours
