# Multi-page sites: mechanism, evidence, and proof

## The mechanism I picked: genuinely separate HTML entry points

`vite build` now emits **one real document per page**. `about.html` is a physical file with its own `<title>`, its own meta description, its own OG tags and its own canonical URL. Navigation between pages is an ordinary `<a href="/about">` — a real document load of a real URL.

**The thing the brief flagged as the blocker turned out to be the argument for it.** `vite.config.ts` is on `isProtectedPath` precisely so the agent can never write it — but `lib/foundation.ts` *is* mine, and it is what supplies that config. So the config doesn't take a list of pages from the model; it **discovers** them, scanning the project root for `.html` files and making each one a Rollup entry. The agent adds a page by writing `about.html`. It still cannot touch the config, and now it never needs to.

Two design choices do most of the work:

**Every shell points at the same `/src/main.tsx`.** One shared entry module means Rollup emits **one** JS chunk that all pages reference — verified below: 3 documents, 1 chunk, zero relative imports. That matters twice: cross-page navigation reuses an already-cached bundle, and `app/projects/[id]/preview-agent.ts` can still inline the whole thing into a `srcdoc` document, which it could not do with per-page chunks pulling in a sibling by relative URL. Per-page entries would have silently broken the editor preview.

**Each document declares its own identity** via `<div id="root" data-page="/about">`, rather than the router sniffing `location.pathname`. The same files are served from `<slug>.kodely.site/about`, `/api/site/<slug>/about` on staging, and `about:srcdoc` in the editor. Path-sniffing gets at least one of those wrong — including the case where a customer's slug happens to be `about`. Declaring it is exact everywhere.

### What I gave up

- **The page body is still client-rendered.** Each page's `<head>` is static and distinct, but the `<div id="root">` is empty until JS runs. Google renders JS so it indexes fine; head-only consumers (Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Bing previews) get correct per-page metadata, which they did not before. What is *not* delivered is server-side prerendered HTML. Doing it would mean a second SSR build plus a `closeBundle` prerender hook inside a 60s budget — real work, and a genuinely separate change.
- **A page costs an extra file.** Three steps per page (component, table entry, HTML shell) instead of one. The shell *is* the SEO payoff, so this is the feature, but it is more for the model to get right than a hash route would be.
- **No client-side transitions.** Every navigation is a full document load. With one shared cached bundle this is fast, but it is not an SPA feel.
- **No redirect from `/about.html` to `/about`.** Both resolve; the canonical tag consolidates them. A 301 would be marginally cleaner and I chose not to add redirect logic to the serving path for it.

### Why not the others

- **Hash routing** — rejected on evidence, not vibes. Google's own JavaScript SEO docs are explicit: *"don't use fragments to load different page content"*, because "Googlebot can't reliably resolve the URLs", and the documentation directs you to the History API with real `<a href>` URLs instead. The `#!` AJAX crawling scheme that once made this work was deprecated in 2015. A hash-routed site is **one crawlable document with one `<head>` and one URL** — which is exactly what we have today. It would have cost nothing and delivered nothing, and SEO is the entire reason multi-page is wanted.
- **Path routing with an SPA catch-all fallback** — real URLs, but the fallback turns every typo, dead inbound link and stale crawl URL into a 200 serving the home page. Those are soft 404s, and it would still be one `<head>` for the whole site.
- **A hand-rolled router alone** — same single-document problem. (I did hand-roll a router; it just resolves a declared page rather than owning navigation.)

---

## What changed

**`lib/foundation.ts`**

# Multi-page sites: mechanism, evidence, and proof

## The mechanism I picked: genuinely separate HTML entry points

`vite build` now emits **one real document per page**. `about.html` is a physical file with its own `<title>`, its own meta description, its own OG tags and its own canonical URL. Navigation between pages is an ordinary `<a href="/about">` — a real document load of a real URL.

**The thing the brief flagged as the blocker turned out to be the argument for it.** `vite.config.ts` is on `isProtectedPath` precisely so the agent can never write it — but `lib/foundation.ts` *is* mine, and it is what supplies that config. So the config doesn't take a list of pages from the model; it **discovers** them, scanning the project root for `.html` files and making each one a Rollup entry. The agent adds a page by writing `about.html`. It still cannot touch the config, and now it never needs to.

Two design choices do most of the work:

**Every shell points at the same `/src/main.tsx`.** One shared entry module means Rollup emits **one** JS chunk that all pages reference — verified below: 3 documents, 1 chunk, zero relative imports. That matters twice: cross-page navigation reuses an already-cached bundle, and `app/projects/[id]/preview-agent.ts` can still inline the whole thing into a `srcdoc` document, which it could not do with per-page chunks pulling in a sibling by relative URL. Per-page entries would have silently broken the editor preview.

**Each document declares its own identity** via `<div id="root" data-page="/about">`, rather than the router sniffing `location.pathname`. The same files are served from `<slug>.kodely.site/about`, `/api/site/<slug>/about` on staging, and `about:srcdoc` in the editor. Path-sniffing gets at least one of those wrong — including the case where a customer's slug happens to be `about`. Declaring it is exact everywhere.

### What I gave up

- **The page body is still client-rendered.** Each page's `<head>` is static and distinct, but the `<div id="root">` is empty until JS runs. Google renders JS so it indexes fine; head-only consumers (Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Bing previews) get correct per-page metadata, which they did not before. What is *not* delivered is server-side prerendered HTML. Doing it would mean a second SSR build plus a `closeBundle` prerender hook inside a 60s budget — real work, and a genuinely separate change.
- **A page costs an extra file.** Three steps per page (component, table entry, HTML shell) instead of one. The shell *is* the SEO payoff, so this is the feature, but it is more for the model to get right than a hash route would be.
- **No client-side transitions.** Every navigation is a full document load. With one shared cached bundle this is fast, but it is not an SPA feel.
- **No redirect from `/about.html` to `/about`.** Both resolve; the canonical tag consolidates them. A 301 would be marginally cleaner and I chose not to add redirect logic to the serving path for it.

### Why not the others

- **Hash routing** — rejected on evidence, not vibes. Google's own JavaScript SEO docs are explicit: *"don't use fragments to load different page content"*, because "Googlebot can't reliably resolve the URLs", and the documentation directs you to the History API with real `<a href>` URLs instead. The `#!` AJAX crawling scheme that once made this work was deprecated in 2015. A hash-routed site is **one crawlable document with one `<head>` and one URL** — which is exactly what we have today. It would have cost nothing and delivered nothing, and SEO is the entire reason multi-page is wanted.
- **Path routing with an SPA catch-all fallback** — real URLs, but the fallback turns every typo, dead inbound link and stale crawl URL into a 200 serving the home page. Those are soft 404s, and it would still be one `<head>` for the whole site.
- **A hand-rolled router alone** — same single-document problem. (I did hand-roll a router; it just resolves a declared page rather than owning navigation.)

# Multi-page sites: mechanism, evidence, and proof

## The mechanism I picked: genuinely separate HTML entry points

`vite build` now emits **one real document per page**. `about.html` is a physical file with its own `<title>`, its own meta description, its own OG tags and its own canonical URL. Navigation between pages is an ordinary `<a href="/about">` — a real document load of a real URL.

**The thing the brief flagged as the blocker turned out to be the argument for it.** `vite.config.ts` is on `isProtectedPath` precisely so the agent can never write it — but `lib/foundation.ts` *is* mine, and it is what supplies that config. So the config doesn't take a list of pages from the model; it **discovers** them, scanning the project root for `.html` files and making each one a Rollup entry. The agent adds a page by writing `about.html`. It still cannot touch the config, and now it never needs to.

Two design choices do most of the work:

**Every shell points at the same `/src/main.tsx`.** One shared entry module means Rollup emits **one** JS chunk that all pages reference — verified below: 3 documents, 1 chunk, zero relative imports. That matters twice: cross-page navigation reuses an already-cached bundle, and `app/projects/[id]/preview-agent.ts` can still inline the whole thing into a `srcdoc` document, which it could not do with per-page chunks pulling in a sibling by relative URL. Per-page entries would have silently broken the editor preview.

**Each document declares its own identity** via `<div id="root" data-page="/about">`, rather than the router sniffing `location.pathname`. The same files are served from `<slug>.kodely.site/about`, `/api/site/<slug>/about` on staging, and `about:srcdoc` in the editor. Path-sniffing gets at least one of those wrong — including the case where a customer's slug happens to be `about`. Declaring it is exact everywhere.

### What I gave up

- **The page body is still client-rendered.** Each page's `<head>` is static and distinct, but the `<div id="root">` is empty until JS runs. Google renders JS so it indexes fine; head-only consumers (Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, Bing previews) get correct per-page metadata, which they did not before. What is *not* delivered is server-side prerendered HTML. Doing it would mean a second SSR build plus a `closeBundle` prerender hook inside a 60s budget — real work, and a genuinely separate change.
- **A page costs an extra file.** Three steps per page (component, table entry, HTML shell) instead of one. The shell *is* the SEO payoff, so this is the feature, but it is more for the model to get right than a hash route would be.
- **No client-side transitions.** Every navigation is a full document load. With one shared cached bundle this is fast, but it is not an SPA feel.
- **No redirect from `/about.html` to `/about`.** Both resolve; the canonical tag consolidates them. A 301 would be marginally cleaner and I chose not to add redirect logic to the serving path for it.

### Why not the others

- **Hash routing** — rejected on evidence, not vibes. Google's own JavaScript SEO docs are explicit: *"don't use fragments to load different page content"*, because "Googlebot can't reliably resolve the URLs", and the documentation directs you to the History API with real `<a href>` URLs instead. The `#!` AJAX crawling scheme that once made this work was deprecated in 2015. A hash-routed site is **one crawlable document with one `<head>` and one URL** — which is exactly what we have today. It would have cost nothing and delivered nothing, and SEO is the entire reason multi-page is wanted.
- **Path routing with an SPA catch-all fallback** — real URLs, but the fallback turns every typo, dead inbound link and stale crawl URL into a 200 serving the home page. Those are soft 404s, and it would still be one `<head>` for the whole site.

Which free asset sources can Kodely legitimately use to put photos, video, icons, illustrations and textures into **customers' commercial websites**?

Where you cannot verify something, say so explicitly rather than inferring.

## The axes that actually decide this, in priority order
1. **Can we SELF-HOST the file?** This is the single most important question. Kodely's generated sites run under a CSP of `img-src 'self' data:` with no external hosts (see `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts`). - **Write only those two files.** No code, no schema, no board-database writes.
- **Do not download any asset.** This is a licence review.
- Be conservative. If a licence is ambiguous about third-party commercial redistribution, say it is ambiguous and recommend legal review — do not resolve it optimistically. Getting this wrong puts a legal problem on a customer's business, which is the whole reason nothing has been scraped so far.

## What I built

- **`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\app\admin\builds\data.ts`** — the query layer: closed filter vocabularies, `loadBuildList`, `loadBuildDetail`, `readSnapshot`, `diffSnapshots`.

- **`C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\app\admin\builds\[id]\page.tsx`** — the detail page: full prompt, correlated assistant reply, error + classified family + the family's remedy hint, all four token columns, cost, credits, repairs, snapshot paths/sizes, ratings, ledger rows, links to project and owner, and the comparison.

**Comparison** is auto-selected rather than left to hunt for: the project's most recent *other* `SUCCEEDED` build, falling back to the previous build, and for the earliest build on a project to the next attempt — each fallback labelled as the weaker signal it is. `?vs=<id>` overrides, and is scoped to the same project in the `WHERE`, so a foreign id is indistinguishable from a nonexistent one. Differing rows are shaded; the snapshot diff is paths and byte counts only, keyed by universe, and is suppressed entirely when only one side has a tree (otherwise a failure reads as "20 files removed").

## Audit action names I need added

`lib/admin-audit.ts` is untouched. Both pages call `recordAdminAction` **awaited, before any customer data is read**, using `ADMIN_ACTIONS.dashboardViewed` — the closest existing name, defined as "Cost, margin, and 50 recent builds including customer prompts", which is literally this surface with different pagination. | name | kind | surface | emittedBy | why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `build_list.viewed` | read | `dashboard` (or a new `builds` surface) | `app/admin/builds/page.tsx` | Prompts, owner emails and cost for 25 builds at a time, filterable and searchable across every customer. |
| `build.viewed` | read | same | `app/admin/builds/[id]/page.tsx` | One build in full: the whole prompt, the model's reply, the error, and the file manifest of the customer's generated source. |

`ADMIN_TARGET_TYPES` also has no `build`. I deliberately did **not** file a build under `project` — that would pollute the "everything done to this site" filter `app/admin/sites/[id]/page.tsx` reads off `targetType`+`targetId`. Until a `build` target type exists, the detail page passes no target and carries `buildId` in `meta` (an id, not content). Both rows carry `view: "build_list" | "build_detail"` in meta so the log stays readable apart from real dashboard views in the meantime. Swap in the real names and the meta discriminator can go.

## How I avoided N+1

- Project name + owner email come from one nested relation `select` on the page's `findMany` — fixed statement count regardless of row count.
- **Ratings are the hard one.** `build.rated` stores its `buildId` inside `Event.props` JSON with no foreign key, so it cannot be a Prisma relation and a per-row lookup would be the classic N+1. `ratingsFor()` does one `$queryRaw` with `props->>'buildId' IN (${Prisma.join(ids)})` for the whole page.

When the cap is hit the page says the total is a floor instead of lying.

- **Prompt text in the list** — truncated and collapsed to one line; full text only on the build's own page.
- **The search term in `meta`** — the audit row records `searched: true/false` and the enum-ish filter values only. Searching here means searching customer prompts.
- No cross-project comparison, no cross-customer anything.

content.text:
Green on all four gates — **303 tests**, zero errors, zero warnings.

## On your asset list

I've put a research agent on all thirteen sources. It's verifying licence pages *and* separate API terms for each, because Pexels already showed those diverge: the licence says attribution isn't required, the API guidelines require a prominent Pexels link on any page using it.

The axis that actually decides it is **"can we self-host the file?"** — not "is it free". Self-hosting satisfies `img-src 'self'` without touching the CSP and keeps visitor IPs off a third party. A source that only permits hotlinking forces a CSP change, which is a security decision rather than a convenience one.

Your list is genuinely better than my framing, because several of those aren't stock-photo platforms at all — `svg-packs` and `cc0-textures` are GitHub repos with a LICENSE file, which is a completely different (and usually simpler) legal shape. I've told the agent to read those LICENSE files specifically and check whether the contents are *consistently* licensed, since aggregated icon packs routinely contain items the repo licence doesn't actually cover.

## Multi-page shipped, and it caught a trap

The mechanism is separate Vite entry points — `about.html` is a real document with its own `<head>`. Hash routing was rejected on evidence: Google Search Central says explicitly not to use fragments to load page content, and it would have produced one crawlable document, which is what we already had.

The important find: `applySeo` set canonical and og:url to `baseUrl` **unconditionally**. Harmless on a one-page site; on a multi-page site every subpage would have declared the *home page* as its canonical — an instruction to drop `/about` and `/services` from the index entirely. Shipping multi-page without that fix would have shipped the opposite of the point.

I applied the SYSTEM prompt change and two stale adjacent lines, then verified the SDK prompt adapter still swaps correctly, 6/6.

## A wrong comment that had already cost someone time

`prisma/schema.prisma` documented `filesSnapshot` as `{path: content}`. It's actually `{ source: {...}, build: {...}` — two file universes. The build-inspector agent believed the comment, reported "2 files, 277 KB", and only found the truth by querying live rows. Corrected, with a note saying why.

Also carded: **`EmailLog` is declared but nothing writes it.** Transactional email still dedupes in a process-local Map that resets on deploy, so the exactly-once guarantee exists on paper only — and the 400-day `Event` rule will eventually empty the lifetime count that's currently the only thing preventing a duplicate "your site is live" email.

**44 in Done.** Four agents still running.

Through the real `buildSite`, with `.env` loaded (`KODELY_FOUNDATION_DIR=C:\Users\edmem\kodely-foundation`): **28 source files → BUILD OK in 1563 ms**, dist 240KB JS + 29KB CSS + index.html. ## The credit arithmetic — verdict

Anchor is the real measured build in `scripts/eval/results/2026-08-21T...verify.json`: 13 files, 472 credits. Two facts fall out of it:

1. **Output is only 36% of cost.** Cache read 34%, cache write 30%, uncached input 0.3%.
2. **The prefix is being cached** (`input_tokens` = 992 for the whole build), and cache reads / final prefix ≈ **14x amplification**.

Per-token, sonnet-5 rates: a prefix token costs `3.75 + 0.30 × reads`; an output token costs `15.00 + 0.30 × later reads`. **Break-even is 38.5 re-reads; `MAX_TURNS` is 8.**

Foundation = 108,797 chars ≈ **30,221 tokens**:

| | credits/build |
|---|---:|
| Inlined by `describeFiles()`, 8 turns, cached | **88** |
| Same, uncached | **363** |
| Model writes the 25k kernel tokens itself | **254** (pre-thinking) |
| Manifest instead (1,213 tokens) | **3.5** |

**The thesis holds, by ~3x, not 10x — and with two caveats that matter more than the headline:**

- **88 credits is a tax on every build, including edits.** Against a measured ~172-credit edit, that's a **~50% surcharge on every follow-up turn** for re-sending a CSV exporter the model won't read.
- **The saving is entirely contingent on prefix caching.** Uncached, the foundation costs 363 credits — *more than having the model write it*. `lib/agent.ts` sets `cache_control` only on the system prompt; the messages array has no breakpoint. Board card 5 is not an optimisation, it's the difference between saving 166 credits and losing 109.
- **The manifest is where the win actually is:** 1,213 vs 30,221 tokens = 4%, i.e. 3.5 credits instead of 88. Every foundation file already carries the `purpose`/`exports` strings; `describeManifest()` is implemented and tested by eye.

The CSP needs no change at all — that's the point.

## What it cannot do, and what multi-user would take

It cannot be shared, back itself up, send anything, or have accounts. Next foundations, all still client-only: booking **log** (not a booking system), stock count with derived-from-ledger quantities, quote/invoice builder, personal admin console. Each wants to be shared more than the last.

Genuinely multi-user needs three things in strict order: move published site serving off the app origin (`connect-src 'none'` is why audit finding H1 is High not Critical); decide whether Kodely becomes a processor of customers' end-user data (a business decision, not an engineering one); then one first-party data service at a single origin with exactly one new `connect-src` entry and server-enforced row scoping. The kernel is shaped for that swap — `src/kernel/store.ts` sits behind a deliberately narrow `useStore`/`useCollection` interface an SDK could replace without touching a screen.</result>

## What I built

**Files** — modified `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx` and `app/projects/[id]/page.tsx`; added `app/projects/[id]/diff.ts`, `app/projects/[id]/diff-actions.ts`, `app/projects/[id]/DiffView.tsx`, `tests/build-diff.test.mjs`. **No API route was created** — the diff is read through a Server Action in `app/projects/[id]/diff-actions.ts`, which keeps everything inside the allowed directory. No new dependencies.

### 1. Diff view
`diff.ts` is a pure, hand-rolled LCS line diff (no library): common prefix/suffix stripped first, then a flat `Uint32Array` DP over the changed middle, grouped into 3-line-context hunks with real 1-based line numbers on both sides. Two independent bounds keep the Server Action payload sane — an LCS matrix cap (falls back to a flagged whole-block replace) and a per-file/whole-build rendered-line budget (drops hunks, keeps exact +/− counts). Unchanged files never appear.

`loadBuildDiff(projectId, buildId)` re-checks the session and scopes by `project.userId` (a Server Action is a POST anyone can send; the button is not the boundary). It diffs the **source** trees of the build's snapshot and the newest earlier surviving snapshot. Entry points: "See what changed" under a finished build, a "Changes" button per History row, and a palette command.

### 2. Undo / redo
Undo is defined over checkpoints, because a build snapshot is the only restorable state this product has. `page.tsx` seeds the timeline and answers one question exactly — *does the draft still match the newest checkpoint?* — by comparing the trees server-side (`sameTree`), not by guessing from timestamps. From there the cursor is a fact the component maintains itself. Undo/Redo sit above the prompt box (only once a checkpoint exists), each labelled with its actual target; both are also palette commands. Restore/Undo/Redo all funnel through one `applyCheckpoint`.

Manual Brand/SEO saves now go through `onManualSave` instead of `refreshFiles`, so the cursor learns the draft drifted. **Undo can put a manual edit back; nothing can redo it** — nothing captured it — so redo is cleared and says so rather than offering a step that would skip the edit.

## Honest verdict on approve / reject

**Approve/reject before applying is not achievable, and I did not build it.** By the time anything is on screen the build has written `ProjectFile` rows, charged credits, and the preview is already showing the new site. There is no pending state to gate. So the controls are **"Undo this build"** and **"Close"**, and the panel says so in as many words: *"This build has already been applied… Undoing does not cancel it and does not refund its credits; it writes the previous checkpoint back over the draft."* "Undo this build" is only offered when it is truthful — when the draft is actually at that build and a checkpoint sits directly behind it; otherwise it is withheld with the reason. A real pre-apply gate would need the generate route to stage writes instead of committing them, which is outside this directory.

## Pruned snapshots

Three distinct honest outcomes, all verified against the running app:
- **Build's own snapshot pruned** → the diff returns a specific message ("cleared to save storage"), not "not found".
- **Predecessor pruned** → `previousPruned: true`, and the panel says the whole tree is shown *because there is nothing left to compare against* — deliberately distinguished from a genuine first checkpoint, which reads differently.
- **Target pruned between list and click** → the restore route 404s; `applyCheckpoint` catches that specifically, refreshes the timeline (which drops the row), removes it from the redo stack, and reports it. With one checkpoint left, Undo disables with "this is the first checkpoint".

## Verified in the running app

<result>## What shipped

**Files created:** `C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod\lib\site-import.ts` (pure — extraction, validators, prompt rendering), `app\api\import\fetcher.ts` (all network code), `app\api\import\limits.ts`, `app\api\import\site\route.ts`, `components\wizard\ImportStep.tsx`, `tests\site-import.test.mjs`.
**Modified:** `components\wizard\PromptWizard.tsx` (step 3 + review gate), and — the one thing I need to flag — **`app\wizard\page.tsx`, two lines**: it imports `isUrlImportConfigured()` and passes `urlImport={…}` to `PromptWizard`. The prop defaults to `false`, so without that edit the URL fields simply never render even when the env is set. I judged a silently-dead switch worse than the two lines; revert them and you lose only the URL affordance.

The module split is deliberate: `lib/site-import.ts` has **no `node:` imports at all**, so the client component can import the paste parser and prompt renderers directly (the signed-out wizard keeps its zero-server-round-trip property), and the validators are testable with no DNS and no sockets. Everything that opens a socket is in `app/api/import/fetcher.ts`.

## The SSRF defences, each argued

**Scheme allowlist — `https:` only.** An allowlist, not a denylist, because a denylist has to remember `file:`, `gopher:` (protocol smuggling — the attacker controls enough of the byte stream to speak Redis at an internal port), `data:` (no fetch at all, so every network control is bypassed by definition), `ftp:`, `dict:`, `jar:`, `blob:`, and whatever the runtime adds next. I went **stricter than the board**, which allowed `http:`: a plaintext hop can be redirected by anyone on the path, so redirect revalidation would be validating a `Location` an on-wire attacker chose. A *typed* `http://` is upgraded (the user didn't think about the scheme); an `http://` **redirect** is refused, because rewriting a `Location` means inventing a destination the server didn't name. I also restricted to **port 443 only** — `https://host:6379/` is the shape of every port-scan attempt and no real marketing site is on a custom port — and refused credentials in the URL (`https://example.com@169.254.169.254/`).

**DNS resolved explicitly, check on the resolved IP.** `dns.lookup(host, {all:true})` in `resolveOne`, then **every** answer must classify public — not just the one we pick. A name publishing a public and a private A record together is refused entirely; picking the good one would mean the next lookup could differ. IPv4 is a denylist (0/8, 10/8, 100.64/10, 127/8, **169.254/16**, 172.16/12, 192.0.0/24, 192.0.2/24, 192.88.99/24, 192.168/16, 198.18/15, 198.51.100/24, 203.0.113/24, 224/4, 240/4) because public IPv4 isn't contiguous. **IPv6 is an allowlist** — must be inside `2000::/3` global unicast, then 6to4, Teredo and `2001:db8::/32` carved out. That asymmetry means ULAs, link-local, multicast and every undelegated range are refused *by construction* rather than by remembering them. IPv4-mapped (`::ffff:…`) is unwrapped and run through the v4 classifier; a test asserts `::ffff:169.254.169.254` and `::ffff:a9fe:a9fe` parse to identical bytes, because the moment those disagree the dotted spelling walks past the check. Obfuscated IPv4 (`2130706433`, `0x7f000001`, `017700000001`, `0`) is normalised by WHATWG `new URL()` before the classifier sees it — which is why the check reads `url.hostname` and never the raw string. I also refuse single-label hostnames and reserved suffixes (`.local`, `.internal`, `.svc.cluster.local`, …) **before** the lookup, so an internal name is never even asked about — a DNS query is itself a timing oracle for which internal names exist.

**The re-bind hole — closed by pinning, not by re-checking.** The naive shape resolves twice: once to validate, once inside the HTTP client. The attacker sets TTL 0, answers the first query publicly and the second with `169.254.169.254`, and retries until it lands. My fix is that **there is only one lookup**: `pinnedLookup(address, family)` is handed to `https.request` as its `lookup`, ignores the hostname, and returns the address already validated. No second resolution exists to disagree. TLS still validates the cert against the real hostname via `servername`, and `Host` still carries it, so virtual hosting works and the server sees an ordinary request. `agent: false` prevents a pooled socket from a different resolution being reused. I verified the mechanism live: a request to `pinned.invalid` — a name that cannot resolve at all — landed on a local server, so it could only have arrived via the pin (`host header was: pinned.invalid | socket peer: 127.0.0.1`).

**Manual redirects.** `https.request` doesn't follow them — one reason it's used instead of `fetch`, which does by default. Each hop goes through `resolveRedirect` (full URL revalidation) then a **fresh DNS resolution, fresh classification, fresh pin**. Cap 3. Verified against a real redirect on the user's own site: `https://kodely.me/pricing/` → `https://kodely.me/pricing`, two entries in the returned `addresses` array proving both hops were re-resolved.

**Bounded.** 5s connect, 10s deadline covering robots + DNS + every hop + the body, 2MB cap enforced byte-by-byte in the `data` handler (`Content-Length` used only as an early reject — a hostile server sends a small one and streams forever), 3 redirects. `Accept-Encoding: identity`, because 2MB of gzip is far more than 2MB of HTML and a decompression bomb is the obvious follow-up.

**Content-Type allowlist — `text/html` only**, checked on the final hop, so a chain ending at an internal service answering JSON stops there even if every address passed.

**Rate limit.** In `app/api/import/limits.ts`, following `checkEnhanceRateLimit`'s in-memory pattern (an import writes no row, so there's nothing to count; `lib/rate-limit.ts` was out of scope anyway). Four counters: per user (5/10min, 20/hr), **per target host** (10/hr across all accounts — the counter an abuse report is actually about, since a hundred accounts on one victim are each inside their own limit), global (200/hr), and a breaker that stops the feature for 15 minutes after 15 blocked addresses. Keyed on **user id, not IP** — the route is authenticated, so `cf-connecting-ip` and the whole spoofable-`x-forwarded-for` argument from `lib/rate-limit.ts` don't arise. That's also why the URL field is signed-in only: "rate limit per user" is meaningless without a user, and an anonymous fetcher is an open proxy with a speed bump.

Also: robots.txt is honoured (same pinned pipeline, RFC 9309 longest-match, group-for-us beats `*`), the UA is `KodelySiteImport/1.0 (+https://kodely.me/contact)`, and every fetch logs user + hop chain + resolved IPs. The route never returns the body — only the struct.

**Verification.** 31 hostile targets through the real `fetchSiteHtml` with the gate forced ON — metadata (v1, ECS, mapped, decimal), loopback, `0.0.0.0`, RFC1918, CGNAT, ULA, link-local, `metadata.google.internal`, `svc.cluster.local`, `file:`/`gopher:`/`data:`/`dict:`/`ftp:`, odd ports, credential tricks. **All 31 refused, every one in ≤1ms**, with TCP tripwires listening on 127.0.0.1:443/80/8080/6379 that saw **zero connections**. Happy path verified end-to-end against kodely.me only (the user's own site): 473ms, one hop, real Cloudflare IP, robots checked, extraction produced real fields; `favicon.ico` refused as non-HTML; a 404 refused.

## Extraction, and where the line is

**Current site → facts.** business name, tagline, description, address, phone, email, services, opening hours, social links — JSON-LD first, then meta/`<title>`/`<h1>`/`tel:`/`mailto:`/`<address>`, with body-text regexes last. Every field carries a `FieldSource` shown in the UI ("from structured data" vs "from the page text"), because an imported fact must stay distinguishable from an invented one. All agents reported. **48 cards in Done**, 303 tests passing, build green, zero lint.

## Your Kodely Pro thesis — measured, and it holds, with a catch

The agent built a real client-only CRM foundation and compiled it, then did the arithmetic against your one real measured build:

| | credits/build |
|---|---:|
| Foundation inlined, **cached** | **88** |
| Foundation inlined, **uncached** | **363** |
| Model writes the kernel itself | 254 |
| A **manifest** instead of the full tree | **3.5** |

So the thesis holds — **by about 3×, not 10×**. But two things matter more than that headline:

**Uncached, the foundation costs more than not having one.** 363 vs 254. And I found the live bug behind that: `lib/agent.ts` set `cache_control` on the system prompt only. The messages array — which carries the **entire file tree** via `describeFiles()` — had no breakpoint, so the largest repeated block in every request was re-sent at full price on all eight turns. **I've fixed it**, and it improves every build, not just Pro ones.

**The real win is the manifest**, not the foundation: 1,213 tokens vs 30,221. Every foundation file already carries `purpose`/`exports` strings and `describeManifest()` is written. Paired with a `read_file` tool, that's 3.5 credits instead of 88.

It also chose the CRM over booking deliberately — a booking system's double-booking guard has to be a *server-side* constraint, so a client-only one would be exactly the pretends-to-work failure the prompt now forbids.

## Site import ships OFF, and that's the right call

The SSRF work is genuinely good — the re-bind hole is closed by **pinning rather than re-checking**, so there's only one DNS lookup and no second resolution exists to disagree. Proven live: a request to a name that can't resolve at all still landed on a local server, which could only happen via the pin. 31 hostile targets refused in under 1ms each, with TCP tripwires that saw zero connections.

But the one control that matters most — egress isolation — can't be provided in application code. So the URL path fails closed behind an env var named after the *service*, not the feature, so it's enabled by whoever stands that worker up. Its own recommendation: if that worker is never built, the URL fields should stay off permanently and paste carries the feature.

## Diff view: the honest answer to your board card

"Approve/reject before applying" **isn't achievable**, and the agent said so rather than faking it. By the time anything is on screen the build has written rows, charged credits, and the preview already shows the new site — there's no pending state to gate. So the control is "Undo this build", and the panel states plainly that undoing doesn't cancel it or refund the credits.

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

**I am not a lawyer and neither is the owner** — that disclaimer leads the document.

## One line per source

| Source | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **pexels.com** | USE WITH CONDITIONS — licence needs no credit, but API guidelines require a "prominent link to Pexels" wherever we make requests; 200/hr, 20k/mo; ToS bans bulk copying, so on-demand only |
| **pixabay.com** | USE WITH CONDITIONS — best fit: their API *forbids* permanent hotlinking and tells you to self-host; 100 req/60s; 24h response caching mandatory; attribution is a soft request tied to search results |
| **unsplash.com** | AVOID as an integration — API mandates hotlinking + UTM attribution + download pings; incompatible with `img-src 'self'`. Licence alone is fine for a hand-picked set |
| **vecteezy.com** | AVOID — "Using Content within software applications which allow a third party to generate on-demand designs is also not permitted"; no sublicence "in a tool or template, not even for free"; free tier needs attribution |
| **kaboompics.com** | AVOID until permission — otherwise excellent terms, but the FAQ says a website builder "requires individual negotiations". One creator, one email away |
| **mixkit.co** | AVOID — Free Licence says "sub-licensable"; Envato User Terms forbid making Items "available to any third party" and aggregating them "on a stock or inventory basis". Contradictory → legal review |
| **coverr.co** | AVOID — bans reuse by "stock video sites, **website builders**, themes providers…" by name |
| **dareful.com** | USE WITH CONDITIONS — clean CC BY 4.0, self-host and sublicence fine, but the credit must appear on the customer's site |
| **iconoop.com** | USE — but vendor upstream (Lucide ISC, Tabler/Phosphor/Devicon MIT, Material Symbols Apache-2.0); no operator named, no terms page; emoji are CC-BY |
| **svgrepo.com** | AVOID pending verification — licensing page 429s behind a Vercel checkpoint from every method; reported to mix CC0/MIT/**GPL**/CC BY |
| **iconsatlas.com** | USE — MIT, no attribution, redistribution permitted |
| **getillustrations.com** | AVOID free tier — free illustrations require a visible credit and exclude client projects (page contradicts itself); paid Standard from $195/yr would be needed |
| **Make-md/svg-packs** | AVOID the mirror — **no LICENSE file on the repo**; 19 packs with mixed terms including CC BY (Font Awesome, coolicons) and brand-logo sets; vendor upstream instead |
| **Kimbatt/cc0-textures** | AVOID — **no LICENSE file**, torrent links not files, last touched 2020, four different upstream sites' terms bundled on a collector's say-so |

## Recommendation
**Pixabay (primary) + Pexels (secondary) for photos, and upstream OSS icon packs vendored in-repo.** Pixabay wins on architecture — its own rules require the self-hosting our CSP forces — and on throughput (100/60s vs 200/hr). Pexels buys curation quality at the price of a builder-UI credit. Icons come from the repos iconoop/iconsatlas are pointing at anyway. Illustrations and textures stay generated in `lib/assets/illustrations.ts` / `patterns.ts` — nothing on the list beats "no licence at all". Optional: Kaboompics if the owner sends the email; Dareful if a CC BY credit on customer sites is acceptable.

## Biggest legal risk
**Every recommended licence grants rights to the downloader; none expressly grants the right to sublicense onward.** Pixabay: "when you download any Content … *we grant you* an irrevocable … right". When Kodely puts that photo on a plumber's site, either the plumber has no licence, or Kodely must be acting as their agent — which has to be true in the ToS, not just in spirit. Four of four sources that addressed the question said no or not-without-a-deal (Vecteezy, Coverr, Kaboompics, Mixkit). Pexels and Pixabay are usable *because they are silent*, and silence is not permission. That is card #12, marked URGENT/blocker.

## Could not verify
svgrepo.com's licensing page (WAF-blocked, every method); unsplash.com/terms (anti-scraping challenge — so I cannot say whether manual bulk download breaches it; assume it does); whether Pexels permits storing downloaded files (unaddressed either way); whether Pexels' "prominent link" reaches the published site (wording ties it to making API requests — flagged for legal); who operates iconoop.com; and the current terms of ambientCG/Poly Haven/cgbookcase/sharetextures behind the textures repo.</result>

| **pexels.com** | USE WITH CONDITIONS — licence needs no credit, but API guidelines require a "prominent link to Pexels" wherever we make requests; 200/hr, 20k/mo; ToS bans bulk copying, so on-demand only |
| **pixabay.com** | USE WITH CONDITIONS — best fit: their API *forbids* permanent hotlinking and tells you to self-host; 100 req/60s; 24h response caching mandatory; attribution is a soft request tied to search results |
| **unsplash.com** | AVOID as an integration — API mandates hotlinking + UTM attribution + download pings; incompatible with `img-src 'self'`. Licence alone is fine for a hand-picked set |
| **vecteezy.com** | AVOID — "Using Content within software applications which allow a third party to generate on-demand designs is also not permitted"; no sublicence "in a tool or template, not even for free"; free tier needs attribution |
| **kaboompics.com** | AVOID until permission — otherwise excellent terms, but the FAQ says a website builder "requires individual negotiations". One creator, one email away |
| **mixkit.co** | AVOID — Free Licence says "sub-licensable"; Envato User Terms forbid making Items "available to any third party" and aggregating them "on a stock or inventory basis". Contradictory → legal review |
| **coverr.co** | AVOID — bans reuse by "stock video sites, **website builders**, themes providers…" by name |
| **dareful.com** | USE WITH CONDITIONS — clean CC BY 4.0, self-host and sublicence fine, but the credit must appear on the customer's site |
| **iconoop.com** | USE — but vendor upstream (Lucide ISC, Tabler/Phosphor/Devicon MIT, Material Symbols Apache-2.0); no operator named, no terms page; emoji are CC-BY |
| **svgrepo.com** | AVOID pending verification — licensing page 429s behind a Vercel checkpoint from every method; reported to mix CC0/MIT/**GPL**/CC BY |
| **iconsatlas.com** | USE — MIT, no attribution, redistribution permitted |
| **getillustrations.com** | AVOID free tier — free illustrations require a visible credit and exclude client projects (page contradicts itself); paid Standard from $195/yr would be needed |
| **Make-md/svg-packs** | AVOID the mirror — **no LICENSE file on the repo**; 19 packs with mixed terms including CC BY (Font Awesome, coolicons) and brand-logo sets; vendor upstream instead |
| **Kimbatt/cc0-textures** | AVOID — **no LICENSE file**, torrent links not files, last touched 2020, four different upstream sites' terms bundled on a collector's say-so |

## Recommendation
**Pixabay (primary) + Pexels (secondary) for photos, and upstream OSS icon packs vendored in-repo.** Pixabay wins on architecture — its own rules require the self-hosting our CSP forces — and on throughput (100/60s vs 200/hr). Pexels buys curation quality at the price of a builder-UI credit. Icons come from the repos iconoop/iconsatlas are pointing at anyway. Illustrations and textures stay generated in `lib/assets/illustrations.ts` / `patterns.ts` — nothing on the list beats "no licence at all". Optional: Kaboompics if the owner sends the email; Dareful if a CC BY credit on customer sites is acceptable.

## Biggest legal risk
**Every recommended licence grants rights to the downloader; none expressly grants the right to sublicense onward.** Pixabay: "when you download any Content … *we grant you* an irrevocable … right". When Kodely puts that photo on a plumber's site, either the plumber has no licence, or Kodely must be acting as their agent — which has to be true in the ToS, not just in spirit. Four of four sources that addressed the question said no or not-without-a-deal (Vecteezy, Coverr, Kaboompics, Mixkit). Pexels and Pixabay are usable *because they are silent*, and silence is not permission. That is card #12, marked URGENT/blocker.

## Could not verify
svgrepo.com's licensing page (WAF-blocked, every method); unsplash.com/terms (anti-scraping challenge — so I cannot say whether manual bulk download breaches it; assume it does); whether Pexels permits storing downloaded files (unaddressed either way); whether Pexels' "prominent link" reaches the published site (wording ties it to making API requests — flagged for legal); who operates iconoop.com; and the current terms of ambientCG/Poly Haven/cgbookcase/sharetextures behind the textures repo.</result>

Every entry ships a second `seeded` variant, so three sections can share one backdrop without looking cloned; output is deterministic across rebuilds (verified).
- **Spots**: storefront, cup, plant, parcel, calendar, marker, document, chat, bag, house, truck, toolbox.

Every coordinate is original. Hand-placed primitives (lines, arcs, circles, rounded rects) on a 120-unit grid, plus paths computed at render time from sine terms and a seeded PRNG. Nothing was copied, traced or adapted from any icon set, illustration pack, CSS library or template, free or licensed. Stated in the file header.

## How the family holds together

One pen (`currentColor`, stroke-width 4, round cap/join, 120-unit height, no second weight, no hand-drawn corner radii — the round join *is* the radius). One accent: a single blob at 13% `currentColor` behind each spot and empty state, generated by the *same* `blobPath` function that draws the hero backdrops. No literal colour anywhere unless the caller passes one, so everything inherits brand colour and works light-on-dark and dark-on-light. Common ground line at y=100. The "no items" open box and the parcel are deliberately the open/closed twins of one isometric construction.

- **house** — door/window/chimney read as floating rectangles; rebuilt symmetric with a centred door and a round gable window.
- **parcel** — a flat rect with a lid line and a full-height tape reads as a *window pane*; rebuilt isometric.
- **coming-soon** — cone too narrow to read; widened.
- **waves** — four layers at 0.16 opacity stacked to near-solid; lightened.
- **sparkle-trio** — the corner-rounding stroke made the small sparkles blobby; 3 → 2.

Also trimmed topo and confetti for size (topo 3,804 → 2,918 B, keeping the 10-point sampling that is the whole reason it reads as contours rather than rings).

Not inspected pixel-by-pixel: the `dataUri` variants (verified programmatically to contain no `currentColor`, which cannot resolve inside one).

`npx tsc --noEmit` clean · `npx eslint app lib components` exit 0, **0 errors 0 warnings** · `node --import ./scripts/test/register.mjs --test "tests/*.test.mjs"` **303/303 pass**. ## Impossible under the CSP

- **Stock photography** — no remote host, and a base64 raster is a context-cost catastrophe, as the brief says. Not attempted.
- **Raster textures of any kind** (paper scans, fabric, bokeh) — same reason. The existing `feTurbulence` grain in patterns.ts is the only honest substitute and it already exists.
- **Web-font-based decorative lettering** — the CSP sets no `font-src`, so fonts fall to `default-src 'self'`, which excludes `data:`. A base64 font is blocked exactly like a remote one, so anything needing a display face has to be drawn as paths.

- What EXACTLY does a project's `status` consist of — is "building" and "archived" representable today?

## 1. Home dashboard — PARTIAL

## 2. My Websites — PARTIAL

Real, with `file:line`:

- **UI** — `app/dashboard/ProjectRow.tsx:263-304` (menu), `app/dashboard/ProjectRow.tsx:317-403` (delete dialog).
- **Dates** — `createdAt`/`updatedAt` exist on the model (`prisma/schema.prisma:260-261`) and are returned by `GET /api/projects` (`app/api/projects/route.ts:24`), but the dashboard does not display them.

Missing:

- **Status** — there is no `status` column on `Project` (`prisma/schema.prisma:255-272`). "Live/draft" is derived from `publishedAt !== null` only (`app/dashboard/page.tsx:87`, rendered `app/dashboard/ProjectRow.tsx:231`).

## 4. Templates — REAL, but understand what it is

`lib/templates.ts` provides exactly:

- `Template` type: `id, name, description, category, prompt` (`lib/templates.ts:38-50`).

There is **no template file tree, no thumbnail, no preview image, no starting HTML**. Application is: write the prompt into `sessionStorage`, create a project, let the Editor auto-fire the first build — `components/templates/TemplateGallery.tsx:69-95`. Every project regardless of template starts from the same `FOUNDATION_FILES` (`app/api/projects/route.ts:43`).

## 5. Usage — PARTIAL

Available:
- **Credits remaining** — `getBalance()` reads `balanceAfter` off the newest ledger row: `lib/credits.ts:153-159`.

The billing page already renders the project name per ledger row: `app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx:85` and `270-276`. A per-site rollup is a `groupBy` away; no schema change needed. Caveat: deleting a project SET NULLs `buildId`, so historical attribution is lost for deleted sites (`prisma/schema.prisma:379`, handled at `app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx:252-258`).

No `Domain` model, no `customDomain` field, no DNS/CNAME/SSL/ACME code, no purchase flow. No customer-facing integrations surface. The only external services in the codebase are Stripe (`lib/stripe.ts`), Google OAuth sign-in (`app/api/auth/google/*`), Discord OAuth for a one-off reward (`app/api/rewards/discord/*`), and nodemailer (`lib/mail.ts`) — none of them are user-configurable. `checkIntegrations()` at `app/admin/health/checks.ts:201` is an admin env-var presence check, not a feature.

- **No ticket model.** No conversation, thread, or ticket table in `prisma/schema.prisma`.
- **`SupportNote` is operator-only and explicitly never shown to the customer** — `prisma/schema.prisma:219-232` ("Never shown to the customer"). Written only from admin: `app/admin/feedback/actions.ts:59`. Read only from `app/admin/feedback/notes/page.tsx:62` and `app/admin/feedback/notes/[userId]/page.tsx:53`. The one exception: it is included in the user's own data export at `app/api/account/export/route.ts:388-391`.
- **What does exist:** an unauthenticated contact form → email, `app/api/contact/route.ts:37+`, gated on `isMailConfigured()` (`app/api/contact/route.ts:38`); and thumbs up/down on a build, which writes an **Event only**, no reply path — `app/api/feedback/route.ts:49-61`.
- `Message` rows (`prisma/schema.prisma:295-305`) are the *build* conversation inside one project, not support.

## 10. Settings — PARTIAL

The entire settings page is 58 lines: `app/settings/page.tsx`.

| Item | State |
|---|---|
| Name | `User.name` exists (`prisma/schema.prisma:22`), set only at signup/Google callback (`app/api/auth/signup/route.ts:81`, `app/api/auth/google/callback/route.ts:113`). **No edit path.** |

| Spend cap | **REAL** — `app/settings/SpendCapForm.tsx`, `app/api/account/spend-cap/route.ts`. |

## 11. Version history — REAL

- **Checkpoints** = successful builds whose `filesSnapshot` survives: `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/route.ts:18-34` (capped at 100, filters `filesSnapshot: { not: DbNull }`).
- **Snapshot shape** is `{ source: {...}, build: {...} }` — `prisma/schema.prisma:330-344`.
- **Restore** — `app/api/projects/[id]/builds/[buildId]/restore/route.ts:24-52`; free, restores both source and compiled trees in one transaction.
- **Compare** — real line-level diff engine, `app/projects/[id]/diff.ts`, loaded via Server Action `app/projects/[id]/diff-actions.ts:44+`, rendered `app/projects/[id]/DiffView.tsx`. Diffs the *source* tree against the previous surviving checkpoint.
- **Undo/redo cursor model** — `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx:32-69`; history panel is a view mode at `app/projects/[id]/Editor.tsx:152`.
- **Caveat for UI copy:** snapshots are pruned — kept only for the newest 20 per project, and only those older than 30 days are eligible (`lib/retention.ts:65`, `lib/retention.ts:74`). So history is bounded, and the list must keep filtering on snapshot survival.

## 12. Website preview — REAL, interactive, and NOT the published site

Two distinct things:

**In-editor preview (draft):**
- Served by `app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts:63-95` — owner-only (`:67-72`), reads `ProjectFile` where `published: false, kind: "build"`, `Cache-Control: no-store`.
- But the iframe is **not** pointed at that URL. It is fed a self-contained document via `srcdoc`: `app/projects/[id]/PreviewFrame.tsx:140`, `sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms"` (no `allow-same-origin`) at `:141`. Assembly/inlining is in `app/projects/[id]/preview-agent.ts`. Reason given at `PreviewFrame.tsx:17-26`: subresource requests from the frame are cross-site and arrive without the session cookie.
- It is a **real interactive iframe** (scripts run, click-to-select handshake at `PreviewFrame.tsx:96-113`), with three widths — desktop / 768 / 380 (`PreviewFrame.tsx:30-36`).
- Empty state is a literal HTML string: `app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts:81`.

**Published site (live):**

| Event name | Line | User-visible-meaningful? |
|---|---|---|
| `user.signed_up` | `lib/events.ts:25` | Marginal — one row, day zero |
| `project.created` | `:26` | **Yes** |
| `project.deleted` | `:30` | **Yes** (though the project is gone; props carry `projectId`, `wasPublished`, `ageHours` — `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:231-240`) |
| `build.started` | `:31` | Noisy — pairs with succeeded/failed |
| `build.succeeded` | `:32` | **Yes** |
| `build.failed` | `:33` | **Yes** |
| `build.rated` | `:36` | No — it is the user's own input echoed back |
| `project.published` | `:37` | **Yes** — the North Star (`lib/events.ts:52`) |
| `credits.exhausted` | `:39` | **Yes** |
| `credits.cap_reached` | `:40` | **Yes** |
| `billing.checkout_started` | `:41` | Marginal — abandoned checkouts would show |
| `billing.credits_purchased` | `:42` | **Yes** (but duplicates the ledger, which is the better source) |

Staging uses the path form `https://staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>` (`app/api/site/[slug]/site-host.ts:28, 59-63`). It is explicitly **not** deployed to external hosting infra — `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts:13-16`.

**No, the preview is not the same thing.** Preview reads `published: false` rows through an owner-authenticated route and is delivered as an inlined `srcdoc` document in a sandboxed iframe; the live site reads `published: true` rows, is public, cached 60s, gets robots/sitemap/SEO backfill, and has working forms. Publishing is the transaction that copies one tree onto the other (`app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts:154-166`).

The ownership model is a single foreign key: `Project.userId` (`prisma/schema.prisma:257`), scoped in every query as `{ id, userId }`. `User.role` is `"CUSTOMER" | "ADMIN"` (`prisma/schema.prisma:23`) — a platform role, not a workspace role. Adding workspaces would touch every route.

**Subscription/plan, or only a credit balance? What does `billingEnabled()` gate?**
**Only a credit balance.** No subscription model, no plan field, no price, no renewal — asserted in code at `app/admin/analytics/page.tsx:50` and `app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx:197-200`. Balance is derived from the append-only `CreditLedger` (`lib/credits.ts:153-159`), never a mutable counter.

`billingEnabled()` is `lib/stripe.ts:55-57` — true only when **both** `STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` and `STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET` are set. It gates exactly four things:
1. `POST /api/billing/checkout` → 503 (`app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts:11-13`)
2. `POST /api/billing/webhook` → 503 (`app/api/billing/webhook/route.ts:14`)
3. The dashboard top-up button and the meter's `canTopUp` (`app/dashboard/page.tsx:42, 44`)
4. The billing page's "Add credits" section (`app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx:89, 194-210`)

It does **not** gate the credit statement, the spend cap, or anything else — deliberately (`app/dashboard/page.tsx:45-48`).

**Is a project thumbnail/screenshot captured anywhere?**
**No.** No `thumbnail`/`screenshot`/`previewImage` field on any model. No headless browser dependency (no puppeteer/playwright in `package.json`). No image generation. The only `og:image` handling is *inside generated sites* (`lib/site-seo.ts:256-258`, `app/projects/[id]/SeoPanel.tsx:71`) and is about the customer's site metadata, not a card image for your dashboard. If you want thumbnails you need a new capture service and storage — neither exists.

**What EXACTLY does a project's `status` consist of? Are "building" and "archived" representable?**
There is **no `status` field on `Project`** (`prisma/schema.prisma:255-272`). The complete state vocabulary is:
- `publishedAt: DateTime?` (`prisma/schema.prisma:263`) → the only binary: **Published** vs **Draft** (`app/dashboard/page.tsx:87`, `app/dashboard/ProjectRow.tsx:231`).
- Everything else is inferred: "has any `kind:"build"` draft file" distinguishes never-built from built (`app/api/preview/.../route.ts:78-85`); `Build.status` is `RUNNING | SUCCEEDED | FAILED` (`prisma/schema.prisma:310`) but belongs to a build, not the project.

- **"Building"** — *transiently* representable: `Build.status = "RUNNING"` scoped to a `projectId` would tell you a build is in flight. But the generate route is a streaming SSE request (`app/api/generate/route.ts:20-21`, `maxDuration = 300`) and the dashboard never queries build status, so today a stale `RUNNING` row from a crashed request would read as "building" forever. Treat this as **derivable but not currently trustworthy** — needs a staleness rule.
- **"Archived"** — **not representable.** No column, no soft-delete. `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:190` says so outright. Delete is the only removal, and it is irreversible and takes the live site down (`:200-205`).

**Is `Event` a usable activity feed for a single customer?**
**Technically yes; product-wise, barely.** `Event` has `@@index([userId, createdAt])` (`prisma/schema.prisma:73`) and is already queried exactly that way — but only by admin: `app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx:135-140`. Nothing customer-facing reads it. Retention is 400 days (`lib/retention.ts:123`, policy row `lib/retention.ts:718-725`). Props are small non-PII only (`prisma/schema.prisma:64`).

The 12 names (`lib/events.ts:23-43`):

| Event name | Line | User-visible-meaningful? |
|---|---|---|
| `user.signed_up` | `lib/events.ts:25` | Marginal — one row, day zero |
| `project.created` | `:26` | **Yes** |
| `project.deleted` | `:30` | **Yes** (though the project is gone; props carry `projectId`, `wasPublished`, `ageHours` — `app/api/projects/[id]/route.ts:231-240`) |
| `build.started` | `:31` | Noisy — pairs with succeeded/failed |
| `build.succeeded` | `:32` | **Yes** |
| `build.failed` | `:33` | **Yes** |
| `build.rated` | `:36` | No — it is the user's own input echoed back |
| `project.published` | `:37` | **Yes** — the North Star (`lib/events.ts:52`) |
| `credits.exhausted` | `:39` | **Yes** |
| `credits.cap_reached` | `:40` | **Yes** |
| `billing.checkout_started` | `:41` | Marginal — abandoned checkouts would show |
| `billing.credits_purchased` | `:42` | **Yes** (but duplicates the ledger, which is the better source) |

Honest read: **7 of 12 are meaningful to a customer**, and a good feed is roughly `project.created`, `build.succeeded`, `build.failed`, `project.published`, `project.deleted`. But note two problems: (a) `props` do **not** carry the project *name*, only `projectId` — so rendering "Published *Acme Cafe*" requires a join, and a deleted project has no name to join to; (b) purchases and credit events are better read from `CreditLedger`, which is never pruned (`prisma/schema.prisma:356-382`). A feed built purely on `Event` will silently thin out after 400 days.

**Where do published sites live, and is the in-editor preview the same thing?**
Published: **`https://<slug>.kodely.site`** (`prisma/schema.prisma:259`, `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts:11` `KODELY_SITES_BASE`, URL at `:180-183`), served from Postgres rows (`ProjectFile` with `published: true, kind: "build"`) by `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts`, routed there by `proxy.ts`. Staging uses the path form `https://staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>` (`app/api/site/[slug]/site-host.ts:28, 59-63`). It is explicitly **not** deployed to external hosting infra — `app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts:13-16`.

**No, the preview is not the same thing.** Preview reads `published: false` rows through an owner-authenticated route and is delivered as an inlined `srcdoc` document in a sandboxed iframe; the live site reads `published: true` rows, is public, cached 60s, gets robots/sitemap/SEO backfill, and has working forms. Publishing is the transaction that copies one tree onto the other (`app/api/projects/[id]/publish/route.ts:154-166`).

input.content:
# Kodely product design system

The contract for the customer-facing portal (`app/(portal)/**`) and the builder
(`app/projects/[id]/**`). Marketing pages (`app/page.tsx`, `/pricing`, `/blog`,
`/templates`, `/wizard`) are a **separate** system — do not repoint their tokens.

## The one-sentence brief

An AI website builder that happens to have a customer portal around it — not a
dashboard that happens to contain a builder. The primary action is always
"build something".

---

## Tokens

Defined in `app/globals.css`, exposed to Tailwind via `@theme inline`. **Use the
Tailwind class, never a raw hex and never an arbitrary-value bracket.**

### Surface

| Class | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `bg-canvas` | The page behind panels. Set by `AppShell`; pages never set it. |
| `bg-surface` | Cards, panels, the sidebar. |
| `bg-surface-2` | Hover, inset rows, quiet fills. |
| `bg-surface-3` | Track of a progress bar, the deepest step. |
| `bg-inset` | Code/preview wells. |

### Line

`border-hair` (default for cards) · `border-line-mid` (inputs, menus) ·
`border-line-strong` (emphasis, pending step outline)

### Text

`text-ink` (primary) · `text-ink-2` (secondary/body) · `text-ink-3` (tertiary,
placeholder, disabled) · `text-ink-inv` (on a brand fill)

### Brand

`text-brand` `bg-brand` `bg-brand-tint` `bg-brand-tint-2` `text-brand-ink`

`--brand-gradient` is a **fill of last resort**. Exactly one element per view may
carry it: the primary button. Do not gradient headings, cards, borders or icons.

### Status

`ok` `warn` `danger` `info`, each with a `-tint` companion
(`text-ok` / `bg-ok-tint`). Status colour is never the brand colour.

### Radius / elevation / motion

`rounded-sm|md|lg|xl|2xl` (8/10/14/20/28px) · `shadow-e1|e2|e3` ·
`duration-[var(--t-1)]` 120ms, `--t-2` 200ms, `--t-3` 380ms ·
`ease-[var(--ease)]`

---

## Utility classes

`k-focus` — **put this on every interactive element.** One focus ring, product-wide.
`k-display` `k-h1` `k-h2` `k-label` — the type scale. `k-label` is the only uppercase.
`k-num` — **required** on any figure: credits, prices, counts, dates in a column.
`k-scroll-x` — wrap any wide table/code block. The page body must never scroll sideways.
`k-msg-in` `k-step-in` `k-step-active` — entrance and progress animations.
`k-preview-busy` / `k-preview-idle` — the preview treatment while the AI works.
`k-wash` — ambient brand glow inside a hero panel. Sparingly: one per page, at most.
`k-gradient-border` — gradient hairline. Reserve for the single most important panel.

---

## Components (`components/ui/`)

Import these. **Do not hand-roll a second version of any of them.**

| Component | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `Button` `ButtonLink` `IconButton` `buttonClass` | Variants `primary\|secondary\|ghost\|soft\|danger`, sizes `xs\|sm\|md\|lg`. **One `primary` per view.** `IconButton` requires `label`. |
| `Card` `CardHeader` `SectionHeader` | `interactive` only if it truly responds. |
| `Badge` | `tone` + `dot` + `pulse`. Set `dot` on anything conveying live state — colour alone is not a status channel. |
| `Input` `Textarea` `Select` `SearchInput` | Label/hint/error/aria wiring is built in. Never hand-write a bare `<input>`. |
| `Progress` `toneForUsage` | Recolours as it fills. `indeterminate` for work with no known end. |
| `Skeleton` `SkeletonList` | Stagger with `delay`. |
| `EmptyState` | `kind` is required: `empty` (none yet) / `no-results` (filter too narrow) / `unavailable` (does not exist yet). These need different sentences. |
| `Menu` | Keyboard + Escape + click-outside already handled. `unavailableReason` greys an item and says why. |
| `Modal` `ConfirmModal` | Native `<dialog>`. Confirm buttons are labelled with the verb, never "OK". |
| `ToastProvider` `useToast` | Provider is already mounted by `AppShell`. Errors and toasts with an action do not auto-dismiss. |
| `Segmented` | Real radios. Used for grid/list and device toggles. |
| `AIProgress` `stepsAt` | **The** progress component. See below. |
| `Stat` `StatRow` | Any number the customer must understand. |
| `Avatar` | Initials only — there is no avatar upload. |
| `Spinner` | |

## Shell (`components/app/`)

`AppShell` wraps every portal page and already provides the sidebar, mobile
drawer, bottom bar and toast host. **A page renders content only** — no page
supplies its own nav, no page sets a background, no page mounts a second
`ToastProvider`.

Navigation lives in `components/app/nav.ts`. An item may only be added there
once it is backed by real data; `soon: true` marks the ones that are not.

---

## AI progress is one object, not three spinners

`AIProgress` is rendered by the initial build overlay, by the chat panel during
an edit, and beside the preview. All three must show the **same steps in the
same state**, because the customer reads them as one thing happening.

**Drive `state` from real build signals.** A timer that walks the list forward on
its own is a fake — and it will still be sitting on "Finalizing" long after a
build has failed. The build genuinely does not know its percentage (it is an
agent loop of unknown length), which is exactly why this is a named-step list
and not a progress bar.

---

## What does not exist (audited — do not build UI that pretends otherwise)

| Thing | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| **Plans / subscriptions** | None. No plan, price, or renewal date. Checkout is one-off `payment` mode for credit packs. **Never render a "Pro" chip or "$X/month".** |
| **Credit reset date** | Credits never expire. There is no monthly allowance and no reset day — the spend cap is a *rolling* 30 days chosen so there is no reset. |
| **Invoices / payment method** | Not fetched from Stripe. The credit ledger is the only history. |
| **Thumbnails** | Nothing captures a screenshot. No headless browser. |
| **Project status** | Only `publishedAt` → Published / Draft. No `archived`. "Building" is derivable from `Build.status = RUNNING` but has no staleness rule, so it is not yet trustworthy. |
| **Domains** | No model, no field, no route. Sites live at `<slug>.kodely.site` only. |
| **Integrations** | Nothing customer-facing. |
| **Support tickets** | No ticket model. `SupportNote` is admin-write-only and explicitly never shown to the customer. |
| **Storage / bandwidth** | Not measured anywhere. |
| **Workspaces / members / roles** | No concept of it. Ownership is one FK: `Project.userId`. |
| **Avatar upload, password change, 2FA, notification prefs** | None. |

**Sessions list and revoke, and editing `User.name`, ARE cheaply real** — the
`Session` model is per-user and queryable.

### The rule

A screen that looks operable and is not is worse than an absent one. A screen
that says "this does not exist yet, here is what you have instead" is neither.
Use `EmptyState kind="unavailable"` and say plainly what is missing.

## TASK 1 — Home dashboard (`/dashboard`)
