<result>## Method note

All four parallel vendor-research agents were stopped mid-run, so I completed the vendor research directly. Two consequences: (a) I hit the session's web-search cap, so the last few gaps were filled by direct doc fetches only, and (b) **Webflow's help center (`help.webflow.com`) returns 403 to automated fetching**, so Webflow's record values are from a secondary source and should be re-verified by a human against Site settings → Publishing. Everything marked UNSURE below is genuinely unverified, not guessed.

---

# 1. Vendor-by-vendor

## Wix

**Buy in product.** Yes. Every annual Premium/Studio plan includes a 1-year free domain voucher, valid 2 months from plan purchase, new registrations only (not renewals) — [Wix: About your free domain voucher](https://support.wix.com/en/article/about-your-free-domain-voucher). Renewal ≈ **$21.35/yr for .com** (secondary: [HostAdvice](https://hostadvice.com/hosting-company/wix-com-reviews/wix-domains-pricing/); Wix's own [Price of Wix Domain Renewals](https://support.wix.com/en/article/price-of-wix-domain-renewals-6790543) is the primary page). **Registrar of record: UNSURE.**

**Connect an owned domain — two named methods.** [Pointing](https://support.wix.com/en/article/connecting-a-domain-to-wix-using-the-pointing-method):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `185.230.63.107` |
| CNAME | `www` | `pointing.wixdns.net` |

Note this is **not** the old `23.236.62.147` / `wwwNNN.wixdns.net` pair that most third-party tutorials still publish — a live example of stale record values circulating on the web.

**Nameservers as the easy path.** Yes, and Wix actively pushes it: they say they *do not recommend* pointing, because they cannot help you inside another host's DNS panel ([Pointing vs. Name Servers](https://support.wix.com/en/article/pointing-vs-name-servers-domain-connection-methods)). Gains: DNS managed in Wix, MX records auto-imported, and it's **mandatory** for Wix Email Marketing, Multilingual subdomains and Photo Albums. Loses: Wix becomes the DNS authority, so every non-web record (email, verification TXT, subdomains at other hosts) has to be re-created.

**Apex/www.** Both records required. Wix's own doc states plainly that if you don't update *both* the A and the CNAME, the site appears unsecure. Their FAQ also documents the `www.www` address-bar loop as a misconfiguration symptom.

**Pending states / timing.** "Up to 48 hours" on both articles. Richer status vocabulary: UNSURE.

**Non-payment.** UNSURE — I could not reach a verified Wix page on plan expiry behaviour.

**Non-technical verdict.** Best-in-class *routing* of the user toward the safer option (nameservers), and honest about the failure mode ("your site will appear unsecure"). Worst-in-class in that the pointing path is a two-record, all-or-nothing operation where getting one right and one wrong produces a browser security warning — the single scariest outcome for a non-technical customer.

## Squarespace

**Buy in product.** Yes — Squarespace Domains, which absorbed Google Domains (~10M domains, ~$180M) — [Squarespace newsroom](https://newsroom.squarespace.com/blog/googledomains). Free first year on annual plans, limited to TLDs priced at the .com rate; cancelling during the free year forfeits the offer; renewal at standard rate ([Free Squarespace domain offer](https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/206541787-Free-Squarespace-domain-offer)). .com renewal ≈ **$20/yr** (secondary; not on a Squarespace page I could fetch).

**Connect an owned domain.** The most record-heavy flow in the set — [Squarespace: connecting a third-party domain](https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/205812378):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `198.185.159.144` |
| A | `@` | `198.185.159.145` |
| A | `@` | `198.49.23.144` |
| A | `@` | `198.49.23.145` |
| CNAME | *(unique per-site code)* | `verify.squarespace.com` |
| CNAME | `www` | `ext-cust.squarespace.com` |

Six records, one of which is a per-site random string. That is six chances to typo.

**Nameserver alternative.** Not offered for third-party domains; the alternative Squarespace pushes is *transferring the domain in*. **UNSURE** whether any NS-delegation option exists.

**Pending states / timing.** 24–48 hours; success is a green **Connected** label in the Domains panel. Intermediate/error state names: UNSURE.

**Non-payment.** UNSURE (the expiry/redemption help articles 404'd on the URLs I tried).

**Non-technical verdict.** The verification CNAME with a random host label is where support tickets come from — many registrar UIs mangle or auto-append the domain to the host field. Four apex A records is also the worst case for "customer adds three, leaves one old record in place" partial failure.

## Webflow

**Buy in product.** UNSURE — I could not verify that Webflow resells domains.

**Connect an owned domain — two flows.** Webflow ships both **Quick connect** (powered by **Entri**) and **Manually connect**. Quick connect detects the registrar, has the user authorize Entri, and writes the records for them; supported registrars include GoDaddy, Namecheap, Squarespace/Google Domains, Domain.com and others. Manual values (⚠️ *secondary source — Webflow's help center blocks automated fetch*; verify in Site settings → Publishing):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `75.2.70.75` |
| A | `@` | `99.83.190.102` |
| CNAME | `www` | `proxy-ssl.webflow.com` |

Source: [thecssagency guide](https://www.thecssagency.com/blog/how-to-connect-webflow-to-domain); official pages are [Quick connect](https://help.webflow.com/hc/en-us/articles/33961266716307-Quick-connect-a-custom-domain) and [Manually connect](https://help.webflow.com/hc/en-us/articles/33961239562387-Manually-connect-a-custom-domain).

**This is the single most load-bearing data point in the whole report.** Entri publishes Webflow-attributed outcome numbers for the Quick-connect flow: **2× domain-connect rate, ~30% faster time-to-connect, 97% fewer DNS support tickets**, and an overall "20% → 80%" connection-success figure — [Entri Connect](https://www.entri.com/products/connect). Vendor-published, so discount accordingly, but the direction is unambiguous: automating the record write, not explaining the records better, is what moves the number.

**Apex/www.** Add both; a star icon designates the default domain and the other redirects to it.

**Non-payment / status strings / timing.** UNSURE (help center inaccessible).

## Vercel

**Buy in product.** Yes, positioned as **"at-cost"** ([vercel.com/domains](https://vercel.com/domains)). Free first-year domain on paid Pro — but only `.online`, `.site`, `.space`, `.store`, `.tech`, `.website`, one per team, excludes trials, renews at standard rate ([Pro plan](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/pro-plan)). Domain purchases and renewals are **final, no refunds**. Registrar of record: UNSURE.

**Connect an owned domain.** Two important corrections to the folklore:

- Apex: an **A record**. `76.76.21.21` still appears as the documented example, but the docs now instruct you to use the value shown on your project's Domains settings ([Domains Overview](https://vercel.com/docs/domains)).
- Subdomain: the CNAME is now **per-project**, e.g. `d1d4fc829fe7bc7c.vercel-dns-017.com` — *not* the old shared `cname.vercel-dns.com` ([Adding a domain](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/add-a-domain)).
- The CNAME value includes a **trailing dot** and must be copied exactly ([Troubleshooting](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/troubleshooting)).
- **No IPv6/AAAA support** for third-party domains.

**Nameservers.** `ns1.vercel-dns.com` / `ns2.vercel-dns.com`. Optional for normal domains, **mandatory for wildcards** because wildcard certs require the ACME DNS-01 challenge. Cost of switching: email breaks until MX records are re-added (Vercel has a dedicated KB article about exactly this).

**Verification.** TXT at `_vercel` — required only when the domain is already attached to another Vercel account.

**Apex/www.** Vercel prompts you to add `www` when you add an apex, and recommends `www` as canonical; redirects are configured by adding both and setting `redirect` on one.

**Pending states.** The clearest published state model of the mainstream hosts: **Invalid Configuration / Valid Configuration / Pending Verification**. Their drop-in [Custom Domain block for platforms](https://vercel.com/docs/platforms/platform-elements/blocks/custom-domain) **re-checks every 20 seconds**, auto-detects whether TXT / CNAME / A is the right instruction, and renders a DNS table with copy buttons.

**Timing.** Certificate: 5–10 minutes after verification. Nameserver change: 24–48h. Notably, Vercel is the only mainstream vendor that publishes the actually-correct advice: **lower your TTL to ~60s before the cutover, then raise it after** — that is the honest fix for the 48-hour problem.

**Documented SSL failure modes** (a good checklist to steal): missing/blocking `CAA` records (need `0 issue "letsencrypt.org"`), a stale `_acme-challenge` TXT left over from a previous host, and any rewrite/redirect of `/.well-known`.

**Non-payment / downgrade.** Domains cost nothing extra within plan limits (Hobby 50/project; Pro soft limit 100,000). Downgrading Pro→Hobby requires **manually transferring domains out first**, and all members except the original owner are removed.

## Netlify

**Buy in product.** Still active (TLD list expanded Nov 2025). 1-year terms, auto-renew on by default; if it lapses there's a **30-day window to email support**, and after **60 days** the domain returns to the public pool ([Register and buy a domain](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/register-and-buy-a-domain/)). Registrar of record and prices: **UNSURE** (not on that page).

**Connect an owned domain.** Netlify is the only one here that leads with the *correct* apex answer ([Configure external DNS](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/configure-external-dns/)):

| Case | Type | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Apex, provider supports it (**recommended**) | ALIAS / ANAME / flattened CNAME | `apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com` |
| Apex, fallback | A | `75.2.60.5` |
| Subdomain | CNAME | `<your-site>.netlify.app` |

They explicitly call the ALIAS form "more resilient" than the hard-coded IP — which it is, because an IP change breaks every customer's A record simultaneously.

**Nameservers.** Netlify DNS runs on **NS1** — nameservers are per-domain from a pool in the form `dns1.p01.nsone.net`, shown in the dashboard rather than published as a fixed list ([Netlify name servers](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/netlify-name-servers/)).

**Pending states / timing.** "Pending DNS verification"; docs say it may take a full day.

**Non-payment:** UNSURE.

## Framer

**Buy in product.** Yes — via a **Hover** partnership; yearly plans get a "Claim a free custom domain" flow that redirects to Hover and auto-connects afterwards ([Framer: connect a custom domain](https://www.framer.com/help/articles/how-to-connect-a-custom-domain/)). Renewal price: UNSURE.

**Connect an owned domain.**

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `31.43.160.6` |
| A | `@` | `31.43.161.6` |
| CNAME | `www` | `sites.framer.app` |

Subdomain-only setups get a single CNAME. Framer explicitly warns to **remove any other A/AAAA records** first.

**Nameservers:** UNSURE. **Status states:** UNSURE (not documented on that page). **Timing:** up to 48h, "typically faster". **Non-payment:** UNSURE.

## Lovable

The most directly comparable competitor to Kodely, and the most interesting.

**Buy in product.** Yes, and the automatic connect path is **Entri**: Lovable detects the customer's DNS provider, the customer logs in and authorizes Entri, and Entri writes the records ([Lovable: custom domain](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/custom-domain)).

**Connect an owned domain (manual).**

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `185.158.133.1` |
| TXT | `_lovable` | `lovable_verify=…` |
| CNAME | *(alt.)* | for CDN/proxy setups |

They chose A + TXT over CNAME precisely because CNAME is illegal at the apex. `www` is **not** auto-included for externally-purchased domains — it must be added separately (a known ticket generator).

**Pending states.** A named five-step ladder: **Unpublished → Ready → Verifying → Setting up → Live**, plus fail/offline states. This is the closest thing to the model I'd recommend Kodely copy.

**Timing.** "Up to 72 hours, though most updates are live within a few hours" — more conservative than everyone else's 48.

**Non-payment.** Custom domains need a paid plan; after downgrading to Free you **cannot add or buy** domains, but **already-connected domains keep serving**. That's a customer-friendly choice worth matching. A Lovable-purchased domain that isn't renewed stops resolving and enters the registrar's ~30-day redemption window.

## Shopify

**Buy in product.** Yes — Shopify is a **reseller through accredited registrar partners**, not the registrar itself; domains registered in the customer's name. From **~$9 USD/yr**, billed annually, 1-year terms, auto-renew on by default, WHOIS privacy free on most eligible TLDs ([shopify.com/domains](https://www.shopify.com/domains)). No free-first-year offer; the free tier is the `.myshopify.com` subdomain.

**Connect an owned domain** ([Connect manually](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/domains/add-a-domain/connecting-domains/connect-domain-manual)):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `23.227.38.65` |
| AAAA | `@` | `2620:0127:f00f:5::` |
| CNAME | `www` | `shops.myshopify.com.` *(trailing period)* |

Regional variation in the A record's last octet (e.g. `23.227.38.32`) is documented as normal — worth knowing, because it means "the value I see doesn't match the docs" is *not* an error. Warnings: delete pre-existing A/AAAA records; only one A and one www CNAME; nameservers must be the provider's defaults.

**Nameservers.** Shopify only runs DNS for domains bought/transferred in — third-party domains stay at their host. (Consistent with the "use provider defaults" warning; not separately confirmed as policy — treat as inference.)

**Pending states.** Shopify defines "connected" as a **three-part conjunction**: DNS points to Shopify **and** the domain is live in all regions **and** the TLS certificate is provisioned. That tri-part definition is the best framing I found for what a green checkmark should actually mean. Timing: up to 48h.

**Non-payment / pause.** UNSURE — the Pause and Build article doesn't address domain behaviour.

## Cloudflare Pages

**Buy in product.** Cloudflare Registrar sells **at cost**: registry fee + the $0.18 ICANN fee, no markup, and registration price = renewal price. **.com ≈ $10.44/yr** (= $10.26 + $0.18). See [Cloudflare low-cost domains](https://www.cloudflare.com/application-services/solutions/low-cost-domain-names/). No free-first-year offer — the pitch is "no year-two surprise" instead.

**Connect an owned domain** ([Pages custom domains](https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/configuration/custom-domains/)):
- **Subdomain:** CNAME `shop.example.com` → `<your-site>.pages.dev`.
- **Apex:** the domain must be a Cloudflare zone — i.e. **nameservers moved to Cloudflare** — after which Cloudflare creates the record itself and CNAME-flattens the apex.
- Hard constraint worth noting: you must add the domain in the dashboard **before** creating the DNS record, or you get a **522**.

**Nameserver alternative.** For Pages apex it isn't an alternative, it's the requirement. Gain: apex works, DNS is managed for you, everything else Cloudflare. Loss: Cloudflare becomes your DNS authority and you must migrate every existing record.

**Status states / timing:** UNSURE — not documented on that page.

## Cloudflare for SaaS — the reference implementation

This is the "one CNAME and we do the rest" pattern in its canonical form ([Getting started](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/start/getting-started/)).

**What the end customer does:** exactly one CNAME, from their hostname to the SaaS provider's published target (e.g. `customers.saasprovider.com`), which resolves onward to the provider's fallback origin. Nothing else. No IPs, no per-tenant values.

**Validation:** three options — TXT, HTTP-automatic (fires once the CNAME is live), or **Delegated DCV** (the customer delegates `_acme-challenge` once, and every future renewal is hands-off). Pre-validation before cutover avoids a downtime window; HTTP-automatic after cutover creates a short one.

**State machine** ([Validation status](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/domain-support/hostname-validation/validation-status/)) — two **independent** axes, which is the key design insight:
- `status`: `pending` → `active` / `active re-deploying` / `blocked` (abuse) / `moved` (stopped pointing at the fallback origin, or exceeded the validation backoff) / `deleted` (after 7+ days in `moved`).
- `ssl.status`: tracks issuance and deployment separately; `active` when issued **and** deployed.

Production-ready = `status: active` **and** `ssl.status: active`. Exact backoff schedule: UNSURE.

**Pricing** ([Plans](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/plans/)): **100 custom hostnames free on Free/Pro/Business**, then **$0.10 per hostname/month** up to 50,000. Wildcard custom hostnames, mTLS and custom certificates are Enterprise-only.

---

# 2. The "one CNAME and we do the rest" pattern

Three distinct commercial shapes:

**a) Edge-terminated proxy (Cloudflare for SaaS, Approximated).** The customer points one record at your edge; the edge does ACME and TLS termination and forwards to your origin.
- [Approximated](https://approximated.app/docs/) supports both apex-A and CNAME-to-intermediary. Their honest note: if you publish a raw IP for apex A records, **changing that IP means every customer must edit their DNS individually** — the argument for an intermediary hostname or an ALIAS-capable answer.
- Approximated's status enum is *diagnosis-shaped* rather than progress-shaped, which is worth stealing wholesale: `ACTIVE_SSL`, `DNS_INCORRECT` (resolving, but pointed somewhere else), `DNS_NOT_RESOLVING` (no records at all), `TARGET_NOT_LOADING` (reaching us, origin dead) — plus booleans `apx_hit`, `is_resolving`, `has_ssl`.
- Pricing ([Approximated](https://approximated.app/pricing)): **$0.20/domain/month**, $20/mo minimum under 100 domains, 400 GB included; self-hosted hybrid $199/mo + $0.10/vhost.

**b) Platform API on an existing host (Vercel for Platforms).** You call `addProjectDomain`, poll `getDomainConfig`, and render the returned records. Verification via `_vercel` TXT only when contested. **No per-domain charge within plan limits.** Vercel additionally ships the front-end as a **drop-in block** with 20-second polling and automatic record-type selection.

**c) Write the customer's DNS for them (Domain Connect / Entri).** This is the category that actually removes the DNS step rather than explaining it.
- [Domain Connect](https://www.domainconnect.org/) is the open, MIT-licensed standard (originated at GoDaddy, submitted to the IETF) for a service provider to hand a DNS provider a templated set of records the user approves in one click.
- [Entri](https://developers.entri.com/connect/overview) is the commercial implementation: JWT from your backend → `entri.connectDomain(config)` → provider auto-detected → user logs into their registrar inside a whitelabeled modal → records written → **webhook to your server when the records go live**. **70+ providers** with direct API login; unsupported providers fall back to registrar-specific step-by-step instructions rather than failing.
- Pricing ([Entri plans](https://www.entri.com/plans)): Startup **$249/mo, 600 domains/year, 1,200 monitored**; Growth 2,400/yr; Premium 12,000/yr; Enterprise beyond. No free tier. Named results: ClickFunnels, Fourthwall (97% fewer DNS tickets).
- **Webflow and Lovable both use Entri.** That is the competitive fact that matters most for Kodely: your two nearest comparables have already bought their way out of the DNS-instructions problem.

**Two constraints any of these designs must respect:**
- **Apex can't be a CNAME** — RFC 1034 forbids other data alongside a CNAME, and the apex must carry SOA/NS (and usually MX). Hence A records, or provider-specific ALIAS/ANAME/CNAME-flattening. Netlify and Cloudflare handle this correctly; most builders just hand out a raw IP.
- **Let's Encrypt rate limits** ([official](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/)): 50 certs per registered domain / 7 days; 5 duplicate certs / 7 days; 300 new orders per account / 3 hours; 5 failed validations per identifier / hour. Let's Encrypt explicitly recommends large integrators use **one account for many customers**, with an override request form (takes weeks). Heroku's docs add the practical corollary: repeatedly toggling cert management off/on gets you rate-limited and support cannot bypass it.

# 3. Honest status copy for DNS/TLS pending states

**Finding: there is no canonical published style guide for this.** I looked for one in design-system content guidelines (Polaris, GOV.UK) and found nothing DNS-specific. What exists is three separate bodies of material you have to assemble yourself.

**(a) The "propagation is a myth" literature — use it to replace the copy, not just to feel superior.**
- [Julia Evans, "DNS 'propagation' is actually caches expiring"](https://jvns.ca/blog/2021/12/06/dns-doesn-t-propagate/) is the best single source. DNS is **pull, not push**: nothing propagates; you are waiting for cached records to expire. A brand-new record is available instantly. The delay only exists when you're *replacing* something already cached.
- Her two gotchas matter enormously for a builder product: **negative caching** — if a customer (or your own checker) queries a record before it exists, the *absence* is cached, governed by the SOA MINIMUM/TTL, often an hour — and **nameserver changes are genuinely the slowest case** because both the registry update and the cached NS records (typically 1-day TTL) have to clear.
- [Tiger Computing](https://www.tiger-computing.co.uk/myth-dns-propagation/) traces the "24–48 hours" number to a worst case of a 24h TTL plus resolvers that ignore TTLs. [ManagingWP](https://managingwp.io/2023/11/02/why-dns-propagation-is-misunderstood-and-abused-by-support-representives/) makes the customer-facing argument: it's used as a scapegoat answer instead of troubleshooting, when in practice changes usually go live in minutes.
- **Important nuance so you don't overcorrect:** a [Let's Encrypt community thread](https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/dont-say-propagation-in-dns/171127) records staff pushing back — there *is* real propagation *inside* a DNS provider's own infrastructure (zone distribution to their anycast edge), on the order of seconds to minutes. So "nothing propagates" is also wrong. The honest line is: *a short real delay at your DNS provider, then cache expiry governed by your old record's TTL.*

**(b) Generic progress research.** [NN/g on progress indicators](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/progress-indicators/): past ~10 seconds you owe the user more than a spinner; when you genuinely cannot estimate a duration, show **a list of completed and remaining steps** and a deliberately vague-but-honest estimate rather than a precise number that will be wrong. Their explicit warning against overpromising speed is exactly the failure mode of "usually takes a few minutes!" copy that then takes six hours.

**(c) De-facto best practice, read off products that got it right.** No one wrote the guide, but four products effectively demonstrate it:

- **Heroku ACM** publishes a full status table with the distinction almost everyone else omits — **`Failing`** (couldn't verify, *still retrying for up to an hour*) vs **`Failed`** (*stopped trying*). Plus `In Progress` → `DNS Verified` → `Cert Issued`, and a concrete anchor: **45–60 minutes** to generate the certificate ([Heroku ACM](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/automated-certificate-management)). "We are still trying" vs "we gave up, act now" is the highest-value single distinction in the whole problem space.
- **Approximated** models states as *diagnoses*, not progress: no records at all vs records pointing elsewhere vs reaching us but origin down. Each maps to a different customer instruction.
- **Cloudflare for SaaS** separates hostname validation from certificate status as two independent axes, so "DNS is right but the cert isn't ready" is representable — a state most builder UIs collapse into a single misleading spinner.
- **Vercel** re-checks every 20 seconds rather than making the user hit refresh, auto-selects which record type to instruct, and — uniquely — publishes the actually-correct mitigation: **lower the TTL to ~60s before cutover, raise it after**.

**The copy pattern these converge on**, which I'd recommend for Kodely:
1. Name the specific check that hasn't passed, not the phase. "We can't see the A record for `example.com` yet" beats "Pending DNS".
2. **Show observed vs expected.** "We see `76.76.21.21`; we expect `185.x.x.x`." This turns a mystery into a diff a non-technical person can act on.
3. Anchor the ETA on the **TTL you actually read** from their current record, not on folklore. "Your DNS provider is caching the old value for 1 hour" is checkable and true.
4. Distinguish **still-retrying** from **stopped** and say when you'll next check.
5. Never conflate DNS-correct with certificate-issued with live-everywhere. Shopify's three-part definition of "connected" is the right bar.
6. Warn about negative caching before the customer trips it: if they visit the domain before the record exists, their own browser/ISP may cache the NXDOMAIN for ~an hour and they will conclude your product is broken.

**The uncomfortable finding:** even Vercel — which publishes the TTL-lowering advice — still ships "DNS changes take 24 to 48 hours to propagate" in its own multi-tenant docs. Every vendor here says 48 hours (Lovable says 72). So honest copy is currently an **unoccupied competitive position**, not a table-stakes catch-up.

---

# 4. Cross-cutting failure modes to design against

These recur across every vendor's forums and docs:

- **"Not secure" warning.** Caused by half-completed record sets (Wix warns about this explicitly), or by the certificate not yet issued while DNS already resolves. The customer sees a browser security interstitial on their own brand — the highest-severity outcome, and it's reachable by doing 50% of the instructions correctly.
- **`DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN` after a correct setup.** Usually negative caching (the customer checked too early) or local OS/browser cache. Mitigation: tell them not to check yet, and give them a "check from our servers" button so they're not diagnosing from their own poisoned cache.
- **Cloudflare orange-cloud proxy in front of your host.** With SSL/TLS mode **Flexible** plus an origin that redirects HTTP→HTTPS, you get `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` ([Cloudflare docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/troubleshooting/too-many-redirects/)). Detect proxied Cloudflare records and warn explicitly. Heroku goes further and recommends *not* using its automated certs behind Cloudflare at all.
- **Both A records and nameservers set.** Nameservers win; the A records at the old provider become dead config the customer keeps re-checking. Wix maintains a whole article on switching connection methods because of this. If you offer both paths, detect and state which one is actually in force.
- **CAA records blocking Let's Encrypt** and **stale `_acme-challenge` records** from a previous host — both silently prevent certificate issuance with no DNS-level symptom. Vercel documents both; check for them automatically.
- **Conflicting pre-existing A/AAAA records.** Framer and Shopify both warn to delete them first. Non-technical customers add rather than replace.
- **60-day ICANN transfer lock** after registration or a prior transfer — surfaces as "why can't I move my domain" immediately after they buy one from you.
- **Registrar UI mangling the host field** — the biggest cause of failed TXT/verification-CNAME entries. Providers variously want `_lovable`, `_lovable.example.com`, or `@`; trailing dots are required by some (Shopify, Vercel) and rejected by others.

**Economics footnote if Kodely resells domains:** Verisign's wholesale .com is **$10.26**, rising **7% to $10.97 on 1 November 2026**, with up to three further 7% hikes permitted this contract cycle ([Domain Name Wire](https://domainnamewire.com/2026/04/23/breaking-verisign-raising-wholesale-com-prices/)). Add the $0.18 ICANN fee and at-cost is ~$10.44 today, ~$11.15 from November. A free-first-year offer therefore costs you roughly $10–11 per activated customer, and the market has bifurcated: Wix/Squarespace/Framer give year one free and recoup at $20–21 renewals; Cloudflare and Vercel sell at cost and compete on the absence of a year-two surprise.

# 1. Vendor-by-vendor

## Wix

**Buy in product.** Yes. Every annual Premium/Studio plan includes a 1-year free domain voucher, valid 2 months from plan purchase, new registrations only (not renewals) — [Wix: About your free domain voucher](https://support.wix.com/en/article/about-your-free-domain-voucher). Renewal ≈ **$21.35/yr for .com** (secondary: [HostAdvice](https://hostadvice.com/hosting-company/wix-com-reviews/wix-domains-pricing/); Wix's own [Price of Wix Domain Renewals](https://support.wix.com/en/article/price-of-wix-domain-renewals-6790543) is the primary page). **Registrar of record: UNSURE.**

**Connect an owned domain — two named methods.** [Pointing](https://support.wix.com/en/article/connecting-a-domain-to-wix-using-the-pointing-method):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `185.230.63.107` |
| CNAME | `www` | `pointing.wixdns.net` |

Note this is **not** the old `23.236.62.147` / `wwwNNN.wixdns.net` pair that most third-party tutorials still publish — a live example of stale record values circulating on the web.

**Nameservers as the easy path.** Yes, and Wix actively pushes it: they say they *do not recommend* pointing, because they cannot help you inside another host's DNS panel ([Pointing vs. Name Servers](https://support.wix.com/en/article/pointing-vs-name-servers-domain-connection-methods)). Gains: DNS managed in Wix, MX records auto-imported, and it's **mandatory** for Wix Email Marketing, Multilingual subdomains and Photo Albums. Loses: Wix becomes the DNS authority, so every non-web record (email, verification TXT, subdomains at other hosts) has to be re-created.

**Apex/www.** Both records required. Wix's own doc states plainly that if you don't update *both* the A and the CNAME, the site appears unsecure. Their FAQ also documents the `www.www` address-bar loop as a misconfiguration symptom.

**Pending states / timing.** "Up to 48 hours" on both articles. Richer status vocabulary: UNSURE.

**Non-payment.** UNSURE — I could not reach a verified Wix page on plan expiry behaviour.

**Non-technical verdict.** Best-in-class *routing* of the user toward the safer option (nameservers), and honest about the failure mode ("your site will appear unsecure"). Worst-in-class in that the pointing path is a two-record, all-or-nothing operation where getting one right and one wrong produces a browser security warning — the single scariest outcome for a non-technical customer.

## Squarespace

**Buy in product.** Yes — Squarespace Domains, which absorbed Google Domains (~10M domains, ~$180M) — [Squarespace newsroom](https://newsroom.squarespace.com/blog/googledomains). Free first year on annual plans, limited to TLDs priced at the .com rate; cancelling during the free year forfeits the offer; renewal at standard rate ([Free Squarespace domain offer](https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/206541787-Free-Squarespace-domain-offer)). .com renewal ≈ **$20/yr** (secondary; not on a Squarespace page I could fetch).

**Connect an owned domain.** The most record-heavy flow in the set — [Squarespace: connecting a third-party domain](https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/205812378):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `198.185.159.144` |
| A | `@` | `198.185.159.145` |
| A | `@` | `198.49.23.144` |
| A | `@` | `198.49.23.145` |
| CNAME | *(unique per-site code)* | `verify.squarespace.com` |
| CNAME | `www` | `ext-cust.squarespace.com` |

Six records, one of which is a per-site random string. That is six chances to typo.

**Nameserver alternative.** Not offered for third-party domains; the alternative Squarespace pushes is *transferring the domain in*. **UNSURE** whether any NS-delegation option exists.

**Pending states / timing.** 24–48 hours; success is a green **Connected** label in the Domains panel. Intermediate/error state names: UNSURE.

**Non-payment.** UNSURE (the expiry/redemption help articles 404'd on the URLs I tried).

**Non-technical verdict.** The verification CNAME with a random host label is where support tickets come from — many registrar UIs mangle or auto-append the domain to the host field. Four apex A records is also the worst case for "customer adds three, leaves one old record in place" partial failure.

**Buy in product.** UNSURE — I could not verify that Webflow resells domains.

**Connect an owned domain — two flows.** Webflow ships both **Quick connect** (powered by **Entri**) and **Manually connect**. Quick connect detects the registrar, has the user authorize Entri, and writes the records for them; supported registrars include GoDaddy, Namecheap, Squarespace/Google Domains, Domain.com and others. Manual values (⚠️ *secondary source — Webflow's help center blocks automated fetch*; verify in Site settings → Publishing):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `75.2.70.75` |
| A | `@` | `99.83.190.102` |
| CNAME | `www` | `proxy-ssl.webflow.com` |

Source: [thecssagency guide](https://www.thecssagency.com/blog/how-to-connect-webflow-to-domain); official pages are [Quick connect](https://help.webflow.com/hc/en-us/articles/33961266716307-Quick-connect-a-custom-domain) and [Manually connect](https://help.webflow.com/hc/en-us/articles/33961239562387-Manually-connect-a-custom-domain).

## Vercel

**Buy in product.** Yes, positioned as **"at-cost"** ([vercel.com/domains](https://vercel.com/domains)). Free first-year domain on paid Pro — but only `.online`, `.site`, `.space`, `.store`, `.tech`, `.website`, one per team, excludes trials, renews at standard rate ([Pro plan](https://vercel.com/docs/plans/pro-plan)). Domain purchases and renewals are **final, no refunds**. Registrar of record: UNSURE.

**Connect an owned domain.** Two important corrections to the folklore:

- Apex: an **A record**. `76.76.21.21` still appears as the documented example, but the docs now instruct you to use the value shown on your project's Domains settings ([Domains Overview](https://vercel.com/docs/domains)).
- Subdomain: the CNAME is now **per-project**, e.g. `d1d4fc829fe7bc7c.vercel-dns-017.com` — *not* the old shared `cname.vercel-dns.com` ([Adding a domain](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/add-a-domain)).

**Verification.** TXT at `_vercel` — required only when the domain is already attached to another Vercel account.

**Apex/www.** Vercel prompts you to add `www` when you add an apex, and recommends `www` as canonical; redirects are configured by adding both and setting `redirect` on one.

**Pending states.** The clearest published state model of the mainstream hosts: **Invalid Configuration / Valid Configuration / Pending Verification**. Their drop-in [Custom Domain block for platforms](https://vercel.com/docs/platforms/platform-elements/blocks/custom-domain) **re-checks every 20 seconds**, auto-detects whether TXT / CNAME / A is the right instruction, and renders a DNS table with copy buttons.

**Timing.** Certificate: 5–10 minutes after verification. Nameserver change: 24–48h. Notably, Vercel is the only mainstream vendor that publishes the actually-correct advice: **lower your TTL to ~60s before the cutover, then raise it after** — that is the honest fix for the 48-hour problem.

**Documented SSL failure modes** (a good checklist to steal): missing/blocking `CAA` records (need `0 issue "letsencrypt.org"`), a stale `_acme-challenge` TXT left over from a previous host, and any rewrite/redirect of `/.well-known`.

**Non-payment / downgrade.** Domains cost nothing extra within plan limits (Hobby 50/project; Pro soft limit 100,000). Downgrading Pro→Hobby requires **manually transferring domains out first**, and all members except the original owner are removed.

**Buy in product.** Still active (TLD list expanded Nov 2025). 1-year terms, auto-renew on by default; if it lapses there's a **30-day window to email support**, and after **60 days** the domain returns to the public pool ([Register and buy a domain](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/configure-domains/register-and-buy-a-domain/)). ## Lovable

The most directly comparable competitor to Kodely, and the most interesting.

**Buy in product.** Yes, and the automatic connect path is **Entri**: Lovable detects the customer's DNS provider, the customer logs in and authorizes Entri, and Entri writes the records ([Lovable: custom domain](https://docs.lovable.dev/features/custom-domain)).

**Connect an owned domain (manual).**

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `185.158.133.1` |
| TXT | `_lovable` | `lovable_verify=…` |
| CNAME | *(alt.)* | for CDN/proxy setups |

They chose A + TXT over CNAME precisely because CNAME is illegal at the apex. `www` is **not** auto-included for externally-purchased domains — it must be added separately (a known ticket generator).

**Pending states.** A named five-step ladder: **Unpublished → Ready → Verifying → Setting up → Live**, plus fail/offline states. This is the closest thing to the model I'd recommend Kodely copy.

**Timing.** "Up to 72 hours, though most updates are live within a few hours" — more conservative than everyone else's 48.

**Non-payment.** Custom domains need a paid plan; after downgrading to Free you **cannot add or buy** domains, but **already-connected domains keep serving**. ## Shopify

**Buy in product.** Yes — Shopify is a **reseller through accredited registrar partners**, not the registrar itself; domains registered in the customer's name. From **~$9 USD/yr**, billed annually, 1-year terms, auto-renew on by default, WHOIS privacy free on most eligible TLDs ([shopify.com/domains](https://www.shopify.com/domains)). No free-first-year offer; the free tier is the `.myshopify.com` subdomain.

**Connect an owned domain** ([Connect manually](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/domains/add-a-domain/connecting-domains/connect-domain-manual)):

| Type | Host | Value |
|---|---|---|
| A | `@` | `23.227.38.65` |
| AAAA | `@` | `2620:0127:f00f:5::` |
| CNAME | `www` | `shops.myshopify.com.` *(trailing period)* |

Regional variation in the A record's last octet (e.g. `23.227.38.32`) is documented as normal — worth knowing, because it means "the value I see doesn't match the docs" is *not* an error. Warnings: delete pre-existing A/AAAA records; only one A and one www CNAME; nameservers must be the provider's defaults.

**Nameservers.** Shopify only runs DNS for domains bought/transferred in — third-party domains stay at their host. (Consistent with the "use provider defaults" warning; not separately confirmed as policy — treat as inference.)

**Pending states.** Shopify defines "connected" as a **three-part conjunction**: DNS points to Shopify **and** the domain is live in all regions **and** the TLS certificate is provisioned. That tri-part definition is the best framing I found for what a green checkmark should actually mean. Timing: up to 48h.

**Non-payment / pause.** UNSURE — the Pause and Build article doesn't address domain behaviour.

## Cloudflare Pages

**Buy in product.** Cloudflare Registrar sells **at cost**: registry fee + the $0.18 ICANN fee, no markup, and registration price = renewal price. **.com ≈ $10.44/yr** (= $10.26 + $0.18). See [Cloudflare low-cost domains](https://www.cloudflare.com/application-services/solutions/low-cost-domain-names/). No free-first-year offer — the pitch is "no year-two surprise" instead.

**Connect an owned domain** ([Pages custom domains](https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/configuration/custom-domains/)):
- **Subdomain:** CNAME `shop.example.com` → `<your-site>.pages.dev`.
- **Apex:** the domain must be a Cloudflare zone — i.e. **nameservers moved to Cloudflare** — after which Cloudflare creates the record itself and CNAME-flattens the apex.
- Hard constraint worth noting: you must add the domain in the dashboard **before** creating the DNS record, or you get a **522**.

**Nameserver alternative.** For Pages apex it isn't an alternative, it's the requirement. Gain: apex works, DNS is managed for you, everything else Cloudflare. Loss: Cloudflare becomes your DNS authority and you must migrate every existing record.

**Status states / timing:** UNSURE — not documented on that page.

## Cloudflare for SaaS — the reference implementation

This is the "one CNAME and we do the rest" pattern in its canonical form ([Getting started](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/start/getting-started/)).

**What the end customer does:** exactly one CNAME, from their hostname to the SaaS provider's published target (e.g. `customers.saasprovider.com`), which resolves onward to the provider's fallback origin. Nothing else. No IPs, no per-tenant values.

**Validation:** three options — TXT, HTTP-automatic (fires once the CNAME is live), or **Delegated DCV** (the customer delegates `_acme-challenge` once, and every future renewal is hands-off). Pre-validation before cutover avoids a downtime window; HTTP-automatic after cutover creates a short one.

**State machine** ([Validation status](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/domain-support/hostname-validation/validation-status/)) — two **independent** axes, which is the key design insight:
- `status`: `pending` → `active` / `active re-deploying` / `blocked` (abuse) / `moved` (stopped pointing at the fallback origin, or exceeded the validation backoff) / `deleted` (after 7+ days in `moved`).
- `ssl.status`: tracks issuance and deployment separately; `active` when issued **and** deployed.

Production-ready = `status: active` **and** `ssl.status: active`. Exact backoff schedule: UNSURE.

**Pricing** ([Plans](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/plans/)): **100 custom hostnames free on Free/Pro/Business**, then **$0.10 per hostname/month** up to 50,000. Wildcard custom hostnames, mTLS and custom certificates are Enterprise-only.

---

# 2. The "one CNAME and we do the rest" pattern

Three distinct commercial shapes:

**a) Edge-terminated proxy (Cloudflare for SaaS, Approximated).** The customer points one record at your edge; the edge does ACME and TLS termination and forwards to your origin.
- [Approximated](https://approximated.app/docs/) supports both apex-A and CNAME-to-intermediary. Their honest note: if you publish a raw IP for apex A records, **changing that IP means every customer must edit their DNS individually** — the argument for an intermediary hostname or an ALIAS-capable answer.
- Approximated's status enum is *diagnosis-shaped* rather than progress-shaped, which is worth stealing wholesale: `ACTIVE_SSL`, `DNS_INCORRECT` (resolving, but pointed somewhere else), `DNS_NOT_RESOLVING` (no records at all), `TARGET_NOT_LOADING` (reaching us, origin dead) — plus booleans `apx_hit`, `is_resolving`, `has_ssl`.
- Pricing ([Approximated](https://approximated.app/pricing)): **$0.20/domain/month**, $20/mo minimum under 100 domains, 400 GB included; self-hosted hybrid $199/mo + $0.10/vhost.

**b) Platform API on an existing host (Vercel for Platforms).** You call `addProjectDomain`, poll `getDomainConfig`, and render the returned records. Verification via `_vercel` TXT only when contested. **No per-domain charge within plan limits.** Vercel additionally ships the front-end as a **drop-in block** with 20-second polling and automatic record-type selection.

**c) Write the customer's DNS for them (Domain Connect / Entri).** This is the category that actually removes the DNS step rather than explaining it.
- [Domain Connect](https://www.domainconnect.org/) is the open, MIT-licensed standard (originated at GoDaddy, submitted to the IETF) for a service provider to hand a DNS provider a templated set of records the user approves in one click.
- [Entri](https://developers.entri.com/connect/overview) is the commercial implementation: JWT from your backend → `entri.connectDomain(config)` → provider auto-detected → user logs into their registrar inside a whitelabeled modal → records written → **webhook to your server when the records go live**. **70+ providers** with direct API login; unsupported providers fall back to registrar-specific step-by-step instructions rather than failing.
- Pricing ([Entri plans](https://www.entri.com/plans)): Startup **$249/mo, 600 domains/year, 1,200 monitored**; Growth 2,400/yr; Premium 12,000/yr; Enterprise beyond. No free tier. Named results: ClickFunnels, Fourthwall (97% fewer DNS tickets).
- **Webflow and Lovable both use Entri.** That is the competitive fact that matters most for Kodely: your two nearest comparables have already bought their way out of the DNS-instructions problem.

**Two constraints any of these designs must respect:**
- **Apex can't be a CNAME** — RFC 1034 forbids other data alongside a CNAME, and the apex must carry SOA/NS (and usually MX). Hence A records, or provider-specific ALIAS/ANAME/CNAME-flattening. Netlify and Cloudflare handle this correctly; most builders just hand out a raw IP.
- **Let's Encrypt rate limits** ([official](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/)): 50 certs per registered domain / 7 days; 5 duplicate certs / 7 days; 300 new orders per account / 3 hours; 5 failed validations per identifier / hour. Let's Encrypt explicitly recommends large integrators use **one account for many customers**, with an override request form (takes weeks). Heroku's docs add the practical corollary: repeatedly toggling cert management off/on gets you rate-limited and support cannot bypass it.

---

# 3. Honest status copy for DNS/TLS pending states

**Finding: there is no canonical published style guide for this.** I looked for one in design-system content guidelines (Polaris, GOV.UK) and found nothing DNS-specific. What exists is three separate bodies of material you have to assemble yourself.

**(a) The "propagation is a myth" literature — use it to replace the copy, not just to feel superior.**
- [Julia Evans, "DNS 'propagation' is actually caches expiring"](https://jvns.ca/blog/2021/12/06/dns-doesn-t-propagate/) is the best single source. DNS is **pull, not push**: nothing propagates; you are waiting for cached records to expire. A brand-new record is available instantly. The delay only exists when you're *replacing* something already cached.
- Her two gotchas matter enormously for a builder product: **negative caching** — if a customer (or your own checker) queries a record before it exists, the *absence* is cached, governed by the SOA MINIMUM/TTL, often an hour — and **nameserver changes are genuinely the slowest case** because both the registry update and the cached NS records (typically 1-day TTL) have to clear.
- [Tiger Computing](https://www.tiger-computing.co.uk/myth-dns-propagation/) traces the "24–48 hours" number to a worst case of a 24h TTL plus resolvers that ignore TTLs. [ManagingWP](https://managingwp.io/2023/11/02/why-dns-propagation-is-misunderstood-and-abused-by-support-representives/) makes the customer-facing argument: it's used as a scapegoat answer instead of troubleshooting, when in practice changes usually go live in minutes.
- **Important nuance so you don't overcorrect:** a [Let's Encrypt community thread](https://community.letsencrypt.org/t/dont-say-propagation-in-dns/171127) records staff pushing back — there *is* real propagation *inside* a DNS provider's own infrastructure (zone distribution to their anycast edge), on the order of seconds to minutes. So "nothing propagates" is also wrong. The honest line is: *a short real delay at your DNS provider, then cache expiry governed by your old record's TTL.*

**(b) Generic progress research.** [NN/g on progress indicators](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/progress-indicators/): past ~10 seconds you owe the user more than a spinner; when you genuinely cannot estimate a duration, show **a list of completed and remaining steps** and a deliberately vague-but-honest estimate rather than a precise number that will be wrong. Their explicit warning against overpromising speed is exactly the failure mode of "usually takes a few minutes!" copy that then takes six hours.

**(c) De-facto best practice, read off products that got it right.** No one wrote the guide, but four products effectively demonstrate it:

- **Heroku ACM** publishes a full status table with the distinction almost everyone else omits — **`Failing`** (couldn't verify, *still retrying for up to an hour*) vs **`Failed`** (*stopped trying*). Plus `In Progress` → `DNS Verified` → `Cert Issued`, and a concrete anchor: **45–60 minutes** to generate the certificate ([Heroku ACM](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/automated-certificate-management)). "We are still trying" vs "we gave up, act now" is the highest-value single distinction in the whole problem space.
- **Approximated** models states as *diagnoses*, not progress: no records at all vs records pointing elsewhere vs reaching us but origin down. Each maps to a different customer instruction.
- **Cloudflare for SaaS** separates hostname validation from certificate status as two independent axes, so "DNS is right but the cert isn't ready" is representable — a state most builder UIs collapse into a single misleading spinner.
- **Vercel** re-checks every 20 seconds rather than making the user hit refresh, auto-selects which record type to instruct, and — uniquely — publishes the actually-correct mitigation: **lower the TTL to ~60s before cutover, raise it after**.

**The copy pattern these converge on**, which I'd recommend for Kodely:
1. Name the specific check that hasn't passed, not the phase. "We can't see the A record for `example.com` yet" beats "Pending DNS".
2. **Show observed vs expected.** "We see `76.76.21.21`; we expect `185.x.x.x`." This turns a mystery into a diff a non-technical person can act on.
3. Anchor the ETA on the **TTL you actually read** from their current record, not on folklore. "Your DNS provider is caching the old value for 1 hour" is checkable and true.
4. Distinguish **still-retrying** from **stopped** and say when you'll next check.
5. Never conflate DNS-correct with certificate-issued with live-everywhere. Shopify's three-part definition of "connected" is the right bar.
6. Warn about negative caching before the customer trips it: if they visit the domain before the record exists, their own browser/ISP may cache the NXDOMAIN for ~an hour and they will conclude your product is broken.

**The uncomfortable finding:** even Vercel — which publishes the TTL-lowering advice — still ships "DNS changes take 24 to 48 hours to propagate" in its own multi-tenant docs. Every vendor here says 48 hours (Lovable says 72). So honest copy is currently an **unoccupied competitive position**, not a table-stakes catch-up.

---

# 4. Cross-cutting failure modes to design against

These recur across every vendor's forums and docs:

- **"Not secure" warning.** Caused by half-completed record sets (Wix warns about this explicitly), or by the certificate not yet issued while DNS already resolves. The customer sees a browser security interstitial on their own brand — the highest-severity outcome, and it's reachable by doing 50% of the instructions correctly.
- **`DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN` after a correct setup.** Usually negative caching (the customer checked too early) or local OS/browser cache. Mitigation: tell them not to check yet, and give them a "check from our servers" button so they're not diagnosing from their own poisoned cache.
- **Cloudflare orange-cloud proxy in front of your host.** With SSL/TLS mode **Flexible** plus an origin that redirects HTTP→HTTPS, you get `ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` ([Cloudflare docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/troubleshooting/too-many-redirects/)). Detect proxied Cloudflare records and warn explicitly. Heroku goes further and recommends *not* using its automated certs behind Cloudflare at all.
- **Both A records and nameservers set.** Nameservers win; the A records at the old provider become dead config the customer keeps re-checking. Wix maintains a whole article on switching connection methods because of this. If you offer both paths, detect and state which one is actually in force.
- **CAA records blocking Let's Encrypt** and **stale `_acme-challenge` records** from a previous host — both silently prevent certificate issuance with no DNS-level symptom. Vercel documents both; check for them automatically.
- **Conflicting pre-existing A/AAAA records.** Framer and Shopify both warn to delete them first. Non-technical customers add rather than replace.
- **60-day ICANN transfer lock** after registration or a prior transfer — surfaces as "why can't I move my domain" immediately after they buy one from you.
- **Registrar UI mangling the host field** — the biggest cause of failed TXT/verification-CNAME entries. Providers variously want `_lovable`, `_lovable.example.com`, or `@`; trailing dots are required by some (Shopify, Vercel) and rejected by others.

**Economics footnote if Kodely resells domains:** Verisign's wholesale .com is **$10.26**, rising **7% to $10.97 on 1 November 2026**, with up to three further 7% hikes permitted this contract cycle ([Domain Name Wire](https://domainnamewire.com/2026/04/23/breaking-verisign-raising-wholesale-com-prices/)). Add the $0.18 ICANN fee and at-cost is ~$10.44 today, ~$11.15 from November. A free-first-year offer therefore costs you roughly $10–11 per activated customer, and the market has bifurcated: Wix/Squarespace/Framer give year one free and recoup at $20–21 renewals; Cloudflare and Vercel sell at cost and compete on the absence of a year-two surprise.

<result>## 1. Atomic deploys for static sites

### 1.1 The symlink-swap pattern and why it's atomic

**Capistrano's layout** is the canonical reference implementation: a `releases/` directory of timestamped release folders, a `shared/` directory for data that persists across releases, `repo/` for VCS data, and `current` — "a symlink pointing to the latest release. This symlink is updated at the end of a successful deployment. If the deployment fails in any step the `current` symlink still points to the old release." ([capistranorb.com/documentation/getting-started/structure](https://capistranorb.com/documentation/getting-started/structure/))

**Why `ln -sfn` + `mv` is atomic.** `ln -sfn new_target link` does *not* atomically replace an existing symlink on all platforms — GNU coreutils `ln -f` may unlink-then-symlink, which leaves a window where the path does not exist. The reliable idiom is therefore:

```sh
ln -sfn /srv/sites/<id>/releases/<deploy_id> /srv/sites/<id>/current.tmp
mv -Tf /srv/sites/<id>/current.tmp /srv/sites/<id>/current    # rename(2)
```

`mv -T` on a symlink issues `rename(2)`, and that syscall is where the atomicity guarantee lives:

- Linux: "If *newpath* already exists, it will be atomically replaced, so that there is no point at which another process attempting to access *newpath* will find it missing." And critically for this pattern: "If *oldpath* refers to a symbolic link, the link is renamed; if *newpath* refers to a symbolic link, the link will be overwritten." ([man7.org rename(2)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/rename.2.html))
- POSIX: "a link named *new* shall remain visible to other threads throughout the renaming operation and refer either to the file referred to by *new* or *old* before the operation began." ([pubs.opengroup.org rename](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/functions/rename.html))

Both require the source and destination be on the same filesystem (`EXDEV` otherwise) — so `current.tmp` must live in the same directory/mount as `current`, not in `/tmp`.

Linux also offers `renameat2()` with `RENAME_EXCHANGE` ("Atomically exchange *oldpath* and *newpath*") and `RENAME_NOREPLACE`. `RENAME_EXCHANGE` is a nice primitive for a two-slot blue/green swap where you want the previous target preserved at a known path.

**In-flight requests are safe.** Because the swap replaces the *symlink*, any request nginx has already resolved holds an open file descriptor to the old release's inode. POSIX keeps that inode alive until the fd closes, so in-flight responses complete correctly even if you `rm -rf` the old release directory immediately after (the space is reclaimed when the last fd closes). This is why release pruning is safe without draining.

### 1.2 Does nginx pick up the swapped symlink immediately?

**Yes — provided `open_file_cache` is off (the default).** nginx resolves `root` + URI and calls `open()`/`stat()` per request, so the next request after the rename traverses the new symlink.

**Caveat 1 — `open_file_cache`.** `open_file_cache` "stores open file descriptors, their sizes and modification times; information on directory existence; file lookup errors". Default is `off`. `open_file_cache_valid` (default `60s`) "sets the time after which `open_file_cache` elements should be validated." ([nginx.org ngx_http_core_module](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html#open_file_cache)) So with the cache enabled, nginx can serve from a stale fd for up to `open_file_cache_valid` seconds after a swap. This is documented behaviour, not a bug: in [nginx trac #1235](https://trac.nginx.org/nginx/ticket/1235) a user rotating symlinks every minute with `open_file_cache_valid 1h` was told by Maxim Dounin that "Changing files once per minute with such a setting simply doesn't make sense, nginx certainly won't notice"; the ticket was closed invalid. **Recommendation:** for a multi-tenant static host, either leave `open_file_cache off`, or set `open_file_cache_valid` to a small value (1–5s) and accept a bounded stale window, and make your deploy path never serve mixed old/new HTML+assets (see 1.5).

**Caveat 2 — `disable_symlinks`.** This directive will *break* the symlink-swap pattern if misconfigured. `disable_symlinks on` → "If any component of the pathname is a symbolic link, access to a file is denied." `if_not_owner` → denied if link and target have different owners. `from=part` skips checking the initial part of the path. Available only where `openat()`/`fstatat()` exist (FreeBSD, Linux, Solaris), and "parameters `on` and `if_not_owner` add processing overhead." Default is `off`. ([nginx.org disable_symlinks](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html#disable_symlinks))

If you want symlink hardening in a multi-tenant box (to stop a customer's uploaded symlink escaping their docroot) while still using `current`, the shape is:

```nginx
root /srv/sites/$site_id/current;
disable_symlinks if_not_owner from=/srv/sites;   # skip the /srv/sites prefix
```
…but note `current` itself sits *after* `from=`, so it will still be checked. Practical resolutions: (a) put `current` outside the checked prefix by setting `from=$document_root` **and** having `$document_root` already be the resolved release path (resolve the symlink at config-generation/reload time), or (b) keep `disable_symlinks off` and rely on the fact that you, not the customer, write the docroot — which is the case here, since files come from Postgres, not from customer SFTP.

### 1.3 Alternatives to symlink swap

| Approach | How the switch happens | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Symlink swap** (`releases/` + `current`) | single `rename(2)` | Simplest; instant rollback; same-filesystem constraint; open_file_cache caveat |
| **Blue/green docroots** | two fixed dirs `a/`/`b/`, swap via `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` or an nginx `map` of site→docroot + reload | Config reload is not atomic per-request the way rename is; adds a reload cost per deploy |
| **Content-addressed asset dirs** | assets stored under `/blobs/<sha256>`, release dir is a tree of hardlinks/symlinks into the blob store | Dedupes across releases and across sites; makes "N previous releases" nearly free in disk terms; pairs naturally with `rsync --link-dest` |
| **Object storage + CDN origin** | upload immutable objects, then flip a pointer (manifest/alias) | Removes per-box state entirely; introduces CDN purge as the new correctness problem |

**Netlify** publishes definitions for the model you're copying: an *atomic deploy* means "make updates available only when they are complete and totally in place" — "the new version of the site only begins receiving requests when all assets and configurations are available"; an *immutable deploy* means "guarantee the integrity of previous deploys by insulating them from future actions," where a deploy "becomes an artifact which will not change" and "deploys result in new versions or instances of the site, and traffic is routed to them accordingly." ([netlify.com/blog terminology-explained-atomic-and-immutable-deploys](https://www.netlify.com/blog/2021/02/23/terminology-explained-atomic-and-immutable-deploys/)) Netlify does **not** publish the underlying storage mechanism on that page — but their deploy API (§2.1) reveals it is content-addressed by SHA1.

**Vercel** frames the same thing as *Instant Rollback*: "Vercel points your domains back to the selected deployment" and "The rollback happens instantaneously." Eligibility: "Deployments previously aliased to a production domain are eligible for Instant Rollback." Note a design detail worth stealing: after a rollback, "Vercel turns off auto-assignment of production domains" so the next push doesn't silently clobber the rolled-back state — you must explicitly `vercel promote` to undo. ([vercel.com/docs/instant-rollback](https://vercel.com/docs/instant-rollback))

### 1.4 Rollback: keeping N releases

Capistrano's model: keep the last N releases (`keep_releases`, **default 5**), prune the rest with `deploy:cleanup`. `cap deploy:rollback` runs `deploy:reverting` — "identifies the last known good release by examining the releases folder... sets the `release_path` to the second-most recent release" — and `deploy:finishing_rollback`, which archives and removes the bad release. A specific target can be chosen: `cap staging deploy:rollback ROLLBACK_RELEASE=20160614133327`. Capistrano itself warns: "Capistrano provides basic rollback support, but... it is up to the individual to test and validate that rollback behaves correctly for their use case." ([capistranorb.com rollbacks](https://capistranorb.com/documentation/getting-started/rollbacks/))

For your product, the clean design is:
- `deployments` table row per deploy with a `deploy_id`, content manifest hash, and status; `releases/<deploy_id>` on disk.
- Rollback = re-run the swap step pointing `current` at an older `deploy_id`. It should be the *same code path* as deploy, minus the file transfer (files already present). That makes rollback ~1 syscall.
- Keep N (5–10) or N-days, whichever is larger, and never prune the currently-live release or the one immediately prior.
- Copy Vercel's "pin" semantics: after a rollback, set a `pinned_deploy_id` so an automatic republish doesn't re-break the site.

### 1.5 The stale-index / fresh-asset problem

The failure: a visitor's browser has `index.html` cached from the old deploy but requests assets from the new deploy (or vice versa). Two independent fixes, both required:

**(a) Different caching policy per resource class.** MDN's normative guidance:

- Hashed/fingerprinted assets: `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable` — "When you use a cache-busting pattern for resources and apply them to a long `max-age`, you can also add `immutable` to avoid revalidation." ([MDN Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control))
- HTML: `Cache-Control: no-cache`. MDN is explicit that this is widely misread: "`no-cache` does not mean 'don't cache'. `no-cache` allows caches to store a response but requires them to revalidate it before reuse."

web.dev says the same thing more tersely: versioned URLs get `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000`; unversioned URLs (HTML) get `Cache-Control: no-cache` paired with an `ETag` (preferred over `Last-Modified`), yielding cheap `304 Not Modified` responses. ([web.dev/articles/http-cache](https://web.dev/articles/http-cache))

Normative sources for the directives:
- **RFC 9111, HTTP Caching** (June 2022) — `no-cache` (§5.2.2.4): "The response MUST NOT be used to satisfy any other request without forwarding it for validation"; `max-age` (§5.2.2.1): "The response is to be considered stale after its age is greater than the specified number of seconds"; `must-revalidate` (§5.2.2.2): "Once the response has become stale, a cache MUST NOT reuse that response... until it has been successfully validated by the origin." ([rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html))
- **`immutable` is *not* in RFC 9111** — it's **RFC 8246, "HTTP Immutable Responses"**: "the immutable Cache-Control extension indicates that the origin server will not update the representation of that resource during the freshness lifetime of the response," and clients "SHOULD NOT issue a conditional request during the response's freshness lifetime (e.g., upon a reload)." ([rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8246.html](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8246.html)) That reload behaviour is the actual value of `immutable` — it kills the revalidation storm when a user hits refresh.

Consider also `stale-while-revalidate=<n>` on HTML to hide origin latency without serving indefinitely-stale markup.

**(b) Keep old assets alive.** Even with correct headers, a cached `index.html` will request the *old* hashed asset filenames. If you deleted the old release, those 404 and the page breaks. This is the strongest argument for content-addressed asset storage: `/assets/<sha256>.js` files from prior releases stay resolvable for as long as any HTML might reference them (retain ≥ your HTML `max-age` + a margin; with `no-cache` HTML the window is short, but proxies and offline caches make "a few days minimum" the safe answer). A symlink-swap docroot where each release is a full independent tree only satisfies this if you serve assets from a shared, union'd path rather than from `current/` alone.

Concrete nginx shape:

```nginx
location ~* ^/assets/ {            # hashed filenames only
    root /srv/sites/$site_id/blobs_view;   # shared across releases
    add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" always;
}
location / {
    root /srv/sites/$site_id/current;
    add_header Cache-Control "no-cache" always;
    etag on;
}
```

### 1.6 CDN / proxy cache invalidation

Three strategies, in increasing order of robustness:

1. **Cache-busting (no purge at all)** — change the URL. Works perfectly for hashed assets, impossible for `/` and `/about`.
2. **Purge by URL** — precise, but you must enumerate every changed path, and wildcards aren't supported. Cloudflare notes "Wildcards are not supported on single file purge, and you must use purge by hostname, prefix, or implement cache tags as an alternative." ([Cloudflare purge-by-single-file](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/how-to/purge-cache/purge-by-single-file/))
3. **Purge by tag / surrogate key** — the right primitive for "invalidate everything belonging to deploy X". Fastly: tag "related assets... with surrogate keys, and these grouped URLs can be purged in a single request"; `POST /service/{id}/purge/{surrogate_key}` for one key, `POST /service/{id}/purge` for up to 256 keys in a batch; `Fastly-Soft-Purge: 1` "marks the affected object as stale rather than making it inaccessible," which lets you revalidate instead of stampeding your origin. ([Fastly purging API](https://www.fastly.com/documentation/reference/api/purging/))

Cloudflare offers all five methods — purge everything, by prefix (max 30 prefixes per API call), by hostname, by URL, and by cache-tag (`Cache-Tag` response header; max 1,024 chars per tag in an API call) — and as of April 2025 all methods are available on all plans. ([Cloudflare purge-cache docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/how-to/purge-cache/), [purge-by-tags](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cache/how-to/purge-cache/purge-by-tags/), [changelog 2025-04-01](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2025-04-01-purge-for-all/))

**nginx `proxy_cache_purge` — verified: NGINX Plus only.** The directive *is* documented on nginx.org, but the page marks it "This functionality is available as part of our commercial subscription." Syntax `proxy_cache_purge string ...;` — "If at least one value of the string parameters is not empty and is not equal to '0' then the cache entry with a corresponding cache key is removed. The result of successful operation is indicated by returning the 204 (No Content) response." It supports a trailing `*` wildcard on the cache key. The OSS build ships `proxy_cache`, `proxy_cache_valid`, `proxy_cache_bypass`, `proxy_cache_use_stale`, `proxy_cache_background_update`, and `proxy_cache_revalidate`, but **no purge**. ([nginx.org ngx_http_proxy_module#proxy_cache_purge](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_cache_purge))

**Practical consequence for an OSS-nginx hosting product:** don't try to purge. Put the deploy ID in the cache key so a new deploy is a new key namespace and the old entries age out on their own:

```nginx
proxy_cache_key "$scheme$request_method$host$request_uri|$deploy_id";
```
(with `$deploy_id` from a `map` or from the upstream's response). This is purge-by-cache-busting applied at the proxy layer, and it needs no commercial license. A third-party `ngx_cache_purge` module exists for OSS nginx, but I did not verify its current maintenance status — **UNSURE**; treat it as a risk if you plan to depend on it.

---

## 2. Transferring files to a server safely

### 2.1 Handoff options

| Option | Credentials | Idempotency | Partial failure | Retry |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HTTP API accepting a tarball/zip** | Short-lived bearer token per deploy, scoped to one site. Easiest to rotate. | Natural: `Idempotency-Key`/`deploy_id` header | Whole-artifact: either the tarball landed or it didn't. Atomic by construction. | Trivial — POST again with same key |
| **HTTP API, content-addressed manifest + per-blob upload** (Netlify's model) | Same | Per-blob idempotency is free (blob name *is* the hash) | Resumable at blob granularity; missing blobs re-requested | Best-in-class |
| **rsync over SSH** | Long-lived SSH key on the app server that can write to hosting boxes. Blast radius if leaked. Needs `command=` forced-command + `rrsync` restriction. | Not idempotent as a unit — see below | Leaves a half-updated tree unless you rsync into a *new* release dir | Re-run is safe only into a fresh release dir |
| **S3-compatible object storage as handoff** | App writes with its own creds; box pulls with read-only creds or presigned URLs. No inbound port on the box. | Object keys can be `deploys/<deploy_id>/...` | Box retries the pull independently | Excellent; also gives you a durable artifact store for free |
| **Pull-based agent on the box** | Box holds an outbound-only credential; **no inbound SSH/HTTP from the internet** | Agent reconciles to desired state (§3.3) | Agent retries locally; app never blocks | Best for fleets; worst for latency-to-first-deploy |

**rsync specifics.** rsync is *not* atomic across a file set. Its closest option is `--delay-updates`: "This option puts the temporary file from each updated file into a holding directory until the end of the transfer, at which time all the files are renamed into place in rapid succession. This attempts to make the updating of the files **a little closer to atomic**." It conflicts with `--inplace`/`--append`, implies `--no-inc-recursive`, and needs disk headroom for a second copy. The man page itself points elsewhere for real atomicity: "See also the 'atomic-rsync' python script in the 'support' subdirectory for an update algorithm that is even closer to atomic (it uses `--link-dest` and a parallel hierarchy of files)." ([rsync man page](https://download.samba.org/pub/rsync/rsync.1))

That `--link-dest` + parallel-hierarchy trick is exactly the `releases/` + `current` model: rsync into `releases/<new>` with `--link-dest=../<previous>` so unchanged files become hardlinks (near-zero disk cost per release), then rename the symlink. If you go the rsync route, use that — not `--delay-updates` into a live docroot.

**Recommendation for your architecture.** Files already live as rows in Postgres, so you control the manifest cheaply. The strongest fit is a **content-addressed HTTP API modeled on Netlify's digest deploy**:

1. `POST /deploys` with `{"deploy_id": "...", "files": {"/index.html": "<sha256>", ...}}`
2. Server replies with `required: [<hashes it doesn't already have>]`
3. `PUT` each required blob
4. `POST /deploys/{id}/publish` → server materializes `releases/<deploy_id>` and does the rename

Netlify's published API does precisely this: POST a JSON map of path → SHA1, get back `{"id": "1234", "required": ["907d14fb..."]}`, then `PUT /api/v1/deploys/{deploy_id}/files/index.html` with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` for each required hash. "If you have duplicate files with the same SHA1, you only upload once." Deploys expected to exceed 30s pass `"async": true` and are polled via `GET /api/v1/sites/{site_id}/deploys/{deploy_id}`. A single-zip alternative exists with a 25,000-file limit. ([docs.netlify.com/api/get-started](https://docs.netlify.com/api/get-started/))

This gives you: dedupe across deploys and across sites, resumability, free integrity verification, and a natural blob store for the "keep old hashed assets alive" requirement from §1.5.

**Tarball security note.** If you do accept archives, the extraction step is the attack surface: reject absolute paths, `..` components, symlinks/hardlinks pointing outside the tree, device nodes, and setuid bits; enforce entry-count, per-entry-size, and total-decompressed-size limits (zip bombs). Extract to a fresh `releases/<deploy_id>` owned by an unprivileged per-site uid, never into `current/`.

### 2.2 Idempotency keys / deploy IDs

Stripe's `Idempotency-Key` is the canonical pattern and its exact semantics are worth copying verbatim ([docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)):

- "Stripe's idempotency works by saving the resulting status code and body of the first request made for any given idempotency key, **regardless of whether it succeeds or fails**. Subsequent requests with the same key return the same result, including `500` errors."
- "we suggest using V4 UUIDs, or another random string with enough entropy to avoid collisions. Idempotency keys are up to 255 characters long. Avoid using sensitive data... as idempotency keys."
- Retention: "You can remove keys from the system automatically after they're at least 24 hours old. We generate a new request if a key is reused after the original is pruned."
- Parameter mismatch: "The idempotency layer compares incoming parameters to those of the original request and errors if they're not the same to prevent accidental misuse."
- Concurrency and validation failures: "We save results only after the execution of an endpoint begins. If incoming parameters fail validation, or the request conflicts with another request that's executing concurrently, we don't save the idempotent result... You can retry these requests."
- "All `POST` requests accept idempotency keys. Don't send idempotency keys in `GET` and `DELETE` requests."

Two deliberate divergences for a deploy system:

1. **Use the `deploy_id` as the idempotency key, not a per-request UUID.** The deploy is the business object; the retry should converge on "deploy N is live," not "this HTTP call ran once." Make publish idempotent at the *state* level: `publish(deploy_id)` where `current` already points at `deploy_id` is a no-op returning success.
2. **Retain much longer than 24 hours.** Deploy records are cheap and you already have Postgres. Retain for the life of the deploy record so a retry weeks later still short-circuits rather than re-executing.

Guard against out-of-order publishes with a monotonic sequence: reject `publish(deploy_id)` if the site's live deploy has a higher sequence number than the one being published, *unless* the request is an explicit rollback (which carries a flag and bumps the sequence). Otherwise a slow retry of deploy #7 can silently undo deploy #8.

### 2.3 Content integrity

Ship a manifest and verify on both sides:

```json
{
  "deploy_id": "dpl_01J...",
  "algorithm": "sha256",
  "files": [{"path": "/index.html", "size": 4211, "sha256": "..."}],
  "manifest_sha256": "..."
}
```

- Verify each blob's digest **after write, before rename into the release tree**. A blob whose computed hash ≠ its name is discarded and re-requested.
- Verify the *set*: after materializing `releases/<deploy_id>`, walk it and confirm the file list and digests match the manifest exactly (catches truncation, missing files, and stray files).
- Only then do the symlink rename. This is the whole point of the two-phase design: transfer failures can never produce a live half-site.
- Store `manifest_sha256` on the deploy row. It's your deploy identity, your dedupe key, and your "is this box actually serving what we think it is?" probe for the reconciler in §3.3.

Netlify uses SHA1 for files (and SHA256 for functions); use SHA256 throughout — SHA1 is fine for dedupe but you're also using this for integrity, and there's no reason to defend the choice later.
