## 5. Failure-mode taxonomy: published status enums from real products

### 5.1 Cloudflare for SaaS — custom hostnames (the richest published model)

Two independent status fields, which is the key structural insight: **hostname validation and certificate issuance are separate state machines.** Cloudflare's own guidance: a hostname is production-ready only when "the hostname should have `status: active`, `ssl.status: active`, and DNS that points to your SaaS target," and "If `result.status` is `active` but `result.ssl.status` is not `active`, Cloudflare has validated the hostname, but the certificate has not completed issuance and deployment." ([Cloudflare hostname validation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/domain-support/hostname-validation/))

**Custom hostname `status`** — "Status of the hostname's activation" (exact enum from Cloudflare's published OpenAPI schema, [github.com/cloudflare/api-schemas](https://github.com/cloudflare/api-schemas)):

```
active, pending, active_redeploying, moved, pending_deletion, deleted,
pending_blocked, pending_migration, pending_provisioned, test_pending,
test_active, test_active_apex, test_blocked, test_failed, provisioned, blocked
```

Cloudflare's human-readable descriptions for the main ones ([validation-status](https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-for-platforms/cloudflare-for-saas/domain-support/hostname-validation/validation-status/)):
- **Pending** — "Custom hostname is pending hostname validation."
- **Active** — "Custom hostname has completed hostname validation and is active."
- **Active re-deploying** — "Customer hostname is active and the changes have been processed."
- **Blocked** — "Custom hostname cannot be added to Cloudflare at this time."
- **Moved** — "Custom hostname is not active after **Pending** for the entirety of the Validation Backoff Schedule or it no longer points to the fallback origin."
- **Deleted** — "Custom hostname was deleted from the zone."

**Custom hostname `ssl.status`** — "Status of the hostname's SSL certificates" (exact enum):

```
initializing, pending_validation, deleted, pending_issuance, pending_deployment,
pending_deletion, pending_expiration, expired, active, initializing_timed_out,
validation_timed_out, issuance_timed_out, deployment_timed_out, deletion_timed_out,
pending_cleanup, staging_deployment, staging_active, deactivating, inactive,
backup_issued, holding_deployment
```

Note the design: every `pending_X` has a matching `X_timed_out`. That is the single most valuable idea to copy — **a pending state without a corresponding timeout state is a bug**, because it means something can hang forever with no operator signal and no user-facing explanation.

Related enums from the same schema, for context:
- Certificate pack `status`: same 21-value list as `ssl.status` above.
- Certificate `status` (individual cert): `initializing, authorizing, active, expired, issuing, timing_out, pending_deployment`
- Fallback origin `status`: `initializing, pending_deployment, pending_deletion, active, deployment_timed_out, deletion_timed_out`

Cloudflare's prose descriptions of the certificate stages ([Certificate statuses](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ssl/reference/certificate-statuses/)) also note "Pending Cleanup — Old certificates are not deleted until the replacement has been successfully issued," and "Holding Deployment" for custom certificates when the zone status is Pending or Moved.

### 5.2 Vercel

Vercel splits the problem into **verification** (do you own it?) and **configuration** (does DNS actually point at us?), exposed as two different endpoints.

**Project domain object** (`GET /v9/projects/{idOrName}/domains/{domain}`) — required fields `apexName`, `name`, `projectId`, `verified`:

- `verified` (boolean): "`true` if the domain is verified for use with the project. If `false` it will not be used as an alias on this project until the challenge in `verification` is completed."
- `verification` (array): "A list of verification challenges, one of which must be completed to verify the domain for use on the project. After the challenge is complete `POST /projects/:idOrName/domains/:domain/verify` to verify the domain. Possible challenges: - If `verification.type = TXT` the `verification.domain` will be checked for a TXT record matching `verification.value`." Each entry requires `type`, `domain`, `value`, `reason`.
- Also: `redirect`, `redirectStatusCode` (`301, 302, 307, 308, null`), `gitBranch`, `customEnvironmentId`.

([vercel.com/docs/rest-api/projects/get-a-project-domain](https://vercel.com/docs/rest-api/reference/endpoints/projects/get-a-project-domain))

**Domain config object** (`GET /v6/domains/{domain}/config`) — this is where `misconfigured` lives:

- `misconfigured` (boolean): "Whether or not the domain is configured AND we can automatically generate a TLS certificate."
- `configuredBy`: enum `"A" | "CNAME" | "dns-01" | "http" | null` — "How we see the domain's configuration. - `CNAME`: Domain has a CNAME pointing to Vercel. - `A`: Domain's A record is resolving to Vercel. - `http`: Domain is resolving to Vercel but may be behind a Proxy. - `dns-01`: Domain is not resolving to Vercel but dns-01 challenge is enabled. - `null`: Domain is not resolving to Vercel."
- `acceptedChallenges`: array of `"dns-01" | "http-01"` — "Which challenge types the domain can use for issuing certs."
- `recommendedIPv4` / `recommendedCNAME`: ranked lists — "rank=1 is the preferred value(s) to use."

([openapi.vercel.sh](https://openapi.vercel.sh/) — the machine-readable spec; human docs at [vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/add-a-domain](https://vercel.com/docs/domains/working-with-domains/add-a-domain))

The `configuredBy: "http"` value — "resolving to Vercel but may be behind a Proxy" — is a real failure mode you will hit constantly: customers who put Cloudflare's orange cloud in front of your CNAME. Have a distinct state and a distinct error message for it.

**Domain `status`** — Heroku's published Platform API JSON schema (`GET https://api.heroku.com/schema`, `Accept: application/vnd.heroku+json; version=3`) defines `status` only as `{"description": "status of this record's cname", "type": ["string"], "example": "pending", "readOnly": true}` — **no `enum` is published**. Same for `acm_status` ("status of this record's ACM", example `"pending"`) and `acm_status_reason` ("reason for the status of this record's ACM", example `"Failing CCA check"`). The only enumerated field on the Domain resource is `kind`: `["heroku", "custom"]`.

**Verdict: UNSURE.** The commonly quoted `none` / `pending` / `succeeded` / `failing` set is *not* documented as an enum by Heroku anywhere I could find. Don't cite it as a published enum. ([devcenter.heroku.com/articles/platform-api-reference](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/platform-api-reference))

**Heroku ACM certificate statuses, however, *are* published** with descriptions ([devcenter.heroku.com/articles/automated-certificate-management](https://devcenter.heroku.com/articles/automated-certificate-management)):

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Cert Issued** | "A certificate has been issued for the domain." |
| **In Progress** | "Heroku is verifying your custom domain's DNS." |
| **DNS Verified** | "Heroku verified your custom domain's DNS and is in the process of generating the certificate." |
| **Waiting** | "Heroku is currently waiting to process your certificate." |
| **Failing** | "Heroku is unable to verify your DNS. We will keep trying to verify for up to an hour." |
| **Failed** | "Heroku is unable to verify your DNS. We have stopped trying to verify this domain." |

Timing: cert generation takes "between 45 and 60 minutes"; Failing retries for up to 1 hour before Failed; a notification goes out "after 3 days of attempts." Manual retry is `heroku certs:auto:refresh`. And a warning directly relevant to your rate-limit exposure: "Do not turn off ACM in an attempt to fix or speed up the ACM process. This can cause your account to reach a rate limit with Let's Encrypt."

Note the **`Failing` → `Failed` distinction** — retryable vs. terminal, surfaced to the user as different words. Copy this.

### 5.4 Netlify

**UNSURE / not published as enums.** Netlify's OpenAPI spec ([github.com/netlify/open-api](https://github.com/netlify/open-api), `swagger.yml`) types `site.state`, `deploy.state`, and `sniCertificate.state` as bare `type: string` with **no enum constraint**. The only enums in the spec are unrelated (env-var contexts and scopes). So there is no authoritative machine-readable status taxonomy to quote.

Netlify's docs do surface UI labels for domain state — "Awaiting External DNS", "Check DNS configuration", "Netlify DNS", "Waiting on DNS propagation" — plus certificate-level error strings like "`<domain>` doesn't appear to be served by Netlify" and "`<domain>` is not resolvable with a resolver that validates DNSSEC". ([docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/troubleshooting-tips](https://docs.netlify.com/manage/domains/troubleshooting-tips/))

That DNSSEC error is worth noting as a real failure mode: a customer with DNSSEC enabled and a stale DS record will fail ACME validation in a way that looks like a generic DNS problem. Give it its own state.

### 5.5 Recommended synthesis for your own state machine

From the above, the design that generalizes:

**Two orthogonal state machines per custom domain, plus one per deploy.**

```
domain.verification_status:
  pending_dns          -- awaiting customer DNS change
  verifying            -- our checker is polling
  verified             -- records correct and stable
  misconfigured        -- records present but wrong (has a `reason`)
  proxied              -- resolves to us but through a third-party proxy (Vercel's "http")
  conflict             -- in use by another tenant
  verification_timed_out  -- backoff schedule exhausted (Cloudflare's "moved")
  deleted

domain.cert_status:
  none
  pending_validation      / validation_timed_out
  pending_issuance        / issuance_timed_out
  pending_deployment      / deployment_timed_out
  active
  pending_expiration | expired
  renewal_failing         -- retryable (Heroku's "Failing")
  renewal_failed          -- terminal, needs human (Heroku's "Failed")
  rate_limited            -- CA said no; carries a retry_after

deploy.status:
  queued | transferring | verifying_integrity | publishing
  live | superseded | rolled_back
  failed_transfer | failed_integrity | failed_publish
```

Non-negotiable rules extracted from the sources:
1. **Every `pending_*` needs a `*_timed_out` sibling** (Cloudflare's schema is built entirely on this).
2. **Distinguish retryable failure from terminal failure in the enum itself**, not in a boolean elsewhere (Heroku's `Failing` vs `Failed`).
3. **Carry a machine-readable `reason` alongside the status** (Vercel's `verification[].reason`, Heroku's `acm_status_reason` — "Failing CCA check").
4. **Never collapse verification and certificate state into one field.** Cloudflare's docs exist largely to explain the case where `status: active` but `ssl.status != active`; a single field would make that case unrepresentable and your support burden much worse.
5. **Give a bounded validation budget with a defined terminal outcome** (Cloudflare: 7 days / 75 attempts, then the hostname is deleted). Unbounded pending states are how you end up with 40,000 zombie domains polling DNS forever.

The **2013 RAA HTML mirror on `itp.cdn.icann.org` works** and is the primary source below. Where I only have a search snippet and not a fetched page, I say so.

---

## 1. Legal / policy framing

### Definitions (2013 RAA, fetched: https://itp.cdn.icann.org/en/files/accredited-registrars/registrar-accreditation-agreement-21jan24-en.htm)

- **§1.18 Registered Name Holder** — *"means the holder of a Registered Name."* Deliberately circular: the RNH is whoever is in the registrant field of the registry/registrar record. There is no ICANN test of "who really paid" or "whose brand it is."
- **§1.19 Registrar** — *"a person or entity that contracts with Registered Name Holders and with a Registry Operator and collects registration data about the Registered Name Holders and submits registration information for entry in the Registry Database."*
- **§1.26 Reseller** — *"a person or entity that participates in Registrar's distribution channel for domain name registrations (a) pursuant to an agreement, arrangement or understanding with Registrar or (b) with Registrar's actual knowledge, provides some or all Registrar Services, including collecting registration data about Registered Name Holders, submitting that data to Registrar, or facilitating the entry of the registration agreement between Registrar and the Registered Name Holder."*

Note the structure: the registration agreement is **between the Registrar and the Registered Name Holder**. The reseller *facilitates* that agreement; it is not a party to the registration relationship in ICANN's model.

### The single most load-bearing clause for a website builder

**RAA §3.7.7.3** (verbatim):

> *"Any Registered Name Holder that intends to license use of a domain name to a third party is nonetheless the Registered Name Holder of record and is responsible for providing its own full contact information and for providing and updating accurate technical and administrative contact information adequate to facilitate timely resolution of any problems that arise in connection with the Registered Name."*

This is the clause that decides the design question. If a platform registers a customer's domain in the **platform's** name and lets the customer "use" it, the platform is the RNH of record and is *responsible* — including under **§3.7.7.9** (RNH represents that the registration *"does not infringe the legal rights of any third party"*) and **§3.7.7.12** (RNH indemnifies the Registry Operator). The platform absorbs the customer's trademark and content liability, and would be the respondent in a UDRP.

Other relevant RAA text (verbatim):
- **§3.7.7.1** — *"The Registered Name Holder shall provide to Registrar accurate and reliable contact details and correct and update them within seven (7) days of any change during the term of the Registered Name registration."*
- **§3.12.2** — *"Any registration agreement used by reseller shall include all registration agreement provisions and notices required by the ICANN Registrar Accreditation Agreement and any ICANN Consensus Policies."*
- **§3.12.3** — Registrar must ensure *"Its Resellers identify the sponsoring registrar upon inquiry from the customer."*
- **§3.12.5** — Reseller customers must be *"provided with a link to an ICANN webpage detailing registrant educational information."*
- §3.12 opener: the **Registrar remains responsible for provision of Registrar Services regardless of reseller involvement**.

**UNSURE / important nuance:** the 2013 RAA contains **no clause literally saying "the reseller must not be the Registered Name Holder."** I searched the RAA text for such a sentence and it is not there. The prohibition is *structural and indirect*: §1.19/§3.7.7 make the registration agreement a Registrar↔RNH contract; §3.7.7.3 makes whoever is in the registrant field the RNH of record with full liability; and §3.12.3 forces disclosure of the sponsoring registrar. So a reseller *can* physically put itself in the registrant field — that is exactly the "domain hostage" pattern — but it then legally *is* the registrant, with all attendant duties, and the customer is a mere licensee with no ICANN-recognized standing.

### Registrant vs. admin / tech / billing contact — and the 2025 change that matters

Historically gTLD registrations carried four contact sets (Registrant, Admin, Tech, Billing). Only the **Registrant** is the RNH; Admin/Tech/Billing are operational contacts with no ownership meaning. Under the **ICANN Registration Data Policy** (published 21 Feb 2024, in force 21 Aug 2025) this collapsed:

Tucows/OpenSRS, fetched: https://opensrs.com/blog/what-icanns-updated-registration-data-policy-rdp-means-for-opensrs-resellers/
> *"We'll stop collecting the administrative, billing, and technical contact sets unless specifically required by the registry."*

Registrant contact remains mandatory (name, address, country, telephone, email). Key operational dates from that page: 30 June 2025 admin/billing/tech collection ceases; 28 July 2025 API returns only the minimum data set; **21 August 2025 the updated RDP takes effect**.

**Design consequence:** the classic advice "put the client as registrant, the agency as admin/tech contact" is now partly obsolete — in most gTLDs *there is no admin/tech contact slot left to occupy*. A platform's operational control has to come from account access and DNS delegation, not from a contact record.

And the Organization-field trap, from the same OpenSRS page:
> *"They should leave the organization field blank, unless they want the organization to be the legal registrant."*

Putting the platform's company name in the registrant **Organization** field makes the platform the legal registrant, regardless of whose personal name is in the first/last name fields. (A secondary, non-primary source — search snippet from smartbranding.com, not fetched — states the same: from 21 Aug 2025, if the Organization field is populated, that organization is treated as the legal owner and the personal name is only a point of contact.)

---

## 2. What each platform actually does

### Wix — accredited registrar for some TLDs, reseller for the rest; customer is registrant

- **ICANN-accredited:** Wix.com Ltd. appeared on the ICANN registrar list with **IANA ID 3817** in July 2018. Before that Wix was a reseller: *"Wix currently acts as a reseller for Network Solutions, a Web.com company."* — fetched: https://domainincite.com/23243-wix-com-obtains-icann-accreditation-bad-news-for-web-com
- **Still resells.** Wix's own help center links out to **two** upstream registration agreements: *"Domain Registration Agreement for Web.com"* and *"Domain Registration Agreement for Tucows"* — fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/change-in-terms-of-use-mailbox-and-domain-renewals. Third-party summary (fetched: https://www.certifiedcode.us/resources/article/is-wix-a-domain-registrar) says Wix is *"an ICANN-accredited domain registrar"* supporting *"over 75 different top-level domains"* and acts as *"the Registrar of Record, entering your information into the WHOIS database."* Search snippets (not fetched) claim Wix is directly accredited for **.com/.net** and resells everything else — **UNSURE**, I could not verify the exact TLD split from a Wix-owned page.
- **Who is registrant:** the customer. Wix's ownership doc is explicit that the ICANN record wins over billing: *"Recognize the domain registrant (listed in databases like ICANN) as the domain's owner"* and *"If billing details and domain owner details conflict, Wix may prioritize the domain's registrant as the owner."* — fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/wix-site-and-content-ownership
- **Transfer out** (fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/transferring-your-wix-domain-away-from-wix-2477749): *"We'll send a transfer authorization code (EPP code) to your domain's registrant contact email address."* — i.e., the code goes to the **registrant email**, not the Wix account login. *"Your domain must be unlocked before you begin the transfer."* *"You cannot transfer a domain within 60 days of purchase. Changing your registrant contact information locks your domain from transfer for 60 days."* Transfer takes up to 7 days.
- **60-day lock** (fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/icanns-60-day-lock-policy): triggered by *"Registering the domain, Changing the registrant contact information, Transferring your domain between different domain providers"*, and *"cannot be changed by Wix."* Wix explicitly warns: transfer **before** changing contact info to avoid tripping the lock.

### Squarespace — genuinely accredited (two accreditations), plus reseller relationships

- **Accredited entities:** the DRA (fetched: https://www.squarespace.com/domain-registration-agreement) names **Squarespace Domains LLC (SDL)**, **Squarespace Domains II LLC (SD2L)**, and **Squarespace Domains Canada Inc. (SDC)**, and states *"Each US Squarespace Registrar Entity is an ICANN-accredited registrar"* with its own RAA (SDC is CIRA-accredited).
- **Registrant definition** (same DRA, verbatim): *"you or the organization you are acting for or on behalf of as the registered name holder of the domain name registration."* The customer is the RNH.
- **Squarespace also resells:** *"Squarespace Domains LLC, Squarespace Domains II LLC, the Tucows family of registrars, and the Key-Systems family of registrars"* — fetched: https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/205812338-Transferring-a-domain-away-from-Squarespace. So even an accredited platform runs a mixed portfolio.

Squarespace is a Domains Registrar."* / *"Domain Reseller: An organization enabled to register domains on behalf of a Registrar."*
- **Google Domains acquisition:** completed **7 September 2023** — fetched: https://www.squarespace.com/press-releases/2023/9/7/squarespace-completes-acquisition-of-google-domains-assets. The release says Squarespace *"will, after a transition period, initiate the transfer of Google Domains accounts to its Squarespace Domains platform"* and commits to *"making it a globally recognized, independent domain registrar."* Price and exact domain count are **not** in the press release. **Squarespace Domains II LLC carries IANA ID 895** (fetched: https://domaindetails.com/registrars/squarespace-domains-ii-llc) — 895 was Google LLC's accreditation, i.e. the accreditation itself was transferred rather than the domains being bulk-migrated to a new IANA ID. ### Shopify — pure reseller of Tucows; merchant is the Registered Name Holder

- **Registrar:** **Tucows Domains Inc.** Shopify's own Domain Registration Agreement (fetched: https://app.shopify.com/legal/domain_registration_agreement.html) is a Tucows agreement, describing services *"offered through Shopify, the Reseller participating in Tucows' distribution channel."*
- **Registrant:** verbatim from that agreement — *"the person named as Registrant on the Whois shall be the 'Registered Name Holder.'"* The registrant is the merchant, contracting **with Tucows**, paying fees **to Shopify** as reseller. This is textbook RAA §1.26 / §3.12.
- Shopify's marketing page states it flatly (fetched: https://www.shopify.com/domains): *"Your domain is registered in your name and managed from your Shopify admin, and you can transfer it out at any time (subject to ICANN/registry rules)"* and *"Shopify sells domains as a reseller through accredited registrar partners."*
- **Designated Agent:** the agreement contains *"Registrant explicitly authorizes Tucows to act as their Designated Agent, as stipulated by the ICANN Transfer Policy, to approve a Change of Registrant on their behalf."* Same clause appears in the upstream Tucows Master Domain Registration Agreement (fetched: https://assets.opensrs.com/Uploads/Master_Domain_Registration_Agreement.html), which also confirms *"The person named as Registrant on record with Tucows shall be the 'Registered Name Holder.'"* This matters: the Designated Agent mechanism is what lets a platform change registrant details without a two-sided email confirmation dance.

### Vercel — reseller of Name.com and Tucows; registrant is the Team Owner

Fetched: https://vercel.com/legal/domain-name-registration-and-services-terms

(Design note: tying the registrant to a *Team Owner* role rather than to the legal entity is a real-world failure mode when that employee leaves.)
- Vercel disclaims the registrar role — registration data flows to *"the applicable Registrar, which acts as the data controller."*
- **Exit obligation, verbatim:** *"You may terminate the Domain Name Terms by allowing to lapse, assigning, or transferring to an alternative registrar the registration of all Domain Names currently using Vercel's Registration Services."* On termination Vercel will *"assist Customer to transfer any Domain Name registrations that have not expired to an alternative registrar of choice"* within 14 days if requested. The terms contain **no** "auth code," "Registered Name Holder," or "reseller" language — **UNSURE** whether Vercel documents a 60-day lock anywhere in its legal terms.
- **Mechanically**, Vercel exposes the whole registrar surface as API: `GET .../registrar/…/auth-code` ("Retrieve authorization codes for domain transfers"), buy, transfer-in, transfer-status, renew, auto-renew, nameservers, contact-info schema — https://vercel.com/docs/domains/registrar-api. The purchase endpoint requires a full `contactInformation` object — `firstName`, `lastName`, `email`, `phone`, `address1`, `city`, `state`, `zip`, `country` required, with **optional `companyName`** — https://vercel.com/docs/rest-api/domains-registrar/buy-a-domain. That optional `companyName` maps to the registrant Organization field, i.e. it is the field that decides legal ownership under the 2025 RDP. This is the closest thing to a reference API shape for a builder implementing option (c).

Conflicting evidence, and I could not fetch Webflow's own pages (help.webflow.com 403, webflow.com/integrations 403 header-overflow):

|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wix | Yes, Wix.com Ltd, IANA 3817 (2018) — but also resells | Web.com, Tucows | Customer | Emailed to **registrant contact email** |
| Squarespace | Yes — SDL, SD2L (IANA 895), SDC(CIRA) — also resells | Tucows family, Key‑Systems family | Customer ("registered name holder") | Emailed to **registrant email**, ≤24h |
| Shopify | No | Tucows Domains Inc. | Merchant ("named as Registrant on the Whois") | **Self-service in admin** |
| Vercel | No | Name.com, Tucows Domains Inc. | Customer / **Team Owner** | **API + dashboard** |
| Webflow | UNSURE | UNSURE | UNSURE | UNSURE |

**Nobody in this set registers customer domains in the platform's own name.** That is the strongest single finding.

---

## 3. Transfer-out mechanics and the hazard

### The auth code / TAC obligation

- **Deadline: 5 calendar days.** *"The registrar is required to provide the Auth-Code to the domain name owner within five calendar days of the owner's request, and ICANN accepts complaints about registrars that do not."* — fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auth-Code. Corroborated by registrar KB, fetched: https://help.101domain.com/kb/finding-the-auth-epp-code — *"The Registrar must provide you with the Auth-Info code within 5 calendar days of your request."*
- **The 2024 Transfer Policy renamed and re-scoped the code.** Per https://seo.domains/seo-resources/transfer-process/epp-code-auth-code/ (fetched): the **TAC** is *"generated on demand and lives no more than 14 calendar days"* — it is no longer a static, always-present value; the registry stores it as a one-way hash; it is single-use. The policy also removed the Form of Authorization (FOA) email dance. Effective **19 November 2024** (search snippet, ICANN page not fetchable — **UNSURE on the exact date**; ICANN also published a 21 Feb 2024 revision for Registration Data Policy alignment, mandatory by 21 Aug 2025).
- **Practical implication for a builder:** you cannot cache or pre-generate the TAC. Transfer-out UX must be a live "generate TAC now" action against the upstream registrar's API — exactly what Vercel's `get-the-auth-code-for-a-domain` endpoint does and what Shopify surfaces on the domain info page.

### Grounds for denial

**UNSURE on verbatim text** — every primary source (icann.org HTML, the itp.cdn and gnso PDFs, registrar mirrors) was unreachable or unparseable. From search snippets, the permitted denial grounds are narrow and enumerated: domain on hold for non-payment of a prior registration period (including chargebacks); express written objection from the holder; domain in Lock status; within 60 days of initial registration; within 60 days of a prior transfer; plus evidence of fraud, UDRP/court order, and reasonable dispute over identity. On denial, the Registrar of Record **must give the registrant and the gaining registrar the reason**.

What is *not* on the list is the point for a website builder: **"the customer owes us money for hosting/subscription" is not a valid reason to deny a transfer.** Only debt for a *prior domain registration period* qualifies. A platform that withholds a TAC because a site plan lapsed is putting its sponsoring registrar in breach.

### Escalation path

- **ICANN Contractual Compliance transfer complaint form:** https://icann-nsp.my.site.com/compliance/s/transfer (JS-rendered, so I could not extract its text — **UNSURE on the exact complaint categories**). General complaints entry point: https://www.icann.org/compliance/complaint (403 to fetch).
- **The reseller gap — the key hazard.** ICANN's compliance page states (search snippet, page not fetchable): if the complaint concerns a **reseller**, contact the reseller or the registrar, because ICANN's authority is limited to obligations in its agreements with registrars and registries. **ICANN has no contract with resellers and cannot sanction one directly.** So a builder acting as reseller is not directly enforceable by ICANN — but its *sponsoring registrar* is, and the registrar carries §3.12.6's duty to take *"reasonable steps to enforce"* reseller compliance. The realistic consequence of misbehavior is not an ICANN fine; it is your registrar terminating your reseller account and your entire book of domains going into a de-accreditation-style migration.

---

## 4. Reputational / legal hazard: documented cases

### ICANN compliance action — Net 4 India (the canonical example)

Fetched: https://domainnamewire.com/2021/03/01/icann-terminates-net-4-india/
- ICANN received **400 complaints between 5 June 2019 and 30 September 2020**, primarily about **domains failing to renew and customers being unable to transfer them out**.
- Escalation ladder: first contact April 2019 → suspension notice June 2019 → third breach notice January 2021 → **termination announced 26 February 2021**.
- ICANN then ran its **De-Accredited Registrar Transition Procedure** to move affected registrants' domains to a new registrar.
- Primary ICANN announcements (surfaced in search, **not fetched** — icann.org 403s): `icann.org/en/announcements/details/icann-terminates-registrar-accreditation-agreement-raa-with-net-4-india-limited-26-2-2021-en` and `icann.org/en/blogs/details/an-update-for-net-4-india-registrants-26-4-2021-en`. A secondary source (search snippet) puts total complaints at ~2,600 from 1 Jan 2020 to 26 Feb 2021, and notes an Indian tribunal (NCLT) stayed the termination, leaving customers stranded longer.

**Read-through for a builder:** the failure mode isn't a lawsuit, it's a slow accumulation of transfer complaints that eventually costs the registrar its accreditation and strands every customer at once.

### The "domain hostage" pattern

Fetched: https://domainnamewire.com/2008/10/22/web-designers-holding-domain-names-hostage/ — the pattern and three concrete incidents:
- Designers bundle "site design, web hosting, and registering the domain name," and *"The domain is registered in the web design firms' name."*
- **Easton, Connecticut** hired Lightning PC Inc., which registered EastonCT.org **in its own name** and *"pulled the plug on the site"* during a payment dispute.
- A **Texas** business owner *"spent tens of thousands of dollars getting a web site created. When she wanted to switch web developers, the company held the domain hostage and demanded more money."*
- **OICBC (2009)** — ex-designer deleted content, renewed the domain without authorization, and refused to hand over credentials.
- The stated remedy is exactly design option (a)/(c): list the client as registrant; if you must register on their behalf, use *"[your company] on behalf of [client name]"*; never use the domain as leverage for unpaid bills.

### TDRP — and why it does *not* help your customer

- **Only registrars can file.** Verbatim from a registrar-hosted copy (fetched: https://nicproxy.com/en/legal/tdrp_policy.asp): *"Either the Gaining or Registrar of Record ('Filing Registrar') may submit a Request for Enforcement."* And: *"A dispute must be filed no later than six (6) months after the alleged violation of the Transfer Policy."*
- ICANN's own page: https://www.icann.org/en/contracted-parties/accredited-registrars/registrar-transfer-dispute-resolution-policy-21-02-2024-en (403 to fetch; current version dated **21 February 2024**).
- **Caution:** a widely-circulated third-party guide (fetched: https://www.domainindia.com/client/knowledgebase/688/The-Ultimate-Comprehensive-Guide-to-Mastering-ICANNs-Inter-Registrar-Transfer-Dispute-Resolution-Policy-TDRP.html) claims *"Domain Owners: The registrant of the domain must provide proof of ownership..."* can file. **This appears to be wrong** and contradicts the policy text above. Do not rely on it in a design doc.
- TDRP is also scoped to *transfers that happened* (fraudulent transfer, improper NACK) — it is **not** a remedy for a registrar/reseller simply refusing to release. That leaves an aggrieved registrant with only: the ICANN transfer complaint form (against the registrar, not you), and civil litigation.

**Net hazard picture:** if you are the RNH and you refuse to release, your customer has **no ICANN remedy at all** — ICANN's transfer machinery protects the *Registered Name Holder*, and in that configuration the Registered Name Holder is you. Their only path is a conversion/breach-of-contract suit. That asymmetry is precisely what makes registrant-in-platform-name a reputational bomb.

---

## 5. Practical design options

### (a) Register in the customer's name, platform as tech/admin contact
- **Largely obsolete as stated.** Post-RDP (in force 21 Aug 2025), admin/billing/tech contact sets are no longer collected in most gTLDs — see the OpenSRS quote in §1. There is often no contact slot for the platform to occupy.
- The surviving, correct version: customer in the **registrant** fields (leave `Organization` blank unless the customer *is* a company that should legally own it), and the platform's operational control comes from **nameserver delegation + account/API access**, not from a contact record.
- Wix, Squarespace, Shopify and Vercel all effectively do this.

### (b) Register in the platform's name, assign to the customer later
- **Do not.** RAA §3.7.7.3 makes you the RNH of record and puts the customer in a licensee position; §3.7.7.9 and §3.7.7.12 attach infringement representations and registry indemnity to you; you become the UDRP respondent for every customer's brand choice.
- The "assign later" step is itself expensive: a **Change of Registrant** trips a **60-day transfer lock** at Wix, Squarespace and Shopify (all three documented above). So the handoff you intended as customer-friendly creates a two-month window where the customer cannot leave — which reads externally as exactly the hostage pattern.
- **No major platform in this survey does this.** That absence is itself the strongest argument.

### (c) Act as reseller of an accredited registrar, customer as Registered Name Holder
- **This is the industry norm.** Shopify (Tucows) and Vercel (Name.com + Tucows) are pure resellers; Wix and Squarespace hold their own accreditations *and still resell* for TLDs outside their direct coverage.
- Contract shape: registration agreement runs **Registrar ↔ Customer**; money runs **Customer → You → Registrar** (Shopify's Tucows DRA: fees paid *"to Reseller"*); you must **identify the sponsoring registrar on request** (RAA §3.12.3) and surface ICANN's registrant education link (§3.12.5).
- **Designated Agent** is the mechanism that makes this workable operationally — the Tucows agreements have the registrant pre-authorize Tucows as Designated Agent under the Transfer Policy to approve Change of Registrant, which avoids blocking on customer email confirmations.
- **Getting your own accreditation** (the Wix/Squarespace path) buys margin and control but converts every §3.12 "reasonable steps" obligation into a direct RAA obligation enforceable by ICANN against you, with de-accreditation as the terminal sanction (Net 4 India).

### Non-negotiables to write into the design doc

1. **Customer in the registrant fields. Always.** Never the platform's legal entity, and never the platform's name in `Organization` — that field alone determines legal ownership post-RDP.
2. **Self-service TAC retrieval, generated on demand** against the upstream registrar (Shopify and Vercel both do this). Never gate it on subscription status: subscription debt is not an ICANN-valid denial ground; only debt for a prior *domain registration* period is.
3. **Hard SLA of well under 5 calendar days** for TAC delivery, since that is the ICANN deadline and the trigger for a compliance complaint.
4. **Send the code to the registrant email**, and expose to the customer that the registrant email may differ from their platform login (Squarespace and Wix both hit this confusion in their docs).
5. **Surface the sponsoring registrar in-product**, not only in the ToS — RAA §3.12.3 requires disclosure on inquiry.
6. **Warn before any registrant-contact edit** that it may trigger a 60-day transfer lock, and advise transferring first (Wix's help center does exactly this).
7. **Plan the wind-down path now**: Vercel's terms commit to assisting transfer to another registrar within 14 days of a request on termination. Having that written commitment is cheap insurance against the hostage narrative.</result>

<result>## Findings: "Who is the registrant of record" when a website builder sells a domain

**Fetch caveat:** `www.icann.org` returns HTTP 403 to WebFetch on every path tried (`/en/contracted-parties/...`, `/resources/pages/auth-...`, `/compliance/complaint`). `icannwiki.org`, `help.webflow.com`, `namecheap.com/legal`, `publicdomainregistry.com`, `tucowsdomains.com`, `billhartzer.com`, `inmotionhosting.com/legal` also 403'd. ICANN PDFs on `itp.cdn.icann.org` and `gnso.icann.org` download but are image/compressed-stream PDFs that could not be text-extracted (no poppler in this environment). The **2013 RAA HTML mirror on `itp.cdn.icann.org` works** and is the primary source below. Where I only have a search snippet and not a fetched page, I say so.

---

## 1. Legal / policy framing

### Definitions (2013 RAA, fetched: https://itp.cdn.icann.org/en/files/accredited-registrars/registrar-accreditation-agreement-21jan24-en.htm)

- **§1.18 Registered Name Holder** — *"means the holder of a Registered Name."* Deliberately circular: the RNH is whoever is in the registrant field of the registry/registrar record. There is no ICANN test of "who really paid" or "whose brand it is."
- **§1.19 Registrar** — *"a person or entity that contracts with Registered Name Holders and with a Registry Operator and collects registration data about the Registered Name Holders and submits registration information for entry in the Registry Database."*
- **§1.26 Reseller** — *"a person or entity that participates in Registrar's distribution channel for domain name registrations (a) pursuant to an agreement, arrangement or understanding with Registrar or (b) with Registrar's actual knowledge, provides some or all Registrar Services, including collecting registration data about Registered Name Holders, submitting that data to Registrar, or facilitating the entry of the registration agreement between Registrar and the Registered Name Holder."*

Note the structure: the registration agreement is **between the Registrar and the Registered Name Holder**. The reseller *facilitates* that agreement; it is not a party to the registration relationship in ICANN's model.

### The single most load-bearing clause for a website builder

**RAA §3.7.7.3** (verbatim):

> *"Any Registered Name Holder that intends to license use of a domain name to a third party is nonetheless the Registered Name Holder of record and is responsible for providing its own full contact information and for providing and updating accurate technical and administrative contact information adequate to facilitate timely resolution of any problems that arise in connection with the Registered Name."*

This is the clause that decides the design question. If a platform registers a customer's domain in the **platform's** name and lets the customer "use" it, the platform is the RNH of record and is *responsible* — including under **§3.7.7.9** (RNH represents that the registration *"does not infringe the legal rights of any third party"*) and **§3.7.7.12** (RNH indemnifies the Registry Operator). The platform absorbs the customer's trademark and content liability, and would be the respondent in a UDRP.

Other relevant RAA text (verbatim):
- **§3.7.7.1** — *"The Registered Name Holder shall provide to Registrar accurate and reliable contact details and correct and update them within seven (7) days of any change during the term of the Registered Name registration."*
- **§3.12.2** — *"Any registration agreement used by reseller shall include all registration agreement provisions and notices required by the ICANN Registrar Accreditation Agreement and any ICANN Consensus Policies."*
- **§3.12.3** — Registrar must ensure *"Its Resellers identify the sponsoring registrar upon inquiry from the customer."*
- **§3.12.5** — Reseller customers must be *"provided with a link to an ICANN webpage detailing registrant educational information."*
- §3.12 opener: the **Registrar remains responsible for provision of Registrar Services regardless of reseller involvement**.

**UNSURE / important nuance:** the 2013 RAA contains **no clause literally saying "the reseller must not be the Registered Name Holder."** I searched the RAA text for such a sentence and it is not there. The prohibition is *structural and indirect*: §1.19/§3.7.7 make the registration agreement a Registrar↔RNH contract; §3.7.7.3 makes whoever is in the registrant field the RNH of record with full liability; and §3.12.3 forces disclosure of the sponsoring registrar. So a reseller *can* physically put itself in the registrant field — that is exactly the "domain hostage" pattern — but it then legally *is* the registrant, with all attendant duties, and the customer is a mere licensee with no ICANN-recognized standing.

### Registrant vs. admin / tech / billing contact — and the 2025 change that matters

Historically gTLD registrations carried four contact sets (Registrant, Admin, Tech, Billing). Only the **Registrant** is the RNH; Admin/Tech/Billing are operational contacts with no ownership meaning. Under the **ICANN Registration Data Policy** (published 21 Feb 2024, in force 21 Aug 2025) this collapsed:

Tucows/OpenSRS, fetched: https://opensrs.com/blog/what-icanns-updated-registration-data-policy-rdp-means-for-opensrs-resellers/
> *"We'll stop collecting the administrative, billing, and technical contact sets unless specifically required by the registry."*

Registrant contact remains mandatory (name, address, country, telephone, email). Key operational dates from that page: 30 June 2025 admin/billing/tech collection ceases; 28 July 2025 API returns only the minimum data set; **21 August 2025 the updated RDP takes effect**.

**Design consequence:** the classic advice "put the client as registrant, the agency as admin/tech contact" is now partly obsolete — in most gTLDs *there is no admin/tech contact slot left to occupy*. A platform's operational control has to come from account access and DNS delegation, not from a contact record.

And the Organization-field trap, from the same OpenSRS page:
> *"They should leave the organization field blank, unless they want the organization to be the legal registrant."*

Putting the platform's company name in the registrant **Organization** field makes the platform the legal registrant, regardless of whose personal name is in the first/last name fields. (A secondary, non-primary source — search snippet from smartbranding.com, not fetched — states the same: from 21 Aug 2025, if the Organization field is populated, that organization is treated as the legal owner and the personal name is only a point of contact.)

---

## 2. What each platform actually does

### Wix — accredited registrar for some TLDs, reseller for the rest; customer is registrant

- **ICANN-accredited:** Wix.com Ltd. appeared on the ICANN registrar list with **IANA ID 3817** in July 2018. Before that Wix was a reseller: *"Wix currently acts as a reseller for Network Solutions, a Web.com company."* — fetched: https://domainincite.com/23243-wix-com-obtains-icann-accreditation-bad-news-for-web-com
- **Still resells.** Wix's own help center links out to **two** upstream registration agreements: *"Domain Registration Agreement for Web.com"* and *"Domain Registration Agreement for Tucows"* — fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/change-in-terms-of-use-mailbox-and-domain-renewals. Third-party summary (fetched: https://www.certifiedcode.us/resources/article/is-wix-a-domain-registrar) says Wix is *"an ICANN-accredited domain registrar"* supporting *"over 75 different top-level domains"* and acts as *"the Registrar of Record, entering your information into the WHOIS database."* Search snippets (not fetched) claim Wix is directly accredited for **.com/.net** and resells everything else — **UNSURE**, I could not verify the exact TLD split from a Wix-owned page.
- **Who is registrant:** the customer. Wix's ownership doc is explicit that the ICANN record wins over billing: *"Recognize the domain registrant (listed in databases like ICANN) as the domain's owner"* and *"If billing details and domain owner details conflict, Wix may prioritize the domain's registrant as the owner."* — fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/wix-site-and-content-ownership
- **Transfer out** (fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/transferring-your-wix-domain-away-from-wix-2477749): *"We'll send a transfer authorization code (EPP code) to your domain's registrant contact email address."* — i.e., the code goes to the **registrant email**, not the Wix account login. *"Your domain must be unlocked before you begin the transfer."* *"You cannot transfer a domain within 60 days of purchase. Changing your registrant contact information locks your domain from transfer for 60 days."* Transfer takes up to 7 days.
- **60-day lock** (fetched: https://support.wix.com/en/article/icanns-60-day-lock-policy): triggered by *"Registering the domain, Changing the registrant contact information, Transferring your domain between different domain providers"*, and *"cannot be changed by Wix."* Wix explicitly warns: transfer **before** changing contact info to avoid tripping the lock.

### Squarespace — genuinely accredited (two accreditations), plus reseller relationships

- **Accredited entities:** the DRA (fetched: https://www.squarespace.com/domain-registration-agreement) names **Squarespace Domains LLC (SDL)**, **Squarespace Domains II LLC (SD2L)**, and **Squarespace Domains Canada Inc. (SDC)**, and states *"Each US Squarespace Registrar Entity is an ICANN-accredited registrar"* with its own RAA (SDC is CIRA-accredited).
- **Registrant definition** (same DRA, verbatim): *"you or the organization you are acting for or on behalf of as the registered name holder of the domain name registration."* The customer is the RNH.
- **Squarespace also resells:** *"Squarespace Domains LLC, Squarespace Domains II LLC, the Tucows family of registrars, and the Key-Systems family of registrars"* — fetched: https://support.squarespace.com/hc/en-us/articles/205812338-Transferring-a-domain-away-from-Squarespace. So even an accredited platform runs a mixed portfolio.
- **Squarespace's own reseller program** defines the roles plainly (fetched: https://reseller.squarespace.com/domain-glossary): *"Registrant: The customer who purchases the domain."* / *"Registrar: An ICANN-approved entity that registers and sells domain names to the customer. Squarespace is a Domains Registrar."* / *"Domain Reseller: An organization enabled to register domains on behalf of a Registrar."*
- **Google Domains acquisition:** completed **7 September 2023** — fetched: https://www.squarespace.com/press-releases/2023/9/7/squarespace-completes-acquisition-of-google-domains-assets. The release says Squarespace *"will, after a transition period, initiate the transfer of Google Domains accounts to its Squarespace Domains platform"* and commits to *"making it a globally recognized, independent domain registrar."* Price and exact domain count are **not** in the press release. **Squarespace Domains II LLC carries IANA ID 895** (fetched: https://domaindetails.com/registrars/squarespace-domains-ii-llc) — 895 was Google LLC's accreditation, i.e. the accreditation itself was transferred rather than the domains being bulk-migrated to a new IANA ID. The domaindetails page does **not** state the Google history, so treat the "895 = former Google LLC" identification as **UNSURE-but-strongly-indicated** (search snippets assert it; I could not fetch ICANN's registrar list to confirm).
- **Transfer out** (same support article): unlock via Domain Lock toggle in the domains dashboard (password/2FA re-auth); *"The transfer authentication code should be received within 24 hours"*, sent **to the registrant's email address, which may differ from the Squarespace login email**; 60-day locks apply after registration, after transfer-in, and after contact updates; full transfer takes *"up to 15 days."*

### Shopify — pure reseller of Tucows; merchant is the Registered Name Holder

- **Registrar:** **Tucows Domains Inc.** Shopify's own Domain Registration Agreement (fetched: https://app.shopify.com/legal/domain_registration_agreement.html) is a Tucows agreement, describing services *"offered through Shopify, the Reseller participating in Tucows' distribution channel."*
- **Registrant:** verbatim from that agreement — *"the person named as Registrant on the Whois shall be the 'Registered Name Holder.'"* The registrant is the merchant, contracting **with Tucows**, paying fees **to Shopify** as reseller. This is textbook RAA §1.26 / §3.12.
- Shopify's marketing page states it flatly (fetched: https://www.shopify.com/domains): *"Your domain is registered in your name and managed from your Shopify admin, and you can transfer it out at any time (subject to ICANN/registry rules)"* and *"Shopify sells domains as a reseller through accredited registrar partners."*
- **Designated Agent:** the agreement contains *"Registrant explicitly authorizes Tucows to act as their Designated Agent, as stipulated by the ICANN Transfer Policy, to approve a Change of Registrant on their behalf."* Same clause appears in the upstream Tucows Master Domain Registration Agreement (fetched: https://assets.opensrs.com/Uploads/Master_Domain_Registration_Agreement.html), which also confirms *"The person named as Registrant on record with Tucows shall be the 'Registered Name Holder.'"* This matters: the Designated Agent mechanism is what lets a platform change registrant details without a two-sided email confirmation dance.
- **Transfer out** (fetched: https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/domains/managing-domain-ownership/transferring-shopify-domains): *"For your domain to be eligible for transfer, you need to wait 60 days after performing the following tasks: purchasing the domain, transferring the domain to Shopify, changing your contact information."* Auth code is **self-service in admin** — *"The domain authorization code is displayed on your domain's information page."* Transfers take up to 7 days; the domain re-locks if not completed within 30 days. Seven TLDs (.be, .co.uk, .de, .ec, .eu, .se, .ph) can't be self-transferred and require Shopify Support. The page does not name Tucows; the Tucows relationship surfaces to merchants only via the consent-settings email and the DRA.

### Vercel — reseller of Name.com and Tucows; registrant is the Team Owner

Fetched: https://vercel.com/legal/domain-name-registration-and-services-terms

- **Sponsoring registrars, verbatim:** *"Vercel currently provides Registration Services through Name.com, Inc and Tucows Domains Inc."*
- **Registrant, verbatim:** *"the individual or entity registering a Domain Name ('Registrant')"*, and where a team registers, *"the Registrant will be the individual designated as the 'Team Owner'."* So Vercel puts a **natural person from the customer's team** in the registrant field, not Vercel Inc. (Design note: tying the registrant to a *Team Owner* role rather than to the legal entity is a real-world failure mode when that employee leaves.)
- Vercel disclaims the registrar role — registration data flows to *"the applicable Registrar, which acts as the data controller."*
- **Exit obligation, verbatim:** *"You may terminate the Domain Name Terms by allowing to lapse, assigning, or transferring to an alternative registrar the registration of all Domain Names currently using Vercel's Registration Services."* On termination Vercel will *"assist Customer to transfer any Domain Name registrations that have not expired to an alternative registrar of choice"* within 14 days if requested. Renewal reminders at 60 and 30 days before expiry. The terms contain **no** "auth code," "Registered Name Holder," or "reseller" language — **UNSURE** whether Vercel documents a 60-day lock anywhere in its legal terms.
- **Mechanically**, Vercel exposes the whole registrar surface as API: `GET .../registrar/…/auth-code` ("Retrieve authorization codes for domain transfers"), buy, transfer-in, transfer-status, renew, auto-renew, nameservers, contact-info schema — https://vercel.com/docs/domains/registrar-api. The purchase endpoint requires a full `contactInformation` object — `firstName`, `lastName`, `email`, `phone`, `address1`, `city`, `state`, `zip`, `country` required, with **optional `companyName`** — https://vercel.com/docs/rest-api/domains-registrar/buy-a-domain. That optional `companyName` maps to the registrant Organization field, i.e. it is the field that decides legal ownership under the 2025 RDP. ### Summary table

| Platform | Accredited registrar? | Upstream registrar(s) | Registrant of record | Auth code delivery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wix | Yes, Wix.com Ltd, IANA 3817 (2018) — but also resells | Web.com, Tucows | Customer | Emailed to **registrant contact email** |
| Squarespace | Yes — SDL, SD2L (IANA 895), SDC(CIRA) — also resells | Tucows family, Key‑Systems family | Customer ("registered name holder") | Emailed to **registrant email**, ≤24h |
| Shopify | No | Tucows Domains Inc. | Merchant ("named as Registrant on the Whois") | **Self-service in admin** |
| Vercel | No | Name.com, Tucows Domains Inc. | Customer / **Team Owner** | **API + dashboard** |
| Webflow | UNSURE | UNSURE | UNSURE | UNSURE |

**Nobody in this set registers customer domains in the platform's own name.** That is the strongest single finding.

---

## 3. Transfer-out mechanics and the hazard

### The auth code / TAC obligation

- **Deadline: 5 calendar days.** *"The registrar is required to provide the Auth-Code to the domain name owner within five calendar days of the owner's request, and ICANN accepts complaints about registrars that do not."* — fetched: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auth-Code. Corroborated by registrar KB, fetched: https://help.101domain.com/kb/finding-the-auth-epp-code — *"The Registrar must provide you with the Auth-Info code within 5 calendar days of your request."*
- **The 2024 Transfer Policy renamed and re-scoped the code.** Per https://seo.domains/seo-resources/transfer-process/epp-code-auth-code/ (fetched): the **TAC** is *"generated on demand and lives no more than 14 calendar days"* — it is no longer a static, always-present value; the registry stores it as a one-way hash; it is single-use. The policy also removed the Form of Authorization (FOA) email dance. Effective **19 November 2024** (search snippet, ICANN page not fetchable — **UNSURE on the exact date**; ICANN also published a 21 Feb 2024 revision for Registration Data Policy alignment, mandatory by 21 Aug 2025).
- **Practical implication for a builder:** you cannot cache or pre-generate the TAC. Transfer-out UX must be a live "generate TAC now" action against the upstream registrar's API — exactly what Vercel's `get-the-auth-code-for-a-domain` endpoint does and what Shopify surfaces on the domain info page.

### Grounds for denial

**UNSURE on verbatim text** — every primary source (icann.org HTML, the itp.cdn and gnso PDFs, registrar mirrors) was unreachable or unparseable. From search snippets, the permitted denial grounds are narrow and enumerated: domain on hold for non-payment of a prior registration period (including chargebacks); express written objection from the holder; domain in Lock status; within 60 days of initial registration; within 60 days of a prior transfer; plus evidence of fraud, UDRP/court order, and reasonable dispute over identity. On denial, the Registrar of Record **must give the registrant and the gaining registrar the reason**.

What is *not* on the list is the point for a website builder: **"the customer owes us money for hosting/subscription" is not a valid reason to deny a transfer.** Only debt for a *prior domain registration period* qualifies. A platform that withholds a TAC because a site plan lapsed is putting its sponsoring registrar in breach.

### Escalation path

- **ICANN Contractual Compliance transfer complaint form:** https://icann-nsp.my.site.com/compliance/s/transfer (JS-rendered, so I could not extract its text — **UNSURE on the exact complaint categories**). General complaints entry point: https://www.icann.org/compliance/complaint (403 to fetch).
- **The reseller gap — the key hazard.** ICANN's compliance page states (search snippet, page not fetchable): if the complaint concerns a **reseller**, contact the reseller or the registrar, because ICANN's authority is limited to obligations in its agreements with registrars and registries. **ICANN has no contract with resellers and cannot sanction one directly.** So a builder acting as reseller is not directly enforceable by ICANN — but its *sponsoring registrar* is, and the registrar carries §3.12.6's duty to take *"reasonable steps to enforce"* reseller compliance. The realistic consequence of misbehavior is not an ICANN fine; it is your registrar terminating your reseller account and your entire book of domains going into a de-accreditation-style migration.

---

## 4. Reputational / legal hazard: documented cases

### ICANN compliance action — Net 4 India (the canonical example)

Fetched: https://domainnamewire.com/2021/03/01/icann-terminates-net-4-india/
- ICANN received **400 complaints between 5 June 2019 and 30 September 2020**, primarily about **domains failing to renew and customers being unable to transfer them out**.
- Escalation ladder: first contact April 2019 → suspension notice June 2019 → third breach notice January 2021 → **termination announced 26 February 2021**.
- ICANN then ran its **De-Accredited Registrar Transition Procedure** to move affected registrants' domains to a new registrar.
- Primary ICANN announcements (surfaced in search, **not fetched** — icann.org 403s): `icann.org/en/announcements/details/icann-terminates-registrar-accreditation-agreement-raa-with-net-4-india-limited-26-2-2021-en` and `icann.org/en/blogs/details/an-update-for-net-4-india-registrants-26-4-2021-en`. A secondary source (search snippet) puts total complaints at ~2,600 from 1 Jan 2020 to 26 Feb 2021, and notes an Indian tribunal (NCLT) stayed the termination, leaving customers stranded longer.

**Read-through for a builder:** the failure mode isn't a lawsuit, it's a slow accumulation of transfer complaints that eventually costs the registrar its accreditation and strands every customer at once.

### The "domain hostage" pattern

Fetched: https://domainnamewire.com/2008/10/22/web-designers-holding-domain-names-hostage/ — the pattern and three concrete incidents:
- Designers bundle "site design, web hosting, and registering the domain name," and *"The domain is registered in the web design firms' name."*
- **Easton, Connecticut** hired Lightning PC Inc., which registered EastonCT.org **in its own name** and *"pulled the plug on the site"* during a payment dispute.
- A **Texas** business owner *"spent tens of thousands of dollars getting a web site created. When she wanted to switch web developers, the company held the domain hostage and demanded more money."*
- **OICBC (2009)** — ex-designer deleted content, renewed the domain without authorization, and refused to hand over credentials.
- The stated remedy is exactly design option (a)/(c): list the client as registrant; if you must register on their behalf, use *"[your company] on behalf of [client name]"*; never use the domain as leverage for unpaid bills.

### TDRP — and why it does *not* help your customer

- **Only registrars can file.** Verbatim from a registrar-hosted copy (fetched: https://nicproxy.com/en/legal/tdrp_policy.asp): *"Either the Gaining or Registrar of Record ('Filing Registrar') may submit a Request for Enforcement."* And: *"A dispute must be filed no later than six (6) months after the alleged violation of the Transfer Policy."*
- ICANN's own page: https://www.icann.org/en/contracted-parties/accredited-registrars/registrar-transfer-dispute-resolution-policy-21-02-2024-en (403 to fetch; current version dated **21 February 2024**).
- **Caution:** a widely-circulated third-party guide (fetched: https://www.domainindia.com/client/knowledgebase/688/The-Ultimate-Comprehensive-Guide-to-Mastering-ICANNs-Inter-Registrar-Transfer-Dispute-Resolution-Policy-TDRP.html) claims *"Domain Owners: The registrant of the domain must provide proof of ownership..."* can file. **This appears to be wrong** and contradicts the policy text above. Do not rely on it in a design doc.
- TDRP is also scoped to *transfers that happened* (fraudulent transfer, improper NACK) — it is **not** a remedy for a registrar/reseller simply refusing to release. That leaves an aggrieved registrant with only: the ICANN transfer complaint form (against the registrar, not you), and civil litigation.

**Net hazard picture:** if you are the RNH and you refuse to release, your customer has **no ICANN remedy at all** — ICANN's transfer machinery protects the *Registered Name Holder*, and in that configuration the Registered Name Holder is you. Their only path is a conversion/breach-of-contract suit. That asymmetry is precisely what makes registrant-in-platform-name a reputational bomb.

---

## 5. Practical design options

### (a) Register in the customer's name, platform as tech/admin contact
- **Largely obsolete as stated.** Post-RDP (in force 21 Aug 2025), admin/billing/tech contact sets are no longer collected in most gTLDs — see the OpenSRS quote in §1. There is often no contact slot for the platform to occupy.
- The surviving, correct version: customer in the **registrant** fields (leave `Organization` blank unless the customer *is* a company that should legally own it), and the platform's operational control comes from **nameserver delegation + account/API access**, not from a contact record.
- Wix, Squarespace, Shopify and Vercel all effectively do this.

### (b) Register in the platform's name, assign to the customer later
- **Do not.** RAA §3.7.7.3 makes you the RNH of record and puts the customer in a licensee position; §3.7.7.9 and §3.7.7.12 attach infringement representations and registry indemnity to you; you become the UDRP respondent for every customer's brand choice.
- The "assign later" step is itself expensive: a **Change of Registrant** trips a **60-day transfer lock** at Wix, Squarespace and Shopify (all three documented above). So the handoff you intended as customer-friendly creates a two-month window where the customer cannot leave — which reads externally as exactly the hostage pattern.
- **No major platform in this survey does this.** That absence is itself the strongest argument.

### (c) Act as reseller of an accredited registrar, customer as Registered Name Holder
- **This is the industry norm.** Shopify (Tucows) and Vercel (Name.com + Tucows) are pure resellers; Wix and Squarespace hold their own accreditations *and still resell* for TLDs outside their direct coverage.
- Contract shape: registration agreement runs **Registrar ↔ Customer**; money runs **Customer → You → Registrar** (Shopify's Tucows DRA: fees paid *"to Reseller"*); you must **identify the sponsoring registrar on request** (RAA §3.12.3) and surface ICANN's registrant education link (§3.12.5).
- **Designated Agent** is the mechanism that makes this workable operationally — the Tucows agreements have the registrant pre-authorize Tucows as Designated Agent under the Transfer Policy to approve Change of Registrant, which avoids blocking on customer email confirmations.
- **Getting your own accreditation** (the Wix/Squarespace path) buys margin and control but converts every §3.12 "reasonable steps" obligation into a direct RAA obligation enforceable by ICANN against you, with de-accreditation as the terminal sanction (Net 4 India).

### Non-negotiables to write into the design doc

1. **Customer in the registrant fields. Always.** Never the platform's legal entity, and never the platform's name in `Organization` — that field alone determines legal ownership post-RDP.
2. **Self-service TAC retrieval, generated on demand** against the upstream registrar (Shopify and Vercel both do this). Never gate it on subscription status: subscription debt is not an ICANN-valid denial ground; only debt for a prior *domain registration* period is.
3. **Hard SLA of well under 5 calendar days** for TAC delivery, since that is the ICANN deadline and the trigger for a compliance complaint.
4. **Send the code to the registrant email**, and expose to the customer that the registrant email may differ from their platform login (Squarespace and Wix both hit this confusion in their docs).
5. **Surface the sponsoring registrar in-product**, not only in the ToS — RAA §3.12.3 requires disclosure on inquiry.
6. **Warn before any registrant-contact edit** that it may trigger a 60-day transfer lock, and advise transferring first (Wix's help center does exactly this).
7. **Plan the wind-down path now**: Vercel's terms commit to assisting transfer to another registrar within 14 days of a request on termination. Having that written commitment is cheap insurance against the hostage narrative.</result>

# Kodely product design system

The contract for the customer-facing portal (`app/(portal)/**`) and the builder
(`app/projects/[id]/**`). Marketing pages (`app/page.tsx`, `/pricing`, `/blog`,
`/templates`, `/wizard`) are a **separate** system — do not repoint their tokens.

## The one-sentence brief

An AI website builder that happens to have a customer portal around it — not a
dashboard that happens to contain a builder. The primary action is always
"build something".

---

## Tokens

Defined in `app/globals.css`, exposed to Tailwind via `@theme inline`. **Use the
Tailwind class, never a raw hex and never an arbitrary-value bracket.**

### Surface

| Class | Use |
| --- | --- |
| `bg-canvas` | The page behind panels. Set by `AppShell`; pages never set it. |
| `bg-surface` | Cards, panels, the sidebar. |
| `bg-surface-2` | Hover, inset rows, quiet fills. |
| `bg-surface-3` | Track of a progress bar, the deepest step. |
| `bg-inset` | Code/preview wells. |

### Line

`border-hair` (default for cards) · `border-line-mid` (inputs, menus) ·
`border-line-strong` (emphasis, pending step outline)

### Text

`text-ink` (primary) · `text-ink-2` (secondary/body) · `text-ink-3` (tertiary,
placeholder, disabled) · `text-ink-inv` (on a brand fill)

### Brand

`text-brand` `bg-brand` `bg-brand-tint` `bg-brand-tint-2` `text-brand-ink`

`--brand-gradient` is a **fill of last resort**. Exactly one element per view may
carry it: the primary button. Do not gradient headings, cards, borders or icons.

### Status

`ok` `warn` `danger` `info`, each with a `-tint` companion
(`text-ok` / `bg-ok-tint`). Status colour is never the brand colour.

### Radius / elevation / motion

`rounded-sm|md|lg|xl|2xl` (8/10/14/20/28px) · `shadow-e1|e2|e3` ·
`duration-[var(--t-1)]` 120ms, `--t-2` 200ms, `--t-3` 380ms ·
`ease-[var(--ease)]`

---

## Utility classes

`k-focus` — **put this on every interactive element.** One focus ring, product-wide.
`k-display` `k-h1` `k-h2` `k-label` — the type scale. `k-label` is the only uppercase.
`k-num` — **required** on any figure: credits, prices, counts, dates in a column.
`k-scroll-x` — wrap any wide table/code block. The page body must never scroll sideways.
`k-msg-in` `k-step-in` `k-step-active` — entrance and progress animations.
`k-preview-busy` / `k-preview-idle` — the preview treatment while the AI works.
`k-wash` — ambient brand glow inside a hero panel. Sparingly: one per page, at most.
`k-gradient-border` — gradient hairline. Reserve for the single most important panel.

---

## Components (`components/ui/`)

Import these. **Do not hand-roll a second version of any of them.**

| Component | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `Button` `ButtonLink` `IconButton` `buttonClass` | Variants `primary\|secondary\|ghost\|soft\|danger`, sizes `xs\|sm\|md\|lg`. **One `primary` per view.** `IconButton` requires `label`. |
| `Card` `CardHeader` `SectionHeader` | `interactive` only if it truly responds. |
| `Badge` | `tone` + `dot` + `pulse`. Set `dot` on anything conveying live state — colour alone is not a status channel. |
| `Input` `Textarea` `Select` `SearchInput` | Label/hint/error/aria wiring is built in. Never hand-write a bare `<input>`. |
| `Progress` `toneForUsage` | Recolours as it fills. `indeterminate` for work with no known end. |
| `Skeleton` `SkeletonList` | Stagger with `delay`. |
| `EmptyState` | `kind` is required: `empty` (none yet) / `no-results` (filter too narrow) / `unavailable` (does not exist yet). These need different sentences. |
| `Menu` | Keyboard + Escape + click-outside already handled. `unavailableReason` greys an item and says why. |
| `Modal` `ConfirmModal` | Native `<dialog>`. Confirm buttons are labelled with the verb, never "OK". |
| `ToastProvider` `useToast` | Provider is already mounted by `AppShell`. Errors and toasts with an action do not auto-dismiss. |
| `Segmented` | Real radios. Used for grid/list and device toggles. |
| `AIProgress` `stepsAt` | **The** progress component. See below. |
| `Stat` `StatRow` | Any number the customer must understand. |
| `Avatar` | Initials only — there is no avatar upload. |
| `Spinner` | |

## Shell (`components/app/`)

`AppShell` wraps every portal page and already provides the sidebar, mobile
drawer, bottom bar and toast host. **A page renders content only** — no page
supplies its own nav, no page sets a background, no page mounts a second
`ToastProvider`, and no page sets a title suffix (the group layout owns the
`"%s — Kodely"` template; a page declares only its own noun).

Navigation lives in `components/app/nav.ts`. An item may only be added there
once it is backed by real data; `soon: true` marks the ones that are not.

`SidebarFooter` carries the brand-gradient credits card, the theme toggle and
the bug/feature link (`/support?topic=bug`, `?topic=feature`). It appears in
both the desktop rail and the mobile drawer.

**The credits card has no progress bar and no "X of Y" figure, deliberately.**
There is no allowance for the balance to be a fraction of — credits are bought
in packs and never expire — so a bar would have to invent a denominator. It
shows the balance and "about N more builds" from `averageBuildCredits()`.
**Anything else in the product showing credits must agree with it.** A card
elsewhere claiming a monthly total would contradict the rail sitting beside it.

### Where the brand gradient may be used as a fill

Three places, and nowhere else: the single `primary` button on a view, the
sidebar credits card, and the `/support` credits card. Not on headings, cards,
borders, icons or section dividers.

---

## AI progress is one object, not three spinners

`AIProgress` is rendered by the initial build overlay, by the chat panel during
an edit, and beside the preview. All three must show the **same steps in the
same state**, because the customer reads them as one thing happening.

**Drive `state` from real build signals.** A timer that walks the list forward on
its own is a fake — and it will still be sitting on "Finalizing" long after a
build has failed. The build genuinely does not know its percentage (it is an
agent loop of unknown length), which is exactly why this is a named-step list
and not a progress bar.

---

## What does not exist (audited — do not build UI that pretends otherwise)

| Thing | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| **Plans / subscriptions** | None. No plan, price, or renewal date. Checkout is one-off `payment` mode for credit packs. **Never render a "Pro" chip or "$X/month".** |
| **Credit reset date** | Credits never expire. There is no monthly allowance and no reset day — the spend cap is a *rolling* 30 days chosen so there is no reset. |
| **Invoices / payment method** | Not fetched from Stripe. The credit ledger is the only history. |
| **Thumbnails** | Nothing captures a screenshot. No headless browser. |
| **Project status** | Only `publishedAt` → Published / Draft. No `archived`. "Building" is derivable from `Build.status = RUNNING` but has no staleness rule, so it is not yet trustworthy. |
| **Domains** | No model, no field, no route. Sites live at `<slug>.kodely.site` only. |
| **Integrations** | Nothing customer-facing. |
| **Support tickets** | No ticket model. `SupportNote` is admin-write-only and explicitly never shown to the customer. |
| **Storage / bandwidth** | Not measured anywhere. |
| **Workspaces / members / roles** | No concept of it. Ownership is one FK: `Project.userId`. |
| **Avatar upload, password change, 2FA, notification prefs** | None. |

**Sessions list and revoke, and editing `User.name`, are now BUILT** — see
`/settings/security` and `/settings`. Note what `Session` actually records:
`id · userId · tokenHash · expiresAt · createdAt`, and nothing else. There is no
user agent, no IP, no last-seen and no device. Do not add a column for them
casually: `/legal/rights` and the data export both enumerate in writing
everything the database holds, so a new personal-data field silently makes two
published documents wrong.

### The rule

A screen that looks operable and is not is worse than an absent one. A screen

content.text:
All green — tsc, lint, **315/315 tests**.

## The consistency pass earned its keep

It couldn't get an authenticated session (minting one was denied three times, and I won't route around that), so nothing is visually verified. But reading the code it found real defects, and the two biggest were in **my** files:

**Seven portal pages had no `<h1>` at all.** `SectionHeader` hardcoded `<h2>`, and seven pages used it as their page title — so those documents started their outline at h2. Fixed with an `as` prop, defaulted to `h2` rather than flipping to `h1`, because most pages render it more than once and a component silently emitting a second h1 is worse than the bug being fixed.

**The focus ring had drifted into three separate systems** — and two of them *cancelled* the outline they were meant to replace. `Field.tsx` used `focus:outline-none` plus its own 4px ring, covering every form control in the product. `Segmented` hand-rolled a third copy. `RewardsCard` had `k-focus` **and** `focus:outline-none` on the same element — a control with a focus class and no visible focus state. All now on one rule, with a `k-focus-within` sibling for controls whose real input is visually hidden (a `<label>` wrapping an sr-only radio never matches `:focus-visible` itself). That's a second *selector*, not a second system, and the CSS says so.

It also caught a live contradiction I'd written: `nav.ts` claimed both Domains and Integrations carried `soon`, but only Integrations did. The **code** was right — Domains is genuinely useful today because every published site has a real address there; only the custom-domain section is unavailable.

And one it found mid-flight that mattered: the support-ticket models landed underneath it, which meant **the account-deletion dialog was under-reporting what erasure destroys**. That's exactly the thing `_deletion.ts` warns against — asking for consent to something unstated.

## Heads up on two things

**`prisma db push` is now required** — `SupportTicket` and `SupportMessage` are in the schema and have never been pushed.

**`/support`'s copy currently contradicts itself.** It says "no ticket list, no status to refresh and no inbox inside Kodely" — written when that was true, and now false. The support agent is still running and owns that reconciliation.

## The Nxeon research that survived is worth reading

Two sub-agents finished before you stopped it. I've saved the findings to [custom-domains.md](docs/research/custom-domains.md) because they apply to any custom-domain implementation, whoever hosts it.

The headline is uncomfortable: **Webflow and Lovable — your two nearest comparables — have both bought their way out of the DNS problem** using Entri, which detects the customer's registrar and *writes the records for them*. Entri publishes Webflow-attributed numbers: 97% fewer DNS support tickets, connection success moving 20% → 80%. Vendor-published so discount it, but the direction is clear — what moves the number is automating the record write, not explaining the records better.

Also worth knowing: **Cloudflare for SaaS gives you 100 custom hostnames free**, then $0.10/hostname/month, and it's the one-CNAME reference implementation. And honest DNS status copy is an *unoccupied* position — every vendor including Vercel still ships "24–48 hours to propagate", which is largely folklore.

`lib/nxeon/` exists as 1,013 lines of typed interface and a not-configured stub. Nothing imports it, so it's inert. Say the word if you want it removed.

Still running: support ticketing, template picker, inline wizard, marketing nav. Queued behind them: the Usage/Billing/Domains restyle to your mockups, the Create-page prompt-box port, and thumbnails.
