  form named `contact` is normal; a multi-page site may use a different name
  per page (`/__forms/booking-request`).
- `method="post"` only. No `fetch`, no `onsubmit`, no client-side validation
  logic beyond `required` — the whole point is that this works with
  JavaScript disabled.

  fields maximum. A field literally named `email` is what lets the owner
  reply — include one whenever the brief implies contact.

  unless the brief explicitly asks for it to be left out — they are what
  keeps spam out of the site owner's inbox. `_`-prefixed field names are
  reserved for this control channel and are never stored as content.

`transform: rotate()` + `overflow: hidden` clipping: no @property, no
          CSS masking (both dropped after they didn't visibly work even in a
          fresh, verified non-cached browser). Two layers: a thin bright one
          and a soft blurred halo.

          The blur lives on the CLIP element, not on the rotating child. That
          ordering matters: filters apply AFTER the element (and its
          overflow:hidden clipping) is rendered, so the blur softens the clip's
          hard outer cutoff and lets the light bleed beyond the clip's bounds —
          a real falloff. With the blur on the child instead, the clip's crisp
          edge survives and the result reads as a chunky solid border.

          below is the right place for a focus affordance; this ring stays

content.text:
This is careful, considered schema design — well worth the wait. Everything's landed and verified.

## Status: all clear

The three agents that died from the session limit had each finished more than their last message suggested — I found and fixed three small integration seams left mid-edit, not incomplete features:

1. **A literal `*/` inside a JSX comment** in `PromptBox.tsx` (the ported homepage prompt box) closed the comment early and broke parsing — one-word fix.
2. **`CreateFlow.tsx` still called the old `image`/`setImage` names** after `Composer` was renamed to `logo`/`setLogo` during the reference-image removal you asked for.
3. **`onAssist` was never wired** — the prop `Composer` needs to receive results from the template picker and inline wizard existed on the child but had no handler on the parent. Added one that replaces the box's contents wholesale (a chosen template should replace placeholder text, not argue with it) and threads `templateName` through so the "Started from…" badge tracks whichever helper flow was actually used.

Full gate run after fixes: **tsc clean, eslint clean, 336/336 tests, and a full production build** — every route compiles, including the new `/support/[id]` ticket thread.

## What actually landed

- **Contact forms are now real in generated sites.** I found `lib/site-forms.ts` was a fully-built, secured feature (honeypot, timing check, three-layer rate limiting) that `lib/agent.ts` categorically forbade the model from using. Fixed the SYSTEM prompt to teach the exact markup contract, and flagged the 23 template prompts as now overly cautious about it (that's a content pass, not urgent).
- **Support ticketing** — `SupportTicket`/`SupportMessage`, customer threads, staff replies, and the admin side with a cross-link from Feedback. Status vocabulary is intentionally three values because only three are real — no "pending" or "priority" column nobody would ever set.
- **Usage & Billing rebuilt to your mockup's structure**, avoiding both traps I flagged: no fake "75% of 1,000 monthly credits," no donut with money on failed builds (they're never charged, so that slice would be a lie).
- **The Create page prompt box** is now the homepage's actual glow/voice-to-text component, reference-image control removed as asked.

**`prisma db push` is still required** before any of this reaches a database — the support ticket models exist only in the schema file.

Confirms it: 157 uncommitted files, HEAD still at `4ff10e8`, and the DB uses `db push` (no migrations), so it's fully out of sync with the new schema. Here's the honest full picture.

## What's left, roughly in order of urgency

**Nothing is shipped yet — this is the big one.** 157 changed files sitting uncommitted, HEAD at `4ff10e8`. All the portal/builder/asset-library work exists only on disk. Nothing reaches production until this is committed and deployed.

**`prisma db push` has never been run.** The database has no migration history at all (it's schema-drift-managed, not migration-managed), and `SupportTicket`/`SupportMessage` plus everything else added this session exists only in `schema.prisma`. Nothing in the new portal — support tickets, sessions list, name editing — will work against the real database until this runs.

**Four pre-existing URGENT items nobody has touched while this redesign was underway:**
- The VM can't reach GitHub over SSH — deploys would silently ship stale code even after you commit
- Two live blog posts state false things (a credit figure, an export claim) — public right now
- A live blog post tells dental/chiro visitors their appointment forms "deliver" — they discard the input
- Security audit: 2 critical were fixed locally, 2 high are still open

**Three decisions that are yours, not mine**, sitting in Needs Attention:
- Subscription vs. credit-only (the whole Billing page was built credit-only per your instruction, but it's still a business-model choice worth confirming)
- The site-thumbnail approach (generated cover vs. real screenshot vs. live iframe — a cover was shipped as the pragmatic default)
- Pricing tiers ("Exact tiers: Free / Pro $25 / Rocket $50 / Booster $250") — unresolved from before this redesign started

**Nxeon/hosting/domains — paused per your instruction**, parked with research saved.

## Portal-specific loose ends

- **Nothing has been visually verified in a real browser.** Every consistency pass this session was blocked from getting an authenticated session (by design — I won't route around that). Everything is verified by types, lint, and tests, not by a human or a screenshot looking at it.
- Two small things I flagged but haven't fixed myself: 195 emoji-only country flags rendering as grey boxes on Windows, and a marketing hero photo with no recorded licence.
- `EmailLog` is declared but nothing writes to it — notification dedupe is still in-memory only.

## My recommendation

Before adding anything new: get someone with real credentials to **log in and click through the portal once** — that's the one gap none of this session's work can close on its own. Then commit, fix the VM→GitHub SSH problem, run `db push`, and deploy. The urgent live-content fixes (the false dental-form claim especially) should probably jump the queue ahead of all of it.

What this wires up

A Kodely user can link their existing Nxeon account (or create a real one on the spot — not a Kodely-specific credential), then from inside Kodely: buy a custom domain, deploy a VPS, or get shared hosting for their generated site — all billed through ONE shared Nxeon wallet.         │   Existing customers just log in; brand-new users click "Create

Async completion  →  Nxeon POSTs a signed webhook to YOUR /api/nxeon/webhook

import "server-only";

const BASE = process.env.NXEON_BASE_URL ?? "https://nxeon.cloud";
const KEY = process.env.NXEON_PARTNER_KEY!;
const REDIRECT_URI = process.env.NXEON_REDIRECT_URI!;

async function partner<T>(path: string, body: unknown): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "x-api-key": KEY, "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
    cache: "no-store",
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`nxeon ${path} -> ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.json() as Promise<T>;
}

/** Where to send the user's browser to link + log into their Nxeon account. */
export function nxeonAuthorizeUrl(state: string): string {
  const u = new URL(`${BASE}/sso/authorize`);
  u.searchParams.set("client_id", "kodely");
  u.searchParams.set("redirect_uri", REDIRECT_URI);
  u.searchParams.set("state", state);
  return u.toString();
}

/** Exchange the code from /sso/authorize for the linked Nxeon identity. */
export function exchangeSsoCode(code: string) {
  return partner<{ userId: string; email: string; name: string; balanceCents: number }>(
    "/api/partner/sso/token",
    { code, redirect_uri: REDIRECT_URI },
  );
}

/** Shared wallet balance for a linked Nxeon user. */
export function nxeonWallet(nxeonUserId: string) {
  return partner<{ balanceCents: number }>("/api/partner/wallet", { userId: nxeonUserId });
}

/** Live availability + retail price for up to 20 domains (name.com). */
export function nxeonCheckDomains(domains: string[]) {
  return partner<{
    results: Array<{
      domain: string;
      available: boolean;
      premium: boolean;
      priceCents: number | null;
      renewCents: number | null;
    }>;
  }>("/api/partner/domains/check", { domains });
}

/** A pre-filled Nxeon wizard URL — redirect the browser here to buy. */
export function nxeonCheckoutUrl(nxeonUserId: string, product: "domain" | "vps" | "hosting", domain?: string) {
  return partner<{ url: string }>("/api/partner/checkout", { userId: nxeonUserId, product, domain });
}

"use server";

import { redirect } from "next/navigation";
import { requireUser } from "@/lib/auth";
import { nxeonCheckoutUrl, nxeonCheckDomains, nxeonWallet } from "@/lib/nxeon";

/** "Get hosting" / "Custom domain" / "Get a VPS" button in the publish panel. */
export async function buyFromNxeon(product: "domain" | "vps" | "hosting", domain?: string) {
  const me = await requireUser();
  if (!me.nxeonUserId) redirect("/api/nxeon/connect"); // link (and log into Nxeon) first
  const { url } = await nxeonCheckoutUrl(me.nxeonUserId, product, domain);
  redirect(url); // lands in Nxeon's real wizard, already signed in
}

/** Live availability + price for a domain the user is typing into the publish panel. */
export async function checkDomainAvailability(domain: string) {
  const { results } = await nxeonCheckDomains([domain]);
  return results[0] ?? null;
}

/** Shared wallet balance, for display in the publish panel. Null if not yet linked. */
export async function getNxeonBalance(): Promise<number | null> {
  const me = await requireUser();
  if (!me.nxeonUserId) return null;
  const { balanceCents } = await nxeonWallet(me.nxeonUserId);
  return balanceCents;
}

import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
import { requireUser } from "@/lib/auth";
import { nxeonAuthorizeUrl } from "@/lib/nxeon";

/** Start the Nxeon account link. Redirects to Nxeon's own login/register — the
 *  user signs in with their REAL Nxeon credentials (or creates one), not a Kodely
 *  password. `state` guards against CSRF on the callback. */
export async function GET() {
  const me = await requireUser().catch(() => null);
  if (!me) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/login", process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? "https://kodely.me"));

  const state = randomBytes(16).toString("hex");
  const res = NextResponse.redirect(nxeonAuthorizeUrl(state));
  res.cookies.set("nxeon_sso_state", state, {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: true,
    sameSite: "lax",
    maxAge: 600,
    path: "/",
  });
  return res;
}

File: app/api/nxeon/callback/route.ts

import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import { db } from "@/lib/db";
import { requireUser } from "@/lib/auth";
import { exchangeSsoCode } from "@/lib/nxeon";

const APP_URL = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? "https://kodely.me";

/** Finish the Nxeon account link. Verifies the CSRF state, exchanges the code for
 *  the linked identity, and stores it on the Kodely user. */
export async function GET(req: Request) {
  const url = new URL(req.url);
  const code = url.searchParams.get("code");
  const state = url.searchParams.get("state");

  const jar = await cookies();
  const expected = jar.get("nxeon_sso_state")?.value;

  if (!code || !state || !expected || state !== expected) {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/dashboard?nxeon=error", APP_URL));
  }

  const me = await requireUser().catch(() => null);
  if (!me) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/login", APP_URL));

  let link: { userId: string; email: string; name: string; balanceCents: number };
  try {
    link = await exchangeSsoCode(code);
  } catch {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/dashboard?nxeon=error", APP_URL));
  }

  await db.user.update({ where: { id: me.id }, data: { nxeonUserId: link.userId } });

  const res = NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/dashboard?nxeon=linked", APP_URL));
  res.cookies.delete("nxeon_sso_state");
  return res;
}

import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";
import { db } from "@/lib/db";

const SECRET = process.env.NXEON_WEBHOOK_SECRET!;

/** Receives Nxeon's provision-complete callbacks. Only fires for orders placed
 *  through the Nxeon checkout link (?ref=kodely) — never for Nxeon's other
 *  customers. Verifies the HMAC signature against the RAW body before parsing. */
export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const raw = await req.text();
  const sig = req.headers.get("x-nxeon-signature") ?? "";
  const expected = createHmac("sha256", SECRET).update(raw).digest("base64url");

  const a = Buffer.from(sig);
  const b = Buffer.from(expected);
  if (a.length !== b.length || !timingSafeEqual(a, b)) {
    return new Response("bad signature", { status: 401 });
  }

  const { event, payload } = JSON.parse(raw) as { event: string; payload: Record<string, unknown> };

  switch (event) {
    case "vps.provisioned": {
      // payload: { userId, serverId, hostname, ipAddress }
      const nxeonUserId = String(payload.userId ?? "");
      if (nxeonUserId) {
        await db.user.updateMany({
          where: { nxeonUserId },
          data: {
            /* TODO: whatever field(s) surface "you have a live server" in your UI,
               e.g. nxeonServerId: String(payload.serverId), nxeonServerIp: String(payload.ipAddress) */
          },
        });
      }
      break;
    }
    case "domain.registered": {
      // payload: { userId, domain, expiresAt }
      const nxeonUserId = String(payload.userId ?? "");
      if (nxeonUserId) {
        // TODO: attach payload.domain to the user's project, prompt DNS setup, etc.
      }
      break;
    }
    case "hosting.provisioned": {
      // payload: { userId, accountId, domain }
      const nxeonUserId = String(payload.userId ?? "");
      if (nxeonUserId) {
        // TODO: whatever field(s) surface "your site is hosted" in your UI,
        // e.g. store payload.accountId / payload.domain against the project.

      break;

import "server-only";

const BASE = process.env.NXEON_BASE_URL ?? "https://nxeon.cloud";
const KEY = process.env.NXEON_PARTNER_KEY!;
const REDIRECT_URI = process.env.NXEON_REDIRECT_URI!;

async function partner<T>(path: string, body: unknown): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(`${BASE}${path}`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "x-api-key": KEY, "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
    cache: "no-store",
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`nxeon ${path} -> ${res.status}: ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.json() as Promise<T>;
}

/** Where to send the user's browser to link + log into their Nxeon account. */
export function nxeonAuthorizeUrl(state: string): string {
  const u = new URL(`${BASE}/sso/authorize`);
  u.searchParams.set("client_id", "kodely");
  u.searchParams.set("redirect_uri", REDIRECT_URI);
  u.searchParams.set("state", state);
  return u.toString();
}

/** Exchange the code from /sso/authorize for the linked Nxeon identity. */
export function exchangeSsoCode(code: string) {
  return partner<{ userId: string; email: string; name: string; balanceCents: number }>(
    "/api/partner/sso/token",
    { code, redirect_uri: REDIRECT_URI },
  );
}

/** Shared wallet balance for a linked Nxeon user. */
export function nxeonWallet(nxeonUserId: string) {
  return partner<{ balanceCents: number }>("/api/partner/wallet", { userId: nxeonUserId });
}

/** Live availability + retail price for up to 20 domains (name.com). */
export function nxeonCheckDomains(domains: string[]) {
  return partner<{
    results: Array<{
      domain: string;
      available: boolean;
      premium: boolean;
      priceCents: number | null;
      renewCents: number | null;
    }>;
  }>("/api/partner/domains/check", { domains });
}

/** A pre-filled Nxeon wizard URL — redirect the browser here to buy. */
export function nxeonCheckoutUrl(nxeonUserId: string, product: "domain" | "vps" | "hosting", domain?: string) {
  return partner<{ url: string }>("/api/partner/checkout", { userId: nxeonUserId, product, domain });
}

import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { randomBytes } from "node:crypto";
import { requireUser } from "@/lib/auth";
import { nxeonAuthorizeUrl } from "@/lib/nxeon";

/** Start the Nxeon account link. Redirects to Nxeon's own login/register — the
 *  user signs in with their REAL Nxeon credentials (or creates one), not a Kodely
 *  password. `state` guards against CSRF on the callback. */
export async function GET() {
  const me = await requireUser().catch(() => null);
  if (!me) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/login", process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? "https://kodely.me"));

  const state = randomBytes(16).toString("hex");
  const res = NextResponse.redirect(nxeonAuthorizeUrl(state));
  res.cookies.set("nxeon_sso_state", state, {
    httpOnly: true,
    secure: true,
    sameSite: "lax",
    maxAge: 600,
    path: "/",
  });
  return res;
}

import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { cookies } from "next/headers";
import { db } from "@/lib/db";
import { requireUser } from "@/lib/auth";
import { exchangeSsoCode } from "@/lib/nxeon";

const APP_URL = process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_APP_URL ?? "https://kodely.me";

/** Finish the Nxeon account link. Verifies the CSRF state, exchanges the code for
 *  the linked identity, and stores it on the Kodely user. */
export async function GET(req: Request) {
  const url = new URL(req.url);
  const code = url.searchParams.get("code");
  const state = url.searchParams.get("state");

  const jar = await cookies();
  const expected = jar.get("nxeon_sso_state")?.value;

  if (!code || !state || !expected || state !== expected) {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/dashboard?nxeon=error", APP_URL));
  }

  const me = await requireUser().catch(() => null);
  if (!me) return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/login", APP_URL));

  let link: { userId: string; email: string; name: string; balanceCents: number };
  try {
    link = await exchangeSsoCode(code);
  } catch {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/dashboard?nxeon=error", APP_URL));
  }

  await db.user.update({ where: { id: me.id }, data: { nxeonUserId: link.userId } });

  const res = NextResponse.redirect(new URL("/dashboard?nxeon=linked", APP_URL));
  res.cookies.delete("nxeon_sso_state");
  return res;
}

Cookies

Kodely sets four cookies, and every one of them is strictly necessary:

  • kodely_session keeps you signed in for up to 30 days. It holds a random token, and the corresponding record in our database holds only a hash of it, so a database read never yields a usable cookie.
  • kodely_auth records nothing except that you are signed in — its only value is the digit 1. It carries no name, no email address and no part of the token above. It exists so a page served from cache, which cannot know who is asking for it, can still show you “Portal” rather than “Sign in”. It is written and removed at exactly the same moments as the session cookie, and on its own it grants access to nothing.
  • kodely_google_oauth_state is set only when you click “Sign in with Google”, lives ten minutes, and exists to prove the reply from Google answers your own request rather than someone else's forgery.
  • kodely_discord_reward_state does the same job, only when you choose to connect a Discord account for reward credits.

There is no advertising pixel, no third-party analytics cookie and no tracker that follows you to another site — which is why you are not shown a cookie banner. The full reasoning, and what your browser stores locally, is on{" "} Your data and your rights.

content.content:
Support tickets

If you open a ticket from the support page inside your account, we store its subject, the category you chose, the site you attached if you attached one, its status, and every message on the thread — both what you write and what we reply. Unlike the contact form below, these are held in the product database, because the thread is the mechanism: it is where you read the reply and where you answer back. Whoever answers is recorded on their own message for our records; you are shown “Kodely support” rather than an individual's address.

Separately, support staff can write internal notes about an account so the next person picking up a thread has the history. Those are never shown to you inside the product, but they are disclosed in full — text and date — if you ask for your data.

Technical data

Requests to kodely.me pass through a CDN and web servers that keep standard access logs, which include IP addresses and timestamps. Our contact form holds the sender IP in memory for up to an hour purely to rate-limit spam; it is not written to the database.

If you email us through the contact form

The name, email address and message you submit are emailed to our own inbox so we can reply. They are not stored in the product database. This is the public form on{" "} /contact, and it is a different thing from a support ticket — a ticket is stored, has a status, and can be read back later; an emailed message is not and cannot. Nxeon is a separate company with its own product and its own login — connecting an account is optional and only happens if you choose to buy a domain, a VPS or shared hosting. Actually the placement is close enough to the reference layout, so it's not a major mismatch. The real divergence is on the Billing page, which collapsed to single-column instead of the requested two-column grid, so I'll concentrate the fix there.

Since the user's mockups likely include richer visual styling (colored accents, avatars, gradient cards) than my more muted, dense implementation, and I can't be certain exactly what "nothing like" refers to, the safest path is to actually rebuild the Billing page into the correct two-column structure, and then check in with the user about whether they're flagging layout structure or overall visual style so I can calibrate correctly.

Two things landed. Here's where they stand.

## Nxeon is wired up

All five routes, schema, and honesty guardrails are in and green (tsc, eslint, 336/336 tests, full production build):

- **`/api/nxeon/connect` → `/callback`** — real SSO into Nxeon's own login, never a Kodely password. I added one thing the kit didn't handle: if the Nxeon account is already linked to a *different* Kodely account, the link is refused outright rather than silently overwritten — otherwise one customer's session could end up spending from another customer's wallet.
- **`/api/nxeon/webhook`** — verifies the HMAC, then I added idempotency the kit was missing entirely. Its documented payload has no event id, so a raw retry would have applied every provisioning event twice; I fall back to hashing the request body when no id is present.
- **The Domains page is real now** where Nxeon is configured — connect button, live domain-availability pricing while you type, buttons for VPS and hosting, and a fact list of anything already provisioned. Where it isn't configured, the honest "not supported yet" page is untouched.
- **One boundary I made sure the copy states plainly, on the page itself**: buying a domain through Nxeon doesn't point it at your Kodely site, and a VPS or hosting account doesn't get your Kodely-built site deployed onto it. The kit only covers identity, billing, and provisioning notification — actually shipping files onto Nxeon infrastructure is separate, unbuilt work.
- Updated the privacy policy (a new cookie, a new data-sharing section), the account export, and account deletion to null out every Nxeon identifier — that part's as personal as a Google account link.

**You still need to paste the two secrets into `.env` yourself** — I didn't touch that file:
```
NXEON_BASE_URL=https://nxeon.cloud
NXEON_PARTNER_KEY=<from the kit>
NXEON_WEBHOOK_SECRET=<from the kit>
NXEON_REDIRECT_URI=https://kodely.me/api/nxeon/callback
```

I'd specified a two-column layout in my own brief and the shipped page came back as a single stacked column — a real miss, not a style disagreement. Fixed: left column now carries "Add credits" and the statement (where the plan card and invoice history sat in your reference), right column carries the account facts, spend cap, and cost ranges (where the subscription and usage panels sat).    NO CHARTING DEPENDENCY. This is plain SVG in a Server Component: it ships no
   JavaScript at all, which for a static bar chart is not a compromise — it is
   the better answer.

   THEMING. Every colour is a Tailwind class bound to a design token
   (`fill-brand`, `stroke-hair`, `fill-ink-3`), never an attribute and never a
   hex, so light and dark are handled by the same variable swap as the rest of
   the product. Presentational SVG attributes lose to CSS, which is why the
   classes work at all.

   ACCESSIBILITY. Three channels, in order of who they serve:
     1. A prose summary above the chart — the shape of the data in a sentence,
        for everyone including people who skim.
     2. The <svg> is role="img" with an aria-label carrying that same summary,
        so a screen reader gets the gist instead of 30 unlabelled <rect>s.
     3. A real <table> in a <details>, keyboard-operable, carrying every figure
        the bars encode. The bars are not individually focusable BECAUSE the
        table exists: 30 tab stops that each announce one number is worse than
        one tab stop that opens all of them.
   The chart is also legible at any width — it scales uniformly with its
   viewBox, so no label is ever clipped or squashed.

   GRANULARITY. A bar may cover one UTC day or a whole week — see groupBuckets

   660-unit plot are 1px apart. Every label, the summary and the table read the

// The "— Kodely" suffix comes from the title template on the (portal) layout.
export const metadata: Metadata = { title: "Usage" };

/* /dashboard/usage — what the credits went ON.
   ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   The brief for this screen asked for storage, bandwidth, a plan allowance and
   a reset date. None of the four exist (docs/design-system.md, "What does not
   exist"), so none of the four are drawn here. What IS real turns out to be
   more useful anyway: every credit ever charged is a successful build, every
   build belongs to a website, and both facts are already in the database.

   Every figure on this page is in CREDITS. Build.costMicros is real model
   spend — the cost side of the retail prices in lib/stripe.ts — and it is used
   only inside the arithmetic in ./data.ts, never rendered as money.

   THREE THINGS THIS LAYOUT DELIBERATELY DOES NOT DO, all of which the visual
   reference for it showed:
     1. The gradient card does NOT read "75% of 1,000 monthly credits" or
        "resets in 18 days". There is no allowance to be a percentage of and no
        reset date to count down to. It shows the balance and what it buys, in
        the same words as components/app/SidebarFooter.tsx and the /support
        card, because those three sit in front of the same customer.
     2. There is NO donut splitting spend across successful, failed and "other"
        builds. Failed builds are charged zero — chargeForBuild is only reached
        on the SUCCEEDED path in app/api/generate/route.ts, and both failure
        paths write creditsCharged: 0 and no ledger row — so that donut would
        be one 100% slice and two empty ones. The honest breakdown of spend is
        by WEBSITE, which is what "Where your credits went" draws, and the
        zero-charge story is the "What isn't charged" strip at the bottom.
     3. Deltas appear on exactly ONE stat, and only when the account is old

input.new_string:
WHAT A VISUAL REFERENCE FOR THIS PAGE SHOWED, and what stands in its place:
     1. "75% of 1,000 monthly credits" / "resets in 18 days" — there is no
        allowance to be a percentage of and no reset date. In that exact slot,
        the gradient card instead shows the customer's own SPEND CAP when one
        is set (a real number, a real rolling-30-day bar against it) and a
        plain sentence when it isn't. Uncapped is not hidden behind a fake bar.
     2. A donut splitting spend across successful, failed and "other" builds —
        impossible here, since a failed build is charged zero (chargeForBuild
        is only reached on the SUCCEEDED path in app/api/generate/route.ts),
        which would draw one 100% slice and two empty ones. SpendKindDonut.tsx
        draws the real split instead: each project's first charged build
        ("new sites") against every build after it ("edits") — a genuine
        category recovered from data that already exists, not invented to
        fill the shape.
     3. A "you're using less than last month!" banner, shown unconditionally —
        here it only renders when `spendingLess` is true, i.e. spend really is
        down by a real margin against a real comparable prior window. Spend
        going up is exactly as likely as it going down, and a banner that
        would still be praising an increase is worse than no banner.
     4. Six "what's free" tiles naming things Kodely does not have (custom
        domains, team invites) — the tiles below name six things that ARE
        free and real: editing, previewing, publishing, version history, a
        failed build, and a repaired one. */

Good, redirecting to login as expected (no session). Everything's green: tsc, eslint, 336/336 tests, full build.

## Nxeon is live

`nxeonEnabled()` now returns true — I appended the two secrets you pasted to the gitignored `.env` (verified it's ignored before touching it) and restarted the dev server to pick them up. The connect route redirects correctly. To actually finish verifying the OAuth round-trip and provisioning, someone needs to click through it with a real account — I can't create one myself.

## Usage & Billing — done a real pass at matching your screens

I went back through both pages and closed the gaps that were genuinely about layout fidelity, not just honesty:

- **A real donut**, not a missing one. Your reference split spend into successful/failed/other — that's impossible here since failed builds are charged zero. Instead it splits by something real and recoverable from existing data: **new sites vs. edits**, this month.
- **A real progress bar on the gradient card**, when there's something real to show — your own spend cap, with its actual number, in the exact visual slot your "75% of 1,000 monthly credits" occupied. No cap set → no bar, just a plain sentence.

die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree dirty — commit first"

git fetch -q origin main || die "cannot reach GitHub from here"
if [ -n "$(git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD)" ]; then
  say "Pushing to origin/main"
  git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | sed 's/^/  /'
  git push -q origin main
fi
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
echo "  main = $NEW"

ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

# --------------------------------------------------------------- transport
# Bundle only what the VM is missing, using prod's current HEAD as the base.
say "Bundling commits for the VM"
# Base on the OLDER of the two environments, not just prod: staging is
# routinely behind, and a bundle cut from prod's HEAD would be missing the
# commits staging still needs. merge-base gives the common ancestor.
PROD_HEAD=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse HEAD')
STAGING_HEAD=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely-staging && git rev-parse HEAD')
for c in "$PROD_HEAD" "$STAGING_HEAD"; do
  git cat-file -e "${c}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null || die "the VM is on commit ${c:0:7}, which this checkout does not have — fetch/rebase first"
done
BASE=$(git merge-base "$PROD_HEAD" "$STAGING_HEAD")
echo "  prod=${PROD_HEAD:0:7}  staging=${STAGING_HEAD:0:7}  base=${BASE:0:7}"

if [ "$BASE" = "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" ]; then
  echo "  both environments already at $NEW — nothing to transport"
  rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle
  vm "rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle" || true
else
  # Must be `..main`, not `..HEAD`: a bundle cut against HEAD is written with a
  # ref literally named "HEAD", and the VM's `git fetch <bundle> main` then
  # fails with "couldn't find remote ref main".
  git bundle create /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle "$BASE..main" >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "  $(git rev-list --count "$BASE..HEAD") commit(s), $(du -h /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle | cut -f1)"
  base64 -w0 /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle > /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64
  B64=$(cat /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64)
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" \
    "echo '$B64' | ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM 'base64 -d > /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle'" \
    || die "could not transfer the bundle to the VM"
  vm "cd /opt/kodely && git bundle verify /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle >/dev/null 2>&1" \
    || die "bundle failed verification on the VM"
  echo "  transferred and verified"
fi

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_env staging /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging https://staging.kodely.me

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

deploy_env prod /opt/kodely kodely https://kodely.me

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK"

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --skip-generate >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# deploy.sh — push this checkout's committed work to kodely.me.
#
#   ./deploy.sh            staging -> verify -> prod -> verify
#   ./deploy.sh --staging  stop after staging
#
# Transport note: the VM cannot currently reach GitHub over SSH (see the board
# card "VM cannot reach GitHub over SSH"). Its own /home/kodely/deploy.sh runs
# `git fetch origin main && git reset --hard origin/main`, and when that fetch
# fails it resets to a STALE remote-tracking ref and reports a healthy deploy
# of the WRONG commit — it did that twice on 2026-08-21.
#
# So this script does not rely on the VM pulling. It still pushes to GitHub
# (that works from here, and keeps origin authoritative), then ships the actual
# commits over the existing SSH path as a git bundle and builds in place. When
# the VM's GitHub access is restored, the bundle step can be dropped.
set -euo pipefail

HOST=root@51.79.162.96
VM=kodely@10.20.0.30
STAGING_ONLY="${1:-}"

say() { printf '\n\033[1m== %s\033[0m\n' "$*"; }
die() { printf '\n\033[31mABORT: %s\033[0m\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }
vm()  { ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM \"$1\""; }

say "Pre-flight"
[ "$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD)" = "main" ] || die "not on main"
[ -z "$(git status --porcelain)" ] || die "working tree dirty — commit first"

git fetch -q origin main || die "cannot reach GitHub from here"
if [ -n "$(git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD)" ]; then
  say "Pushing to origin/main"
  git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD | sed 's/^/  /'
  git push -q origin main
fi
NEW=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
echo "  main = $NEW"

ROLLBACK=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse --short HEAD')
say "Rollback point (current prod): $ROLLBACK"

# --------------------------------------------------------------- transport
# Bundle only what the VM is missing, using prod's current HEAD as the base.
say "Bundling commits for the VM"
# Base on the OLDER of the two environments, not just prod: staging is
# routinely behind, and a bundle cut from prod's HEAD would be missing the
# commits staging still needs. merge-base gives the common ancestor.
PROD_HEAD=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely && git rev-parse HEAD')
STAGING_HEAD=$(vm 'cd /opt/kodely-staging && git rev-parse HEAD')
for c in "$PROD_HEAD" "$STAGING_HEAD"; do
  git cat-file -e "${c}^{commit}" 2>/dev/null || die "the VM is on commit ${c:0:7}, which this checkout does not have — fetch/rebase first"
done
BASE=$(git merge-base "$PROD_HEAD" "$STAGING_HEAD")
echo "  prod=${PROD_HEAD:0:7}  staging=${STAGING_HEAD:0:7}  base=${BASE:0:7}"

if [ "$BASE" = "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" ]; then
  echo "  both environments already at $NEW — nothing to transport"
  rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle
  vm "rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle" || true
else
  # Must be `..main`, not `..HEAD`: a bundle cut against HEAD is written with a
  # ref literally named "HEAD", and the VM's `git fetch <bundle> main` then
  # fails with "couldn't find remote ref main".
  git bundle create /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle "$BASE..main" >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "  $(git rev-list --count "$BASE..HEAD") commit(s), $(du -h /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle | cut -f1)"
  base64 -w0 /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle > /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64
  B64=$(cat /tmp/kodely-deploy.b64)
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" \
    "echo '$B64' | ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM 'base64 -d > /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle'" \
    || die "could not transfer the bundle to the VM"
  vm "cd /opt/kodely && git bundle verify /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle >/dev/null 2>&1" \
    || die "bundle failed verification on the VM"
  echo "  transferred and verified"
fi

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --skip-generate >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_env staging /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging https://staging.kodely.me

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

deploy_env prod /opt/kodely kodely https://kodely.me

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK"

## What's built, matching your spec

Find the actual layout bug: likely a missing `overflow-hidden` on the outer dialog frame, a max-height that isn't being respected by a flex/grid child, or a scroll container that isn't correctly bounded. Fix it so the ENTIRE wizard — header, stage indicator, stage content, footer buttons — renders fully inside one bounded, rounded modal frame, with exactly one internal scroll region for the stage content when it's taller than available space. Verify the same fix (or lack of the same bug) in `TemplatePickerModal.tsx`.

## BUG 2 — the Features stage should be an icon grid, not a scrolling checkbox list

Currently it's a tall list of rows, each with a checkbox and no icon. Redesign it as a responsive grid of icon cards (2–3 columns depending on width), each card showing: an icon, the feature name, its one-line honest description, and a clear selected/unselected state (border + tint change, not just a checkbox — though the checkbox can remain for accessibility). Every feature in `lib/features.ts` (both offered and the `NOT_OFFERED` list, if the stage currently shows both) needs an icon — check what's already there and add `lucide-react` icons for any that are missing a sensible one. Keep every existing honest caveat sentence exactly as strong as it is now (e.g. "Kodely cannot run bookings, availability or payments itself") — do not soften or hide these while making the layout prettier.

## FIX 3 — the logo message is technically true but reads as "your upload does nothing"

The current copy says: "The image file itself can't go on the page — Kodely sites carry no uploaded pictures. The brief asks for a clearly-marked space where your logo goes instead." That's accurate but incomplete, and it currently reads as though the upload is discarded.

If your trace finds the pipeline is NOT actually connected (a real bug), fix that instead and say so in your report — do not just take my word for it.

1. **A "+" button** inside or beside the prompt box that opens a file picker.

All 11 refusal reasons check out as legitimate structural constraints — no database, no server, no outbound connections, and CSP gaps on frame-src, img-src, font-src, and form-action. This confirms that "mailing-list" specifically refers to posting directly to Mailchimp's servers, which is genuinely blocked by the form-action 'self' policy, distinct from the separately offered "keep me posted" feature.

Now I'm going through each unoffered item to see if any could realistically become achievable with genuine backend investment rather than fabrication. Online booking, accounts, and checkout all require real server-side infrastructure — databases, auth systems, payment processing — that would mean Kodely building entirely new platform capabilities, well beyond a quick fix. Search similarly needs a real database and query engine, and connect-src 'none' blocks any API call, so it can't be resolved without Kodely hosting a dedicated search service.

That said, I realize there's a genuinely real middle ground worth flagging: a purely client-side filter over a small, fixed list of already-rendered items requires no network calls at all and wouldn't violate the CSP — this is just JS array filtering. That's a legitimate, immediately buildable feature I could propose adding as an honest offering: "filter/search over your own static content," distinct from search over a real growing database. Next I'm considering map-embed, which is blocked by CSP frame-src/img-src rules and could only work if Kodely relaxed the CSP for a specific trusted domain.

Actually, wait — the CSP already permits `data:` URIs for images, so a base64-embedded photo would technically render just fine and pass the CSP. The real blocker isn't the CSP at all, it's that no mechanism exists today to get the customer's actual photo into the generated HTML — the reference image only ever reaches the model as vision input, never gets written into the file tree.

Actually, the lib/features.ts wording is slightly imprecise — remote images are blocked, but same-origin data URIs aren't; the real limitation is the lack of an upload mechanism plus the context-cost of embedding raster data, which isn't worth fixing in this pass since it'd require object storage and a whole upload infra. Live-chat is a separate, harder blocker: it needs remote scripts and outbound connections, which CSP's script-src and connect-src rules structurally prevent.

Kodely could theoretically build a first-party chat widget hosted at its own origin, but that's a full product effort involving a hosted backend, well beyond current scope. Analytics has the same problem — a first-party privacy-respecting script would need to live on kodely.me, but since generated sites are served from `<slug>.kodely.site`, that script would actually be cross-origin, requiring CSP whitelisting and connect-src exceptions that would weaken the strict "connect-src none" stance, making this another sizable feature project rather than a quick fix.

Social-feed and video-embed fall into the same bucket — video especially is blocked not just by CSP but by the complete absence of any video hosting infrastructure, making it a major infra undertaking that's clearly out of scope. Custom-fonts, though, looks like the most tractable case: adding `font-src 'self'` to the CSP is a small, low-risk change since fonts aren't a typical XSS vector, and Kodely could self-host a curated set of open-source webfonts the same way it already self-hosts icons and illustrations — achieving custom fonts with zero security compromise, unlike the network-dependent features above.

Still, this isn't a trivial add — it means vetting and vendoring 5-10 quality open-source font families with proper licensing checks (mirroring the discipline shown in the earlier asset-license audit), updating the CSP, integrating the font files into the site's build foundation, and wiring up `lib/agent.ts` to reference them. It's a legitimate feature project, not something to slip in as a quick fix this turn.

Then there's the mailing-list integration going directly to Mailchimp, which is structurally blocked by `form-action 'self'` — genuinely impossible to fix without relaxing that CSP directive, which is a real security tradeoff.

But there's a cleaner alternative: since Kodely's own server already receives form submissions via `/__forms/<name>`, that receiving endpoint could let customers configure a Mailchimp API key, and Kodely's backend would then forward the submission server-to-server using the existing site-forms.ts intake pipeline. This avoids any CSP change on the generated site entirely, since the site itself never talks to Mailchimp directly. It's a genuinely buildable, architecturally clean finding — mailing-list sign-ups reaching Mailchimp is achievable through this server-side integration.

That said, it's a scoped feature project requiring new settings UI, sensitive credential storage, and a new server-side call path, so it needs the user's go-ahead rather than being built in this pass. Weighing everything, I count 8 of 11 capabilities as genuinely not achievable without a fundamentally new backend service, while 1 (this Mailchimp case) is nearly real already.

The Mailchimp proxy also needs new UI and credential handling, making it a real feature project rather than a quick fix. Map-embed and photos involve real security/cost tradeoffs that are the owner's call, not something I should decide silently — so I shouldn't attempt to build the font system or Mailchimp proxy right now.

Instead, I'll add the one genuinely trivial win — a real search/filter feature — to lib/features.ts since it's cheap and safe, and report the other findings honestly as a costed menu of follow-up work, consistent with the "report don't fabricate" pattern from this session.

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is part of this read — decided, not defaulted: a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, so it fits only when the user asked for Markdown or the content is bound for a Markdown-native destination; never pick it to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits — link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=…&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Glob, Grep, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## 4bdddc46-3b80-45ec-bc37-523e74d4fda6
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f

Here's where things stand across the multi-part request:

**Done and verified (tsc + eslint clean):**
- Removed the suggestion chips and the "120–550 credits" range paragraph from the Create page; the prompt box is now vertically centered ([Composer.tsx](app/(portal)/dashboard/new/Composer.tsx), [CreateFlow.tsx](app/(portal)/dashboard/new/CreateFlow.tsx)).
- Added a site-wide custom scrollbar, themed off your existing `--border-strong`/`--brand-ring` tokens ([globals.css](app/globals.css)).
- Usage page charts now use real gradients instead of flat fills — the bar chart has a brand→purple vertical gradient plus a soft radial wash, the donut's two arcs each run a distinct gradient (pink→purple for new sites, purple→peach for edits), and the four top stat tiles each got a colored gradient icon chip instead of the same flat pink tile four times over ([UsageChart.tsx](app/(portal)/dashboard/usage/UsageChart.tsx), [SpendKindDonut.tsx](app/(portal)/dashboard/usage/SpendKindDonut.tsx), [page.tsx](app/(portal)/dashboard/usage/page.tsx)). These are new local SVG/CSS gradients, not your reserved `--brand-gradient` — that's still only on the primary CTA and credits cards, per the standing rule.
- Added one genuinely real feature to the library: a client-side filter/search box over a small fixed list (menu, price list, portfolio) — pure JS, no network call, no CSP change needed, so it's honest to offer today ([features.ts](lib/features.ts)).

**Agent B finished** — the prompt box now has a "+" attach button, image paste, and drag-and-drop, all funneling into the one real attachment path. Video/PDF get a clear toast explaining Kodely can't read them, rather than being silently accepted. tsc/eslint clean.

**Agent A (InlineWizard modal fix, features-as-icon-grid, logo copy) is still running.**

**On "we should be able to support all of these features":** I went through all 11 refused items in `lib/features.ts`. Bottom line — none of them can be flipped on as a quick fix, because each is blocked by something real: no database/server (booking, accounts, checkout), the CSP's `connect-src 'none'` and no `frame-src` (live chat, analytics, social feed, video, maps), or `img-src`/`font-src`/`form-action` restrictions (photos, custom fonts, Mailchimp). Two are worth a real look as future projects if you want them:
- **Custom fonts** — could genuinely work: vendor a curated set of open-source fonts (same pattern as your self-hosted icons) plus add `font-src 'self'` to the CSP. Low security risk, moderate effort.
- **Mailchimp sign-ups** — could genuinely work via a server-side proxy: Kodely's own backend (which already receives form submissions) forwards them to a customer-supplied Mailchimp API key, so the generated site never talks to Mailchimp directly. Needs new settings UI and credential storage, so it's a real feature project, not a tweak.

The rest (booking, accounts, checkout, search-over-real-data, live chat, analytics, social feeds, video hosting, live maps) would each need Kodely to build actual backend infrastructure — not something to build into this pass. I didn't touch any of this in code; just flagging what's real vs. not.

Now I'm cross-checking the mockup against real data constraints, since Kodely credits don't expire or reset monthly. That means the mockup's "resets in 18 days" and "% of allowance" framing is fabricated and must be replaced with real balance and spend cap info instead, while metrics like credits used and average build cost can stay since they map to real computed values, though the "vs last month" trend for average build cost isn't currently tracked and would need to be added or omitted.

I'm also confirming that the donut chart attributing spend to "failed builds" is a fabrication I already caught and fixed previously with an honest new-sites-vs-edits breakdown. Now I just need to restyle that existing honest donut to match the mockup's more vivid look with a thicker ring, glow, and larger center number, without reintroducing the fabricated categories.

For the "recent credit activity" table, since the user wants a layout similar to the mockup's date/website/action/credits/status columns, I can restyle my existing compact activity component into a proper table format using real ledger data — project name, reason, delta, timestamp — with status always shown as "Completed" since that's accurate for ledger rows. I'll skip adding fake search boxes or filter dropdowns that don't actually work, since that would duplicate the real statement page dishonestly.

Usage alert toggles with 80%/100% thresholds would be another exact fabrication I flagged earlier since there's no notification system behind them, so I'll keep the real spend cap panel but just restyle it visually without fake toggles. Similarly "Upgrade plan" was already rejected since there's no subscription tier, so I'll keep only the real "Buy credits" button restyled with warmer colors. The "Where your credits went" section can reuse real site data with gradient bars instead of flat colors for visual polish.

The left sidebar in the mockup showing a "Pro Plan" card is a fictitious tier and out of scope entirely -- I won't touch the sidebar since it's a separate real component and no such plan exists; I'll focus only on the Usage page content itself. For the "Credits over time" graph, I can convert my bar chart to a smooth filled area chart with gradient fill and a hover tooltip showing date/credit values, which is a legitimate visual upgrade using the same real bucketed data.

<result>## Summary

**Setup note**: dashboard auth couldn't be reached (no credentials, and creating one is prohibited), so I built a temporary unauthenticated route (`app/tmp-wizard-preview/page.tsx`, outside all forbidden paths) to render both modals directly, drove them with `javascript_exec`/DOM measurement (screenshots aren't available in this headless pane), and deleted the route before finishing. `git status` confirms no leftover files and edits confined to `components/wizard/InlineWizard.tsx` and `components/templates/TemplatePickerModal.tsx`.

### Bug 1 — overflow / double scrollbar (root cause, empirically confirmed)

Two independent, additive causes, both in code I own (Modal.tsx's `<dialog>` was never touched):

1. **No height budget tied to the dialog's actual space.** The stage-content region used `max-h-[min(56vh,30rem)]`, sized against the viewport in isolation. The native `<dialog>` has no explicit height/overflow of its own, so it falls back to the UA default (`overflow: auto`, `max-height: calc(100% - Npx)` of viewport). When the wizard's real total (header + rail + that region + footer) exceeded that clamp, the **dialog itself** started scrolling as a second container around the first — verified: at 1280×600 the Features stage showed `dialog.scrollHeight(601) > clientHeight(560)` *and* the inner region overflowing simultaneously.
2. **A second, subtler leak, independent of (1).** Every `sr-only` radio (category chips, look cards, tone chips) is `position: absolute` with no positioned ancestor. Its containing block became the `<dialog>` itself (`dialog:modal` is `position: fixed` in the UA sheet), so its off-screen hypothetical position pierced straight through both `overflow-hidden` and `overflow-y-auto` wrappers and inflated the dialog's own scrollable area — confirmed via `dialog.scrollTop` being draggable to 71px even after fix (1), dragging the header off-screen.

3. Implement the PDF path: new `document` field end to end (Composer -> route -> agent.ts, attempt-1 gated like the image).
4. Implement the video path: client-side first-frame extraction reusing the image pipeline exactly.
5. Update all user-facing copy (attach button label/aria, thumbnail caption, any "what happens to this file" text) to honestly describe what actually happens for each of the three file kinds now supported.
6. Keep rejecting anything else with a clear, honest toast.

content.text:
Here's a concrete phased plan for real backend capability, scoped so it doesn't blow up the current security model:

**The core tension, restated:** every generated site today is a static bundle with a locked-down CSP (`connect-src 'none'`, no `frame-src`, no server of its own). That's *why* the AI can be trusted to generate code unsupervised — there's nothing dangerous it can do. The moment a site can talk to a real backend, "the AI writes arbitrary code that runs with real permissions" becomes true, and that's the part that needs a deliberate boundary, not an accidental one.

**The boundary I'd draw:** the AI never gets to write and run its own server code. Instead, Kodely offers a fixed menu of real, Kodely-owned backend *primitives* that the AI wires a generated UI to. The AI's job stays "write the frontend, call these APIs" — never "write and execute a server."

**Phase 0 — foundation (what "prepare a foundation" should actually mean):**
- A real per-project data table: a generic `records` store (projectId, a JSON payload, a "kind" tag) that any primitive below can write into. One shared schema, not a new table per feature.
- A scoped API layer generated sites can call: same-origin relative paths like `/api/site/{projectId}/...`, so the CSP can allow *that one origin* (`connect-src 'self'` scoped to Kodely's own API) without opening the floodgates to arbitrary outbound requests.
- Rate limiting and per-project quotas on that API from day one — this is the thing that turns "someone's generated contact form" into "an abuse vector" if skipped.

**Phase 1 — the first two primitives** (highest value, lowest new-surface):
- **Bookings/calendar**: a real table (service, date/time, contact info), a real availability check, real emails on confirm — no arbitrary logic, just a defined shape the AI fills in with the business's actual services.
- **Simple CRUD data** (menus, listings, inventory) that a client can edit through a lightweight admin view Kodely hosts — this is most of what "a client portal" means for a small business in practice.

**Phase 2 — accounts**: a real, Kodely-hosted auth primitive a generated site can drop a login into (magic link or password, Kodely's session, not the AI's). This is what unlocks "customer accounts" and "client portal" without the AI ever touching auth/session code, which is the single riskiest thing to let an LLM improvise.

**Deliberately NOT in scope, maybe ever:** arbitrary server-side code execution, arbitrary outbound network calls from a generated site, and full payment processing beyond linking out to Stripe/Square (that's a licensing and liability question, not just an engineering one).

**What I'd actually start on now, if you want to move:** Phase 0's data table + scoped API layer, since everything else depends on it, and it's genuinely just infrastructure — no product surface changes yet, so it doesn't lock in a feature decision I haven't scoped with you. I'd treat that as its own dedicated piece of work (schema, API route, rate limiting, CSP change), not something to fold into the current batch of UI fixes. Want me to start there, or do you want to look at the phase list first and reorder/cut anything?

This is a great precedent to follow: a plain HTML form POST with no JavaScript or fetch, hitting the site's own origin at a forms endpoint that gets proxied back into Kodely's app. It's elegant because it means Phase 0 doesn't need any CSP relaxation at all—connect-src can stay locked down if I mirror this same same-origin POST pattern.

I can extend this exact mechanism into a generic data primitive: the existing forms endpoint handles arbitrary submissions like contact enquiries, and I could add a parallel same-origin path for structured data (bookings, CRUD-style listings) that's still just a static form post, keeping the same trust model and rate limits. For reading data back—like a client portal showing existing bookings—I'd need a same-origin GET-based read path proxied through that same site route handler.

Since the generated site is a static bundle rather than server-rendered, reading data into the page would mean a client-side fetch to that same-origin data path, which means `connect-src 'self'` alone suffices without opening any external domain—this is a much smaller, more contained relaxation than I first assumed, since the proxy already treats the per-site subdomain as its own origin for form submissions.

Alternatively, an even simpler path exists: reuse Kodely's existing dashboard pattern where project owners already view their form submissions on a Kodely-rendered admin page, not embedded in the generated static site. Applying this same pattern for bookings or CRUD listings would deliver "client portal" value fast and safely for the MVP without touching CSP at all.

For booking-specific logic like checking slot availability, I realize that can be handled server-side in the same route handler that receives the POST, doing a read-then-validate before writing, similar to how the existing rate-limit checks work — no client-side fetch or connect-src changes needed if we're okay rejecting conflicts at submit time with an honest reply page. Though for a better experience, showing live availability before submission would require some additional mechanism.
