65	//     relative URL on the page, which is a way to smuggle a remote origin back
66	//     in past the directives above.
67	//   object-src 'none' — plugin content has no use on a static generated page,
68	//     and it does not fall back to default-src either.
69	//
70	// MUST STAY IN SYNC with the copy in app/api/preview/[id]/[[...path]]/route.ts,
71	// which serves the same generated markup to the editor's iframe. It is a
72	// separate constant in a separate file on purpose (that route is owner-only
73	// and has its own MIME table); there is no shared module for the two.
74	const SANDBOX_CSP =
75	  "default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'";

77	/**
78	 * Which stored build file answers a requested URL path.
79	 *
80	 * Generated sites are multi-page (lib/foundation.ts): `vite build` emits a real
81	 * document per page — index.html, about.html, blog/index.html — and visitors
82	 * ask for /about, not /about.html. This is the whole server-side cost of that.
83	 *
84	 * Deliberately NOT the SPA catch-all ("serve index.html for anything unknown").
85	 * That shape is what a client-side router needs, and it turns every typo, every
86	 * dead inbound link and every stale crawl URL into a 200 serving the home page —
87	 * soft 404s, which Google treats as a quality problem on the whole site. Here a
88	 * path resolves only to a file that actually exists under one of two well-known
89	 * spellings, and everything else still 404s exactly as it did before.
90	 *
91	 * Anything carrying an extension resolves to itself and nothing else, which is
92	 * what keeps robots.txt, sitemap.xml and /assets/* on their existing single
93	 * path — no candidate list can shadow them.
94	 */
95	function candidatePaths(filePath: string): string[] {
96	  if (/\.[A-Za-z0-9]+$/.test(filePath)) return [filePath];
97	  const clean = filePath.replace(/\/+$/, "");
98	  if (!clean) return ["index.html"];
99	  // Order matters: about.html wins over about/index.html when a site has both.
100	  return [`${clean}.html`, `${clean}/index.html`];
101	}
102	
103	/**
104	 * Form submissions from a published site: `POST /__forms/<formName>`, which
105	 * arrives here as `/api/site/<slug>/__forms/<formName>` via proxy.ts.
106	 *
107	 * Everything — host check, published check, caps, abuse control, storage and
108	 * the owner notification — is in lib/site-forms.ts. Anything that is not that
109	 * exact path shape is a 404 there, so this does not become a general POST
110	 * surface on the sites domain.
111	 */
112	export async function POST(
113	  req: Request,
114	  { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string; path?: string[] }> },
115	) {
116	  const { slug, path } = await params;
117	  return submitSiteForm(req, slug, path ?? []);
118	}
119	
120	export async function GET(
121	  req: Request,
122	  { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string; path?: string[] }> },
123	) {
124	  const { slug, path } = await params;
125	  const filePath = path && path.length > 0 ? path.join("/") : "index.html";
126	
127	  // Generated pages are only ever first-party to the sites domain. proxy.ts
128	  // turns this request away earlier for the same reason, but a route handler
129	  // must not depend on that: the proxy's own matcher can miss paths, and the
130	  // proxy is explicit (see its header comment) that it is never the only gate.
131	  //
132	  // The response is byte-identical to the "no such site" 404 below, so it does
133	  // not confirm that a slug exists to someone probing the wrong host.
134	  if (!siteHostAllowed(req.headers.get("host") ?? "", slug)) {
135	    return new Response("Site not found.", { status: 404 });
136	  }
137	
138	  const project = await db.project.findUnique({ where: { slug } });
139	  if (!project || !project.publishedAt) {
140	    return new Response("Site not found.", { status: 404 });
141	  }
142	
143	  const baseUrl = siteBaseUrl(req, slug);
144	  const seoHeaders = {
145	    "Content-Security-Policy": SANDBOX_CSP,
146	    "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=60",
147	  };
148	
149	  // robots.txt and sitemap.xml are generated, not stored — they depend on the
150	  // visitor-facing host (which differs between the branded subdomain and the
151	  // staging path form), so a file baked at build time would be wrong on one of
152	  // them. A site that ships its own copy still wins: we only synthesise these
153	  // when the project has no such file.
154	  if (filePath === "robots.txt" || filePath === "sitemap.xml") {
155	    const own = await db.projectFile.findFirst({
156	      where: { projectId: project.id, path: filePath, published: true, kind: "build" },
157	    });
158	    if (!own) {
159	      if (filePath === "robots.txt") {
160	        return new Response(robotsTxt(baseUrl), {
161	          headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME.txt },
162	        });
163	      }
164	      const pages = await db.projectFile.findMany({
165	        where: { projectId: project.id, published: true, kind: "build", path: { endsWith: ".html" } },
166	        select: { path: true },
167	      });
168	      return new Response(
169	        sitemapXml(baseUrl, pages.map((p) => p.path), project.publishedAt ?? undefined),
170	        { headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME.xml } },
171	      );
172	    }
173	  }
174	
175	  // One query for both spellings of a page, then the caller's preference order
176	  // decides — /about must not cost two round trips to answer.
177	  const candidates = candidatePaths(filePath);
178	  const matches = await db.projectFile.findMany({
179	    where: { projectId: project.id, path: { in: candidates }, published: true, kind: "build" },
180	  });
181	  const file = candidates.map((c) => matches.find((m) => m.path === c)).find(Boolean);
182	  if (!file) {
183	    return new Response("Not found.", { status: 404 });
184	  }
185	
186	  const ext = file.path.split(".").pop() ?? "";
187	
188	  // Backstop so no site can ship with the foundation's placeholder <title>.
189	  // Only fills gaps — anything the builder wrote itself is preserved.
190	  //
191	  // pageUrl(), not baseUrl: canonical and og:url must name THIS page. Keyed off
192	  // the file that actually answered, so /about and /about.html both canonicalise
193	  // to /about and Google sees one page rather than two competing duplicates.
194	  const body =
195	    ext === "html"
196	      ? applySeo(file.content, {
197	          projectName: project.name,
198	          baseUrl,
199	          pageUrl: pageUrl(baseUrl, file.path),
200	        })
201	      : file.content;
202	
203	  return new Response(body, {
204	    headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME[ext] ?? "application/octet-stream" },
205	  });
206	}

This confirms Composer.tsx was touched by multiple background agents, with the hero-card work present but the PDF/video rejection logic not yet updated—so those agents are still in-flight. More importantly, I've verified that published sites are served dynamically per request via force-dynamic rendering with fresh DB queries on each GET, not as static pre-rendered snapshots.

This means I could inject live server-side data into a page at request time without any client-side JS or CSP changes, either by having the agent's generated HTML contain a marker the route fills server-side, or by exposing small "live" endpoints under a data path that render HTML fragments server-side—same-origin GET requests don't need any connect-src changes since only fetch/XHR does. So I'm sketching a clean, CSP-respecting design: generalizing the existing FormSubmission pattern into a new SiteRecord table to support this live-data model.

Defining schema fields...

I'm designing the write path so bookings post to a proxied endpoint mirroring the existing forms handler, but with a new site-records module that shares rate-limiting, origin checks, and body caps with the forms code via a common helper rather than copy-pasting. For availability, the server checks existing active bookings at the same project/date/time before creating the record and rejects conflicts with a plain reply page, keeping everything server-side with no client JS or CSP changes needed.

For the initial version, I'm deciding to skip a live-availability preview and instead make the submission itself authoritative -- if the slot's taken, the user finds out on submit and tries again, similar to a "username taken" flow. For the owner's side, I'm planning to reuse the existing submissions page pattern, adding a parallel records view or a kind filter so project owners can see their bookings and listings.

This keeps everything inside Kodely's own authenticated dashboard rather than the untrusted generated site, which is the safer approach to a client portal MVP -- generalizing the one proven-safe pattern instead of inventing something new, and it works without loosening the CSP. Given the scope -- a new Prisma model and migration, a records module mirroring the forms safety logic, wiring into the POST handler, an availability check, and an owner view page -- this is well-defined enough to hand off to a background agent now that I've worked out the architecture, though I'll keep control over the security decisions myself.

Since I shouldn't run migrations myself, I'll have the agent write the schema change and hand the exact migration command to the user rather than executing it. I'm also reconsidering scope: rather than building both bookings and generic listings, Phase 0 should really just be the generic SiteRecord foundation -- schema, write pipeline, rate limiting, and owner viewing page -- leaving the booking-specific availability logic for Phase 1 once the foundation is proven.

I want Phase 0 to stay purely about the generic storage/write/read foundation, demonstrated minimally by letting a generated site write any structured record the same safe way it already handles contact forms, with the owner able to view them grouped by kind in the dashboard. This matches "prepare a foundation" literally, so I'll finalize this as a well-specified agent task now, giving it the exact schema, the file to mirror, the route wiring point, and the non-negotiables like no CSP changes, no client-side fetch, mirroring existing safety machinery, and reporting the migration command instead of running it.

Read the key precedent — `lib/site-forms.ts` and its route wiring. This confirms something important that changes the plan for the better: published sites are already served **dynamically per-request** (not static snapshots), and the existing contact-form pipeline proves a whole data-write path that needs **zero CSP changes** — a plain HTML form POSTs to the site's own origin (`form-action 'self'`), which the proxy routes back into Kodely's own database. Phase 0 should generalize that exact pattern rather than touch the CSP at all.

Here's the concrete design, then I'll hand it to an agent to build:

- **New `SiteRecord` model** (generalizing `FormSubmission`): `projectId`, `kind` (e.g. `"booking"`, `"listing"`), a JSON `fields` payload, `status`, timestamps — one reusable table any future primitive (bookings, CRUD listings) writes into, instead of a new table per feature.
- **Write path**: a new `lib/site-records.ts` mirroring `lib/site-forms.ts`'s entire safety model (same-origin-only via `form-action 'self'`, origin check, body caps, honeypot, three-layer rate limiting) — factored to share that plumbing rather than copy-pasted, since the validation logic (e.g. checking a booking slot isn't already taken) genuinely differs per `kind` but the safety rails don't.
- **No CSP change, no client-side fetch, no new attack surface** — same trust model that's already proven safe for contact forms.
- **Owner-side viewing**: a real, authenticated page in Kodely's own dashboard (mirroring `/projects/[id]/submissions`) where the project owner sees their site's records — the actual "client portal" lives in Kodely's dashboard, not inside the untrusted generated bundle.

This is deliberately just the foundation — no booking-specific logic yet, that's Phase 1. Dispatching now:

Rather than assume unlimited scope, I should propose a concrete expanded Phase 1 — likely folding in real accounts/auth from Phase 2 and giving the AI explicit patterns in the system prompt for using SiteRecord to build CRMs, portals, inventory systems, etc. Given how decisive the user has been throughout this conversation, I'll lay out this concrete plan directly and confirm it looks right rather than asking another open-ended question.

The bigger idea taking shape: instead of hardcoding "bookings" and "CRUD listings" as two separate features, teach the agent itself to design record shapes — field names, kinds — for whatever business the user describes, using SiteRecord as a generic foundation with consistent conventions for create/list/edit/status actions, essentially a mini form-builder pattern the AI can apply to any structured data need.

I also want to pull real accounts/auth into Phase 1 rather than leaving it for later, since a genuine client portal needs login so each client only sees their own records — plus a generic read/search mechanism so the generated site can display data back to users, not just accept form submissions. Since sites already run force-dynamic, authenticated server-rendered read pages are naturally supported, which makes this the logical next capability to add alongside owner-side edit/delete/export tools in the dashboard.

I'm using magic-link email via the existing mail library instead of password handling, since it's simpler and safer for AI-generated auth logic. I also want to extend the record pattern into real CRUD with update/delete support, plus improve the owner's dashboard with edit/export/delete capabilities — though I recognize this is turning into a substantial infrastructure effort spanning real auth and dynamic templated pages.

Given the scope, I think it's worth checking back with the user before committing to all of it — specifically confirming whether they want auth included in this first phase or just the expanded data capabilities without login yet, since that's the single biggest addition with its own tradeoffs to consider.

content.text:
Here's a genuinely bigger Phase 1, built on the same foundation:

**A. Teach the AI to design its own data, not just fill in a fixed template.** Right now the plan implied hardcoded "booking" and "listing" features. Bigger version: extend `lib/agent.ts`'s prompt so the AI can invent whatever `kind`/`fields` shape fits the business it's building — a CRM's contacts, a restaurant's reservations, a shop's inventory, a gym's class roster — all through the same `SiteRecord` primitive, with the AI choosing field names and a matching UI, the way it already chooses layout and copy today.

**B. Real reads, not just writes.** Phase 0 only covers a visitor *submitting* data (safe, no CSP change, proven pattern). A real CRM/portal needs to *show* data back — "your upcoming bookings," "current inventory." Since published sites are already rendered per-request server-side (not frozen static files), Kodely can inject live `SiteRecord` data into a page at request time, with zero client-side JS and zero CSP relaxation. This is what actually turns "a form that stores things" into "a working app."

**C. Real CRUD, not just create.** Extend the safe same-origin write path to also update and delete/cancel records (with ownership checks — a visitor should only be able to touch their own record, not anyone's), not just append new ones.

**D. A real accounts primitive.** This is the one genuinely new, bigger piece: a Kodely-hosted login (magic-link email, no passwords for the AI to mishandle) so a generated site can have actual "sign in to see my own bookings/orders" — the thing that makes "client portal" real instead of an open form anyone can see.

(D) is the biggest lift and the one I'd want to confirm before diving in — it's a new trust primitive (real sessions, real per-visitor identity on someone else's site), separate from the data-layer work in A–C. Want me to include real accounts in this round, or start with A–C (which alone turns this into a real, general-purpose CRUD system) and treat accounts as its own follow-up?

content.thinking:
With scope confirmed to A-C, I want to work through the architecture myself before handing off to an agent, given the security sensitivity around ownership checks and server-side rendering. I'm sketching how to extend the agent's system prompt so it can design its own SiteRecord shapes for custom data models.

For real reads, the tricky part is how a static page's stored HTML gets live data injected at request time — I'm thinking through whether to use placeholder markers that get swapped during serving, or a separate dynamic page type.

The cleanest fit is a lightweight convention where the builder emits a container marked with something like a data attribute naming the record kind and a fallback empty state, and the GET handler recognizes that marker, queries matching SiteRecords, and injects the rendered (fully escaped) results into that slot before serving — keeping everything string-level rather than requiring a full templating engine.

For the actual repeating structure, I'm having the builder also author a small template block inside the same container using `{{field}}` placeholders, which Kodely clones once per active record and fills in with escaped values — this stays consistent with how site-forms.ts already treats stored content as untrusted-in-HTML, requires no client JS or CSP changes, and is a genuinely buildable server-side-rendered feature.

For safety, I'm limiting interpolation to text content only for v1 rather than attributes, since that avoids any injection risk through `src=`, `href=`, or event-handler attributes while still letting builders display record data. I'll also default to newest-first ordering with an optional ascending flag, and cap rendered records per page (around 100) to keep things performant.

Next I'm turning to the harder problem: building real CRUD operations — update, delete, and cancel — with proper ownership checks on the existing POST endpoint.

Since accounts are being deferred, the only honest way to let an anonymous creator later modify or cancel their own record is through a possession token: a random unguessable `editToken` generated at creation time and stored on the record, likely hashed the same way IPRateLimit entries are, so a database leak wouldn't expose live tokens.

The token gets returned to the submitter as part of a manage link, following the standard no-login cancellation pattern used by real booking systems ("cancel your reservation" links in confirmation emails). Update and delete endpoints would then check the submitted token against the stored hash for a real ownership check without requiring login, and if no email exists to send the link, the confirmation page itself can display it for the user to save.

The project owner also gets the ability to edit or delete any record directly through their existing authenticated dashboard, since they already have full authenticated ownership over their own project — no token needed there. Given how large this feature is, spanning schema changes, new library methods, agent prompt updates, template rendering logic, owner UI controls, and token generation/validation, I want to work through the concrete design carefully before implementing.

Since the templating engine and the token-based CRUD both touch the same files — site-records.ts, the site route, and the owner UI — I'll dispatch a single comprehensive background agent to handle all three pieces together rather than splitting the work and risking merge conflicts. I need to write an extremely explicit and detailed prompt for it, especially around the security-sensitive parts like escaping rules and token hashing, plus the schema addition for an edit token field on records.

I'm also deciding that "delete" for token-authenticated users should really be a soft cancel — setting status to "cancelled" rather than removing the row — consistent with how the status field was designed to preserve history, while a true hard delete can be reserved for the owner's authenticated dashboard where purging their own data is reasonable.

Dispatching now with a precise spec, since the read/write security details need to be exact.

THE GOAL (confirmed scope — do NOT include real user accounts/login, that is explicitly deferred to later separate work):

**A — Teach the builder to design its own record shapes.** Extend lib/agent.ts's system prompt with a new section (parallel in tone/rigor to the existing forms section) explaining SiteRecord to the model: it can `POST /__records/<kind>` to store structured data for whatever the business actually needs — a CRM's contacts, a restaurant's reservations, a shop's inventory, a gym's class roster, anything — by choosing its own `kind` (URL-safe token, same regex discipline as form names) and its own field names (same regex/cap discipline as form fields: validated key names, capped value lengths, `_`-prefixed control fields never stored). It is NOT a fixed template — the model picks the shape that fits the brief. Explain the full lifecycle it now has available (write via A, read-back via B, update/cancel via C) so it can build something that is actually a working data-backed feature, not just a write-only form. Be exact about the mechanics (exact path shape, exact control-field names, exact content-type) since this text steers a model that will generate real markup — copy the existing forms section's level of precision.

**B — Real reads: live data rendered back into the page, server-side, per request, with zero client JS and zero CSP change.** Design and implement a minimal, SAFE server-side templating convention:
- The builder authors a container element with `data-kodely-records="<kind>"` and, inside it, exactly one `<template data-kodely-record-template>` child whose innerHTML is the per-record markup, using `{{fieldName}}` placeholders ONLY in text content (never inside tag attributes like `src=`/`href=`/`on*=` — do not implement attribute interpolation at all, text-content-only, to close off any injection vector through attributes). The container's own children OTHER than the `<template>` (e.g., a paragraph inside it) serve as the empty-state fallback the builder authors itself.
- At GET-request time (in the same route that already reads db.projectFile and serves HTML — app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts), after loading an `.html` file's content and BEFORE the existing applySeo() step, scan for every `data-kodely-records="<kind>"` container, query `SiteRecord` where `projectId` matches and `kind` matches and `status: "active"` and `spam: false`, ordered newest-first, capped at a sane max (e.g. 100) so a page can never render unboundedly large. For EACH matching record, clone the `<template>`'s inner markup and replace every `{{fieldName}}` occurrence in TEXT NODES with that record's `fields[fieldName]` value, HTML-escaped exactly the way lib/site-forms.ts already escapes stored field values before they reach any HTML/email context (reuse or mirror escapeHtml exactly — never trust a field value in HTML unescaped). A field name with no matching value in that record renders as empty string, not as the literal `{{...}}` or an error — a record simply may not have every field the template expects. If there are zero matching records, leave the container's original static children in place (the builder's own empty-state) instead of an empty div. Remove the `<template>` tag itself from the served output in both cases (it's a build-time-authored template, not something a browser should ever be asked to render). This must run efficiently for a page with several containers (batch the SiteRecord queries per kind rather than one query per container if a page happens to have more than one of the same kind — should not normally happen, but don't do an unbounded number of separate queries per request either).
- No client-side JavaScript, no fetch, no CSP relaxation anywhere. This is pure server-side string/DOM templating done once per request in the existing route handler.
- Write a focused unit-style sanity check is not required (no test framework mandate here) but DO manually reason through: a record whose field VALUE contains `</template>`, `<script>`, or `{{` must render as inert escaped text, never break out of its slot or execute. State in your final report how you verified this (e.g., a specific field value you traced through the code by hand).

**C — Real update/cancel without accounts, via an unguessable per-record link (the same pattern real-world "manage your booking" email links use).**
- When a `SiteRecord` is created via `POST /__records/<kind>`, generate a cryptographically random token (Node's `crypto.randomBytes`, no new dependency), store only its SHA-256 hash on the row (add an `editTokenHash` nullable String column to the `SiteRecord` model — mirror how `ipHash` is already salted-hashed in this codebase, same salt-env-var pattern), and return the RAW token to the submitter exactly once, in the same-origin HTML response page (the existing `page()`-style reply in site-records.ts) as a real, copyable "manage this" link: `/__records/<kind>/<id>?token=<rawToken>`. If the submitted fields include a plausible email address (reuse the existing `replyToFor`-style strict email regex from lib/site-forms.ts, do not invent a looser one), ALSO state in that reply that the same link can be reached again by anyone with the record's id+token, so losing it isn't necessarily fatal, but do NOT implement actual emailing of this link in this pass — that's an enhancement for later, keep this pass's scope to generating and returning the token.
- New endpoint(s), same-origin only (extend the existing dispatch in app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts's POST handler): `POST /__records/<kind>/<id>` with a `_token` control field and either `_action=update` (replace the stored `fields` with the newly submitted ones, same validation discipline as create) or `_action=cancel` (set `status` to `"cancelled"`, do NOT hard-delete — matches the existing schema comment that status exists precisely so history isn't destroyed). Reject with an honest, generic "that link isn't valid" reply (do not distinguish "wrong token" from "record not found" in the response — same anti-enumeration discipline lib/site-forms.ts already uses for its 404s) if the id doesn't exist, the token hash doesn't match, or the kind doesn't match the record's actual kind.
- The project OWNER (authenticated, in app/projects/[id]/records/) does not need a token — they already have real ownership via the existing auth+project-ownership check that page uses. Add real update/cancel controls there too (the owner can cancel/edit any record on their own project without a token, since they're already authenticated as its owner) — read that page's existing patterns (Card/Badge/Button usage) and match them.
- All of this stays inside the exact same safety machinery as Phase 0: same host/origin checks, same body caps, same rate limiting (reuse lib/site-endpoint.ts's shared helpers, don't duplicate).

CONSTRAINTS (non-negotiable):
- Do not build any accounts/login/session system — explicitly deferred.
- Do not add `connect-src` or any other CSP relaxation to SANDBOX_CSP in app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts. Everything in B and C must work via server-side rendering and same-origin form POSTs only.
- Do not implement attribute-position `{{}}` interpolation (text-content only, per B above) — this is a deliberate security boundary, not an oversight to "complete later."
- Do not hard-delete SiteRecord rows from the visitor-facing cancel path — only the status change.
- Keep `kind` and `fields` fully generic everywhere you touch them — no hardcoded "booking"/"reservation"/"listing" special-casing in validation or rendering logic (illustrative examples in lib/agent.ts's prompt text are fine and expected, since the model needs concrete examples to learn the pattern from — the constraint is on the CODE's logic, not on illustrative prose).
- Schema change: add `editTokenHash` to `SiteRecord` (nullable). Do NOT run `prisma migrate dev`, `prisma db push`, or any DB-touching command yourself — write the schema change and tell me in your final report that `npx prisma db push` (this project's established convention, confirmed working) needs to be run, so I can do it.

STEPS:
1. Read every file listed above in full before writing code.
2. Implement A (lib/agent.ts prompt section).
3. Implement B (the template-rendering step in the site route's GET handler, with the escaping discipline stated above).
4. Implement C (token generation on create, the new update/cancel endpoint, the owner-side UI controls).
5. Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean before you finish. If `tsc` complains about the new `editTokenHash` field not existing on the Prisma client type, that's expected until the schema is pushed and the client regenerated — note it in your report rather than trying to run the DB command yourself.

Report back: exactly how the `{{fieldName}}` escaping is enforced (walk through the injection-attempt trace you reasoned through), the exact new endpoint shapes, where the owner-side edit/cancel controls live, and the exact command I need to run.

content.text:
Fair question — it's gotten deep into implementation. Zooming out:

**The original problem:** you didn't want Kodely limited to brochure-style static pages. You wanted people to describe "a booking system," "a client portal," "a CRM," and actually get one — not a form that goes nowhere.

**The obstacle:** the only safe way to let an AI generate code unsupervised, for strangers, at scale, is to make sure that code can't do anything dangerous. That's why every generated site until now has been a static page with no backend, no database, no way to call out anywhere — the AI literally couldn't cause harm even if it tried, because there was nothing there to misuse.

**What all of this actually is:** a real, working backend that generated sites can use — but one Kodely owns and controls, not one the AI writes itself. Concretely, as of right now, if someone asks Kodely to build:

- **A photographer's booking form** → the AI designs the fields (name, date, package), the visitor's submission is genuinely stored, the photographer sees real bookings in their dashboard, and the visitor gets a real link to cancel or change their own booking later — no login needed.
- **A simple CRM for a small agency** → same underlying mechanism, different shape of data (contacts, deals, notes) — the AI just chooses different fields.
- **A site that shows live inventory or availability** → the page now genuinely reflects real stored data every time it loads, not a frozen snapshot.

None of that existed a few hours ago — sites could only ever collect a contact-form message and email it to the owner. This is the difference between "a website" and "a website with an actual working feature behind it."

**What's still missing** is real customer logins (so "my account" pages can exist properly instead of link-based access) and, if you want it, real payment checkout. Those are the next two pieces, and they build cleanly on top of what's already there rather than requiring a redesign — which was the whole point of doing the foundation first.

content.thinking:
I'm working out how to auto-email the manage-link: recordSavedReply() currently just returns the raw token, so I need to detect a plausible email field and send the manage link via lib/mail.ts, mirroring how site-forms.ts's notifyOwner already handles this.

But here the recipient is the visitor who submitted the form, not a trusted site owner—meaning we'd be sending real emails to whatever address someone types into an arbitrary POST body. That's a real spam/phishing relay risk (someone could flood the form with other people's addresses to spam them via Kodely's mail server), so I need to think through abuse mitigations like rate limiting before wiring this up.

I should keep the email content minimal and neutral, avoid reflecting attacker-controlled text that could be crafted for phishing, only expose the site's already-public name, apply the same per-project rate cap used in site-forms.ts, and make sure the reply-to isn't the visitor's own address the way owner notifications do.

Now I'm moving to think through the real accounts primitive—designing a way for a generated site to offer visitor sign-in that creates a persistent identity scoped to that specific project, enabling genuine account pages.

I'm designing a per-project SiteVisitor model with email uniqueness scoped to (projectId, email), so the same person's identity stays isolated between different generated sites for privacy and simplicity. Login would work via a passwordless magic-link flow so the AI never touches credentials directly.

I'm working through the token flow now: a hashed, expiring one-time token stored in a SiteLoginToken record, emailed as a verification link, which on visit sets a secure, HTTP-only session cookie scoped to that site's own subdomain and marks the token used. I still need to figure out whether this can reuse Kodely's existing portal session cookie logic or whether it needs a completely separate, site-scoped session system to avoid mixing identities between the platform and generated sites.

Given the two trust domains, I'm now planning a separate SiteSession table keyed to the visitor and project, distinct from Kodely's own auth cookies entirely. With that in place, I need to modify SiteRecord to include an optional siteVisitorId so the record-render step can filter results down to only what the authenticated visitor created themselves.

This also enables session-based update/cancel: if the authenticated visitor's session matches the record's siteVisitorId, they can act on it without the token-in-URL flow, though I'd keep tokens as a fallback for sites without accounts. For CSRF, the existing Origin-header check in site-endpoint.ts already serves as the CSRF-equivalent control for POSTs, so I'd extend that same approach rather than introduce something new.

Login-request emails need rate limiting to avoid becoming an enumeration oracle — responses should always look identical whether the email is registered or not, matching the anti-enumeration pattern already used elsewhere in this codebase. Logout is a simple same-origin POST to /__auth/logout that clears the cookie and deletes the SiteSession row, and I need to update the agent prompt so the model understands the new /__auth/request → confirmation → magic link → session flow.

CSP stays same-origin only since this is plain navigation-based login, no passwords are ever implemented, and session expiry should use an explicit, documented default like a 30-day sliding window. Critically, this new site-level auth must stay completely isolated from Kodely's own portal auth in lib/auth.ts — separate cookie namespace with no Domain attribute so it's scoped strictly to the exact host.

This is genuinely the biggest piece of work yet: new models for visitors, login tokens, and sessions, new same-origin auth endpoints, cookie handling, integration into existing record flows, and careful anti-enumeration and CSRF discipline. I'm now ready to write a thorough agent prompt covering all of this, emphasizing no passwords, no cross-domain leakage with portal auth, and reuse of existing patterns.

I realize both the email-link agent and the accounts agent touch overlapping code — specifically lib/site-records.ts, where one modifies the record-creation/reply flow to send email and the other stamps visitor IDs into that same flow. Given this real conflict risk, I've decided to sequence them rather than run in parallel, starting with the smaller email-link agent first.

Since the user explicitly said "start the accounts and email-link agents" together, I'll honor that intent but sequence them sensibly and just note why, rather than asking permission — consistent with making the reasonable call in auto-mode. I'll kick off the email-link agent first since it's smaller and faster, touching the reply function in site-records.ts.

I'll queue accounts to launch right after, waiting for the email-link agent's completion notification before starting it, as I've done in similar cases. Now let me draft the prompt for the email-link agent.

Repo: C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Windows paths, Git-Bash/PowerShell environment). Kodely, an AI website builder. No new npm dependencies allowed.

CONTEXT — read fully first:
- lib/site-records.ts — specifically `recordSavedReply()` and the create flow around it. Right now, when a `SiteRecord` is created via `POST /__records/<kind>`, a raw manage-link token is shown ONCE in the same-origin HTML response page. If the submitted fields contain a plausible email address (checked via `STRICT_EMAIL_RE`, now exported from lib/site-endpoint.ts), the reply currently just states in text that no auto-email is sent yet. Your job: actually send that email.
- lib/mail.ts — the existing mail-sending wrapper (`sendMail`, `isMailConfigured`) used everywhere else in this codebase.
- lib/site-forms.ts — read `notifyOwner()` and `submissionEmail()` fully as your pattern reference: same escaping discipline (`escapeHtml`), same `headerSafe()` header-injection guard, plain-text + HTML alternative, "best effort, always" semantics (never block or fail the main request if the email send fails), and the `EMAIL_MAX_PER_HOUR`-style per-project cap that already exists there to stop a form flood from becoming a mail flood.

THE IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE FROM site-forms.ts's EXISTING EMAIL: that one notifies the PROJECT OWNER (a known, trusted address already on file in the User table). This new one sends to an ARBITRARY ADDRESS TYPED INTO A PUBLIC FORM BY WHOEVER SUBMITTED IT. That is a real abuse surface distinct from anything already built: without care, this becomes a way to make Kodely's mail server send email to any address a stranger picks (spam relay / harassment vector — "someone keeps getting emails from a Kodely site they never visited because an attacker keeps typing their address into a booking form"). Design against this specifically:

1. **Strict, separate rate limiting on this send path**, independent of (in addition to) the existing record-creation rate limits: cap how many of these visitor-confirmation emails can go out per project per hour AND per exact-recipient-address per hour (so even a project under its normal creation-rate-limit can't be used to spam one specific victim address repeatedly). Reuse `lib/site-endpoint.ts`'s existing rate-limiting building blocks (e.g. `createBurstLimiter`) rather than inventing new machinery — read what's already there before adding anything.
2. **Fixed, minimal, non-reflective email content.** The email must NOT echo arbitrary submitted field values verbatim as free text that could be crafted to look like phishing bait. It should say, plainly and factually: which published site (project name — already public, since only published sites can receive submissions), which `kind` of record, that a manage-link was requested/created, and the link itself. Do not include the record's other field values in the email body. Everything interpolated (project name, kind) must go through the exact same `escapeHtml`/`headerSafe` discipline already used in site-forms.ts.
3. **No reply-to set to anything.** Unlike `notifyOwner()` (which sets reply-to to the visitor's address so the OWNER can reply), this email goes TO the visitor — there is no reason to invite a reply, and the `From` must stay Kodely's own sending address exactly as `sendMail()` already enforces elsewhere (never derived from anything user-submitted).
4. **Never block the main response on this.** Exactly like `notifyOwner()`: fire-and-forget, `void sendMail(...).catch(...)`, logged on failure, never awaited by the request handler, never changes what the visitor sees in the same-origin reply page (the reply page's own text can still mention "we've also emailed this link to the address you gave us" — but only state that if the send was actually attempted, not if it was skipped by a rate limit or `isMailConfigured()` being false).
5. **Skip silently and honestly if `isMailConfigured()` is false** — same as everywhere else in this codebase; the HTML reply's wording must not claim an email was sent if it wasn't.

Also update the same-origin reply text in `recordSavedReply()` to accurately reflect the new real behavior instead of the current "no auto-email is sent yet" placeholder — say plainly whether an email is going out or not, and never claim something happened that didn't (e.g. if the per-recipient rate limit is hit and the email is skipped for that reason, the reply must not falsely say it was sent).

STEPS:
1. Read lib/site-records.ts, lib/site-forms.ts, lib/site-endpoint.ts, and lib/mail.ts in full before writing anything.
2. Implement the confirmation email exactly as scoped above, with the two-axis rate limiting (per-project AND per-recipient-address).
3. Update the reply page's wording to be accurate in every case (sent / not sent because mail isn't configured / not sent because rate-limited).
4. Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean before you finish.

Note: a separate agent will start immediately after you finish, working on a real visitor-accounts primitive that ALSO touches lib/site-records.ts's create flow. Keep your changes to the specific functions you need (the reply generation and the new email-sending logic) rather than a broad refactor of that file, so the next agent's diff against your version stays easy to reason about.

Report back: the exact rate-limit numbers you chose and why, the email's exact content, and confirmation both checks passed clean.

- Anti-enumeration on both the login-request reply and the verify-failure reply — never reveal whether an email has an account.
- One-time-use, time-limited login tokens, `timingSafeEqual` for hash comparisons (matching how the existing manage-link token check already does this — read that code and mirror it).
- Keep `kind`/`fields` on SiteRecord exactly as generic as before — `siteVisitorId` is just an optional linkage, not a new constraint on what a record can be.
- Do not touch the still-independent token-based manage-link flow's core behavior for anonymous (non-visitor-linked) records — it must keep working unchanged.

2. Implement the schema additions.
3. Implement request/verify/logout endpoints, dispatched from app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts alongside the existing `/__forms/`, `/__records/` dispatch.

content.thinking:
I need to scope out Stripe Checkout properly, similar to how I approached the SiteRecord phase-0 design. The core question is what "Stripe Checkout for generated sites" actually means, and there seem to be two distinct approaches: either using Stripe Connect where site owners link their own Stripe accounts via OAuth, or some alternative model — I need to weigh which is safer and avoids taking on liability I shouldn't.

With Connect, money goes directly to the site owner's account with Kodely potentially taking a fee, but this drags in real regulatory and compliance weight — OAuth flows, storing connected account IDs, platform-of-record obligations, payment facilitator concerns, webhook management, and being on the hook if something breaks for a merchant. It's a legitimate business model that companies like Shopify use, but it amounts to a whole subsystem, not a quick feature. That makes me want to consider the simpler alternative: having site owners just paste in their own existing Stripe Payment Link URL instead.

Since Stripe already lets anyone generate a no-code hosted checkout link from their dashboard, Kodely's job would shrink to simply wiring that URL into a button on the site — no different technically from a mailto or tel link. This needs zero new infrastructure on Kodely's end: no Connect OAuth, no API calls on the merchant's behalf, no webhooks, no custody of funds, no added liability, and it actually matches the existing "pricing" feature already documented in the codebase around sending buy buttons to Etsy, Shopify, Square, or Stripe payment links.

I realize Stripe Payment Links already support redirecting the buyer's browser to a custom "after completion" URL, which could point back to a same-origin confirmation page on the merchant's site to log the order — but trusting that redirect alone is spoofable, since anyone could hit that URL without actually paying, so real verification would need server-side confirmation via Stripe's API.

That pushes me toward recommending Payment Links over Stripe Connect: the business owner sets up their own free Stripe Payment Link with zero Kodely API keys or OAuth involved, then pastes that link into a new settings field similar to the subdomain editor, and the AI wires "Buy now" CTAs directly to it in place of the current generic contact flow.

Explicitly staying away from Stripe Connect, holding merchant credentials, taking a platform fee, or verifying webhooks — those are a much bigger, separate decision if ever pursued. This scoped-down version is genuinely buildable safely and fits directly into the existing architecture around features.ts, project settings, and the agent prompt.

I'll present this as my recommendation, contrasted clearly against full Stripe Connect, and let the user decide — similar to how I handled the "real react apps" question, since Connect is a legitimately much bigger business decision (third-party payment flows, platform compliance, MSB-adjacent scrutiny, support burden) while Payment Links is just storing a URL and linking to it, matching the existing pattern already live in the product. I'll present this as scoping output directly rather than jumping to code.

content.text:
Two very different things could be called "Stripe Checkout" here, and they're not close in scope:

**Option A — Stripe Payment Links (recommended).** The business owner creates a free Payment Link in their own Stripe dashboard (no code, ~2 minutes) — Kodely never touches their Stripe account, never holds an API key, never sees a transaction. Kodely's whole job is: store that URL for the project (a real settings field, same pattern as the subdomain editor) and have the AI wire "Buy now" buttons directly to it. This is actually already the *documented* honest workaround in `lib/features.ts` today ("send the buy button to your Etsy, Shopify, Square or Stripe payment link") — this would just upgrade that from prose advice into a real, validated, structured feature. Zero new trust boundary, zero new liability, ships fast. As a bonus, Stripe Payment Links support a custom "redirect after payment" URL, so the AI can build a real thank-you/confirmation page on the site — cosmetic only, not a source of truth on whether payment succeeded (that stays in the merchant's own Stripe dashboard).

**Option B — Stripe Connect (full checkout-as-a-platform).** Kodely becomes a Stripe platform: merchants OAuth-connect their account to Kodely, Kodely creates Checkout Sessions and holds/routes real money on their behalf, handles Connect onboarding, webhooks, payout failures, and takes on real payment-facilitator-adjacent obligations. This is a legitimate direction (it's what Shopify/Squarespace do), but it's a business and compliance decision, not an engineering one — ongoing support burden when a connected merchant's payout breaks, Stripe's own platform requirements, and real liability if something goes wrong with someone else's money. Not something to scope as a side feature.

My recommendation is Option A — it gets real "sell things on your site" working now, safely, and doesn't foreclose Option B later if you ever want to become an actual payments platform. Want me to build A, or do you actually want to go the Connect route?

content.thinking: They're asking whether Option A requires linking their Stripe account to Kodely. I should clarify that it doesn't — they'd simply use their own separate Stripe account (existing or newly created for free) to generate a Payment Link, a Stripe-hosted checkout page, and then copy that link over to use elsewhere.

content.text:
No — that's the key distinction. With Option A (Payment Links), there's no "connect" step between Kodely and Stripe at all:

1. The business owner logs into **their own** Stripe account directly at stripe.com (or creates one — free, nothing to do with Kodely).
2. In their own Stripe dashboard, they create a Payment Link for a product/price.
3. They copy that URL (looks like `https://buy.stripe.com/...`) and paste it into a field in Kodely, the same way they'd paste a Calendly link or a Google Maps address.
4. Kodely just stores that URL and points a "Buy now" button at it.

Kodely never authenticates with Stripe, never sees their account, never touches their money, never has an API key for them. It's a plain link, indistinguishable technically from a `mailto:` or `tel:` link — just happens to go to Stripe.

"Connect their own Stripe account" describes Option B instead — that's the literal name of Stripe's OAuth product ("Stripe Connect"), where the owner *does* click something like "Connect with Stripe" inside Kodely, granting Kodely real API access to create charges and move money through their account. That's the one with all the platform/compliance weight I described.

So to be concrete about what you'd be shipping with Option A: a "Payment link" field next to where pricing tiers are described, validated to actually look like a Stripe Payment Link, with the AI wiring real buy buttons to it. Want me to go ahead and scope that into an actual build?

**Step 1, verify before assuming:** The current CSP is `default-src 'self'; ...; connect-src 'none'; ...` with no explicit `font-src` directive. Per the CSP spec, an unset `font-src` falls back to `default-src`. The comment in lib/agent.ts says "The CSP sets no font-src, so fonts fall back to default-src 'self', which does NOT allow data: ... Base your decision on what you actually observe, not on assumption. For each family, only fetch the weights actually needed (typically 400/500/600/700 — do not vendor every available weight), in WOFF2 format only (smallest, universally supported by every browser this product needs to support). Before generating page content, the model must commit to: a real palette (named as 4–6 actual hex values, not "a warm palette"), ONE of the curated font pairings from Part 1 chosen deliberately for a stated reason (a sentence connecting the choice to the specific business/subject — e.g. "a bakery run by hand for 20 years reads better in a warm serif than a geometric sans"), and a one-sentence layout concept for how this specific business's content will be organized (not necessarily unconventional, just deliberate and stated).
2. State plainly that landing on one of these by genuine deliberate choice for a specific brief is fine — the instruction is against defaulting to them unthinkingly on every single build.
3. Keep the existing real, load-bearing constraints from the current quality-bar section intact (real specific copy never invented facts about a real business, responsive to 380px, semantic HTML, focus states, dark-mode treatment) — you are STRENGTHENING this section's design-decision rigor, not removing its existing honesty/accessibility requirements.

## Constraints
- Do not change anything about the NOT_OFFERED features list in lib/features.ts, the SiteRecord/accounts work from prior phases, or any unrelated part of the CSP beyond exactly what Part 1's verification concludes is needed.
- Do not add any new npm dependency — vendored font files are static assets, not packages.

Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean. Additionally, if feasible without spending significant model-generation credits, verify at least once end-to-end that a real generated/preview page can actually load one of the vendored fonts under the real CSP header (reuse the preview pipeline rather than running a full paid build if there's a cheaper way to exercise the same serving path) — describe exactly what you checked and observed.

input.description: Research how competitors avoid generic AI design
input.prompt:
This is research for Kodely, an AI website-builder product (competitors: v0.dev, Lovable, Framer AI, Webflow AI, Durable, 10Web, Wix ADI, Hostinger AI Website Builder). Read-only research task using WebSearch/WebFetch — no local file edits needed, this doesn't require the local repo at all, pure external research.

The core problem: Kodely's AI-generated sites currently "feel generic" — every site uses the same fonts, similar layouts, and safe default visual choices, because the underlying prompt only has one soft sentence of anti-genericness guidance ("give the page one distinctive visual idea"). We're already fixing typography (self-hosting real font pairings) and adding a forced design-plan step + an explicit list of AI-design clichés to avoid.

Research and report back on:
1. What specific, concrete techniques do the strongest AI website/page/design builders (v0.dev, Lovable, Framer AI, and any other notably good ones you find) use to produce genuinely varied, distinctive visual output instead of converging on generic "AI slop" design? Look for: do they use curated design-system/template starting points, style transfer from references, multi-step "plan then build" pipelines, randomized/varied design tokens per generation, human-curated component libraries, or something else?
2. Is there published research, blog posts, or technical writeups (from Vercel/v0, Anthropic, or design-focused AI tooling companies) specifically about WHY LLM-generated UI/web design tends to converge on generic patterns (the "AI design clichés" phenomenon — cream backgrounds with serif+terracotta, purple gradient heroes, Inter-everywhere, rounded-lg cards, emoji bullets) and what concretely counters it? Summarize the actual mechanisms proposed, not just that the problem exists.
3. Are there known best practices for a system prompt or generation pipeline to force genuine per-project visual variety at scale (thousands of independent generations, no shared session/memory between them) — e.g., seeded randomization of a constrained set of design tokens, requiring the model to critique its own plan against genericness before proceeding, using reference imagery, or a library of many distinct "starter aesthetics" the model picks/adapts rather than inventing from scratch each time?
4. What role do curated component/pattern libraries (as opposed to the model hand-writing every layout from scratch) play in the best tools you found — does giving the model a smaller set of well-designed, pre-varied layout patterns to assemble from (rather than infinite freedom) actually produce BETTER, more distinctive results than unconstrained generation? This is directly relevant since Kodely already has a similar asset catalogue (`find_assets`) for icons/gradients/patterns, and the question is whether extending that same idea to LAYOUT PATTERNS (not just decorative assets) is worth investing in.
5. Give a concrete, prioritized recommendation: of everything you found, what are the 3-4 highest-leverage, realistically-implementable-by-a-small-team techniques Kodely should consider next, beyond what's already planned (fonts + design-plan step + cliché list)?

Report in a clear structured format with sources cited. This is research only — no code, no repo changes.

- **`lib/assets/flags.ts`**: emoji generated arithmetically from ISO 3166-1 codes; ~55 hand-authored SVGs from public-domain flag construction specs (not copyrightable subject matter).
- **`lib/assets/patterns.ts`**: gradients/meshes/textures/dividers/patterns/avatar, all pure CSS or arithmetic-generated SVG.
- **`lib/assets/illustrations.ts`**: hand-placed primitives on a 120-unit grid plus seeded-PRNG paths for backdrops/spots/marks/empty-states. ### 3. Variety per category — real convergence risk, confirmed

Checking `services` (trades) and the `plumber`/`electrician`/`mechanic` synonym mappings directly in the source:

- `services` category icons: scissors, dumbbell, wrench, hammer, paw, camera, paint-brush, spray, leaf, sprout, stethoscope, tooth, car, key, home, building, briefcase, graduation-cap, lotus, ticket, bed, mic (22 total, spread across a wide range of trades/verticals).

- Similarly `contact` has only 10 icons total (phone, mail, map-pin, clock, calendar, globe, send, message-circle, compass, printer) — every generated site's contact section is drawing from the same 10-icon pool.
- `food` has 12 icons total (coffee, utensils, pizza, wine, beer, ice-cream, cake, bread, salad, chef-hat, cocktail, bowl) covering cafes, bakeries, restaurants, bars, pubs alike.

1	# Free asset sources for customer sites — licence review
2	
3	**Date of review: 2026-08-22.** Every claim below was checked against the live
4	licence page (and, where one exists, the separate API terms) on that date.
5	Licences change; re-verify before shipping and again at least annually.
6	
7	**I am not a lawyer, and neither is the owner of this project.** This document
8	is engineering due diligence, not legal advice. Three findings in it
9	(§3 Pexels, §3 Pixabay, §3 Mixkit) turn on a question — *is the customer's
10	published site a "third party" that needs its own licence?* — that only a
11	lawyer should answer. Nothing here should be built without that answer.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## 1. What the six axes mean here
16	
17	Kodely is not a designer downloading a photo for one project. Kodely is a
18	machine that hands asset files to strangers' commercial websites, at volume,
19	forever. Almost every "free" licence on the internet was written for the first
20	case. The axes below exist to find out what each licence says about the second.
21	
22	| # | Axis | Why it decides things |
23	|---|------|-----------------------|
24	| 1 | **Self-host** | Generated sites run under `default-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; img-src 'self' data:; connect-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; form-action 'self'; base-uri 'none'; object-src 'none'` — `SANDBOX_CSP`, `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts:74-75`. No external image host. A source that forbids downloading and re-serving is unusable without widening the CSP, which is a security decision, not an asset decision. Hotlinking is not a workaround: it needs the same CSP change *and* leaks every visitor's IP to a third party. |
25	| 2 | **Attribution** | Checked **twice** per source — once in the licence, once in the API terms. Attribution means our supplier's branding in our customer's footer. |
26	| 3 | **3rd-party commercial** | Our customers are businesses. Several licences permit commercial use *by the downloader* and say nothing about the person the file is handed to. |
27	| 4 | **Redistribution / picker** | "Don't put this on another stock platform" clauses. Embedding one image in one generated site and exposing a searchable library inside Kodely are different acts under most of these licences. |
28	| 5 | **API + limits** | A 200/hour ceiling is a real cap on build throughput. |
29	| 6 | **Verified?** | Whether I actually read the page, or was blocked. |
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. The table
34	
35	| Source | 1. Self-host | 2. Attribution (licence / API) | 3. 3rd-party commercial | 4. Redistribution / picker | 5. API + limits | 6. Verified | Verdict |
36	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
37	| **pexels.com** | Yes — download/modify permitted. **Bulk pre-scraping prohibited.** | No / **Yes — "prominent link to Pexels" on any API request** | Permitted, but no express sublicence grant → ambiguous | No selling/redistributing on other stock or wallpaper platforms; "may not replicate core functionality of Pexels" | Yes. 200/hr, 20,000/mo; higher on request | Full | **USE WITH CONDITIONS** |
