51	
52	---
53	
54	## 3. Per-source detail
55	
56	### pexels.com — USE WITH CONDITIONS
57	
58	- **Licence** (<https://www.pexels.com/license/>): "All photos and videos on
59	  Pexels are free to use", "Attribution is not required", "You can modify the
60	  photos and videos". Not allowed: "Don't sell unaltered copies", "Don't
61	  redistribute or sell the photos and videos on other stock photo or wallpaper
62	  platforms", no trademark use, no implied endorsement.
63	- **API guidelines** (<https://www.pexels.com/api/documentation/#guidelines>) —
64	  *this is the trap, and it is real*: "Whenever you are doing an API request
65	  make sure to show a **prominent link to Pexels**." Also "You may not copy or
66	  replicate core functionality of Pexels", and 200 requests/hour, 20,000/month,
67	  raisable on request "given that you've implemented the API properly".
68	- **Terms of Service** (<https://www.pexels.com/terms-of-service/>): "Bulk,
69	  large-scale or systematic copying of Content is strictly prohibited unless
70	  explicit permission has been granted by us", and data mining / scraping is
71	  "strictly prohibited for all unauthorised purposes". **So a pre-scraped local
72	  Pexels library is out.** On-demand API fetch per build is the only compliant
73	  route.
74	- **Reading of the attribution clause.** The obligation attaches to "doing an
75	  API request". Kodely makes the API request in the builder; the customer's
76	  published site makes none. The defensible reading is a Pexels credit in the
77	  Kodely picker UI. It is *not* certain that the published site is exempt, and
78	  Pexels can decide what "proper implementation" means when we ask for a higher
79	  rate limit. Treat the builder-side credit as required and the site-side credit
80	  as an open question for legal.
81	- **The unresolved bit**: the licence grants rights to the user of the site; it
82	  never says the downloader may sublicense to someone else. See §5.
83	
84	### pixabay.com — USE WITH CONDITIONS (best technical fit)
85	
86	- **Content License** (<https://pixabay.com/service/license-summary/> and the
87	  binding full text at <https://pixabay.com/service/terms/> §5): "an
88	  irrevocable, worldwide, perpetual … non-exclusive and royalty-free right to
89	  download, use, copy, modify or adapt the Content for commercial or
90	  non-commercial purposes." No attribution required. Content published before
91	  9 January 2019 is CC0.
92	- **Prohibited Uses** (terms §5): no selling or distributing Content "on a
93	  Standalone basis … including through a stock media platform"; no commercial
94	  use of Content containing recognisable trademarks/logos/brands; no misleading
95	  use; no use as a trade mark. Elsewhere in the ToS: no "bulk, large-scale or
96	  systematic copying", and you may not "use or compile any Content to replicate
97	  a similar or competing service".
98	- **API docs** (<https://pixabay.com/api/docs/>) — the standout finding:
99	  "permanent hotlinking of images (using Pixabay URLs in your app) is **not
100	  allowed**. If you intend to use the images, please download them to your
101	  server first." Pixabay's own rules *require* the architecture our CSP
102	  already forces. Rate limit 100 requests per 60 seconds; "requests must be
103	  cached for 24 hours"; "systematic mass downloads are not allowed".
104	- **Attribution**: "If you make use of the API, show your users where the images
105	  and videos are from, whenever search results are displayed. That's the one
106	  thing we kindly request." Bound to *search results*, i.e. the builder UI. It
107	  is phrased as a request, not a condition of the licence grant.
108	- Same unresolved sublicence question as Pexels (§5).
109	
110	### unsplash.com — AVOID as an integration
111	
112	- **Licence** (<https://unsplash.com/license>) is genuinely permissive:
113	  "irrevocable, nonexclusive, worldwide copyright license to download, copy,
114	  modify, distribute, perform, and use images … for free, including for
115	  commercial purposes, without permission from or attributing the photographer
116	  or Unsplash." Restrictions: no selling unmodified copies, and no "compiling
117	  photos from Unsplash to replicate a similar or competing service".
118	- **API terms** (<https://unsplash.com/api-terms>) and **guidelines**
119	  (<https://help.unsplash.com/en/articles/2511245-unsplash-api-guidelines>)
120	  reverse that for anyone using the API:
121	  - "All API uses must use the hotlinked image URLs returned by the API" —
122	    **self-hosting is forbidden on the API path**;
123	  - "each time you or your Developer App displays an Image, your Developer App
124	    must attribute Unsplash, the Unsplash photographer, and contain a link back
125	    to the photographer's Unsplash profile", with `utm` parameters;
126	  - a download-event ping to `/photos/:id/download` on every use;
127	  - Demo 50 req/hr, Production 1,000 req/hr
128	    (<https://unsplash.com/documentation>).
129	- **Conclusion**: the API is structurally incompatible with `img-src 'self'`,
130	  and complying would put Unsplash + photographer branding on every customer's
131	  page. Going around the API — bulk-downloading from the website — very likely
132	  breaches Unsplash's site terms; I could not verify that page (blocked, §6),
133	  which is itself a reason not to rely on the workaround. A small hand-picked
134	  set, downloaded by a human, is licence-clean; an integration is not.
135	
136	### vecteezy.com — AVOID
137	
138	The Vecteezy License Agreement (<https://www.vecteezy.com/licensing-agreement>,
139	updated 22 June 2026) closes this from three directions:
140	
141	- Free License: "Attribution is required. Content is licensed to an individual
142	  user … Content may not be used on products for resale."
143	- Sub-licensing: "You may not sublicense, resell, share, transfer, or otherwise
144	  redistribute the Content (e.g., as stock, **in a tool or template**, as source
145	  files, etc.), **not even for free**."
146	- No Content Extraction: "**Using Content within software applications which
147	  allow a third party to generate on-demand designs is also not permitted.**"
148	
149	That last sentence is a description of Kodely. Even paid Pro tiers are subject
150	to it.
151	
152	### kaboompics.com — AVOID until written permission
153	
154	The Standard Licence (<https://kaboompics.com/page/license-and-faq>) is one of
155	the friendliest reviewed: commercial use, no attribution, "You may also use
156	Kaboompics photos as part of templates or mockups for your clients", explicit
157	permission for placeholder images in HTML/WordPress templates that are sold.
158	But the FAQ answers our exact question directly: **"Can I put the images in our
159	website builder, plugin (or any other app) for our users? It is possible but
160	requires individual negotiations."**
161	
162	So the door is open but shut until someone walks through it. Single creator
163	(Karolina Grabowska), direct email contact on the page. Also note some photos
164	are "Editorial Use Only" and must never reach a commercial site — any
165	integration would need to filter on that flag.
166	
167	### mixkit.co — AVOID (contradictory)
168	
169	- **Free Licence** (fetched from `https://mixkit.co/license/modal/videoFree/`
170	  and `.../artFree/`, the endpoints the licence page's modal loads): "can be
171	  used in your commercial and non-commercial projects, for free. You're
172	  permitted to download, copy, modify, distribute, publicly perform and
173	  broadcast the Items. Your rights are non-exclusive, worldwide,
174	  **sub-licensable** and ongoing. Attribution is not required." Then: "There are
175	  some important limits to these rights, described in our User Terms."
176	- **User Terms** (<https://mixkit.co/terms/>) supply limits that contradict it:
177	  you must not "rent, license, sublicense, sell, resell or otherwise
178	  commercially exploit or make Mixkit or any Item available to any third
179	  party"; must not "aggregate or collate an Item(s) and make available on a
180	  stock or inventory basis"; must not "use Mixkit … or any Item, to build a
181	  similar or competitive product"; and these apply "even if you sub-license or
182	  transfer use of the Item to a third party".
183	- A licence that says *sub-licensable* and terms that say *not to any third
184	  party* cannot both be applied to our use. Ambiguous against us → do not build
185	  on it. Note also that Mixkit is Envato: there is a commercial route (Envato
186	  Elements) if video ever becomes a priority.
187	
188	### coverr.co — AVOID
189	
190	<https://coverr.co/license> is the only source that names the product category
191	outright: content may not be "resold or offered as part of services to which
192	providing videos can help. This applies to stock video sites, **website
193	builders**, themes providers, mobile apps builders and video editing services."
194	Also: no building "a service that is similar to or competes with Coverr.co", and
195	no AI-training use. Coverr explains it moved off CC0 precisely because other
196	sites redistributed its videos. No ambiguity, nothing to review.
197	
198	### dareful.com — USE WITH CONDITIONS
199	
200	Dareful releases its 4K stock video under **Creative Commons Attribution 4.0
201	International** (<https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/>), stated on
202	<https://dareful.com/> with the requested credit format: "Video courtesy of
203	Dareful" with a link. CC BY is irrevocable, runs to every downstream recipient
204	(so the sublicence problem in §5 does not exist here), and permits self-hosting
205	and commercial use.
206	
207	The cost is that attribution is a **condition of the licence**, not a courtesy:
208	drop the credit and the licence terminates. CC BY 4.0 allows the credit "in any
209	reasonable manner … appropriate to the medium", so a `/credits` page linked from
210	the footer is defensible, but the credit has to be on the customer's site, not
211	in our builder. Library is small (a few hundred clips) and there is no API.
212	`dareful.com/license/` returns 404 — the licence statement lives on the homepage
213	and item pages, which is weaker documentation than I would like.
214	
215	### iconoop.com — USE, but source upstream
216	
217	A clean aggregator of seven upstream open-source sets, each keeping its own
218	licence: Lucide (ISC), Tabler (MIT), Phosphor (MIT), Material Symbols
219	(Apache-2.0), Devicon (MIT), brand logos (CC0), emoji/Twemoji (CC-BY 4.0). Its
220	own summary: "Every collection here is free for commercial use, including
221	inside paid products and client work", and only the emoji "require a credit
222	line". SVG download, no account, no API.
223	
224	Two conditions:
225	1. **Take the icons from the upstream repositories, not from iconoop.** The site
226	   does not identify its operator and publishes no terms; upstream repos give us
227	   pinned versions, real LICENSE files and a provenance trail.
228	2. **Brand logos are a trademark question, not a copyright one** — iconoop says
229	   so itself. A CC0 logo file does not give a customer the right to display
230	   another company's mark. Brand/logo icons must be excluded from anything the
231	   model can place autonomously.
232	
233	### svgrepo.com — AVOID pending verification
234	
235	**Could not verify.** `svgrepo.com/page/licensing/` and the site root returned
236	HTTP 429 behind a Vercel security checkpoint on every attempt (direct fetch,
237	browser user-agent, and a text-extraction proxy). Third-party summaries say the
238	library mixes CC0, MIT, **GPL** and CC BY per icon, with the licence shown on
239	each icon's page — but I did not read that from the source and will not treat it
240	as established.
241	
242	Two reasons to stay away even after verification: a GPL-licensed icon landing in
243	a customer's commercial site is a genuine problem, and per-icon licence metadata
244	maintained by an aggregator is exactly the kind of thing that is wrong 1% of the
245	time — which, at Kodely's volume, means it is wrong. If anyone wants it, the
246	prerequisite is: verify the page in a real browser, then ingest only icons whose
247	recorded licence is CC0/MIT/Apache-2.0/ISC, storing the licence string per icon.
248	
249	### iconsatlas.com — USE
250	
251	Atlas Icons is **MIT licensed** (<https://www.iconsatlas.com/license/>): "Use it
252	in personal, commercial, and open-source projects with no attribution required.
253	Modify, redistribute, and build on it freely." The one obligation MIT does
254	impose is that the copyright and permission notice travels with copies of the
255	files — satisfied by keeping the upstream LICENSE in our vendored copy and a
256	`NOTICES` entry; it does not need to appear on customer sites.
257	
258	### getillustrations.com — AVOID the free tier
259	
260	<https://www.getillustrations.com/license>. The free illustration licence
261	requires "a credit such as 'Illustrations by GetIllustrations.com' in your
262	footer or credits page" and the comparison table marks **client projects ✗** for
263	Free; the FAQ says the Free License "is limited to personal use". (The pricing
264	card on the same page says "Personal and commercial use" — a self-contradiction
265	on a single page, which resolves against us.) Paid **Standard** (from $195/yr,
266	$599 lifetime) does cover client work and products for sale, capped at 500
267	assets per design, with no attribution; **Extended** covers redistributing full
268	packs. There is an API (1,500 calls/month included, Pro 300k for $49/mo).
269	
270	Their "free MIT icons" are re-hosted upstream open-source sets (Feather, Lucide,
271	Phosphor, Tabler, Bootstrap, Material Symbols) — and the page calls all of them
272	MIT, though Material Symbols is Apache-2.0. Another argument for going upstream.
273	
274	### github.com/Make-md/svg-packs — AVOID the mirror, vendor upstream
275	
276	- **The repository has no LICENSE file** (GitHub API reports `license: null`).
277	  The aggregation itself therefore carries no grant at all; only the per-pack
278	  LICENSE files preserved under `svg-originals/<pack>/` do any work.
279	- Contents are 19 upstream packs, and they are **not consistently licensed**:
280	  Apache-2.0 (Material Design Icons, Remix), MIT (Tabler, Heroicons, Phosphor,
281	  Bootstrap, Octicons, Eva, Boxicons, Feather, Icon Brew, CSS.gg, Radix,
282	  Zondicons), ISC (Lucide), CC0 (Simple Icons), Unlicense (System UIcons), and
283	  **CC BY 4.0 — attribution required — for Font Awesome (2,806 icons) and
284	  coolicons (442)**. Font Awesome Brands, Boxicons "logos" and Simple Icons are
285	  brand marks: copyright-clear, trademark-loaded.
286	- It is a one-star, single-snapshot mirror generated 2025-09-26 by a third
287	  party. There is no reason to take a supply-chain dependency on it when every
288	  pack has an upstream repo with releases and a real licence file.
289	
290	### github.com/Kimbatt/cc0-textures — AVOID
291	
292	- **No LICENSE file** (`license: null`). The README asserts CC0 and adds "These
293	  textures were not made by me, I just collected them for easy download" — an
294	  assertion by a collector is not a licence grant.
295	- Distribution is **torrent files**, not the images; last push July 2020.
296	- It aggregates four different sites (cc0textures.com — now ambientCG,
297	  texturehaven.com — now Poly Haven, cgbookcase.com, sharetextures.com), each
298	  with its own current terms. I did not verify any of them (out of scope of the
299	  named list), and sharetextures in particular I would not assume is CC0.
300	- If textures are ever wanted, go to ambientCG / Poly Haven / cgbookcase
301	  directly and verify each. Note that Kodely already synthesises textures,
302	  gradients and patterns as inline SVG/CSS in `lib/assets/patterns.ts`, which
303	  has zero licence surface and zero bytes over the wire.
304	
305	---
306	
307	## 4. Recommendation — build against these
308	
309	**1. Pixabay (photos + video) — primary.**
310	The only source whose own API rules *require* the architecture our CSP forces:
311	"download them to your server first". 100 requests per 60 seconds is 60× the
312	Pexels ceiling. Attribution is a soft request tied to displaying search results,
313	i.e. our UI, not the customer's footer. Licence grant is irrevocable and
314	perpetual, so nothing we ship can be pulled out from under a customer later.
315	
316	**2. Pexels (photos + video) — secondary, for quality and coverage.**
317	Better curation than Pixabay on a lot of business subject matter. Costs us a
318	visible "Photos provided by Pexels" link in the builder UI, and a 200/hr cap
319	that will need raising (they grant increases to implementations that attribute
320	properly — a reason to over-comply on the credit rather than hunt for the
321	minimum).
322	
323	**3. Upstream open-source icon packs (Lucide, Tabler, Phosphor, Material
324	Symbols, Heroicons) — vendored, not fetched.**
325	This is what iconoop and iconsatlas are actually pointing at, minus the
326	aggregator risk. MIT/ISC/Apache-2.0, no attribution on customer sites, pinned
327	versions, licence files shipped in-repo. Excludes the CC BY packs (Font Awesome,
328	coolicons) and all brand-logo sets.
329	
330	**Not recommended but cheap to unlock:** Kaboompics — one email to one person,
331	and its terms otherwise fit better than anything else on the list.
332	**Optional third for video:** Dareful, if a visible CC BY credit on customer
333	sites is acceptable. Decide that as a product question before building it.
334	
335	**Illustrations and textures stay generated.** `lib/assets/illustrations.ts` and
336	`lib/assets/patterns.ts` already cover that ground with geometry that has no
337	licence, no host and no bytes. Nothing on the reviewed list beats "no licence at
338	all" for those two categories.
339	
340	---
341	
342	## 5. The single biggest legal risk
343	
344	**Every one of these licences grants rights to the person who downloads the
345	file. None of the recommended ones expressly grants the right to sublicense
346	those rights onward to someone else.**
347	
348	Pixabay: "when you download any Content … **we grant you** an irrevocable,
349	worldwide, perpetual … right to download, use, copy, modify or adapt the
350	Content". Pexels: "All photos and videos on Pexels are free to use", addressed
351	to the user of the site. Neither says "and you may pass this right to your
352	customers".
353	
354	When Kodely puts a Pixabay photo into a plumber's website, who is the licensee —
355	Kodely, or the plumber? If it is Kodely, the plumber is displaying an image they
356	have no licence to, and Kodely has arguably distributed it to a third party. If
357	it is the plumber, then Kodely has to be acting as their agent, which needs to
358	be true in our terms of service, not just in spirit.
359	
360	The sources that thought about this at all came down against us: Vecteezy
361	forbids "software applications which allow a third party to generate on-demand
362	designs"; Coverr names website builders explicitly; Kaboompics says it needs
363	"individual negotiations"; Mixkit's terms forbid making Items "available to any
364	third party". Four out of four of the sources that addressed the question said
365	no or not-without-a-deal. Pexels and Pixabay are usable *because they are
366	silent* — and silence is not permission.
367	
368	**Mitigations to put in front of a lawyer**, not to self-approve:
369	1. Structure the download so the *customer* is the licensee and Kodely is their
370	   agent, and say so in Kodely's ToS, which should also pass the stock licences'
371	   restrictions (no resale as standalone files, no trademark use, no implied
372	   endorsement) through to the customer.
373	2. Keep a provenance record per asset per site — source, id, licence text,
374	   author, URL, timestamp — so any single image can be evidenced or removed.
375	3. Prefer Pixabay's pre-2019 CC0 content and CC0/MIT/Apache-2.0 vector assets
376	   where quality allows: for those, the sublicence question does not exist.
377	
378	Second-order risks worth naming: **trademarks and identifiable people** in
379	photos (both Pexels and Pixabay put that responsibility on the user — no
380	model-release warranty flows to our customers, and Pixabay explicitly bans
381	commercial use of trademark-bearing content), and **bulk-copying bans** in both
382	Pexels' and Pixabay's ToS, which rule out building a local mirror of either
383	library.
384	
385	---
386	
387	## 6. What I could not verify
388	
389	| Item | Why | Consequence |
390	|---|---|---|
391	| **svgrepo.com licensing page** | HTTP 429 / Vercel security checkpoint on every attempt, including a text proxy | Source is excluded. Everything said about it above is third-party report, not verified fact |
392	| **unsplash.com/terms** (site terms, as distinct from API terms) | Blocked by an anti-scraping challenge | Cannot state whether manual bulk download breaches their site terms. Assume it does |
393	| **Whether Pexels permits caching/storing downloaded files** | Neither licence nor API docs address storage | The licence permits use and modification, which implies keeping the file; not explicit |
394	| **Whether Pexels' "prominent link" obligation reaches the published site** | Wording ties it to "doing an API request"; unaddressed for downstream output | Treat builder-side credit as required, site-side as an open legal question |
395	| **Who operates iconoop.com; any terms of service** | No operator identified, no terms page found | Reason to use upstream repos rather than the site |
396	| **Current terms of ambientCG / Poly Haven / cgbookcase / sharetextures** | Out of scope of the named list | Any texture work needs a separate review |
397	| **Dareful's licence page** | `/license/` is 404; CC BY 4.0 stated on the homepage and item pages | Licence identification is confident, documentation is thin |
398	
399	---
400	
401	## 7. Architecture consequences (see the cards for the work)
402	
403	1. **Do not widen the CSP.** Rejecting Unsplash's API is the price; `img-src
404	   'self' data:` with no external hosts is worth more than any one source.
405	2. **A photo needs a real delivery path**, which does not exist yet:
406	   `lib/assets/index.ts` says so in its own header — "Photography. Not 'not
407	   yet' — there is no host to serve it from". Downloaded binaries have to become
408	   files in the built site, served by the existing site route so `'self'`
409	   covers them.
410	3. **The model must select by id, never by content.** Referencing
411	   `photo:pixabay:1234567` costs a handful of tokens; a base64 hero image costs
412	   ~88,900 tokens and roughly $1 per build. The existing `find_assets` /
413	   `.kodely-assets/INDEX.md` seam (`lib/assets/materialize.ts`) is already
414	   shaped for this: search returns ids and one-line descriptions, and a
415	   post-generation pass resolves the ids into real files and rewrites `src`
416	   attributes.
417	4. **Budget the API calls.** Pexels 200/hr is a hard throughput ceiling on
418	   concurrent builds; Pixabay requires 24h response caching and forbids mass
419	   downloads. Both point at the same design: a shared, cached search layer, one
420	   download per distinct asset, content-addressed storage reused across sites.
421

# Free asset sources for customer sites — licence review

**Date of review: 2026-08-22.** Every claim below was checked against the live
licence page (and, where one exists, the separate API terms) on that date.
Licences change; re-verify before shipping and again at least annually.

**I am not a lawyer, and neither is the owner of this project.** This document
is engineering due diligence, not legal advice. Three findings in it
(§3 Pexels, §3 Pixabay, §3 Mixkit) turn on a question — *is the customer's
published site a "third party" that needs its own licence?* — that only a

| 5 | **API + limits** | A 200/hour ceiling is a real cap on build throughput. |

The only source whose own API rules *require* the architecture our CSP forces:
"download them to your server first". 100 requests per 60 seconds is 60× the
Pexels ceiling. Attribution is a soft request tied to displaying search results,
i.e. our UI, not the customer's footer. Licence grant is irrevocable and
perpetual, so nothing we ship can be pulled out from under a customer later.

**2. Pexels (photos + video) — secondary, for quality and coverage.**
Better curation than Pixabay on a lot of business subject matter. Costs us a
visible "Photos provided by Pexels" link in the builder UI, and a 200/hr cap
that will need raising (they grant increases to implementations that attribute
properly — a reason to over-comply on the credit rather than hunt for the
minimum).

**3. Upstream open-source icon packs (Lucide, Tabler, Phosphor, Material
Symbols, Heroicons) — vendored, not fetched.**
This is what iconoop and iconsatlas are actually pointing at, minus the
aggregator risk. MIT/ISC/Apache-2.0, no attribution on customer sites, pinned
versions, licence files shipped in-repo. Excludes the CC BY packs (Font Awesome,
coolicons) and all brand-logo sets.

**Not recommended but cheap to unlock:** Kaboompics — one email to one person,
and its terms otherwise fit better than anything else on the list.
**Optional third for video:** Dareful, if a visible CC BY credit on customer
sites is acceptable. Decide that as a product question before building it.

**Illustrations and textures stay generated.** `lib/assets/illustrations.ts` and
`lib/assets/patterns.ts` already cover that ground with geometry that has no
licence, no host and no bytes. Nothing on the reviewed list beats "no licence at
all" for those two categories.

## 5. The single biggest legal risk

**Every one of these licences grants rights to the person who downloads the
file. None of the recommended ones expressly grants the right to sublicense
those rights onward to someone else.**

Pixabay: "when you download any Content … **we grant you** an irrevocable,
worldwide, perpetual … right to download, use, copy, modify or adapt the
Content". Pexels: "All photos and videos on Pexels are free to use", addressed
to the user of the site. Neither says "and you may pass this right to your
customers".

When Kodely puts a Pixabay photo into a plumber's website, who is the licensee —
Kodely, or the plumber? If it is Kodely, the plumber is displaying an image they
have no licence to, and Kodely has arguably distributed it to a third party. If
it is the plumber, then Kodely has to be acting as their agent, which needs to
be true in our terms of service, not just in spirit.

The sources that thought about this at all came down against us: Vecteezy
forbids "software applications which allow a third party to generate on-demand
designs"; Coverr names website builders explicitly; Kaboompics says it needs
"individual negotiations"; Mixkit's terms forbid making Items "available to any
third party". Four out of four of the sources that addressed the question said
no or not-without-a-deal. Pexels and Pixabay are usable *because they are
silent* — and silence is not permission.

**Mitigations to put in front of a lawyer**, not to self-approve:
1. Structure the download so the *customer* is the licensee and Kodely is their
   agent, and say so in Kodely's ToS, which should also pass the stock licences'
   restrictions (no resale as standalone files, no trademark use, no implied
   endorsement) through to the customer.
2. Keep a provenance record per asset per site — source, id, licence text,
   author, URL, timestamp — so any single image can be evidenced or removed.
3. Prefer Pixabay's pre-2019 CC0 content and CC0/MIT/Apache-2.0 vector assets
   where quality allows: for those, the sublicence question does not exist.

Second-order risks worth naming: **trademarks and identifiable people** in
photos (both Pexels and Pixabay put that responsibility on the user — no
model-release warranty flows to our customers, and Pixabay explicitly bans
commercial use of trademark-bearing content), and **bulk-copying bans** in both
Pexels' and Pixabay's ToS, which rule out building a local mirror of either
library.

| Item | Why | Consequence |
|---|---|---|

| **unsplash.com/terms** (site terms, as distinct from API terms) | Blocked by an anti-scraping challenge | Cannot state whether manual bulk download breaches their site terms. Assume it does |
| **Whether Pexels permits caching/storing downloaded files** | Neither licence nor API docs address storage | The licence permits use and modification, which implies keeping the file; not explicit |
| **Whether Pexels' "prominent link" obligation reaches the published site** | Wording ties it to "doing an API request"; unaddressed for downstream output | Treat builder-side credit as required, site-side as an open legal question |
| **Who operates iconoop.com; any terms of service** | No operator identified, no terms page found | Reason to use upstream repos rather than the site |
| **Current terms of ambientCG / Poly Haven / cgbookcase / sharetextures** | Out of scope of the named list | Any texture work needs a separate review |
| **Dareful's licence page** | `/license/` is 404; CC BY 4.0 stated on the homepage and item pages | Licence identification is confident, documentation is thin |

---

## 7. Architecture consequences (see the cards for the work)

1. **Do not widen the CSP.** Rejecting Unsplash's API is the price; `img-src
   'self' data:` with no external hosts is worth more than any one source.
2. **A photo needs a real delivery path**, which does not exist yet:
   `lib/assets/index.ts` says so in its own header — "Photography. Not 'not
   yet' — there is no host to serve it from". Downloaded binaries have to become
   files in the built site, served by the existing site route so `'self'`
   covers them.
3. **The model must select by id, never by content.** Referencing
   `photo:pixabay:1234567` costs a handful of tokens; a base64 hero image costs
   ~88,900 tokens and roughly $1 per build. The existing `find_assets` /
   `.kodely-assets/INDEX.md` seam (`lib/assets/materialize.ts`) is already
   shaped for this: search returns ids and one-line descriptions, and a
   post-generation pass resolves the ids into real files and rewrites `src`
   attributes.
4. **Budget the API calls.** Pexels 200/hr is a hard throughput ceiling on
   concurrent builds; Pixabay requires 24h response caching and forbids mass
   downloads. Both point at the same design: a shared, cached search layer, one
   download per distinct asset, content-addressed storage reused across sites.

content.text:
Good news — those links you provided before were already thoroughly researched. There's a full review at `docs/research/asset-sources.md`, dated two days ago, covering exactly this list: Pexels, Pixabay, Unsplash, Vecteezy, Kaboompics, Mixkit, Coverr, Dareful, iconoop, svgrepo, iconsatlas, getillustrations, and two GitHub icon-pack mirrors. Here's where it landed:

**Icons — matches what my research agent just found independently, good convergence:** vendor upstream open-source packs directly (Lucide, Tabler, Phosphor, Heroicons — all MIT/ISC, no attribution needed on customer sites), not from aggregators like iconoop/svgrepo/GitHub mirrors, which either don't identify a license clearly or mix in CC-BY/GPL icons that would poison the well. This is ready to build on.

**Photos/video — usable, but with one real unresolved legal question.** Pixabay is the primary recommendation (its own API rules require self-hosting first, which is exactly what Kodely's CSP already demands, and the license is irrevocable/perpetual). Pexels is a solid secondary. But the doc is explicit about a genuine open problem: **every one of these licenses grants rights to whoever downloads the file — none of them clearly says that right can be passed on to Kodely's customers.** When Kodely puts a Pixabay photo on a plumber's site, is the plumber licensed to display it, or only Kodely? Four of the sources that actually addressed this question (Vecteezy, Coverr, Kaboompics, Mixkit) said no or "needs a deal." Pexels and Pixabay are usable *because they're silent* on it — and the doc is blunt that silence isn't the same as permission. It explicitly says this needs a lawyer's answer before anything is built on it, not an engineering judgment call.

**Avoid entirely:** Unsplash (API forces hotlinking + mandatory attribution, incompatible with the CSP), Vecteezy, Coverr (literally names "website builders" as prohibited), Mixkit (self-contradictory terms), svgrepo (couldn't even verify its licensing page), and the GitHub aggregator mirrors (no LICENSE file on the mirror itself).

So: icons are a clean, ready-to-build yes. Photos have a real product decision sitting in front of them — do you want to get an actual legal answer on the sublicensing question so Pixabay/Pexels can be used, or stick with what Kodely already does today (generated illustrations/patterns, zero license surface, zero photos at all)? That's not something I should decide for you.

It also names something I hadn't scoped: the repeated **"hero + 3-card" layout skeleton** is probably a bigger tell than fonts or color ever were, and it won't be fixed by typography work alone — it needs the same curated-catalogue treatment Kodely already gives icons/gradients, extended to actual section-level layout patterns (multiple genuinely different hero shapes, feature-section arrangements, etc.) that the model assembles from instead of drawing from scratch. This is exactly what v0/shadcn and the template-based builders (Wix, Durable) already prove works.

Still waiting on the multi-page audit and the styling-engine feasibility assessment — I'll fold all four together into one real plan once they land, since this finding changes what the styling-engine question should even mean.

<result># Findings: Is a "Styling Engine" Worth Building for Kodely?

## What I read
- `lib/agent.ts` (748 lines, includes uncommitted Records/Accounts backend work — not font-related)
- `lib/assets/index.ts`, `lib/assets/materialize.ts` (catalogue + `find_assets`)
- `lib/foundation.ts` (project seed files)
- `lib/build-site.ts` (Vite build pipeline)
- `lib/brand-kit.ts`, `lib/wizard.ts`, `lib/features.ts` (adjacent systems that turned out highly relevant)
- CSP definition in `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts`

---

## 1. Does Kodely have any reusable, named "visual style" unit today?

**Almost — one exists, but it's a UI-only artifact, not a builder-time concept.**

`lib/wizard.ts` defines `LOOK_DIRECTIONS`: six named objects (`warm-rustic`, `clean-clinical`, `bold-editorial`, `fresh-natural`, `soft-elegant`, `bright-energetic`), each bundling exactly what a "look profile" would need:
- a resolved `GradientPreset` (palette) from `lib/assets/patterns.ts`
- a `headingFont` (system-stack only), `headingWeight`, `headingTracking`
- a `typography` prose description
- a `density`/`densityLabel` (spacing/layout rhythm)

This is a real, nameable, reusable unit *larger than a single asset*. But its life ends at prompt assembly: `assemblePrompt()` in `lib/wizard.ts` flattens the chosen look into a paragraph of prose (`visualDirection()`) that gets pasted into the textarea a user can edit/delete. The builder model in `lib/agent.ts` never sees `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` as data — it only ever sees whatever prose survived into the final prompt, same as any other line of user text. There's no tool, no catalogue entry, no id the model can look up or ask for more of.

Outside the wizard's 6 pre-baked directions, every build's visual identity is invented fresh from `SYSTEM`'s generic instructions ("Give the page one distinctive visual idea..."), the asset catalogue's individual pieces (one gradient, one icon, one divider at a time), and whatever adjectives are in the user's prompt. `lib/brand-kit.ts` adds a customer's own logo/palette but explicitly has "no typography field... Type is the system stack" — confirmed again in `lib/features.ts`'s `custom-fonts` feature-gap entry: *"The CSP sets no font-src... A base64 font is blocked exactly like a hosted one."* No vendored font pairing system exists yet anywhere in the repo I could find (`grep` for "vendored"/"design plan"/"look profile" turned up nothing outside asset-provenance docs).

So: **there is one half-built precedent (`LOOK_DIRECTIONS`), and it proves the concept but stops one layer short of where the model could use it.**

## 2. What would a layer above the asset catalogue concretely look like — and is it realistic?

Concretely, extending `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` into a real "look profile" catalogue would mean each entry bundling:
- palette (already solved — reuse `GradientPreset` ids, exactly as `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` and `brand-kit.ts` already do)
- font pairing (blocked today — no font-src, no vendoring; this is a prerequisite, not this feature's job)
- component conventions (card radius/shadow, button shape, spacing scale) — currently exists only as prose in `LOOK_DEFS.typography`/`.density`, never as a real convention the model is told to apply consistently across `write_file` calls
- asset-category bias (e.g. "bold-editorial" leans on `divider`/`mark` kinds, "soft-elegant" leans on `illustration`/`gradient`) — doesn't exist at all today; `find_assets` has no awareness of a "current look"

This is realistic to build **on top of** what exists — it is not an architecture change. The asset catalogue (`lib/assets/index.ts`) already has the exact shape for it: an `AssetKind`, an `Entry`, a `render()` function, keyword search via `findAssets()`. A `"look"` kind slots into `ASSET_KINDS` the same way `"gradient"` or `"divider"` did. The hard parts are all curation/design work (choosing 8-15 good profiles, writing their component-convention prose, picking asset biases), not plumbing.

## 3. Is there a natural home in existing patterns?

Yes, directly:
- **As a new `AssetKind`** (`"look"` or `"style"`) in `lib/assets/index.ts`, following the exact pattern gradients/patterns/dividers already use — a data array + a `render()` closure + keywords, folded into `buildCatalog()`.
- **Searched via a variant of `find_assets`** — either the same tool with `kind: "look"`, or a new `pick_look` tool in `TOOLS` in `lib/agent.ts` that returns one profile's full bundle (palette id + font stack + convention notes + biased asset ids) in one call, the same shape `formatMatchesForTool` already produces for other kinds.
- **`lib/wizard.ts`'s `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` becomes the seed data**, not a parallel system — the six existing directions plus more, promoted from wizard-only prose into catalogue entries usable by every build path (composer, wizard, and edits), not just the wizard.

This is the cleanest possible integration point in the codebase — it reuses an established pattern rather than inventing one.

## 4. Engineering cost/risk

Mostly low-risk, but not *purely* prompt engineering — there's one small, well-scoped pipeline change plus curation work:

- **Low-risk (data + prompt work):**
  - Moving `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` (or a superset) into `lib/assets/` as a real catalogue kind — mechanical, same shape as five existing kinds.
  - Writing the component-convention prose per profile (card treatment, button shape, spacing rhythm) — pure content work, no code risk.
  - Biasing `find_assets` results toward a chosen profile's asset categories — a filter/boost, not a new search engine.

- **Real (small) pipeline change:**
  - A new tool definition in `TOOLS` (`lib/agent.ts`) if you want the model to actively *pick* a look rather than just have one handed to it in the prompt (as the wizard does today) — this is a few dozen lines, same shape as `find_assets`'s existing wiring (`normalizePath`-style validation isn't even needed since it takes no path).
  - Deciding *when* the model picks: a pre-generation step (before the main turn) vs. letting it call the tool mid-build like `find_assets`. The latter is basically free — same loop, same `messages.push` pattern already in `runAgent`. A dedicated pre-generation "pick a look profile" step would be new orchestration in `runAgent`/`lib/agent-sdk.ts` and is the one piece that's a genuine (if small) architecture addition.
  - `lib/agent-sdk.ts`'s materialize-to-disk bridge (`lib/assets/materialize.ts`) would need the new kind folded in too, since it mirrors the whole catalogue — trivial, same loop.

- **Not in scope for this feature, but a blocking dependency if "font pairing from the vendored set" is taken literally:** actual web fonts require either (a) a CSP change to add `font-src 'self'` plus vendoring real `.woff2` files as static assets in the build output (`lib/build-site.ts`'s `TEXT_EXTENSIONS` only allows text formats today, so binary font files would need new handling), or (b) staying on system-stack pairings only (e.g., serif-heading/sans-body combos), which needs no infra work at all. The two are separable — a look-profile catalogue can ship with system-stack font pairings today and gain real vendored fonts later without a redesign.

Overall: **incremental and additive, not a rewrite.** The riskiest part is not code, it's curation quality — a shallow set of look profiles that just restates "warm and modern" in different words would add token cost and a new tool round-trip without moving the needle on actual visual variety.

## 5. Recommendation

**Sequence it after the font/vendoring work is evaluated, not before — but scope it now while that's fresh, because it's the natural next step and cheap to plan.**

Reasoning:
- The single highest-leverage unresolved constraint on Kodely's visual range is typography: `custom-fonts` is explicitly listed as unsupported in `lib/features.ts`, and every "look" the wizard offers today is differentiated by palette/density/weight, never by an actual different typeface, because there isn't one available. If the in-flight font/design-plan work makes real font pairings possible, a look-profile catalogue becomes dramatically more valuable overnight — it goes from "6 palettes with prose about density" to "6 genuinely distinct visual identities." Building the look-profile layer first, on system fonts only, means redoing/expanding it the moment fonts land.
- Conversely, if the font work stalls or gets descoped, the look-profile catalogue is still worth doing on its own — `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` already proves users respond to picking a named direction over an adjective, and promoting it from "wizard-only, 6 hardcoded options, flattened to prose" to "first-class catalogue entry, searchable by the model on every build, not just when the wizard was used" is a real improvement to build consistency even without new fonts.
- Priority-wise: this is a "beef up the engine" investment, not an urgent fix — nothing is broken today, and the wizard already gives users *some* of this value in a narrower form. It's reasonable to treat it as the next scoped project once the font work either ships or is confirmed deprioritized, since that determines whether you're curating 6-10 palette-only profiles or a genuinely richer catalogue with real typography — and you don't want to curate the content twice.

**Concrete first step, whenever you pick it up:** promote `LOOK_DIRECTIONS` out of `lib/wizard.ts` into `lib/assets/` as a new `AssetKind`, keep it wizard-compatible (no regression), and only then decide whether the model gets it via a dedicated tool or via the same `find_assets` path with `kind: "look"`.</result>

## Findings

**1. `lib/agent.ts` — the multi-page prompt guidance**

The system prompt's "Multi-page" section (lines ~51–57) is genuinely rigorous, not a throwaway mention:
- Spells out the exact 3-file recipe for adding a page: `src/pages/About.tsx`, an entry in `src/pages.tsx` (`{ path, label, component, nav? }`), and `about.html` at project root with its own `data-page`, `<title>`, description and OG tags.
- Explicitly warns "Skip step 3 and the page does not exist" and explains *why* per-page `<head>` matters (SEO — a shared title/description across pages competes with itself).
- Tells the model to link via `<Link to="/about">` from `src/router.tsx`, never a bare `<a href>`, and explains `SiteNav` self-builds from the page table.
- Gives real judgment guidance on *when* to use pages ("content genuinely differs... Don't manufacture thin pages to look bigger") rather than blindly multiplying pages.
- **Gap**: it documents *adding* a page in detail but has no analogous instructions for *removing* one (no "delete the .html shell, drop the pages.tsx entry, delete the orphaned component" checklist).

**2. `lib/foundation.ts` / `lib/build-site.ts` — is this a first-class shape?**

Yes, genuinely first-class, not a fragile edge case:
- `src/router.tsx` is a real ~40-line hand-rolled router (`PageDef`, `resolvePage`, `href`/`Link`, `navPages`) deliberately built without client-side routing (real document loads, not pushState) so back-button/SEO/preview-iframe all stay simple and correct.
- `src/pages.tsx` is a real, explicit page table (`PAGES: PageDef[]`), separate from the router mechanism by design.
- `SiteNav.tsx` derives its links from `navPages()` — adding an entry to the table alone updates nav everywhere, and it self-hides for one-page sites (`pages.length < 2`).
- `vite.config.ts` in the foundation **discovers** pages by scanning for `.html` files at build time (recursive, depth-capped) and turns each into a Rollup multi-entry — this is exactly why multi-page works with zero config changes even though the agent is barred from touching `vite.config.ts` (that file is `isProtectedPath`). This is a deliberate, well-reasoned design, not an accident.
- All pages share one `/src/main.tsx` bundle (one JS chunk), which the code comments explain is intentional for both cross-page cache reuse and compatibility with the editor's `srcdoc` preview.

**3. `lib/site-seo.ts` — sitemap completeness**

Sitemap generation genuinely enumerates every page and is unlikely to miss one, because it's driven by the actual served artifacts, not by the page table:
- `sitemapXml()` is built from `db.projectFile` rows of `kind: "build"` filtered by `path.endsWith(".html")` — i.e., every HTML file the last Vite build actually emitted, queried fresh per-request (not cached/stale).
- `pageUrl()`/`pagePath()` normalize `about.html` → `/about`, `blog/index.html` → `/blog`, and the sitemap dedupes so two spellings of the same page (`about.html` vs `about/index.html`) collapse to one `<loc>`.
- Canonical/`og:url` tags are stamped per-page via the same `pageUrl()` function the sitemap uses (`applySeo({ pageUrl: pageUrl(baseUrl, file.path) })`), so a page's own canonical and its sitemap entry cannot disagree — this is explicitly tested (`tests/site-seo.test.mjs`, e.g. "a subpage canonicalises to ITSELF, not to the home page", "one entry per page, for a real multi-page site").
- Caveat: since the sitemap enumerates *built* HTML files rather than `pages.tsx` entries, an orphaned `.html` file (still on disk/build output but no longer in the nav table) would still be listed — see point 6.

**4. `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` — path resolution**

Re-verified: `candidatePaths()` correctly handles nested, arbitrary-depth paths, not just flat one level:
- Anything with an extension resolves to itself only (protects `/assets/*`, `robots.txt`, etc.).
- Otherwise it tries `${clean}.html` then `${clean}/index.html`, and `clean` is just the raw joined path — so `/services/plumbing` → tries `services/plumbing.html` then `services/plumbing/index.html`, with no depth limit. This is confirmed to work for nested pages, matching the `vite.config.ts` scanner's own recursive discovery (capped at depth 4, "a site is not nested deeper than this").
- Deliberately not an SPA catch-all — unknown paths 404 rather than soft-404ing to the homepage, which is a correct SEO decision but also means a *broken* nav link (see point 6) will produce a real 404, not silently paper over the mistake.

**5. Customer-facing UI — the real gap**

This is where the story changes. Grepping `InlineWizard.tsx`, `TemplatePickerModal.tsx`, and `lib/templates.ts` for "multi-page"/"multi page"/"second page" returns **zero hits**. Concretely:
- **`lib/templates.ts`**: the file's own top-of-file doc comment states the constraint every one of the 23 templates is written to satisfy: sites must stay "one Vite + React + TS + Tailwind page... no backend... **no second page**." Every single template prompt literally opens with `"Build a one-page website for..."`.
- **`lib/wizard.ts`**: the generic skeleton and the `openingLine()` assembly function used by `InlineWizard` hardcode `"Build a one-page website for [name] — <description>."` as the very first sentence sent to the model — every time, regardless of what the customer typed in the free-text "Describe it" field.
- **`InlineWizard.tsx`** and **`TemplatePickerModal.tsx`**: neither has any stage, toggle, or field for "how many pages" / "which pages do you want." The Features stage (`lib/features.ts`) offers things like contact forms, records, service areas, etc., but nothing about page structure.
- So a customer who types "I want a Home, About, Services, and Contact page" into the wizard's Describe box gets that text appended *after* a hardcoded "Build a one-page website..." opener — actively contradicting their own request rather than staying silent on it. Their only real path to multi-page is: (a) skip the wizard/templates entirely, write a free-form prompt themselves that clearly asks for pages, or (b) get lucky that the model interprets "and a Services and Contact page" strongly enough to override the "one-page" framing that its own stitched-together brief just told it.

This is a genuine, specific UI/prompt-assembly gap, not just "under-explained" — the customer-facing paths actively push toward one-page by default and never surface the capability that clearly exists server-side.

**6. Edit-turn robustness / orphan risk**

- The build pipeline fully regenerates `kind: "build"` rows every publish (`deleteMany` then `createMany` from the fresh `vite build` output — `app/api/generate/route.ts` ~line 339), so the *served* tree can never contain a build artifact for a page whose `.html` source no longer exists. That part is safe.
- However, `kind: "source"` files are only touched by whatever `write_file`/`delete_file` calls the model actually makes (`onWrite`/`onDelete` in `app/api/generate/route.ts`, ~lines 263–282) — there is no code-level referential-integrity check between `src/pages.tsx`'s table and the set of `.html` shells, or between `pages.tsx` and `src/pages/*.tsx` component files.
- Two concrete failure modes are possible, and nothing in code prevents them, only the prompt's care in following its own (page-adding-only) instructions:
  - Model removes a page's `pages.tsx` entry but forgets to `delete_file` the `.html` shell → `vite.config.ts`'s scanner still finds the `.html` file (it scans disk, not `pages.tsx`), so the page keeps building, keeps appearing in `sitemap.xml`, and stays reachable at its URL — orphaned/zombie page, invisible in nav but live and indexed.
  - Model deletes the `.html` shell but forgets to remove the `pages.tsx`/`SiteNav` entry → the nav renders a link to a page whose file no longer exists, and clicking it produces a real 404 (the route deliberately doesn't SPA-fallback).
- No tests exercise this specific scenario (`tests/site-seo.test.mjs` and `tests/build-diff.test.mjs` cover SEO correctness and the diff-viewer's line math, not page-table/file-tree consistency across an edit turn). No comments in the codebase acknowledge this as a known/tracked issue.
- This risk is mitigated somewhat by edit turns receiving the *entire* current file tree as context (`describeFiles()` in `lib/agent.ts`), so a capable model *can* see and fix all three places — but it's relying on the model's general competence and the "change only what the request calls for" instruction, not on an explicit "how to retire a page" checklist the way adding a page gets one.

## Assessment

**The underlying engineering is solid.** Router, page table, per-page `.html` shells + Vite auto-discovery, per-page canonical/OG tags, and sitemap generation are all well-designed, mutually consistent, and covered by real tests for the SEO-correctness half. This is not a fragile edge case bolted on — `vite.config.ts`'s comment block and `site-seo.ts`'s comment block both show deliberate design work specifically for the multi-page case (e.g., the canonical-URL bug this was designed to avoid is explicitly tested against). Nested paths, arbitrary depth, and multiple pages sharing one bundle all work correctly end-to-end for a **single build turn**.

**Two real, distinct problems remain, and they are different in kind:**

1. **A genuine UI/UX gap (needs product/copy work, not backend engineering)**: the customer-facing wizard and template gallery actively steer toward one-page sites — every template and the generic wizard skeleton hardcode "Build a one-page website" as the literal opening instruction sent to the model, and there is no field or toggle anywhere for a customer to say "I want these pages." A customer has no discoverable way to ask for multi-page short of writing a fully custom prompt and hoping their multi-page language overrides the wizard's own "one-page" framing. This is squarely "under-surfaced" — the capability is real, but the funnel actively hides/contradicts it.

2. **A real (if narrower) functional gap in edit-turn reliability (needs engineering)**: removing/renaming a page depends entirely on the model correctly touching three separate files (page component, `pages.tsx` entry, `.html` shell) with no explicit "how to retire a page" prompt guidance and no code-level consistency check. This can silently produce either an orphaned page (still built, still indexed, invisible in nav) or a broken nav link (404). Fixing this well would mean either: (a) adding explicit removal guidance to the `lib/agent.ts` prompt (cheap, quick win), and/or (b) a lightweight server-side consistency check after an edit turn (e.g., warn or auto-clean when a `.html` file exists with no `pages.tsx` entry, or vice versa) — a real, scoped piece of engineering work.

In short: don't rebuild the plumbing — it's good. Do (a) fix the wizard/template funnel so a customer can actually ask for multi-page cleanly, and (b) close the edit-turn consistency gap around page removal, ideally with both a prompt fix and a small backend safety net.</result>

input.prompt:
Repo: C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Windows paths, Git-Bash/PowerShell environment). Kodely, an AI website builder. No new npm dependencies allowed.

CONTEXT — a research audit just found this exact bug, confirmed by direct grep/read, don't re-derive it, just read the cited files and fix it:
- lib/agent.ts's multi-page section (~lines 51-57) is genuinely well-built: a real router (`src/router.tsx`), a real page table (`src/pages.tsx`), per-page `.html` shells with their own SEO, `vite.config.ts` auto-discovering pages by scanning for `.html` files. This works end-to-end and is tested (tests/site-seo.test.mjs).
- BUT: `lib/templates.ts`'s own top-of-file doc comment states every one of its ~23 templates is written to satisfy "no second page," and every single template's prompt literally opens with "Build a one-page website for..." — read the file and confirm this yourself.
- `lib/wizard.ts`'s generic skeleton / `openingLine()` function hardcodes "Build a one-page website for [name] — <description>." as the FIRST sentence sent to the model on every wizard-assembled build, regardless of what the customer actually typed in their own free-text description.
- Neither `components/wizard/InlineWizard.tsx` nor `components/templates/TemplatePickerModal.tsx` has any stage, toggle, or field for page count/structure — a customer who explicitly asks for multiple pages in their own words gets that request appended AFTER an instruction that already told the model to build one page, actively contradicting them.
- Separately, a smaller real gap: lib/agent.ts's multi-page guidance explains how to ADD a page in detail (3-file recipe: page component, pages.tsx entry, .html shell) but has NO analogous guidance for REMOVING one — there's no code-level consistency check either, so a model that forgets to delete one of the three files during an edit turn can leave either an orphaned indexed page (still built, still in sitemap, invisible in nav) or a dead nav link (404).

YOUR JOB — two parts, keep them clearly separated in your work:

## Part 1: stop the wizard/templates from contradicting the customer

The goal is NOT to force every build into being multi-page — most small businesses genuinely are better served by one good page, and lib/agent.ts's own judgment guidance ("use pages when the content genuinely differs... don't manufacture thin pages to look bigger") should stay intact and in charge of that decision. The bug is narrower and more specific: the WIZARD AND TEMPLATES ACTIVELY ASSERT "one-page" as a hardcoded fact before the model even sees what the customer wants, which both overrides customer intent when they DO ask for multiple pages, and denies the model the judgment call lib/agent.ts otherwise wants it to make.

Fix:
1. In `lib/wizard.ts`: find the exact hardcoded "Build a one-page website for..." opening line construction (`openingLine()` or wherever it lives) and change it so it no longer asserts a page count — describe what's being built (the business/description) without prescribing one page vs. many. Let the model's own judgment (per lib/agent.ts's existing "use pages when content genuinely differs" guidance) decide, informed by whatever the customer's own words in the wizard's free-text fields actually say. Read the full wizard assembly flow (`assemblePrompt()` and everything that feeds it) before changing anything, so you don't break the six `LOOK_DIRECTIONS`-driven prose or any other part of the assembled prompt.
2. In `lib/templates.ts`: read the full file and its top-of-file doc comment. For each of the ~23 templates, decide on a per-template basis (don't blanket-find-replace) whether "one-page" is a genuine, deliberate constraint for that specific template's kind of business (e.g., a simple one-off landing page template MIGHT genuinely be better as one page always) or whether it's just inherited boilerplate that should instead let the model judge based on the template's actual content and whatever the customer added on top. Update the top-of-file doc comment to accurately describe the new, non-blanket approach. Do not silently turn every template into "always multi-page" either — the fix is removing an incorrect blanket assertion, not replacing it with the opposite blanket assertion.
3. Confirm (by reading, don't guess) whether `components/wizard/InlineWizard.tsx` or `components/templates/TemplatePickerModal.tsx` themselves construct or display any "one-page" framing in their own UI copy (separate from the prompt text lib/wizard.ts/lib/templates.ts assemble) — if so, fix that copy too so the UI doesn't promise/imply something the backend no longer hardcodes.
4. Do NOT add a new UI control for "how many pages" / "which pages" in this pass — that's future scope, not part of this fix. The fix is purely: stop actively asserting "one page" when nothing in the actual customer input asked for that constraint, and let the model's existing judgment guidance in lib/agent.ts do its job.

## Part 2: close the page-removal gap

1. In lib/agent.ts's multi-page section, add explicit guidance for REMOVING a page, parallel in rigor to the existing page-ADDING recipe: when a page is genuinely no longer wanted (an edit turn removes it), the model must delete all three things — the page component file, the `pages.tsx` table entry, AND the `.html` shell at project root — and explain briefly why missing any one of the three leaves either an orphaned indexed page (the `.html` shell alone keeps it building and in the sitemap even with no nav entry) or a dead nav link (a `pages.tsx`/`SiteNav` entry pointing at a deleted `.html` file 404s, since routing is real per-document navigation, not an SPA catch-all).
2. Consider (use your judgment after reading the actual generation route) whether a lightweight, genuinely useful server-side consistency check is realistically addable in this pass without over-scoping: e.g., after an edit turn's writes are applied and before/during the build step, checking whether `src/pages.tsx`'s table and the set of `.html` shells at project root agree (same set of paths) and surfacing a clear warning (not a build failure — a warning surfaced to the customer, since this is a real edit-turn code-quality signal like an existing repair/warning mechanism might already exist for). Read app/api/generate/route.ts's existing write/build/repair flow fully first to see if there's already a natural hook point (e.g., alongside however a failed-compile repair pass already works) — if adding this cleanly fits in that same pass at low risk, do it; if it would require meaningfully restructuring the generation route, leave it as a documented follow-up in your report instead of forcing it in.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Do not touch anything related to the font/design-plan work (already done, separate agent) — if you see it in lib/agent.ts, leave it as-is, just add your page-removal guidance as its own clearly-separated addition.
- Do not touch lib/features.ts, the SiteRecord/accounts backend work, or anything outside the files named above.
- Keep every template's REAL, already-good copy/business-specificity intact — you're only touching the page-count framing, not rewriting template content.

STEPS:
1. Read lib/wizard.ts, lib/templates.ts, lib/agent.ts's multi-page section, components/wizard/InlineWizard.tsx, components/templates/TemplatePickerModal.tsx, and app/api/generate/route.ts's write/build flow, fully, before changing anything.
2. Implement Part 1.
3. Implement Part 2 (guidance always; the consistency check only if it fits cleanly).
4. Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean before you finish.

Report back: exactly what changed in lib/wizard.ts's opening-line construction, which templates (if any) kept a deliberate one-page constraint and why, what you added to lib/agent.ts for page removal, and whether you added the consistency check or left it as a follow-up (and why).

Repo: C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (Windows paths, Git-Bash/PowerShell environment). Kodely, an AI website builder. No new npm dependencies allowed (icon files are static assets, not packages).

CONTEXT — two independent research passes already confirmed the plan, don't re-derive it, just execute it:
- lib/assets/icons.ts currently has ~147 hand-authored icons across 9 categories. lib/assets/provenance.ts documents (module-level, not per-asset) that everything today is original work, and explicitly states the prerequisite for adding anything third-party: "a per-asset source/license/author/URL record, a license field the tool output can carry, a brand/trademark flag" must exist BEFORE any vendored asset is added. Read lib/assets/provenance.ts in full — it names its own requirements precisely; follow them.
- docs/research/asset-sources.md (§4 "Recommendation") and an independent audit both converged on the same answer: vendor raw SVG source from Lucide (ISC + partial MIT for Feather-derived icons), Tabler Icons (MIT), Phosphor Icons (MIT), and Heroicons (MIT) — all sourced from their own official GitHub repos (lucide-icons/lucide, tabler/tabler-icons, phosphor-icons/core, tailwindlabs/heroicons), never from aggregators (iconoop, svgrepo, GitHub mirror repos) which mix in unverifiable or non-permissive licenses (Font Awesome and coolicons are CC BY 4.0 — attribution required — and must be excluded; any brand/logo icon sets are a trademark issue independent of copyright and must also be excluded).
- The concrete problem being solved: lib/assets/icons.ts's `services`/`trades` category has only 22 icons, and its SYNONYMS map resolves five completely different trade businesses (plumber, plumbing, electrician, handyman, mechanic/garage) all down to the same single `wrench` icon. `contact` has only 10 icons total, shared by every generated site's contact section. This is a real, structural sameness problem, not just an aesthetic one.

YOUR JOB:

## Step 1 — build the provenance infrastructure first (the stated prerequisite)
Read lib/assets/provenance.ts's exact stated requirements and implement them: add a per-asset provenance record capability (source repo name, upstream icon id, license string, upstream version/commit or release tag, retrieved-at date) that the icon catalogue's existing `Entry`/render machinery can carry, and a brand/trademark exclusion mechanism (a boolean flag or category that keeps anything logo/brand-mark-like out of what the model can place autonomously — Lucide/Tabler/Phosphor/Heroicons are all general UI icon sets, not brand-logo packs, so this should mostly be a not-applicable/false flag for everything you vendor here, but the mechanism itself must exist for future use). Update provenance.ts's own module-level claims to accurately reflect that some assets are now vendored-with-recorded-provenance rather than 100% original work — do not leave the file asserting something no longer true.

## Step 2 — source the actual icon files
Fetch real SVG source directly from each project's official GitHub repository (use WebFetch/git — whichever tool actually gets you the raw files; these are real permissively-licensed open-source projects, this is legitimate vendoring, not scraping an unverified site). For each of the four packs:
1. Confirm the LICENSE file's content directly from the repo (don't trust a cached memory of what it says — fetch and read it now) and save a copy locally (e.g. lib/assets/icon-licenses/<pack>/LICENSE).
2. Record the exact commit/tag/version you pulled from.
3. Pull a curated, targeted set of icons that actually fill the gaps found — prioritize the `services`/`trades` and `contact` categories specifically (e.g., real distinct icons for plumbing/pipes, electrical/circuit, carpentry, painting, landscaping, HVAC, cleaning, security, IT/tech support, real distinct additional contact-method icons beyond the current 10) rather than importing entire packs wholesale — this is about closing specific convergence gaps, not maximizing total icon count. A few hundred well-chosen icons across the weak categories is the right scale, not thousands.
4. Exclude anything resembling a brand/company logo from any of the four packs (Tabler and Phosphor in particular sometimes include brand-adjacent icons — check and exclude).

## Step 3 — integrate into the catalogue
Add the vendored icons into lib/assets/icons.ts (or a clearly-named sibling module, following whatever pattern is more consistent with how the existing 147 are organized — read the file's actual structure before deciding) as real `IconDef`-shaped entries with real geometry (not re-drawn/approximated — use the actual upstream path data), each carrying the new provenance record from Step 1. Give them sensible keywords/synonyms so `findAssets()`'s existing token-scoring actually surfaces them for the gap terms identified above (e.g. a real "pipe wrench" or "electrical panel" icon should now outrank the generic wrench for an electrician-specific query, and the SYNONYMS map should be updated so `plumber`/`electrician`/`handyman`/`mechanic` resolve to genuinely different icons instead of all converging on one). Update lib/agent.ts's asset-catalogue description (the "~460 inlinable assets" line) to reflect the new real total once you know it.

## Constraints
- Every vendored icon must have a real, traceable provenance record. No icon without one.
- Exclude anything CC BY (Font Awesome, coolicons) or otherwise non-permissive, and anything brand/logo-shaped.
- Do not touch icons.ts's existing 147 original icons' geometry — pure addition, no modification of existing entries.
- Do not touch anything in the font/design-plan work already done (lib/fonts/, the design-plan section of lib/agent.ts) or the multi-page fix already done (lib/wizard.ts, lib/templates.ts) — if your changes to lib/agent.ts are near either of those, keep your edit narrowly scoped to just the asset-count line.
- Keep the total added payload reasonable — this is inlined SVG source that gets pasted into generated sites' code, not loaded over a network, so bloating the catalogue with thousands of rarely-used icons adds real token cost to every future generation for no benefit. Favor filling the identified gaps precisely over maximizing count.

## Verification
Run `cd /c/Users/edmem/kodely-prod && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `npx eslint app lib components --max-warnings=0` — both must be completely clean before you finish. Also do a quick sanity check: call/trace through `findAssets("plumber")`, `findAssets("electrician")`, and `findAssets("mechanic")` (read the code path, or use a small script if one already exists for testing the catalogue) and confirm they no longer all resolve to the same single icon.

Report back: exactly how many icons you added from each pack, the exact license/version for each, how the provenance record is structured, and the before/after result of the plumber/electrician/mechanic search-convergence check.

vm "rm -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle" || true
else
  # Must be `..main`, not `..HEAD`: a bundle cut against HEAD is written with a
  # ref literally named "HEAD", and the VM's `git fetch <bundle> main` then
  # fails with "couldn't find remote ref main".
  git bundle create /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle "$BASE..main" >/dev/null 2>&1
  echo "  $(git rev-list --count "$BASE..HEAD") commit(s), $(du -h /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle | cut -f1)"
  # Raw bytes over stdin through both hops, NOT base64 embedded as a command
  # argument. The base64 version deadlocked in practice on a real bundle
  # (confirmed live: the exact nested `echo '$B64' | ssh ...` form hung
  # indefinitely on a 1.4M bundle, no error, no progress). Embedding megabytes
  # of text as a single argv element is the failure mode — it has to be fully
  # buffered before anything moves and has no OS-level backpressure. `-J`
  # (ProxyJump) was tried first and is not an option: the jump host refuses
  # port-forwarding ("administratively prohibited"). Piping through the
  # command's own stdin/stdout needs no forwarding permission — verified live
  # at this exact bundle size (1.5M, <1s, sha256-identical) before landing.
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" \
    "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM 'cat > /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle'" \
    < /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle \
    || die "could not transfer the bundle to the VM"
  vm "cd /opt/kodely && git bundle verify /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle >/dev/null 2>&1" \
    || die "bundle failed verification on the VM"
  echo "  transferred and verified"
fi

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --skip-generate >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_env staging /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging https://staging.kodely.me

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

deploy_env prod /opt/kodely kodely https://kodely.me

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK"

  # (ProxyJump) was tried first and is not an option: the jump host refuses
  # port-forwarding ("administratively prohibited"). Piping through the
  # command's own stdin/stdout needs no forwarding permission — verified live
  # at this exact bundle size (1.5M, <1s, sha256-identical) before landing.
  ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=15 "$HOST" \
    "ssh -o BatchMode=yes $VM 'cat > /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle'" \
    < /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle \
    || die "could not transfer the bundle to the VM"
  vm "cd /opt/kodely && git bundle verify /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle >/dev/null 2>&1" \
    || die "bundle failed verification on the VM"
  echo "  transferred and verified"
fi

deploy_env() {
  local env="$1" dir="$2" svc="$3" url="$4"

  say "Deploying $env"
  # Apply the bundle, then build. Every step is chained with && under `set -e`
  # so a failure here fails the deploy instead of leaving stale code running.
  vm "set -e
      cd $dir
      if [ -f /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle ]; then
        git fetch -q /tmp/kodely-deploy.bundle main
        git update-ref refs/remotes/origin/main FETCH_HEAD
        git reset -q --hard FETCH_HEAD
      fi
      npm ci --no-audit --no-fund >/dev/null 2>&1
      npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss --skip-generate >/dev/null 2>&1
      npm run build >/dev/null 2>&1
      sudo systemctl restart $svc" || die "$env deploy failed"
  sleep 5

  say "Verifying $env"
  local head build code
  head=$(vm "cd $dir && git rev-parse --short HEAD")
  build=$(vm "stat -c %y $dir/.next/BUILD_ID | cut -d. -f1")
  echo "  HEAD=$head  BUILD_ID=$build  service=$(vm "systemctl is-active $svc")"
  # The check that catches a stale deploy: HEAD must equal what we just shipped.
  [ "$head" = "$NEW" ] || die "$env is on $head, expected $NEW — deploy did not take"
  for path in /api/health / /pricing /blog /contact; do
    code=$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' -m 25 "$url$path")
    printf '  %-12s %s\n' "$path" "$code"
    [ "$code" = "200" ] || die "$env $path returned $code"
  done
}

deploy_env staging /opt/kodely-staging kodely-staging https://staging.kodely.me

if [ "$STAGING_ONLY" = "--staging" ]; then
  say "Stopped after staging. Prod untouched."
  exit 0
fi

deploy_env prod /opt/kodely kodely https://kodely.me

say "Shipped"
echo "  main:     $NEW"
echo "  live:     https://kodely.me"
echo "  rollback: $ROLLBACK"

Hotfix is live (`1cf1c98`). Root cause and fix:

**What broke:** the icon-vendoring change reworded a "plumber wrench icon" example in `lib/agent.ts` to "plumber icon" (correctly — plumbers don't just get a generic wrench anymore), but `lib/agent-sdk.ts` checks for that exact sentence verbatim at runtime to rewrite it for the SDK engine. The mismatch made every SDK-engine build throw before writing a single file — which is exactly the "Reading the brief and starter files" failure you saw.

**Fixed:**
- Updated the matching string in `lib/agent-sdk.ts`.
- Exported `SYSTEM` and added a real regression test that actually calls `adaptPromptForSdk()` against the live prompt, so this exact class of silent-until-production break fails locally next time instead.
- Also caught and fixed a second, related bug from the same batch: the new solar-panel icon had "electrician" as a stray keyword, which was winning over the intended circuit-board/electric-plug icons — removed it and updated the one test that still encoded the old (buggy) expectation.

All 337 tests pass, staging verified before prod, and prod's health checks are green. Rollback point is `4cee8e8` if needed.
